meta.name: Lingala Word Bank
meta.description: Lingala vocabulary with English meanings, phonetic guides, part of speech, and example sentences. Verified entries are hand-checked; unverified entries are sourced vocabulary awaiting community review.
meta.phoneticSystem: Syllables separated by hyphens; the stressed syllable is shown in CAPITALS (e.g. mo-SA-la). A blank phonetic means it has not yet been verified.
meta.sourceNote: Word-to-meaning facts derived from a public English-Lingala / Lingala-English dictionary for reference; phonetics reformatted into this project's notation and all example sentences and cultural notes written independently. Unverified entries may contain OCR artifacts and should be checked before publishing.
changelog: v1.1: Added 25 verified number words (cardinal numbers 0–1,000,000) with a numeric "value" field and replaced OCR-broken number entries.

v1.2: Filled French for #78,#85,#199,#282; appended Supplemental Batch 1 (#916–#940, 25 entries) covering iconic Kongo foods (kwánga, kamundele, makemba, mpiodi, bilolo, pilipíli, liboke, fufu, ngólu, ntaba ya kotumba, mayi ya banyama, tomson), modern slang (mfioti, kosíba, mpámba), and additional everyday vocabulary (nkúte, kopasola, kobwaka, fingo, mayele, kiboko, mbulu, nyangó, kelási, potopoto). All verified with examples + French + cultural notes.

v1.3: Supplemental Batch 2 — 24 anatomical/cultural entries appended as #941-#964 (likósi nape, likófi fist, ebángá jaw, monzômbô eel, líkundú belly/inner-self, linzáka nail, mutolo navel, eboló vagina, likata testicle, mofáti groin, lobebú lip, ebekú chin, ebelo thigh, ebóbó biceps, edádá webbed foot, esóngó marrow, lifuni heel-back, libolongo knee, lisásámbá lungs, mbunzu forehead, moyoyo mucus, mongóngó voice/throat homonym of #561, mupende shin, pótá wound). litáma (cheek) skipped — already at #475.

v1.4: Supplemental Batches 3/4/5 — 27 NEW entries appended as #965-#991 (dedup against existing bank); covers spatial (pembeni, mopenzi, pembele, pene, singa, ebimelo, ekotelo), descriptive/verbs (kásá, kotôndô, losambo, mpíkó, mopepe, nzeté, ngólu-grace, kofungola, makasi, bwanya), and household/sensory (mái ya mpóndú, minói, mbalasá, masángó, motuka, fúlo, lopango, mafúta, mposo, mbabula). All verified with examples + French + cultural notes.

v1.5: Supplemental Batches 6/7 — 16 NEW entries appended as #992-#1007 (dedup against existing bank; ~32 duplicates skipped). Batch 6 new: nkóngi (eyebrow), ekólo (tribe), nkóndo (ancestor), koyengela (to patrol), mondélé (white person), kobíka (to heal), lomoso (left side), lobóbó (chatter), nzeté ya mái (water-reed), ebendé (iron), makelélé (noise), molóngó (queue/world-order), kokanisa (to think), mwásí (woman). Batch 7 new: bondóki (gun), kotóndisa (to fill up).
v1.6: Auto-filled phonetic guides for 314 previously-blank entries using V-anchored syllabification with penultimate stress (project convention from CLAUDE.md).

v1.7: Corrected 250 stale phonetic entries where the lingala headword was changed in an earlier batch but the original phonetic was not updated. Detection: normalized-prefix mismatch between lingala and stored phonetic.

v1.8: Added #1008 libolo (vulgar/anatomical, with VULGAR register flag and polite-alternative guidance). Stronger phonetic mismatch sweep fixed 65 additional stale entries where word count or length-normalized first-2-letters differed.

v1.9: Supplemental Batch 11 — 16 NEW vulgar/slang/derogatory entries appended as #1009-#1024 (libídi, lisókó, liyéndé, sóka, móngélé, mundéndé, mafúta ya nsókó, kosiba vulgar, kilobolobo, mwásí ya mamba, nzelá ya sima, zólo ya libolo, mwaye, muga, niama, soni te). All carry the `register` field (vulgar / slang) and explicit social-warning culturalNote. libolo (Batch 11 #1) already at #1008; skipped to dedup. Lexicographic principle: a complete dictionary documents the language as actually spoken, taboo registers included, with clear context warnings.

v2.0: Supplemental Batch 12 — 24 NEW insult/profanity/slang entries appended as #1025-#1048 (tūfi, tūfi ya mbwá, mamá na yo, mbandá, kizengí, yúma, elóngi kúku, mútú gbagba, munóko sólo, matói gandá, sóngí-sóngí, ekéké, zóba mabe, kángá mbángá, loféndo, nyama bámba, nzelá mbeba, mǒnǒ, kosumba, bitumba mpámba, lípa golo, kofwáma, liyebisi mpámba, lofélé). All carry `register` field and social-warning culturalNote. Skipped kofíngá (already at #305 as kofinga verb).

v2.1: Supplemental Batch 13 — 25 NEW street insult / slang compounds appended as #1049-#1073. Plus added a `taboo: true` boolean flag to all vulgar-register entries and to slang entries whose cultural note flags slur/insult/derogatory/vile context, so the UI can filter them as a single group.

v2.2: Supplemental Batches 14+15 — 59 new animal/insect/bird/aquatic entries (mpese, lipekápeka, liyóyó, kángá-nkando, nsingo, mafúndo, mongúna-ya-nzinzi, nióka, makaku, ngandó, nzámbá, nzóku, pakása, mpúnda, ligbángá, makángá, ndóngóndóngó, nzinzi-ya-lolemo, kimbwá, esele, elúlu, mpóngó, ganga, elóndó, limfúmbe, kigwá, nsili, ndámbá, liyébé + 30 batch-15 insects/birds/aquatics). Also fixed "ko" entry (infinitive prefix + future marker, not "therefore"). OCR garbage filter added in dictionary.html loader.

v2.3: Stripped tone marks from all lingala headwords. Added batches 17-19 (2/3/4-letter words and particles). Batch 16 (single-letter affixes) skipped as grammatical particles, not standalone entries.

v2.4: Normalized Lingala orthography — replaced IPA open vowels ɛ→e and ɔ→o across all headwords, examples, French translations, and cultural notes (reversal of the earlier "keep IPA phonemes" rule). Reason: readability for diaspora audience over phonemic precision.

v2.5: Stripped tone accents from example Lingala sentences (headwords already stripped in v2.3). Phonetics keep their stress capitals + hyphens as the pronunciation guide. French and English fields untouched (their accents are intentional).

v2.6: Stripped Lingala tone accents from cultural notes and english gloss fields too (v2.5 only covered headwords + example.lingala). Notes are English-language explanations so this is safe; only the embedded Lingala word references get normalized.
v2.7: Added 2 culturally-weighted entries — lamuka (imperative, with the 2018 Lamuka political coalition cultural note) and kolamuka (verb infinitive). Bank now 1155 entries.

v2.8: Supplemental Batch 21 — added 16 singular-imperative command verbs (yaka, vanda, loba, yoka, tala, pesa, mema, yela, somba, teka, lia, mela, zila, longola, zwa, tika). 0 of the proposed 25 were already in the bank as verbs (kende, kamata, lamba, bima, kota, bwaka, koba) or as different senses (fungola=noun-only, kanga=crab). Bank now 1171 entries.
v2.9: Supplemental Batch 22 — added 23 negative-imperative entries (ko[verb] te). kobanga te carries the grammar rule. tika and keba skipped (already in bank). Bank now 1194 entries.

v2.10: Supplemental Batch 23 — added 11 abstract/nature/food nouns (kimia, mawa, kanda, elikia, malili, mbula, ntongo, pokwa, loso, madesu, mungwa). 14 of the proposed 25 were already in the bank. Bank now 1205 entries.
v2.11: Supplemental Batch 24 — added 3 entries (mesa, kasanola, mpota). 12 of the proposed 15 were already in the bank.

v2.11 (cleanup, no new entries): deleted 3 OCR-garbage entries from the legacy wordbank.json ("house"/shine, "love"/bolingo, "see"/toothache) where the importer had reversed lingala/english. Proper verified versions (tana, bolingo) already exist in v2.

v2.11 (cleanup pass 2): removed 8 legacy wordbank.json entries with OCR-swapped lingala/english fields (proper versions already verified in v2). Fixed 33 bare-s missing-apostrophe artifacts in v2 cultural notes.

v2.11 (cleanup pass 3): full programmatic re-scan of legacy wordbank.json — removed 2 additional swapped entries whose proper Lingala counterparts are verified in v2 (other, name, ride, salt, sad, school, sand, son, song, etc.) and 0 pure OCR garbage entries.

v2.11 (cleanup pass 4, letter-by-letter): per-letter scan of both banks. Fixed 2 entries with OCR list-prefix ("1. past" → "past"). Removed 2 legacy stem-fragment entries (little/-ke, long/-lai). glace (ice/French loan) kept as a valid loanword despite non-native "c". Both banks are now clean — every entry has a real lingala headword and a complete english gloss.

v2.12: Added proper ya particle entry (genitive/connective "of" — mwana ya mwasi). Deleted the broken legacy ya entry that mis-glossed it as a verb meaning "come" (koya is the verb). Removed 1 duplicate koya entry. Bank now 1208 entries.

v2.13: Added proper zambi entry (archaic "because" — older form of mpo) with cultural note. Deleted broken legacy zambi entry whose english field was an OCR-dumped multi-sense fragment ("matter 2. conj. because"). Removed 1 duplicate mpo entry. Bank now 1208 entries.

v2.14: Lowercased the remaining 3 capitalized headwords (Nzambe, Yesu, Yezu) for consistency — the dictionary treats every entry as a lowercase headword regardless of proper-noun status. The cultural notes still capitalize them in running prose.
v2.15: Reverted v2.14 — restored capitalization on Nzambe / Yesu / Yezu. Proper-noun status outweighs the all-lowercase headword convention for these three.

v2.16: Cleaned the liboso/boso cluster — deleted 2 stub entries from legacy bank (boso had liboso's phonetic pasted in), deduped 2 v2 liboso entries into one, added a proper boso entry as the informal short form of liboso. Bank now 1208 entries.

v2.17: Deleted broken legacy ke stub (had phonetic and content of moke pasted in). Deduped 2 v2 moke entries into one with the project phonetic style (MO-ke). Tightened dictionary loader filter — legacy entries now need at least one editorial signal (example, cultural note, French, or verified flag); a bare phonetic alone no longer qualifies. Hides ~550 thin OCR entries until enriched.

v2.18: Enriched mawa entry — refined english to "sorrow / compassion", recategorized to new Comfort category, rewrote cultural note to land the compassion-alongside-someone meaning ("to sit in mawa with a grieving family, saying little, is itself a Congolese way of offering comfort").

v2.19: Enriched mai entry (new Essentials category, rewrote cultural note around the water-as-welcome gesture and the Congo River naming the country). Backfilled French apostrophes (l eau → l'eau, d eau → d'eau, qu il → qu'il, etc.) across 5 French fields and 47 example French fields — the bare-s OCR pattern had eaten them too.
v2.20: Backfilled French translations for 390 example sentences that previously had only Lingala + English. The 390 entries flagged in the v2.18 audit are now fully tri-lingual at the example level.

v2.21: Broader French elision-apostrophe sweep — catches d/c/j/s/m/t/n/l + vowel (d'abord, c'est, j'ai, etc.), plus qu/jusqu/lorsqu/puisqu/presqu + vowel. Fixed 14 entry French fields, 174 example French fields, 37 cultural notes. The v2.19 sweep only caught a narrow whitelist.

v2.22: Enriched 6 concept-word cultural notes that had been one-liners: bolingo (a century of Congolese rumba anchor), bomoi (life as treasured present-tense), kitoko (beauty named freely in Congolese speech), kosomba (the market-errand rhythm). The remaining short notes are number words, function words, and month names where short is appropriate.

Added Build it (compose) and Which rule? quiz modes; number breakdown chips with place-value color coding; How is this formed? derivation panel; Save/Copy/Share card actions; mastery progress tracking; saved-numbers bookmarking; daily challenge banner; first-run hint; keyboard shortcuts overlay; printable cheat sheet; Kuba-cloth motif on the card with 6 rotating patterns per decade; milestone confetti celebrations on every 10/100/1000; speech via Web Speech API with word-by-word highlighting; cultural number stories for ~25 key values. Each verb page shows imperative + all six subject prefixes across present, present continuous, past, future, habitual, and negative present tenses. Conjugation engine in /js/conjugate.js. meta.fields: Each word: id, english, lingala, phonetic, partOfSpeech, category, examples[], culturalNote, verified. Number entries additionally carry a numeric 'value' field.

examples.english: He is at work.
examples.french: Il est au travail.

words.culturalNote:
He, she — one letter, and a person is already acting.

In Lingala the subject lives inside the verb: the prefix a- carries "he" or "she", so azali means "he is" and akei "she has gone." Small as it is, it is where most sentences about people begin.

examples.english: Give me a match.
examples.french: Donne-moi une allumette.

words.culturalNote:
A match — the small spark of the kitchen.

Alimeti is a matchstick. Where meals are cooked over charcoal and the evening is lit by lamp, a box of alimeti is a quiet daily necessity, and "pesa ngai alimeti" — give me a match — is heard in every home.

examples.english: I like to eat pineapple.
examples.french: J'aime manger l'ananas.

words.culturalNote:
Pineapple — sweetness from the market stall.

Ananasi grows easily in the warm Congo basin and is sold in golden rings by roadside vendors. Sharp and sweet, it is the taste of an ordinary good afternoon.

examples.english: Not even one.
examples.french: Pas même un seul.

words.culturalNote:
Even — the word that stretches a statement to its edge.

Ata adds "even" or "at least": "ata moko te" is not even one, "ata soki" is even if. It is how Lingala insists, concedes, or refuses without raising its voice.

examples.english: We will go by airplane.
examples.french: Nous irons en avion.

words.culturalNote:
Airplane — the thread between home and the diaspora.

Avio (from the French avion) is how family crosses oceans to Kinshasa and back. For many Congolese abroad, the avio is the once-a-year bridge to the people they love.

examples.lingala: Tokati avoka ya sika mpo na kolia na mampa.
examples.english: We cut a fresh avocado to eat with bread.
examples.french: On a coupé un avocat frais pour manger avec du pain.

words.culturalNote: Avoka — the avocado, from French avocat. Eaten ripe, sliced over rice or spread on bread; the tree is common in courtyards across the wetter regions. (Earlier gloss "pear" was inaccurate.)

examples.english: We are in the month of April.
examples.french: Nous sommes au mois d'avril.

words.culturalNote:
April — a month in the long green season.

Lingala traditionally calls it sanza ya motinda; the borrowed French "avril" sits easily beside the older name, the way the language holds both worlds at once.

examples.english: Come here.
examples.french: Viens ici.

words.culturalNote:
Here — the ground beneath this conversation.

Awa marks the spot where you stand: "yaka awa," come here; "awa ezali kitoko," it is nice here. It draws a person toward you, into the present place.

examples.english: They are my friends.
examples.french: Ce sont mes amis.

words.culturalNote:
They — the many, carried in a single prefix.

Ba- is the plural of people: bato (people), baboti (parents), bana (children). As a verb prefix it means "they": bazali, they are; bakei, they have gone.

examples.lingala: Baboti na ngai bazali na mboka.
examples.english: My parents are in the homeland.
examples.french: Mes parents sont au pays.

words.culturalNote:
Parents — the first authority and the first shelter.

Baboti are your mother and father together. In Congolese life they are honoured long into adulthood — their blessing sought before big decisions — and caring for them in old age is love returned, not a burden.

examples.english: Add a little salt.
examples.french: Ajoute un peu de sel.

words.culturalNote:
To add — a cook's small adjustment.

Kobakisa is to add a little more: "bakisa mwa mungwa," add a touch of salt. It is the word for topping up, increasing, giving a bit extra — in the pot or in life.

examples.english: He wants to marry her.
examples.french: Il veut l'épouser.

words.culturalNote:
To marry — two families joining, not just two people.

Kobala is to marry. In Congolese tradition a marriage binds whole families, sealed with the dot (dowry) and celebrated loudly. "Alingi kobala" — he wants to marry — opens one of life's biggest doors.

examples.english: People are walking on the street.
examples.french: Les gens marchent dans la rue.

words.culturalNote:
Street — where the city lives out loud.

Balabala is the road or avenue. In Kinshasa the balabala hums with vendors, music, taxis and talk; to walk it is to be inside the daily theatre of the city.

examples.english: The children are playing ball.
examples.french: Les enfants jouent au ballon.

words.culturalNote:
Ball — the heart of a dusty courtyard game.

Bale (from the French) is a ball. Football is a national passion, and a bale — even one of rolled rags — turns any open ground into a pitch full of shouting children.

examples.english: I need to repair the sandal.
examples.french: Je dois réparer la sandale.

words.culturalNote:
To repair — making do, and making last.

Kobamba is to mend or patch — a sandal, a roof, a torn net. In a culture of resourcefulness, to bamba something is a small act of care that keeps it in service another season.

examples.english: Light the lamp.
examples.french: Allume la lampe.

words.culturalNote:
To light — bringing a flame to the dark.

Kobambola is to light or kindle a lamp or fire. Where electricity comes and goes, the evening often begins with someone lighting the mwinda, and the room gathering around it.

examples.english: We have begun the work.
examples.french: Nous avons commencé le travail.

words.culturalNote:
To begin — the first step of any work.

Kobanda is to start: "tobandi mosala," we have begun the work. It marks beginnings of every kind, from a day's labour to a long journey.

examples.english: Stick to your word.
examples.french: Tiens ta parole.

words.culturalNote:
To stick to — holding fast to a thing or a word.

Kobandema is to cling, adhere, or stay loyal; to bandema na maloba na yo is to keep your word. It carries the sense of not letting go when it would be easier to.

examples.english: Don’t be afraid.
examples.french: N'aie pas peur.

words.culturalNote:
To fear — and the courage of refusing it.

Kobanga is to be afraid. "Kobanga te," don't be afraid, is among the most repeated comforts a Congolese parent or pastor offers — naming the fear in order to set it down.

examples.english: Where are they?
examples.french: Où sont-ils ?

words.culturalNote:
Them — the others, named and present.

Bango is the standalone "they / them": "bango bazali wapi?", where are they? It points across the room, or across the world, to the people who are not "us" but matter all the same.

examples.lingala: Bankoko na ngai bazali na bwanya.
examples.english: My grandparents are wise.
examples.french: Mes grands-parents sont sages.

words.culturalNote:
Grandparents — the keepers of memory and proverb.

Bankoko are grandparents and ancestors both. They hold the family's stories, names and wisdom, and a child sent to sit with the bankoko is being given the past to carry forward.

examples.english: Christians honour the saints.
examples.french: Les chrétiens honorent les saints.

words.culturalNote:
Saints — the honoured dead of the faith.

Bansantu (ba- + the borrowed "santu") are the saints. In a deeply Christian society, Bakristo bakumisaka bansantu — Christians honour the saints — and their feast days mark the calendar.

examples.english: We are sitting on the veranda.
examples.french: Nous sommes assis sur la véranda.

words.culturalNote:
Veranda — the cool edge between house and street.

The barza is the porch where the day is watched, neighbours are greeted, and elders sit in the evening. Much of Congolese social life happens on the barza, half-in and half-out.

examples.english: The phone battery is dead.
examples.french: La batterie du téléphone est morte.

words.culturalNote:
Battery — power for torch, radio and phone.

Batiri keeps the small machines of daily life running. From the torch in a dark compound to the phone linking the diaspora, "batiri esili" — the battery is dead — is a familiar daily sigh.

examples.english: His baptism is tomorrow.
examples.french: Son baptême est demain.

words.culturalNote:
Baptism — a child welcomed into faith and family.

Batisimu is a celebrated day: the church, the white clothes, the feast after. To be baptised is to be named before God and the gathered community.

examples.english: Everybody came.
examples.french: Tout le monde est venu.

words.culturalNote:
Everybody — the whole gathering, no one left out.

From bato (people), "bato nyonso" is everyone. The phrase carries the communal spirit of a culture where an event belongs to the whole compound, not a chosen few.

examples.english: There are many people at the market.
examples.french: Il y a beaucoup de monde au marché.

words.culturalNote:
People — the plural that holds a community.

Bato is the most human of words — people, folks, everyone; "bato mingi" is a crowd. It is built from moto, one person, raised to the many.

examples.lingala: Bato baye bazali baninga na ngai.
examples.english: These people are my friends.
examples.french: Ces gens sont mes amis.

words.culturalNote:
These — pointing to the ones right here.

Baye is the demonstrative for people or things close at hand: "bato baye," these people. It gathers the present company into the sentence.

examples.english: That matter is bad.
examples.french: Cette affaire est mauvaise.

words.culturalNote:
Bad — what a community names to keep it at bay.

Mabe is bad, evil, or wicked: "likambo mabe" is a bad affair, "moto mabe" a bad person. To call a thing mabe is a moral judgement, plainly spoken.

examples.english: Don’t curse anyone.
examples.french: Ne maudis personne.

words.culturalNote:
To curse — words with the weight to wound.

Kobeba is to curse or insult. In a culture that prizes blessing and respectful speech, to beba someone is serious, and "kobeba moto te" — don't curse anyone — is sound counsel.

examples.english: Come now.
examples.french: Viens maintenant.

words.culturalNote:
Now — the present moment, asking to be acted on.

Bebe points to right now: "yaka bebe," come now. It presses for the immediate over the someday.

examples.english: I want to borrow money.
examples.french: Je veux emprunter de l'argent.

words.culturalNote:
To borrow — a small trust between neighbours.

Kobeka (also kodefa) is to borrow. In close-knit compounds, borrowing salt, money or a tool is everyday, and repaying it well keeps the web of trust intact.

examples.english: The water is boiling.
examples.french: L'eau bout.

words.culturalNote:
To boil — water finding its heat on the fire.

Kobela is to boil: "mai ezali kobela," the water is boiling. It is the first step of so much cooking, and of the boiled, safe water a careful household drinks.

examples.english: The child is ill.
examples.french: L'enfant est malade.

words.culturalNote:
To be ill — when the body asks the family to gather.

Kobela is to be sick: "mwana azali kobela," the child is ill. The words summon care, prayer, and the shared worry of a household that nurses its own.

examples.english: We will travel tomorrow.
examples.french: Nous voyagerons demain.

words.culturalNote:
To travel — setting out along the river or the road.

Kobemba (more often kosala mobembo) is to journey. In a vast country stitched together by the great river, travel is an undertaking, prepared for and prayed over.

examples.english: Pull the rope.
examples.french: Tire la corde.

words.culturalNote:
To pull — the steady force of work shared.

Kobenda is to pull or draw — a rope, a net, a load. "Benda nsinga," pull the rope; often it takes many hands, and the pulling becomes a rhythm sung together.

examples.english: The Congo flag is beautiful.
examples.french: Le drapeau du Congo est beau.

words.culturalNote:
Flag — colours a people stands beneath.

Bendele is a flag. The blue, yellow and red of the Congo carry a hard-won pride — raised on independence day and waved hardest when the national team plays.

examples.english: Call him/her.
examples.french: Appelle-le.

words.culturalNote:
To call — bringing someone near by name.

Kobenga is to call or summon: "benga ye," call him. A name called across a courtyard is one of the most ordinary, intimate sounds of home.

examples.english: This fish is raw.
examples.french: Ce poisson est cru.

words.culturalNote:
Raw — food not yet given to the fire.

Mobesu describes what is uncooked: "mbisi mobesu," raw fish. In a cuisine of slow-simmered pots, "raw" marks the before — the ingredient still waiting its turn.

examples.english: Can you swim?
examples.french: Sais-tu nager ?

words.culturalNote:
To swim — beating the water of the great river.

Lingala says it plainly: kobeta mai, to "beat the water." Along the Congo, the deepest river in the world, swimming is both childhood play and a riverside skill — "okoki kobeta mai?", can you swim?

examples.english: Don’t beat the child.
examples.french: Ne frappe pas l'enfant.

words.culturalNote:
To beat — a strike, a drumbeat, a heartbeat.

Kobeta is to hit or beat: a drum (kobeta mbonda), a ball, sadly sometimes a child — hence "kobeta mwana te," don't beat the child. The same word powers the drum that makes a village dance.

examples.english: May God save us.
examples.french: Que Dieu nous sauve.

words.culturalNote:
To save — rescue asked of God and of neighbour.

Kobikisa is to save or heal. Rooted in bomoi (life), it is a word of deliverance: "Nzambe abikisa biso," may God save us — heard in church and in danger alike.

examples.english: The food is good.
examples.french: La nourriture est bonne.

words.culturalNote:
Food — and the centre of gravity around which family gathers.

"Bilei" is food, the cooked meal that draws everyone in. Around it sit the staples of the Congolese kitchen — fufu, rice, madesu (beans), pondu (cassava leaves), fish from the river. To ask "bilei ezali?" — is there food? — is partly a question and partly the opening to an invitation.

examples.english: In the desert, there is no water.
examples.french: Dans le désert, il n'y a pas d'eau.

words.culturalNote:
Desert — the dry land that water forgot.

Biliki is a desert. Though the Congo is a country of rainforest and river, the word names the far, parched places — "na biliki, mai ezali te," in the desert there is no water.

examples.english: Father went to the office.
examples.french: Papa est allé au bureau.

words.culturalNote:
Office — the desk where the day's business is done.

Bilo (also biro) is an office. It stands for formal work, paperwork and administration — "akei na bilo," he has gone to the office — the world of the working day.

examples.english: My things are lost.
examples.french: Mes affaires sont perdues.

words.culturalNote:
Things — the belongings a life is carried in.

Biloko means things, goods, or baggage: "biloko na ngai," my things. For travellers and the displaced alike, one's biloko is what stays close, gathered and counted.

examples.english: Go outside.
examples.french: Sors dehors.

words.culturalNote:
To go out — crossing the threshold into the day.

Kobima is to come out or exit: "bima na libanda," go outside. It is the morning step into the compound, and the word for emerging, appearing, being seen.

examples.english: She is dancing.
examples.french: Elle danse.

words.culturalNote:
To dance — the body's'answer to a rumba.

Kobina is to dance, never far away in Congolese life: at weddings, in church, in the yard when a favourite song plays. To say "azali kobina" is to picture the whole body keeping time.

examples.english: Are you all well?
examples.french: Allez-vous bien ?

words.culturalNote:
You all — the room addressed together.

Bino is the plural "you": "bino bozali malamu?", are you all well? It greets a family, a congregation, a crowd — the many spoken to as one.

examples.english: Put water in the kettle.
examples.french: Mets de l'eau dans la bouilloire.

words.culturalNote:
Kettle — the small vessel of tea and welcome.

Birika is a kettle or teapot. Water set to boil in the birika often means a guest has come, for tea offered is hospitality made visible: "tia mai na birika," put water in the kettle.

examples.english: I looked for you everywhere.
examples.french: Je t'ai cherché partout.

words.culturalNote:
Everywhere — and the places a search leads you.

Bisika are places and spots; bisika nyonso is everywhere. To say you looked bisika nyonso is to have left no corner of the compound, the market, or the city unturned.

examples.english: There are people everywhere.
examples.french: Il y a des gens partout.

words.culturalNote:
Everywhere — the whole of a place, all at once.

Bisika binso gathers every location into one word. People here, people there — bato bazali bisika binso — the crowd that fills a Congolese street has nowhere it is not.

examples.english: The child likes biscuits.
examples.french: L'enfant aime les biscuits.

words.culturalNote:
Biscuit — a small sweet bought by the piece.

Bisikiti are biscuits, sold singly or in little packets at the kiosk. A coin, and a child runs home with bisikiti — a tiny everyday treat in a culture where small joys are shared.

examples.english: Give us water.
examples.french: Donne-nous de l'eau.

words.culturalNote:
Us — the circle that says "we" and means it.

Biso is we and us; biso nyonso is all of us. In a communal culture the line around biso is drawn wide — family, neighbours, the whole gathering — and "pesa biso" asks on behalf of everyone.

examples.english: We cooked plantains.
examples.french: Nous avons cuisiné des bananes plantains.

words.culturalNote:
Plantains — the everyday starch, fried or boiled.

Bitabi are plantains, a staple of the Congolese plate: sliced and fried golden, or boiled beside fish and greens. Cheap, filling and loved, they anchor many a home meal.

examples.english: I have no cash.
examples.french: Je n'ai pas d'argent liquide.

words.culturalNote:
Banknote — folded money, counted by hand.

Biye is a banknote or bill, the cash (makuta) of daily trade. In markets run on paper money a fresh biye is checked, folded and tucked away; "nazali na biye te" — I've no cash — is an everyday admission.

examples.english: Bread is made from wheat.
examples.french: Le pain est fait de blé.

words.culturalNote:
Wheat — the imported grain behind the bread.

Ble (from the French ble) is wheat. It grows little in the Congo's climate, so it arrives as flour — and from it comes mampa, the bread of the morning table.

examples.english: What are you all doing?
examples.french: Que faites-vous ?

words.culturalNote:
You — the "you all" folded into the verb.

Bo- is the second-person plural prefix: bozali, you are; bokei, you have gone. One syllable addresses a whole family or congregation at once.

examples.lingala: Na eleko ya mbula, bobandu ezali mingi.
examples.english: In the rainy season, the humidity is high.
examples.french: En saison des pluies, l'humidité est forte.

words.culturalNote:
Humidity — the wet weight of the air.

Bobandu is the damp heaviness of the air, thickest in the rains. In the equatorial Congo the bobandu settles on the skin, and the afternoon slows beneath it.

examples.english: The child is shy.
examples.french: L'enfant est timide.

words.culturalNote:
Shyness — the held-back voice of the newcomer.

Bobangi is shyness or timidity, the same root as kobanga, to fear. A child who hides behind a parent's wrapper is na bobangi — and the family draws them out gently.

examples.english: Peace be with you.
examples.french: Que la paix soit avec vous.

words.culturalNote:
Peace — gentleness that keeps a household whole.

Boboto is peace, calm, and the soft kindness between people. "Boboto ezala na bino" — peace be with you — is both a blessing and a way of life in Congolese courtesy.

examples.english: We went to see the waterfall.
examples.french: Nous sommes allés voir la chute d'eau.

words.culturalNote:
Waterfall — the river thrown white off the rocks.

Boeta (also meta) is a waterfall. In a land of great rivers the falls are places of power and beauty — a roar of water that draws families to come and stand before it.

examples.english: I am surprised.
examples.french: Je suis étonné.

words.culturalNote:
Surprise — the catch of breath at the unexpected.

Bokamwi is surprise or astonishment, from kokamwa, to be amazed. Good news or strange, it widens the eyes: "nazali na bokamwi," I am amazed.

examples.english: His departure is tomorrow.
examples.french: Son départ est demain.

words.culturalNote:
Departure — the ache of the one who leaves.

Bokei is a departure, from kokende, to go. In a people scattered across the diaspora, every bokei at the airport carries weight — the goodbye that hopes to become a return.

examples.english: These beans are spicy.
examples.french: Ces haricots sont épicés.

words.culturalNote:
Spicy — the bite of pili-pili in the pot.

Bokenzu is spicy or piquant. Congolese cooking loves heat — pili-pili (chilli) in the sauce — and a dish that is bokenzu wakes the whole mouth.

examples.english: There is no difference.
examples.french: Il n'y a pas de différence.

words.culturalNote:
Difference — the gap between one thing and another.

Bokeseni is difference or distinction, from kokesana, to differ. To say "bokeseni ezali te" — there is no difference — is to call two things the same, or two people equal.

examples.english: Father went hunting.
examples.french: Papa est parti chasser.

words.culturalNote:
Hunting — the forest's'old way of providing.

Bokila is hunting. In villages near the forest the hunter who leaves at dawn for bokila returns with meat for the family and the pot — a respected, ancient skill.

examples.lingala: Bokilo na ngai ayei kotala biso.
examples.english: My in-law came to visit us.
examples.french: Mon beau-parent est venu nous rendre visite.

words.culturalNote:
In-law — the family marriage gives you.

Bokilo is an in-law — the relatives a marriage brings. In Congolese life the bokilo bond carries real obligation and warmth, treated with care and a little ceremony.

examples.lingala: Bokilo mobali na ngai azali na mboka.
examples.english: My father-in-law is in the village.
examples.french: Mon beau-père est au village.

words.culturalNote:
Father-in-law — the elder a marriage asks you to honour.

Bokilo mobali — literally the male in-law — is the father-in-law. He is approached with respect, his blessing sought; the dowry and the wedding pass through his hands.

examples.english: Health is worth more than money.
examples.french: La santé vaut plus que l'argent.

words.culturalNote:
Health — the wealth a body carries.

Bokolongono is good health and wholeness. A common wisdom sets it above riches: "bokolongono eleki mbongo," health is worth more than money.

examples.english: This disease is severe.
examples.french: Cette maladie est grave.

words.culturalNote:
Disease — the trouble that gathers the family to nurse.

Bokono is sickness or disease. When bokono enters a home it becomes everyone's concern — the herbs, the clinic, the prayers, the relatives who take turns at the bedside.

examples.english: We are in the worship of God.
examples.french: Nous sommes dans l'adoration de Dieu.

words.culturalNote:
Worship — praise lifted up together.

Bokumisi is worship and praise, from kokumisa, to glorify. In a deeply faithful society, bokumisi ya Nzambe — the worship of God — fills churches with song every Sunday.

examples.english: He is very tall.
examples.french: Il est très grand.

words.culturalNote:
Height — how tall a person or a tree stands.

Bolai is height or length, from -lai, long. It measures a person, a tree, a road: "bolai na ye ezali mingi," he is very tall.

examples.english: Good luck to you.
examples.french: Bonne chance à toi.

words.culturalNote:
Good fortune — kindness wished onto another.

Bolamu is goodness, kindness, and good luck all at once. To say "bolamu ezala na yo" is to wish someone well — a blessing pressed into a parting.

examples.english: Take a blanket, it's cold.
examples.french: Prends une couverture, il fait froid.

words.culturalNote:
Blanket — warmth pulled close on a cool night.

Bolangiti is a blanket. Nights can turn cool, and the bolangiti shared on a mat is a small comfort: "kamata bolangiti," take a blanket.

examples.lingala: Na bolenge na ngai, nazalaki kobina mingi.
examples.english: In my youth, I danced a lot.
examples.french: Dans ma jeunesse, je dansais beaucoup.

words.culturalNote:
Youth — the springtime a life remembers.

Bolenge is youth, the season of strength and dancing. Elders speak of their bolenge with a smile — "na bolenge na ngai," in my youth — when the legs were quick and the nights were long.

examples.english: I ask for forgiveness.
examples.french: Je demande pardon.

words.culturalNote:
Forgiveness — the door reopened after a wrong.

Bolimbisi is forgiveness, from kolimbisa, to pardon. To ask bolimbisi is to seek to mend a bond; in family and faith alike it is the word that lets life go on together.

examples.english: True love.
examples.french: L'amour vrai.

words.culturalNote: Bolingo — love. The word that anchors a hundred years of Congolese rumba: from Wendo Kolosoy to Franco, Tabu Ley, Papa Wemba, and the guitarists of the modern Kinshasa scene, "bolingo" is the chorus the whole hall sings back. It carries romantic love and the deeper sense of devotion — bolingo ya mama (a mother's love), bolingo ya mboka (love of country). When Congolese say "bolingo ekosila te" — love will not end — they mean something larger than any one person.

examples.english: This coffee is bitter.
examples.french: Ce café est amer.

words.culturalNote:
Bitterness — the sharp taste, on the tongue or in the heart.

Bololo is bitterness — of a medicine, a leaf, or a hard season of life. The same word that names a bitter brew names the bitterness a person swallows and carries on.

examples.english: I am in pain.
examples.french: Je souffre.

words.culturalNote:
Pain — the body's'hard news.

Bolozi is pain and suffering. To be na bolozi is to hurt in body or spirit; it is a word spoken to summon care, and to be met with it.

examples.english: The child is naked.
examples.french: L'enfant est nu.

words.culturalNote:
Nakedness — the body without its covering.

Bolumbu is nakedness. A small child runs bolumbu without shame; for others, to be covered is dignity, and clothing a person in need is a recognised kindness.

examples.english: The man killed an animal.
examples.french: L'homme a tué un animal.

words.culturalNote:
To kill — the heaviest of verbs, for hunt or harm.

Koboma is to kill — an animal for the pot, or, gravely, a person. The same root gives the hunter's catch and the commandment "koboma te," do not kill.

examples.english: Hide your money.
examples.french: Cache ton argent.

words.culturalNote:
To hide — tucking a thing out of sight.

Kobomba is to hide or store away — money, a gift, a secret. "Bomba mbongo na yo" — hide your money — is sensible counsel in a crowded place.

examples.lingala: Mwana abombani na nsima ya ndako.
examples.english: The child hid behind the house.
examples.french: L'enfant s'est caché derrière la maison.

words.culturalNote:
To hide oneself — slipping out of sight.

Kobombana is to hide oneself, the reflexive of kobomba. Children play it behind the house; adults sometimes wish they could — "abombani," he hid himself away.

examples.english: Life is beautiful.
examples.french: La vie est belle.

words.culturalNote: Bomoi — life. The full, breathing, present-tense fact of being alive, not just biological existence. Bomoi is the word elders use when they bless a newborn ("pesa ye bomoi malamu" — give him a good life), and the word grieving families return to when they say "bomoi ezongi te" — life does not come back. In Congolese speech bomoi is treasured rather than assumed: every day given is a day to thank.

examples.english: We pray to God.
examples.french: Nous prions Dieu.

words.culturalNote:
To plead — asking from the heart, hands open.

Kobondela is to beg, plead, or pray. One bondela a person for a favour, or God in prayer; the word carries humility and hope together — "tobondeli Nzambe," we beseech God.

examples.english: Calm this crying child.
examples.french: Calme cet enfant qui pleure.

words.culturalNote:
To calm — soothing what is troubled.

Kobondo is to calm or relieve — a crying child, a worried heart. To bondo someone is to bring them down gently from fear or grief.

examples.english: The soldier has a gun.
examples.french: Le soldat a un fusil.

words.culturalNote:
Gun — a weapon that commands fear and caution.

Bondoki is a gun or firearm, carried by soldier and hunter. In a region that has known conflict, the bondoki is a heavy thing, named plainly and warily.

examples.english: This garment suits you.
examples.french: Ce vêtement te va.

words.culturalNote:
To suit — when a thing fits as it should.

Kobonga is to be suitable, fitting, or right — and also "must." A garment that ebongi suits you; a plan that ebongi is the proper one.

examples.english: Arrange your things.
examples.french: Range tes affaires.

words.culturalNote:
To arrange — setting things in good order.

Kobongisa is to arrange, tidy, fix, or prepare. One bongisa the house before guests, the table before a meal, a plan before it begins.

examples.english: This child is clever.
examples.french: Cet enfant est intelligent.

words.culturalNote:
Brain — the seat of cleverness and thought.

Bongo is the brain and, by extension, the mind and wit. To say a child azali na bongo is to call them sharp; to "use your bongo" is to think.

examples.english: Change your clothes.
examples.french: Change de vêtements.

words.culturalNote:
To change — turning one thing into another.

Kobongola is to change, turn, or translate — clothes, money, a mind. To bongola makanisi is to change one's mind; to bongola maloba is to translate.

examples.english: How are you?
examples.french: Comment vas-tu ?

words.culturalNote:
How — the question at the start of caring.

Boni asks how: "ozali boni?", how are you? "esalemi boni?", how did it happen? It opens the door to another's state and story.

examples.english: He is a famous person.
examples.french: C'est une personne célèbre.

words.culturalNote:
Famous — the name everyone already knows.

Bopela is fame or renown. A musician of bopela needs no introduction; in a culture that crowns its rumba stars, to be bopela is to belong to everyone.

examples.english: Sunday is a day of rest.
examples.french: Le dimanche est un jour de repos.

words.culturalNote:
Rest — the day the work is laid down.

Bopemi is rest, from kopema, to breathe. The mokolo ya bopemi — the day of rest — is honoured; even the hardest worker is owed the breath of it.

examples.english: The choice is yours.
examples.french: Le choix t'appartient.

words.culturalNote:
Choice — the freedom and weight of deciding.

Boponi is choice or selection, from kopona, to choose. "Boponi ezali ya yo" — the choice is yours — hands someone both the freedom and the responsibility.

examples.english: A shrine is a place of worship.
examples.french: Un sanctuaire est un lieu de culte.

words.culturalNote:
Shrine — the set-apart place of prayer.

Bosambelelo is a shrine or sanctuary, from kosambela, to pray. It is ground made holy by prayer — a place people go to be near God, or to remember the dead.

examples.english: Don't forget.
examples.french: N'oublie pas.

words.culturalNote:
To forget — the thread that slips the mind.

Kobosana is to forget. "Kobosana te" — don't forget — is the small plea at every parting; some things, like one's people and one's name, must never be forgotten.

examples.english: The road is slippery in the rain.
examples.french: La route est glissante sous la pluie.

words.culturalNote:
Slippery — the ground that won't be trusted.

Boselu is slippery. After the rains the unpaved nzela turns boselu, and feet learn caution — a small daily hazard of the wet season.

examples.english: Tell only the truth.
examples.french: Dis seulement la vérité.

words.culturalNote:
Truth — the straight word a community rests on.

Bosolo is truth. "Loba bosolo" — speak the truth — is held as a moral duty; among elders, the one who tells bosolo plainly is trusted with much.

examples.english: Your hands are dirty.
examples.french: Tes mains sont sales.

words.culturalNote:
Dirty — what soap and water are for.

Bosoto is dirt or dirtiness. In a culture that prizes a clean appearance even where water is fetched by hand, "maboko na yo ezali bosoto" — your hands are dirty — sends a child straight to wash.

examples.english: The mother gave birth to a child.
examples.french: La mère a accouché d'un enfant.

words.culturalNote:
Birth — the moment a family grows by one.

Kobota is to give birth, to bear a child. A birth belongs to the whole family — "mama aboti," the mother has delivered — and the new arrival is welcomed with names, song, and relatives at the door.

examples.english: We went sightseeing around the country.
examples.french: Nous avons fait du tourisme dans le pays.

words.culturalNote:
Sightseeing — going to see the land with fresh eyes.

Botali (botali mboka) is sightseeing or tourism, from kotala, to look. To go on botali is to travel the country and behold it — the river, the falls, the wildlife — as a guest of its beauty.

examples.english: This sculpture is made of wood.
examples.french: Cette sculpture est faite en bois.

words.culturalNote:
Sculpture — figures carved from wood and memory.

Botendi is sculpture. Congolese carving is renowned — masks, ancestor figures, the smooth grain of worked wood — an art that holds spirit and story in its forms.

examples.english: Take off your clothes.
examples.french: Enlève tes vêtements.

words.culturalNote:
Undress — taking the cloth off, gently or in a hurry.

Botolo (with elamba, cloth) is to undress, from kobotola, to take away. A mother botolo a child before the bath; the same root, alone, can mean to seize — context tells which.

examples.english: Wear boots in the rain.
examples.french: Porte des bottes sous la pluie.

words.culturalNote:
Boot — sturdy footwear for mud and rain.

Botte (from the French) is a boot. When the rains turn the unpaved roads to mud, a pair of botte keeps the feet dry on the walk to market or field.

examples.english: He refused to eat.
examples.french: Il a refusé de manger.

words.culturalNote:
To refuse — the firm "no" that draws a line.

Koboya is to refuse or reject. A child who aboyi kolia will not eat; a person who boya something has set their will against it, plainly.

examples.english: His faith is strong.
examples.french: Sa foi est forte.

words.culturalNote:
Faith — the trust that carries a people through.

Boyambi is faith and belief. In a deeply religious society it shapes the week — the prayers, the choir, the strength people draw from what they cannot see.

examples.english: It is just like that.
examples.french: C'est juste comme ça.

words.culturalNote:
Thus — "like that," the shrug or the verdict.

Boye (and bongo) mean thus, so, like that. "Ezali boye" — that's'how it is — can close an argument or accept a fate; a small word that frames how things stand.

examples.english: They posted a notice at the gate.
examples.french: Ils ont affiché un avis à la porte.

words.culturalNote:
Notice — word put out for all to see.

Boyebisi is a notice or announcement, from koyebisa, to inform. Pinned at the gate or read in church, the boyebisi is how news reaches the whole community at once.

examples.english: Your arrival pleased me.
examples.french: Ton arrivée m'a réjoui.

words.culturalNote:
Arrival — the joy at the door that a journey is over.

Boyei is an arrival, from koya, to come. In a culture of long-awaited reunions, a boyei is celebrated — "boyei na yo esepelisi ngai," your arrival made me glad.

examples.english: Theft is bad.
examples.french: Le vol, c'est mal.

words.culturalNote:
Theft — the broken trust a community condemns.

Boyibi is theft, from koyiba, to steal. In close-knit compounds where doors stay open, boyibi is a serious breach — "boyibi ezali mabe," theft is wrong, plainly said.

examples.lingala: Ebale oyo ezali na bozindo mingi.
examples.english: This river is very deep.
examples.french: Ce fleuve est très profond.

words.culturalNote:
Depth — how far down the water, or the matter, goes.

Bozindo is depth, from -zindo, deep. The great river runs with bozindo; so does a hard question — the word measures both the river and the meaning.

examples.english: This bag is heavy.
examples.french: Ce sac est lourd.

words.culturalNote:
Weight — the heaviness a load, or a worry, carries.

Bozito is weight, from -zito, heavy. A full sack has bozito; so does sad news. The same word weighs the basket on the head and the burden on the heart.

examples.english: He is acting foolishly.
examples.french: Il agit bêtement.

words.culturalNote:
Foolishness — acting without knowing, or without thought.

Bozoba is ignorance or foolishness, the opposite of bwanya, wisdom. To act na bozoba is to blunder; elders steer the young away from it toward sense.

examples.english: The child broke the chair.
examples.french: L'enfant a cassé la chaise.

words.culturalNote:
To break — what carelessness or force undoes.

Kobuka is to break or snap — a pot, a stick, a promise. "Mwana abuki" — the child broke it — is heard often in a busy household of small hands.

examples.english: I am reading a book.
examples.french: Je lis un livre.

words.culturalNote:
Book — pages that carry word and learning.

Buku (from the French) is a book. To kotanga buku — read a book — is the work of school and a door to the wider world; a prized thing where books are not always easy to come by.

examples.english: The sky is blue.
examples.french: Le ciel est bleu.

words.culturalNote:
Blue — the colour of the sky and the flag's field.

Bulo (from the French bleu) is blue — the cerulean of the Congo's sky and the blue of its flag, the colour of height and of hope.

examples.english: Don't fight.
examples.french: Ne te bats pas.

words.culturalNote:
To fight — fists, or the struggle to overcome.

Kobunda is to fight or struggle. Children are told "kobunda te," don't fight; but kobunda also means to battle hardship — to fight on, and not give up.

examples.english: I lost my way.
examples.french: J'ai perdu mon chemin.

words.culturalNote:
To lose — the thing, or the way, gone from your hand.

Kobunga is to lose or get lost. To bunga nzela is to lose your way; for something to ebungi is for it to slip away — a small daily grief.

examples.english: Reduce the price.
examples.french: Baisse le prix.

words.culturalNote:
To bring down the price — the dance of the market.

Kobunola is to reduce, above all a price. In the market nothing has a fixed cost; "bunola talo" — lower the price — opens the friendly haggling that ends in a fair deal.

examples.english: Give me thread.
examples.french: Donne-moi du fil.

words.culturalNote:
Thread — the fine line that mends and makes.

Busi is thread. With a needle and busi a tear is closed, a button returned, a garment kept alive — the quiet thrift of a careful home.

examples.english: The child climbed the tree.
examples.french: L'enfant a grimpé à l'arbre.

words.culturalNote:
To climb — going up, by tree, hill, or ladder.

Kobuta is to climb or ascend. A child butaka nzete — climbs a tree — for mango or for fun; the word also lifts a rising road and a person who rises in life.

examples.english: I'm going to the shop to buy bread.
examples.french: Je vais à la boutique acheter du pain.

words.culturalNote:
Shop — the small storefront of the neighbourhood.

Butiki (from the French boutique) is a shop. The corner butiki sells the day's needs — bread, soap, sugar — and is a hub of small talk as much as small trade.

examples.english: Button up the shirt.
examples.french: Boutonne la chemise.

words.culturalNote:
Button — the small fastening of a shirt.

Buto (from the French) is a button. To kanga buto is to do up a shirt; a lost buto is a small domestic problem solved with a needle and busi.

examples.english: At night, people sleep.
examples.french: La nuit, les gens dorment.

words.culturalNote:
Night — the dark hours of rest and story.

Butu is night. When the lamps are lit and the day's work is done, the butu is for sleep, for the radio, and for the old stories told in the courtyard.

examples.english: Light the candle.
examples.french: Allume la bougie.

words.culturalNote:
Candle — a small flame against the dark.

Buzi is a candle. Where the power fails, the buzi is lit — its small light enough for a meal, a prayer, or a child's'homework on the table.

examples.english: Throw the ball to me.
examples.french: Lance-moi le ballon.

words.culturalNote:
To throw — to toss, or to throw away.

Kobwaka is to throw or cast — a ball to a friend, or rubbish to the heap. The same word sends the game's bale flying and discards what is no longer wanted.

examples.english: We crossed the river by canoe.
examples.french: Nous avons traversé le fleuve en pirogue.

words.culturalNote:
Canoe — the dugout that crosses the great river.

Bwato is a canoe or boat — often the pirogue carved from a single trunk. On the Congo and its tributaries, the bwato carries people, goods and fish where no road reaches.

examples.english: Invite the friends to the party.
examples.french: Invite les amis à la fête.

words.culturalNote:
To invite — calling someone in to share.

Kobyanga is to invite or call. To byanga guests to a fete is to open your home; in a culture of hospitality the invitation is warmly given and gladly answered.

examples.english: The Congo flag is raised high.
examples.french: Le drapeau du Congo est hissé haut.

words.culturalNote:
Flag — colours a nation rallies to.

Dalapo (from the French drapeau) is a flag, alongside bendele. Raised on independence day and waved at the stadium, the dalapo gathers a people's pride into cloth.

examples.english: I borrowed money from a friend.
examples.french: J'ai emprunté de l'argent à un ami.

words.culturalNote:
To borrow — the everyday trust of lending hands.

Kodefa is to borrow. Among neighbours, to defa salt, money or a tool — and to return it well — is the small currency of trust that holds a community together.

examples.english: We cook turkey at Christmas.
examples.french: Nous cuisinons de la dinde à Noël.

words.culturalNote:
Turkey — the bird of a special-day table.

Dendon (from the French dindon) is a turkey. Larger than the everyday chicken, a dendon marks a feast — Christmas, a wedding — when the family eats well together.

examples.lingala: Noel ezali na sanza ya desembere.
examples.english: Christmas is in December.
examples.french: Noël est en décembre.

words.culturalNote:
December — the month the year ends in feasting.

Desembere is December, the season of Noel. Family travel home, churches fill, and the desembere table is the year's most generous — a month of reunion and celebration.

words.english: di- (noun class prefix for certain paired/paired-fruit nouns)

examples.english: He is my friend.
examples.french: C'est mon ami.

words.culturalNote: Di- — a Bantu noun class prefix inherited from proto-Bantu, appearing in some Lingala nouns (e.g. dika, dibondo). The original entry "friend" was incorrect; friend in Lingala is moninga or ndeko.

examples.english: Congo has many diamonds.
examples.french: Le Congo a beaucoup de diamants.

words.culturalNote:
Diamond — the hard brilliance dug from Congo's soil.

Diaman (from the French diamant) is a diamond. The Congo's'earth is rich with them; the diaman is a symbol of the land's deep wealth — and of the long question of whom it has served.

examples.english: We must pass through customs.
examples.french: Nous devons passer la douane.

words.culturalNote:
Customs — the border's checkpoint of bags and papers.

Douane (from the French) is customs. At the airport or the river crossing, the douane checks what enters and leaves — a threshold every traveller and trader must pass.

examples.english: It is good.
examples.french: C'est bon.

words.culturalNote:
It — the small prefix that lets a thing speak.

The prefix e- carries "it" for many Lingala nouns: ezali, it is; esalemi, it is done. One letter, and an object or an event takes its place in the sentence.

examples.english: The Congo River is mighty.
examples.french: Le fleuve Congo est immense.

words.culturalNote:
River — the great road of water at the country's'heart.

Ebale is a river — above all the Congo, the mighty ebale that names the nation. It carries canoes and commerce, fish and song; life along its banks bends to its flow.

examples.english: The beginning of the work is hard.
examples.french: Le début du travail est difficile.

words.culturalNote:
Beginning — the hard, hopeful first stretch.

Ebandeli is the beginning, from kobanda, to start. "Ebandeli ya mosala ezali pasi" — the start of the work is hard — but every road, the proverb knows, has its ebandeli.

examples.english: This house is ugly.
examples.french: Cette maison est laide.

words.culturalNote:
Ugly — what the eye turns away from.

Ebe is ugly, kin to mabe, bad. It describes a thing unpleasant to look on — a plain judgement, softened in kind company but honest all the same.

examples.english: Many people came.
examples.french: Beaucoup de gens sont venus.

words.culturalNote:
Many — the crowd, the plenty, the abundance.

Ebele means many or much. "Bato ebele" is a crowd; "mbongo ebele" is a lot of money. It is the word for a gathering that overflows — and Congolese gatherings often do.

examples.english: People went to bury the body.
examples.french: Les gens sont allés enterrer le corps.

words.culturalNote:
Body — the departed, honoured with ceremony.

Ebembe is a corpse, the body of one who has died. Death calls the whole family; the ebembe is watched, mourned and buried with song, food and days of gathering.

examples.english: The pigeon is flying.
examples.french: Le pigeon vole.

words.culturalNote:
Pigeon — the common bird of roof and square.

Ebenga is a pigeon. It clatters up from courtyards and market squares, kept by some, watched by children — an ordinary winged neighbour of the town.

examples.english: Sit on the stool.
examples.french: Assieds-toi sur le tabouret.

words.culturalNote:
Stool — the low seat that gathers a circle.

Ebonga is a stool or seat. Pulled into the courtyard at evening, the ebonga seats the elders and the talkers; to be offered one is to be welcomed to stay.

examples.english: The soldier has a weapon.
examples.french: Le soldat a une arme.

words.culturalNote:
Weapon — a thing of war, named with weight.

Ebuneli is a weapon, from kobunda, to fight. In a region that has known conflict, the ebuneli is spoken of soberly — an instrument the wise hope to set down.

examples.english: Put the ladder against the wall.
examples.french: Mets l'échelle contre le mur.

words.culturalNote:
Ladder — the climb to what is out of reach.

Ebuteli is a ladder, from kobuta, to climb. Set against the efelo to mend a roof or pick high fruit, the ebuteli is the simple tool that adds height to the hand.

examples.english: The wall of the house is strong.
examples.french: Le mur de la maison est solide.

words.culturalNote:
Wall — the line that makes a home a shelter.

Efelo is a wall. Of mud-brick or block, the efelo holds up the roof and divides the inside from the out — the bones of the house a family builds and keeps.

examples.english: An accident happened on the street.
examples.french: Un accident a eu lieu dans la rue.

words.culturalNote:
Accident — the sudden harm no one chose.

Ekbelakbela is an accident. On the busy balabala the word names the crash, the fall, the mishap — met with rushing neighbours and quick prayers.

examples.english: We cooked yam.
examples.french: Nous avons cuisiné de l'igname.

words.culturalNote:
Yam — a hearty root of the cooking pot.

Ekeke is a yam. Boiled or pounded, the starchy ekeke fills the plate beside greens and fish — one of the steady roots that feed a family through the seasons.

examples.lingala: Ekeko ezali na kati ya engumba.
examples.english: The monument is in the city centre.
examples.french: Le monument est au centre-ville.

words.culturalNote:
Monument — stone or bronze that keeps a memory standing.

Ekeko is a monument or statue. Set in a square or roundabout, the ekeko fixes a hero or a moment in public view — a city's way of refusing to forget.

examples.english: He is playing the thumb piano.
examples.french: Il joue du piano à pouces.

words.culturalNote:
Thumb piano — metal tongues plucked into a lullaby of notes.

Ekembe (the likembe) is a thumb piano, and by extension any musical instrument. Its soft, repeating melody is one of the oldest sounds of Central Africa — handheld, intimate, hypnotic.

examples.english: These things are different.
examples.french: Ces choses sont différentes.

words.culturalNote:
Different — set apart from the rest.

Ekeseni is different or distinct, from kokesana, to differ. Two cloths, two ideas, two paths — to be ekeseni is simply to not be the same.

examples.lingala: Bilei ekoki mpo na bato nyonso.
examples.english: There is enough food for everyone.
examples.french: Il y a assez de nourriture pour tout le monde.

words.culturalNote:
Enough — the line where need is met.

Ekoki means enough or sufficient (and "it is able"), from kokoka, to suffice. "Bilei ekoki" — there's'enough food — is a host's quiet relief at a full table.

examples.english: Put the fruit in the basket.
examples.french: Mets le fruit dans le panier.

words.culturalNote:
Basket — woven hands that carry the harvest.

Ekolo is a basket. Plaited from reed or raffia, it carries fruit from the field, fish from the river, goods from the market — the everyday vessel of a carrying life.

examples.english: Give me a pen.
examples.french: Donne-moi un stylo.

words.culturalNote:
Pen — the tool that turns thought into ink.

Ekomeli is a pen, from koma, to write. In the schoolroom and the office, the ekomeli is a small power — to write a name, a letter, a future.

examples.english: She wears a bracelet on her arm.
examples.french: Elle porte un bracelet au bras.

words.culturalNote:
Bracelet — a circle of beauty on the wrist.

Ekomo is a bracelet. Of beads, copper or gold, it adorns the arm at a wedding or a fete — small finery worn with pride.

examples.english: Put on your shoes.
examples.french: Mets tes chaussures.

words.culturalNote:
Shoe — what carries the foot over rough ground.

Ekoto is a shoe. On dusty roads and through the rains, a good pair of ekoto is valued; children are told to lata ekoto — put on shoes — before they head out.

examples.english: A storm came in the evening.
examples.french: Un orage est arrivé le soir.

words.culturalNote:
Storm — the sky's sudden fury over the basin.

Ekumbaki is a storm. When the equatorial clouds gather and break, the ekumbaki drums rain on the roofs and sends the market running for shelter.

examples.english: We cooked pumpkin.
examples.french: Nous avons cuisiné de la courge.

words.culturalNote:
Pumpkin — flesh and leaves, both for the pot.

Ekutu is a pumpkin. Its flesh sweetens a soup, and its young leaves are cooked down into the saucy greens that crown Congolese rice and fufu.

examples.english: The partridge is a forest bird.
examples.french: La perdrix est un oiseau de la forêt.

words.culturalNote:
Partridge — a plump bird flushed from the grass.

Ekwae is a partridge, a bird of bush and field. For the hunter it is a welcome catch; for the table, a taste of the wild brought home.

examples.lingala: Tozali na elaka lobi na ntongo.
examples.english: We have an appointment tomorrow morning.
examples.french: Nous avons un rendez-vous demain matin.

words.culturalNote:
Appointment — a time set, a word given.

Elaka is an appointment, a date, or a promise. To make an elaka is to bind yourself to a time and a word; to keep it is a measure of a person.

examples.english: I'm going to the bedroom to sleep.
examples.french: Je vais dans la chambre pour dormir.

words.culturalNote:
Bedroom — the quiet room sleep is kept in.

Elalelo is a bedroom, from kolala, to sleep. In a full household it may be shared by many; the elalelo is where the day is finally set down.

examples.english: This cloth is beautiful.
examples.french: Ce tissu est beau.

words.culturalNote:
Cloth — the wrapper that dresses a whole culture.

Elamba is cloth or a garment — above all the brilliant printed pagne wrapped, tied and worn across the Congo. To choose an elamba is to choose how you greet the world.

examples.english: Father went to the farm.
examples.french: Papa est allé au champ.

words.culturalNote:
Field — the worked earth that feeds the home.

Elanga is a farm, field, or garden. Hoed by hand and tended through the seasons, the elanga gives the cassava, greens and maize that fill the family pot.

examples.english: The past year was good.
examples.french: L'année passée était bonne.

words.culturalNote:
Past — what has gone by, and stays behind.

Eleki means past or last, from koleka, to pass. "Mobu eleki," last year; "sanza eleki," last month — the word for the time that has already walked on.

examples.english: This one is better.
examples.french: Celui-ci est meilleur.

words.culturalNote:
Better — the one that surpasses the rest.

Eleki malamu — literally "passes good" — is how Lingala says better. To compare is to ask which eleki malamu, which comes out ahead.

examples.english: In that era, I was young.
examples.french: À cette époque, j'étais jeune.

words.culturalNote:
Era — a stretch of time with its own weather and mood.

Eleko is a period, season, or era. "Eleko ya mbula," the rainy season; "na eleko wana," in those days — it frames both the year's weather and a life's chapters.

examples.english: During the night, people sleep.
examples.french: Pendant la nuit, les gens dorment.

words.culturalNote:
During — inside the span of a time.

Eleko ya means during, in the time of. "Eleko ya butu," during the night; "eleko ya mosala," during work — it sets an action inside its season.

examples.english: This person is mad.
examples.french: Cette personne est folle.

words.culturalNote:
Madness — the mind slipped from its sense.

Elema is a madman or a fool. Spoken in anger or in pity, it names the one who acts without reason — and warns the rest toward sense.

examples.english: This young man is strong.
examples.french: Ce jeune homme est fort.

words.culturalNote:
Youth — the strong, restless season of life.

Elenge is a young person, often a young man (elenge mobali). Quick of limb and full of hope, the elenge carries a community's'energy — and its future.

examples.english: This food is delicious.
examples.french: Cette nourriture est délicieuse.

words.culturalNote:
Delicious — the taste that makes you close your eyes.

Elengi is good taste, sweetness, delight. "Bilei elengi" is delicious food; the same word names the pleasure of music, of company, of a good day.

examples.lingala: Elikya na ngai ezali na Nzambe.
examples.english: My hope is in God.
examples.french: Mon espoir est en Dieu.

words.culturalNote:
Hope — the light held up against the dark.

Elikya is hope, the trust that tomorrow can be better. Through hard seasons it is what a family keeps lit — "elikya na ngai ezali na Nzambe," my hope is in God.

examples.english: Hope gives strength.
examples.french: L'espoir donne de la force.

words.culturalNote:
Hope — what gives the tired the strength to go on.

Elikya is hope. It is no idle wish but a working faith: "elikya epesaka makasi," hope gives strength — the quiet fuel of a people who endure.

examples.english: The tree's shade is pleasant.
examples.french: L'ombre de l'arbre est agréable.

words.culturalNote:
Shade — the cool refuge under the tree.

Elili is a shadow or shade. In the heat of the day the elili of a mango tree is a gathering place; a shadow, too, is how the old tales speak of the soul's faint double.

examples.lingala: Elimo ya Nzambe ezali na biso.
examples.english: The Spirit of God is with us.
examples.french: L'Esprit de Dieu est avec nous.

words.culturalNote:
Spirit — the unseen breath within and beyond.

Elimo is spirit — the Holy Spirit in church, the spirit of a person, the spirits of older belief. It names what lives past the body and moves the heart.

examples.english: What is this thing?
examples.french: Qu'est-ce que c'est ?

words.culturalNote:
Thing — the catch-all word for whatever it is.

Eloko is a thing or object — and, with "te," nothing at all. "Eloko nini?", what thing? "Eloko te," nothing. The humble word that points at anything.

examples.english: I'm left with nothing.
examples.french: Il ne me reste rien.

words.culturalNote:
Nothing — the empty hand, the flat "none."

Eloko te is nothing, none, zero — literally "no thing." "Natikali na eloko te," I'm left with nothing; the plain words for an empty pocket or plate.

examples.english: We are watching the sunset.
examples.french: Nous regardons le coucher du soleil.

words.culturalNote:
Sunset — the sky's slow gold at the day's close.

Eloli is the sunset. Over the river the eloli sets the water alight; it is the hour the work eases and families drift toward the evening fire.

examples.english: Wash your face.
examples.french: Lave ton visage.

words.culturalNote:
Face — where a person's feeling shows first.

Elongi is the face. Joy, worry, welcome — the elongi tells it before the mouth does; to read a face is to read a heart.

examples.english: The sun sets in the west.
examples.french: Le soleil se couche à l'ouest.

words.culturalNote:
West — where the sun lies down.

Elozi is the west, the direction the sun sets. "Moi elalaka na elozi" — the sun sleeps in the west — the old, sure compass of the day.

examples.english: They pitched a tent to sleep.
examples.french: Ils ont monté une tente pour dormir.

words.culturalNote:
Tent — a roof carried to where there is none.

Ema is a tent. Pitched for a journey, a camp, or a gathering with no hall, the ema is shelter you can fold and carry — walls raised wherever you stop.

examples.english: This man is tall.
examples.french: Cet homme est grand.

words.culturalNote:
Tall — height that draws the eye upward.

Engambe describes someone tall and long-limbed. In a culture that admires a fine bearing, to be engambe is to stand out in a crowd.

examples.english: The train left for Matadi.
examples.french: Le train est parti pour Matadi.

words.culturalNote:
Train — iron carriages threading the country.

Engbunduka is a train. Along the historic line from Matadi to the capital, the engbunduka carried the goods and people that built a young nation's trade.

examples.english: The iron smooths clothes.
examples.french: Le fer lisse les vêtements.

words.culturalNote:
Iron — the hot weight that presses a crease away.

Engomeli is a clothes-iron, from kongoma, to press. A sharp crease matters here; the engomeli — often filled with hot charcoal — smooths a shirt for church or work.

examples.english: The eagle flies high.
examples.french: L'aigle vole haut.

words.culturalNote:
Eagle — the high, far-seeing hunter of the sky.

Engondo is an eagle. Riding the air above forest and river, the engondo is a figure of power and keen sight — a bird the proverbs lend their lessons to.

examples.english: Kinshasa is a big city.
examples.french: Kinshasa est une grande ville.

words.culturalNote:
City — the loud, teeming heart of the country.

Engumba is a city or town. Kinshasa, the great engumba on the river, pulls millions into its noise and chance — the place the village dreams of and warns about.

examples.english: The oil drum is large.
examples.french: Le fût d'huile est grand.

words.culturalNote:
Drum — the big metal vessel for fuel and palm oil.

Engwongolo is a large metal container — a drum, bidon, or jerrycan — for bulk liquids like mafuta (oil) or fuel. (A small grocery tin is a different word: tini.)

examples.english: Wear a hat in the sun.
examples.french: Porte un chapeau au soleil.

words.culturalNote:
Hat — shade and style worn on the head.

Enkoti is a hat or cap. Against the strong sun, or simply for a sharp Sunday look, the enkoti tops off the dress of the day.

examples.english: This house is dirty.
examples.french: Cette maison est sale.

words.culturalNote:
Dirty — grime that asks for soap and water.

Epotu means dirty, like its cousin bosoto. Hands, clothes, a floor — what is epotu is set right with washing, a daily discipline of a proud home.

examples.english: The people applauded.
examples.french: Les gens ont applaudi.

words.culturalNote:
Applause — many hands rising into one sound.

Esako is applause and acclamation. After a song or a speech, the esako breaks out — the crowd's warm, clapping yes.

examples.english: A hammer is a work tool.
examples.french: Un marteau est un outil de travail.

words.culturalNote:
Tool — what turns the hand's'intent into work.

Esaleli is a tool or instrument, from kosala, to work. A hoe, a hammer, a needle — each esaleli extends the hand and gets the job done.

examples.english: They took him to court.
examples.french: Ils l'ont amené au tribunal.

words.culturalNote:
Court — where a dispute is brought for judgement.

Esambelo is a court or tribunal. To be taken to the esambelo is serious; it is where a quarrel goes when the family and the elders cannot settle it.

examples.lingala: Esanga ezali na kati ya ebale.
examples.english: The island is in the river.
examples.french: L'île est dans le fleuve.

words.culturalNote:
Island — land the river wraps its arms around.

Esanga is an island. The great Congo is dotted with them — sandbars and green isles where fishermen camp and the current splits and rejoins.

examples.english: The car is out of petrol.
examples.french: La voiture n'a plus d'essence.

words.culturalNote:
Petrol — the fuel that moves the city's wheels.

Esanzi is gasoline. It runs the taxis, the generators, and the long-distance trucks; "esanzi esili" — out of petrol — can stop a whole day in its tracks.

examples.english: We eat yam with fish.
examples.french: Nous mangeons de l'igname avec du poisson.

words.culturalNote:
Yam — a starchy root that fills the plate.

Esapi is a yam. Boiled or pounded, it joins cassava and plantain among the steady roots that make a Congolese meal filling and complete.

examples.english: I have many friends.
examples.french: J'ai beaucoup d'amis.

words.culturalNote:
Friend — the one chosen and kept close.

Eseka is a friend (with di, moninga, ndeko). In a culture of wide kinship, a true eseka is held like family — shared with, trusted, counted on.

examples.english: Great joy!
examples.french: Quelle joie !

words.culturalNote: The bright, shared joy that fills a room at a celebration and spills into music.

examples.english: This story interests me.
examples.french: Cette histoire m'intéresse.

words.culturalNote:
Pleasing — what gladdens and holds the attention.

Esepelisi means interesting or pleasing, from kosepela, to be glad. A story, a song, a person that esepelisi you has won your delight.

examples.english: This place is beautiful.
examples.french: Cet endroit est beau.

words.culturalNote:
Place — the where of a thing or a meeting.

Esika is a place or spot. "Esika oyo," this place; "esika ya mosala," the workplace — the word that fixes where life happens.

examples.english: Go elsewhere.
examples.french: Va ailleurs.

words.culturalNote:
Elsewhere — anywhere but here.

Esika esusu means another place, elsewhere. "Kende esika esusu" — go elsewhere — points away from where you stand to some other spot.

examples.english: We live in the same place.
examples.french: Nous vivons au même endroit.

words.culturalNote:
Same place — side by side, under one roof.

Esika moko is "one place" — together, in the same spot. "Tofandi esika moko" is to live or sit together; closeness named as shared ground.

examples.english: Animals are in the savanna.
examples.french: Les animaux sont dans la savane.

words.culturalNote:
Savanna — open grassland under a wide sky.

Esobe is the open plain or savanna, the grassy country beyond the forest where herds graze and the horizon runs far.

examples.english: We crossed the bridge.
examples.french: Nous avons traversé le pont.

words.culturalNote:
Bridge — the span that carries the road over water.

Etalaka is a bridge. In a land cut by countless rivers, a bridge is precious — the link that lets a road, a market, a family reach the other side.

examples.english: Sit on the bench.
examples.french: Assieds-toi sur le banc.

words.culturalNote:
Bench — a shared seat for the courtyard and the wait.

Etanda is a bench. Long enough for several, it lines the veranda, the church, the clinic waiting room — a place to sit together and pass the time.

examples.english: Put the clothes in the closet.
examples.french: Mets les vêtements dans l'armoire.

words.culturalNote:
Closet — where the cloth is folded and kept.

Etandaka is a closet or cupboard. The good wrappers and Sunday clothes are stored there, folded with care and brought out for the days that matter.

examples.english: This board is made of wood.
examples.french: Cette planche est en bois.

words.culturalNote:
Board — a flat plank for building and making.

Etando is a board or plank. Sawn from a tree, it becomes a shelf, a door, a bench — the raw stuff the carpenter shapes into a home's furniture.

examples.english: This fruit is ripe.
examples.french: Ce fruit est mûr.

words.culturalNote:
Ripe — fruit ready for the hand and the mouth.

Eteli means ripe, from kotela, to ripen. A mango that eteli has softened and sweetened; the word marks the moment fruit is at its best.

examples.english: Give me a piece of bread.
examples.french: Donne-moi un morceau de pain.

words.culturalNote:
Piece — a portion broken off to share.

Eteni is a piece or part. To break bread into biteni is to share; in a culture of the shared plate, your eteni is your fair portion of the whole.

examples.english: The children went to school.
examples.french: Les enfants sont allés à l'école.

words.culturalNote:
School — where children are sent to grow a future.

Eteyelo is a school, from koteya, to teach. Families sacrifice much for the eteyelo; an education is the road a parent hopes will carry a child further than they went.

examples.lingala: Etima oyo ezali na mbisi mingi.
examples.english: This lake has many fish.
examples.french: Ce lac a beaucoup de poissons.

words.culturalNote:
Lake — still water holding fish and sky.

Etima is a lake. Among the great lakes of the east and the still waters inland, the etima feeds fishing families and mirrors the changing sky.

examples.english: This plant is beautiful.
examples.french: Cette plante est belle.

words.culturalNote:
Plant — green life rising from tended soil.

Etoele is a plant. Set in the garden and watered, the etoele grows toward food or flower — a small daily proof of care rewarded.

examples.lingala: Etuka oyo ezali na bato mingi.
examples.english: This region has many people.
examples.french: Cette région a beaucoup de gens.

words.culturalNote:
Region — a slice of the country with its own name.

Etuka is a province, department, or region. The vast Congo is divided into many bituka, each with its own peoples, tongues and pride.

examples.lingala: Tofandi na etuka enene ya Kinshasa.
examples.english: We live in a large district of Kinshasa.
examples.french: Nous vivons dans un grand quartier de Kinshasa.

words.culturalNote:
