District — a large quarter of a sprawling city.

Etuka enene — a "big area" — is a district or large neighbourhood. Kinshasa's bituka enene each teem like cities of their own, with their own markets and music.

examples.english: War is evil.
examples.french: La guerre est un mal.

words.culturalNote:
War — the sorrow a land knows too well.

Etumba is war or battle. A heavy word in a region that has lived through conflict; "etumba ezali mabe" — war is evil — carries hard memory and a longing for peace.

examples.english: Put the bread in the oven.
examples.french: Mets le pain au four.

words.culturalNote:
Oven — the heat that turns dough to bread.

Etumbeli is an oven, from kotumba, to bake. From it comes the morning mampa; the etumbeli is the warm heart of bakery and kitchen alike.

examples.english: The festival is a day of joy.
examples.french: La fête est un jour de joie.

words.culturalNote:
Feast day — the week's bright pause for joy and worship.

Eyenga is a holiday, festival, or Sunday — the day of rest, church and celebration. It gathers families in their best clothes for song, food and one another.

examples.english: In the evening, the sky darkens.
examples.french: Le soir, le ciel s'assombrit.

words.culturalNote:
To darken — when the light drains from the sky.

Eyindi means it darkened, from koyinda, to grow dark. As the sun sets the likolo eyindi — the sky darkens — and the lamps and the evening begin.

examples.english: I live in Kinshasa.
examples.french: Je vis à Kinshasa.

words.culturalNote:
To dwell — to sit, to settle, to make a home.

Kofanda is to sit, stay, or live somewhere. "Nafandi na Kinshasa" — I live in Kinshasa; the same word seats a guest and roots a household.

examples.english: The horse is a fast animal.
examples.french: Le cheval est un animal rapide.

words.culturalNote:
Horse — a swift, uncommon animal in the basin.

Farasa (from the French) is a horse. Rarer here than in the savanna lands, the farasa is a creature of speed and bearing, admired when it appears.

examples.english: February is a short month.
examples.french: Février est un mois court.

words.culturalNote:
February — the short month of the turning year.

Febuari (from the French fevrier) is February. The shortest month, it slips by quickly — borrowed into Lingala beside the older season-names of the year.

examples.english: February is the second month.
examples.french: Février est le deuxième mois.

words.culturalNote:
February — the same short month, an alternate spelling.

Febuary is another way to write February (febuari). The borrowed month-name varies in spelling as French words settle into Lingala writing.

examples.english: The child has a fever.
examples.french: L'enfant a de la fièvre.

words.culturalNote:
Fever — the heat that warns a body is fighting.

Fefele is a fever (also molunge). Where malaria is a constant, a child's fefele is watched closely — the first sign that sends a family to the clinic.

examples.english: This thing is made of iron.
examples.french: Cette chose est faite en fer.

words.culturalNote:
Iron — the hard metal of tool and roof.

Felo (from the French fer) is iron. Beaten into blades and hoes or laid as roofing sheets, the felo is the strong, rust-prone metal of everyday building.

examples.lingala: Fimbo ezali na maboko na ye.
examples.english: The whip is in his hand.
examples.french: Le fouet est dans sa main.

words.culturalNote:
Whip — a feared switch of old discipline.

Fimbo is a whip or cane. A heavy symbol of punishment — once of colonial cruelty, sometimes of strict discipline — the fimbo is a word that lands hard.

examples.english: Do not insult anyone.
examples.french: N'insulte personne.

words.culturalNote:
To insult — words flung to wound.

Kofinga is to insult or curse at someone. In a culture that prizes respectful speech, to finga is a real offence; "kofinga moto te" is plain good counsel.

examples.english: Light the match.
examples.french: Allume l'allumette.

words.culturalNote:
Match — a little stick of fire (also alimeti).

Fololo (or fofolo) is a matchstick, another word beside alimeti. One struck fololo lights the lamp, the stove, the charcoal — small fire on demand.

examples.english: It's my fault.
examples.french: C'est ma faute.

words.culturalNote:
Fault — the slip a person owns up to.

Foti (from the French faute) is a mistake or fault. "Ezali foti na ngai" — it's my fault — three honest words that mend more than they cost.

examples.english: Take my picture.
examples.french: Prends-moi en photo.

words.culturalNote:
Photo — a moment kept to be shared.

Foto is a photograph. At weddings, send-offs and reunions the foto is taken and treasured — proof of a face, a day, a family pulled briefly together.

examples.english: The car's brakes are bad.
examples.french: Les freins de la voiture sont mauvais.

words.culturalNote:
Brake — what stops the wheel in time.

Frein (from the French) is a brake. On Kinshasa's crowded roads a good frein is life and death; bad brakes are no small worry in a shared taxi.

examples.english: We ate fufu with cassava leaves.
examples.french: Nous avons mangé du fufu avec des feuilles de manioc.

words.culturalNote:
Fufu — the soft dough at the centre of the plate.

Fufu is the staple dough of pounded cassava or maize flour, eaten with the fingers and dipped in sauce or greens. "Toliaki fufu na pondu" — we ate fufu with cassava leaves — names a most ordinary, beloved meal.

examples.english: This flower is beautiful.
examples.french: Cette fleur est belle.

words.culturalNote:
Flower — a bright small gift of the garden.

Fulele (from the French fleur) is a flower, beside the older mbe. It brightens a yard, a grave, a welcome — beauty offered with little words.

examples.english: Close the door.
examples.french: Ferme la porte.

words.culturalNote:
To close — to shut against the night or the rain.

Kofunga is to close or shut — a door, a window, a shop. "Funga ekuke" — close the door — keeps in the warmth, the safety, the quiet.

examples.english: Open the window.
examples.french: Ouvre la fenêtre.

words.culturalNote:
To open — to let in light, air, or a guest.

Kofungola is to open or unlock. Fungola the window for air, the door for a visitor, the shop for the day — the welcoming opposite of funga.

examples.english: I paid my debt.
examples.french: J'ai payé ma dette.

words.culturalNote:
To pay — settling what is owed.

Kofuta is to pay — a price, a wage, a debt. To futa what you owe, promptly and in full, is a quiet mark of an honourable person.

examples.english: We rented a house.
examples.french: Nous avons loué une maison.

words.culturalNote:
To rent — paying for the use of another's thing.

Kofutela is to rent or hire — a house, a car, a hand for the day. In the city most live in a futela home, the rent due like clockwork.

examples.english: The river bridge is long.
examples.french: Le pont du fleuve est long.

words.culturalNote:
Bridge — a crossing over the water (also etalaka).

Gbagba is a bridge, a second word beside etalaka. From a felled log over a stream to a span across the great river, the gbagba joins what water divides.

examples.english: Put ice in the drinks.
examples.french: Mets de la glace dans les boissons.

words.culturalNote:
Ice — a cool rarity in the heat.

Glace (from the French) is ice. In the equatorial warmth a block of glace is prized — chilling the drinks at a fete, a small luxury of a hot afternoon.

examples.english: This child is lazy.
examples.french: Cet enfant est paresseux.

words.culturalNote:
Lazy — the one who lets the work wait.

Goigoi means lazy or sluggish. In a culture that honours mosala (work), to be called goigoi stings; the goigoi is gently teased and pushed to rise.

examples.english: Iron my shirt.
examples.french: Repasse ma chemise.

words.culturalNote:
To iron — pressing the day's creases away.

Kogoma is to iron clothes. A crisp, pressed shirt is a point of pride; to goma a garment before church or work is a small daily care for one's'appearance.

examples.english: The iron rusted in the rain.
examples.french: Le fer a rouillé sous la pluie.

words.culturalNote:
To rust — what damp does to forgotten iron.

Koguga is to rust. Left in the rains, the felo eguga — the iron rusts — and roofs and tools wear orange and brittle; a quiet enemy of the wet season.

examples.english: The sun is shining.
examples.french: Le soleil brille.

words.culturalNote:
To shine — light thrown off by sun or polished thing.

Kotana is to shine or glow. "Moi ezali kotana" — the sun is shining; the word lights the sky, the lamp, and a face well pleased.

examples.english: Yes, I will come.
examples.french: Oui, je viendrai.

words.culturalNote:
Yes — the small word of agreement and welcome.

Iyo is yes — assent, acceptance, the open door of a conversation. Said warmly, "iyo" is more than agreement; it is a readiness to go along, to help, to come.

examples.english: He wants to, but he can't.
examples.french: Il veut, mais il ne peut pas.

words.culturalNote:
But — the small hinge that turns a sentence.

Ka (also kasi) is "but." It sets one thing against another — "alingi, ka akoki te," he wants to, but he can't — the everyday word for the catch in the plan.

examples.english: Distribute food to the children.
examples.french: Distribue de la nourriture aux enfants.

words.culturalNote:
To share out — handing round so each one has.

Kokaba is to give out or distribute. To kaba food among the children is the daily arithmetic of a generous house — making sure no one is passed over.

examples.english: The carpenter made a table.
examples.french: Le menuisier a fait une table.

words.culturalNote:
Carpenter — the hands that shape wood into use.

Kabinda is a carpenter. From a plank and a few tools the kabinda makes the bed, the table, the door — a respected maker in every neighbourhood.

examples.english: I'm going to the toilet.
examples.french: Je vais aux toilettes.

words.culturalNote:
Toilet — the small private room of the household.

Kabine (from the French cabinet) is a toilet or latrine. Plain and necessary, the kabine is asked for politely — "nakei na kabine" — and pointed to without fuss.

examples.english: Divide the bread into two pieces.
examples.french: Divise le pain en deux morceaux.

words.culturalNote:
To divide — splitting a whole into shares.

Kokabola is to divide or share out. To kabola the bread, the land, the work fairly keeps the peace; division done well is generosity, done badly is quarrel.

examples.english: We bought cocoa at the market.
examples.french: Nous avons acheté du cacao au marché.

words.culturalNote:
Cocoa — a cash crop of the green hinterland.

Kakao (from the French cacao) is cocoa. Grown on small farms for export, the kakao bean is one of the land's quiet riches — sold at market, shipped to distant sweets.

examples.english: Bargain the price before buying.
examples.french: Marchande le prix avant d'acheter.

words.culturalNote:
To bargain — the friendly contest of the market.

Kokakola is to bargain or haggle. In the market no price is final; to kakola — to push and joke and settle — is half the business and half the fun of buying.

examples.english: That was long ago.
examples.french: C'était il y a longtemps.

words.culturalNote:
Long ago — the deep, settled past.

Kala means before or long ago, the old time. "Kala, bankoko bafandaki na mboka" — long ago, the grandparents lived in the village — opens the elder's stories.

examples.english: In the old days, there were no cars.
examples.french: Autrefois, il n'y avait pas de voitures.

words.culturalNote:
In the old days — when the world wore a different face.

Kalakala is "long, long ago," a doubled emphatic form of kala. It marks the deeper past, the days before today's roads and lights.

examples.english: The clerk is writing in the office.
examples.french: Le clerc écrit au bureau.

words.culturalNote:
Clerk — the patient hand of the office paper.

Kalaki is a clerk or office worker. From the colonial-era bureau to today's ministries, the kalaki keeps the registers, stamps the forms, and lets the day's business pass.

examples.english: Fry the plantains.
examples.french: Fais frire les bananes plantains.

words.culturalNote:
To fry — bright oil and a hot pan.

Kokalanga is to fry. From the sizzle of plantain slices going golden to fish browned for the evening meal, kalanga is the lively sound of a Congolese kitchen.

examples.english: Give me your card.
examples.french: Donne-moi ta carte.

words.culturalNote:
Card — a small printed proof you carry.

Kalati (from the French carte) is a card — an ID, a visiting card, a phone card. The kalati you keep in your wallet is sometimes the difference between a smooth day and a stuck one.

examples.english: Take this money.
examples.french: Prends cet argent.

words.culturalNote:
To take — the hand closing on what is offered.

Kokamata is to take, seize, or pick up. "Kamata" is the everyday word for accepting a thing into your hand — money offered, a child lifted, an opportunity grasped.

examples.english: The camel is a desert animal.
examples.french: Le chameau est un animal du désert.

words.culturalNote:
Camel — a beast of the far drylands.

Kamela (from the French chameau) is a camel. Foreign to the Congo's forests, it is a creature of the open desert and dry north — known from books, stories, and the world's'other corners.

examples.english: My camera is broken.
examples.french: Ma caméra est cassée.

words.culturalNote:
Camera — what catches the day to keep.

Kamera is a camera. At weddings and reunions the kamera comes out, and the moment is fixed — for the album, the wall, the family group chat.

examples.english: The lorry carried many goods.
examples.french: Le camion a transporté beaucoup de marchandises.

words.culturalNote:
Lorry — the heavy hauler of the road.

Kaminyo (from the French camion) is a lorry or truck. Loaded high with goods, fuel or produce, the kaminyo grinds along the long Congolese roads, carrying the country to its markets.

examples.english: Don't twist his arm.
examples.french: Ne lui tords pas le bras.

words.culturalNote:
To twist — turning what shouldn't be turned.

Kokamola is to twist or wrench, often a limb. "Kamola loboko" — to twist the arm — names both real harm and, by figure, forcing a person against their will.

examples.english: Close the door.
examples.french: Ferme la porte.

words.culturalNote:
To close — also to tie, fasten, hold.

Kokanga is to close or to bind. The same root closes a door, ties a knot, fastens a button, and can even mean to arrest — to "close" a person in custody.

examples.english: Open the door.
examples.french: Ouvre la porte.

words.culturalNote:
To open — undoing what was tied or shut.

Kokangola is the undoing of kokanga: to open, untie, release, or set free. To kangola the door, the knot, the prisoner — each is letting something be free again.

examples.english: Think well before speaking.
examples.french: Réfléchis bien avant de parler.

words.culturalNote:
To think — the quiet weighing before the word.

Kokanisa is to think, ponder, or remember. Elders teach the young to kanisa first and speak second; a thought given proper time is the start of wisdom.

examples.lingala: Nalingi koya, kasi nazali na mosala.
examples.english: I want to come, but I have work.
examples.french: Je veux venir, mais j'ai du travail.

words.culturalNote:
But — the small hinge that turns a sentence.

Kasi is the everyday "but" (also ka). It introduces the catch, the exception, the gentle disagreement — "kasi…" opens the room for the other side of the thing.

examples.english: Cut the bread into pieces.
examples.french: Coupe le pain en morceaux.

words.culturalNote:
To cut — dividing with the blade or the word.

Kokata is to cut — bread, cloth, a tree, or the talk that has gone on too long. The same word slices and decides.

examples.english: I drank coffee in the morning.
examples.french: J'ai bu du café le matin.

words.culturalNote:
Coffee — the dark cup that opens the day.

Kate (also kawa; pronounced "kafe") is coffee. Grown in the Congo's'eastern highlands, it goes out as export and stays at home as the steaming bowl of an early morning.

examples.english: Inside the house it is cool.
examples.french: À l'intérieur de la maison, il fait frais.

words.culturalNote:
Inside — the middle, the heart of a place.

Kati means inside, middle, or centre. "Kati ya ndako" is inside the house; "kati ya engumba" is the city centre. It is the word for the within of any space.

examples.english: Fill the bucket with water.
examples.french: Remplis le seau d'eau.

words.culturalNote:
Bucket — the everyday vessel of fetched water.

Katini is a bucket or pail. Where water is carried from a tap or a well, the katini is the household's faithful tool — filled, hauled, and emptied many times a day.

examples.english: Cross the road carefully.
examples.french: Traverse la route avec prudence.

words.culturalNote:
To cross — passing from one side to the other.

Kokatisa is to cross — the road, the river, a border. Heavy traffic and great waters give the word weight; to katisa is to safely reach the other side.

examples.english: Congolese coffee is good.
examples.french: Le café congolais est bon.

words.culturalNote:
Coffee — the second name for the morning cup.

Kawa is another word for coffee (also kate). Heard in homes and markets across the country, kawa carries the rich, slightly bitter flavour of the eastern hills into the everyday cup.

examples.english: Write in your notebook.
examples.french: Écris dans ton cahier.

words.culturalNote:
Notebook — bound paper for the schoolchild and the scribe.

Kaye (from the French cahier) is a notebook. The schoolchild's kaye holds lessons and dictations; the workshop's kaye keeps accounts — paper kept for memory.

examples.english: Wear a coat, it's cold.
examples.french: Porte un manteau, il fait froid.

words.culturalNote:
Coat — a wrap against an unexpected chill.

Kazaka (from the French casaque) is a coat or jacket. The equatorial day rarely calls for it, but the morning hill mist or the rare cool night sends the kazaka over the shoulders.

examples.english: Be careful on the road!
examples.french: Fais attention sur la route !

words.culturalNote:
Take care — the warning from a parent's lips.

Kokeba is to be careful or to watch out. "Keba!" alone is the quick warning shouted as a child runs into traffic; "keba na nzela" is the parting word at the door.

examples.english: The children are in class.
examples.french: Les enfants sont en classe.

words.culturalNote:
Class — the room and the rank both.

Kelasi (from the French classe) is a school class or grade. The morning kelasi gathers children in uniform; the year's progress is measured in kelasi after kelasi climbed.

examples.english: Go to the market.
examples.french: Va au marché.

words.culturalNote:
To go — setting one foot in front of the other.

Kokende is to go. The word starts most journeys: "kende" to the school, "kende" to the field, "kende" home before the dark falls.

examples.english: Guard the house at night.
examples.french: Garde la maison la nuit.

words.culturalNote:
To watch — keeping an eye through the long hours.

Kokengele is to watch, guard, or stand sentinel. The night guard, the older sibling minding the little one, the dog at the gate — each kengele their charge.

examples.lingala: Elamba ya keusa ezali ya ntalo.
examples.english: Silk cloth is expensive.
examples.french: Le tissu en soie est cher.

words.culturalNote:
Silk — a costly cloth for fine occasions.

Keusa is silk. A rarer fabric in everyday life, the elamba ya keusa appears at weddings and grand events — its softness and shine reserved for moments meant to be remembered.

examples.english: He ran away fast.
examples.french: Il s'est enfui vite.

words.culturalNote:
To flee — feet driven by fear or alarm.

Kokima is to flee or run away. From the playground chase to the heavier exodus a danger forces, the word names the urgent run that leaves a place behind.

examples.english: Sit on the chair.
examples.french: Assieds-toi sur la chaise.

words.culturalNote:
Chair — the seat offered to a guest.

Kiti is a chair or seat. The kiti pulled forward for a visitor is hospitality made wood — to be offered the kiti is to be welcomed in.

examples.english: You are beautiful.
examples.french: Tu es beau.

words.culturalNote: Kitoko — beautiful, lovely. Used freely and warmly in Congolese speech: about a person, a song, a meal, a sunset, or a child's drawing. To call someone "kitoko" in Lingala is not flirtation by default — it is recognition. Mothers say it to children, friends say it to friends, strangers say it across a market stall. In a culture where beauty is named out loud, kitoko is one of the most often-spoken adjectives.

examples.english: I will open. (Na + ko + fungola)
examples.french: Je vais ouvrir.

words.culturalNote:
Ko — the most important grammatical particle in Lingala.

1. INFINITIVE PREFIX: placed before any verb root it marks the infinitive ("to..."): kofungola = to open; kokanga = to close; koya = to come.
2. FUTURE TENSE MARKER: placed after the subject pronoun before the verb root it marks the future: Nakofungola = I will open; Tokokanga = We will close.
3. SLANG (Kinshasa street speech): shouted alone as an emphatic filler meaning "man!" or "look!" — e.g. Zoba ko! = "What a fool, man!"

examples.lingala: Koba efelo na langi ya pembe.
examples.english: Paint the wall white.
examples.french: Peins le mur en blanc.

words.culturalNote:
To paint — laying colour over the bare surface.

Koba is to paint. The walls of a fresh house, the door of a new shop — to koba in bright langi (colour) is to declare a place ready for living and trade.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Peindre — étendre la couleur sur la surface nue.

Koba, c'est peindre. Les murs d'une maison neuve, la porte d'une boutique fraîchement ouverte — koba dans une langi (couleur) vive, c'est déclarer un lieu prêt pour la vie et le commerce.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koba — kotia langi na esika oyo ezangi langi.

Koba elimboli kotia langi. Bifelo ya ndako ya sika, porte ya magazini ya sika — koba na langi ya kongenga ezali koloba ete esika oyo ekoki mpo na kovanda mpe mpo na mombongo.

examples.english: I want to add a little sugar.
examples.french: Je veux ajouter un peu de sucre.

words.culturalNote:
To add — putting more in for the right measure.

Kobakisa is the infinitive "to add." The cook bakisa a touch of salt; the trader bakisa interest; the speaker bakisa a final word — small additions that complete a thing.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Ajouter — en mettre davantage pour la juste mesure.

Kobakisa est l'infinitif « ajouter ». Le cuisinier bakisa une pincée de sel ; le commerçant bakisa des intérêts ; l'orateur bakisa un dernier mot — petits ajouts qui complètent une chose.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobakisa — kotia mosusu mpo ya komeka malamu.

Kobakisa elimboli kotia mosusu. Mosalisi-ya-bilei abakisa mungwa moke; motekisi abakisa mbongo ya kobaba; molobi abakisa liloba ya nsuka — mabakiseli mike oyo ekokisi eloko.

examples.english: He needs to repair the house.
examples.french: Il doit réparer la maison.

words.culturalNote:
To repair — patching what wear or weather broke.

Kobamba is to mend, patch, or repair. A torn net, a leaking roof, a worn sandal — to kobamba is the careful art of giving a thing more useful life.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Réparer — recoudre ce que l'usure ou le temps a brisé.

Kobamba, c'est rapiécer, réparer. Un filet déchiré, un toit qui fuit, une sandale usée — kobamba est l'art patient de redonner à une chose une vie utile.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobamba — kobongisa oyo emonisi to ntango ebebisi.

Kobamba elimboli kotonga lisusu, kobongisa. Monyama oyo epasuki, motondo oyo ekosopa mai, sandale oyo eumeli — kobamba ezali mosala ya bopembe oyo epesi eloko bomoyi ya sika.

examples.english: We are starting the work.
examples.french: Nous commençons le travail.

words.culturalNote:
To begin — the first move that sets a thing in motion.

Kobanda is the infinitive "to begin." A road, a song, a school year — "tozali kobanda" announces the start; the rest will follow step by step.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Commencer — le premier geste qui met une chose en marche.

Kobanda est l'infinitif « commencer ». Une route, un chant, une année scolaire — « tozali kobanda » annonce le début ; le reste suivra pas à pas.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobanda — ebandeli oyo etii eloko na nzela.

Kobanda elimboli kobanda. Nzela, loyembo, mbula ya kelasi — « tozali kobanda » ezali kosakola ebandeli; oyo etikali ekolanda litambe na litambe.

examples.english: To fear God is wisdom.
examples.french: Craindre Dieu est sagesse.

words.culturalNote:
To fear — the heart held tight by what may come.

Kobanga is to be afraid, to fear, to dread. The saying "kobanga Nzambe ezali bwanya" — to fear God is wisdom — turns fear into the start of right living.

examples.english: I'm going to call him.
examples.french: Je vais l'appeler.

words.culturalNote:
To call — bringing someone nearer by name.

Kobenga is the infinitive "to call" — by voice, by phone, or by message. "Nakei kobenga ye" — I'm going to call him — sets the small errand of reaching across a distance.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Appeler — rapprocher quelqu'un par son nom.

Kobenga est l'infinitif « appeler » — de la voix, par téléphone, par message. « Nakei kobenga ye » — je vais l'appeler — ouvre la petite démarche de franchir une distance.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobenga — kobenda moto na nkombo na ye.

Kobenga elimboli kobenga — na mongongo, na téléphone, to na nsango. « Nakei kobenga ye » — nakokende kobenga ye — ezali kofungola mosala mokemoke ya koleka mosika.

examples.english: They know how to beat the drum.
examples.french: Ils savent battre le tambour.

words.culturalNote:
To beat — also to strike a drum and a beat.

Kobeta is to hit or beat. Sadly it strikes a child; gladly it strikes a mbonda (drum), and the whole village finds the rhythm and begins to dance.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Frapper — et aussi frapper le tambour et le rythme.

Kobeta, c'est frapper, battre. Tristement, elle frappe un enfant ; joyeusement, elle frappe le mbonda (tambour), et tout le village trouve le rythme et se met à danser.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobeta — mpe kobeta mbonda na kobeta ya rythme.

Kobeta elimboli kobeta. Na mawa, ebetisi mwana; na esengo, ebetisi mbonda, mpe mboka mobimba ezali kozwa rythme mpe ebandi kobina.

examples.english: The wound is bleeding.
examples.french: La plaie saigne.

words.culturalNote:
To bleed — literally "blood coming out."

Kobima makila is to bleed — kobima (to come out) joined to makila (blood). A cut, a nosebleed, a wound — the words come honest and plain, naming what the eye already sees.

examples.english: Knock on the door before entering.
examples.french: Frappe à la porte avant d'entrer.

words.culturalNote:
To knock — the polite hand at the door.

Kobete is to knock — to strike the door for permission before entering. (Kobola means to bruise, squash, or crash; the standard word for knocking is kobete.) A small courtesy that sets the manners of a Congolese visit: announce, wait, then come in.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Frapper à la porte — la main polie qui demande à entrer.

Kobete, c'est frapper — heurter la porte pour demander la permission avant d'entrer. (Kobola signifie meurtrir, écraser, briser ; le mot juste pour frapper à la porte est kobete.) Petite courtoisie qui pose les manières d'une visite congolaise : annoncer, attendre, puis entrer.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobete — loboko ya boboto na porte.

Kobete elimboli kobete porte mpo ya kosenga nzela liboso ya kokota. (Kobola elimboli kobeba, kopanza, to kobuka; liloba ya solo mpo ya kobete porte ezali kobete.) Ezali bonkonde moke oyo etiamaki na bizaleli ya botomboli ya mokongolais: kosakola, kozela, sima kokota.

examples.english: To kill a person is a sin.
examples.french: Tuer quelqu'un est un péché.

words.culturalNote:
To kill — the heaviest verb the language owns.

Koboma is the infinitive "to kill." The hunter's catch and the gravest commandment share this root; "koboma moto ezali lisumu" — to kill a person is a sin — carries the weight of every faith spoken here.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Tuer — le verbe le plus lourd que la langue possède.

Koboma est l'infinitif « tuer ». La prise du chasseur et le commandement le plus grave partagent cette racine ; « koboma moto ezali lisumu » — tuer une personne est un péché — porte le poids de chaque foi qui s'exprime ici.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koboma — liloba ya kilo koleka oyo monoko na biso ezali na yango.

Koboma elimboli kosukisa bomoyi. Mobomi ya nyama na zamba mpe mobeko ya monene ya kondima babombami na motó moko; « koboma moto ezali lisumu » — koboma moto ezali mabe — ememi kilo ya kondima nyonso oyo elobami awa.

examples.english: The mother knows how to comfort the child.
examples.french: La mère sait consoler l'enfant.

words.culturalNote:
To comfort — soothing what is troubled.

Kobondisa (the causative of kobondo, to beg or supplicate) is to calm or console someone. The mother who kobondisa a crying child is the picture: a low voice, gentle hands, fear turned softly down.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Consoler — apaiser ce qui est troublé.

Kobondisa (causatif de kobondo, supplier) signifie calmer, consoler quelqu'un. La mère qui kobondisa un enfant en larmes en est l'image : voix basse, mains douces, peur posée doucement au sol.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobondisa — kokitisa oyo emitungi.

Kobondisa (euti na kobondo, kosenga na boboto) elimboli kokitisa moto, kobondisa. Mama oyo abondisaka mwana oyo azali kolela ezali ndakisa: mongongo ya nse, maboko ya boboto, bobangi oyo bakitisi malembe.

examples.english: This job will suit him.
examples.french: Ce travail lui conviendra.

words.culturalNote:
To suit — when the thing and the person fit.

Kobonga is the infinitive "to be suitable" — and also "must." The garment that ebongi suits the wearer; the plan that ebongi is the proper one to follow.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Convenir — quand la chose et la personne s'accordent.

Kobonga est l'infinitif « être convenable » — et aussi « devoir ». Le vêtement qui ebongi convient à celui qui le porte ; le plan qui ebongi est le bon à suivre.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobonga — ntango eloko na moto bayokani.

Kobonga elimboli kobonga — mpe lisusu « esengeli ». Elamba oyo ebongi ekoki na moto oyo alati yango; mwango oyo ebongi nde malamu mpo na kolanda.

examples.english: I need to tidy the house.
examples.french: Je dois ranger la maison.

words.culturalNote:
To set in order — preparing the place for what's coming.

Kobongisa is the infinitive "to arrange, tidy, fix, or prepare." Before guests, before a meal, before a journey — one kobongisa what is loose so the moment finds the house ready.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Mettre en ordre — préparer le lieu pour ce qui vient.

Kobongisa est l'infinitif « arranger, ranger, réparer, préparer ». Avant les invités, avant un repas, avant un voyage — on kobongisa ce qui traîne, pour que le moment trouve la maison prête.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobongisa — kotia molongo mpo na oyo ezali koya.

Kobongisa elimboli kobongisa, kotia esika malamu, kobongisa, to kolengele. Liboso ya bapaya, liboso ya kolia, liboso ya mobembo — moto akobongisaka biloko mpo ntango ekuta ndako esili kolengele.

examples.english: I want to change money.
examples.french: Je veux changer de l'argent.

words.culturalNote:
To change — turning one form into another.

Kobongola is the infinitive "to change" or translate. Clothes, money, a mind, a language — to kobongola is to turn one thing into a different one, fit for the next use.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Changer — transformer une forme en une autre.

Kobongola est l'infinitif « changer » ou « traduire ». Des vêtements, de l'argent, un esprit, une langue — kobongola, c'est faire passer une chose d'un état à un autre, pour le prochain usage.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobongola — kobongola ndenge moko na ndenge mosusu.

Kobongola elimboli kobongola to koloba na monoko mosusu. Bilamba, mbongo, makanisi, monoko — kobongola ezali kosala ete eloko ekoma ndenge mosusu, ekoki na bosaleli ya sika.

examples.english: I can't forget it.
examples.french: Je ne peux pas l'oublier.

words.culturalNote:
To forget — the slip the mind makes against the heart.

Kobosana is the infinitive "to forget." Some things one cannot kobosana — a parent's voice, a name spoken in love, a hardship endured together. The heart keeps what the mind would lose.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Oublier — le faux pas que l'esprit fait contre le cœur.

Kobosana est l'infinitif « oublier ». Il y a des choses qu'on ne peut pas kobosana — la voix d'un parent, un nom prononcé avec amour, une épreuve traversée ensemble. Le cœur garde ce que l'esprit laisserait perdre.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobosana — likambo oyo mutú esali na boyokani te na motema.

Kobosana elimboli kobosana. Ezali na makambo mosusu oyo moto akoki kobosana te — mongongo ya tata to mama, nkombo elobamaki na bolingo, mpasi oyo bakutanaki na yango elongo. Motema ebombi oyo mutú akoki kobwaka.

examples.english: The soldier confiscated his things.
examples.french: Le soldat a confisqué ses affaires.

words.culturalNote:
To confiscate — taking by authority or force.

Kobotola is to seize, snatch, or confiscate. The soldier or official who kobotola goods leaves a sting — and the word lives in everyday speech for any heavy-handed taking.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Confisquer — prendre par autorité ou par force.

Kobotola, c'est saisir, arracher, confisquer. Le soldat ou l'officiel qui kobotola laisse une morsure — et le mot vit dans la langue quotidienne pour toute saisie brutale.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobotola — kozwa na bokonzi to na makasi.

Kobotola elimboli kosimba na makasi, kobotola. Soda to motambwisi oyo abotolaka biloko atiki mpasi — mpe liloba ezali bomoyi na maloba ya mokolo na mokolo mpo na kobotola nyonso ya makasi.

examples.english: This medicine will heal you.
examples.french: Ce médicament te guérira.

words.culturalNote:
To heal — bringing the body back to itself.

Kobikisa (rooted in bomoi, life) is to heal, cure, or save. The clinic and the church share this verb; "nkisi oyo ekobikisa yo" — this medicine will heal you — is the steady reassurance of care. (Kobowa is an older, less standard form.)
words.culturalNoteFr:
Guérir — ramener le corps à lui-même.

Kobikisa (de bomoi, la vie) signifie guérir, soigner, sauver. La clinique et l'église partagent ce verbe ; « nkisi oyo ekobikisa yo » — ce médicament te guérira — est la promesse régulière du soin. (Kobowa est une forme plus ancienne, moins standard.)
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobikisa — kozongisa nzoto na esika na yango.

Kobikisa (oyo euti na bomoyi) elimboli kobikisa, kosalisa, mpe kobikisa moto. Lopitalo na ndako ya Nzambe basangani na liloba moko; « nkisi oyo ekobikisa yo » — nkisi oyo ekobikisa yo — ezali maloba ya kondima oyo ekitisi motema. (Kobowa ezali ndenge ya kala mpe oyo basaleli mingi te.)

examples.english: Breaking the rules is bad.
examples.french: Enfreindre les règles, c'est mal.

words.culturalNote:
To break — the verb of the slipped hand and the broken word.

Kobuka is the infinitive "to break or snap" — a pot, a stick, a promise. To kobuka mibeko — break the rules — is the social fracture; both kinds of breaking the same word names.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Briser — le verbe de la main qui glisse et de la parole rompue.

Kobuka est l'infinitif « casser ou rompre » — un pot, un bâton, une promesse. Kobuka mibeko — enfreindre les règles — est la rupture sociale ; le même mot dit les deux ruptures.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobuka — kobuka eloko, mpe kobuka liloba.

Kobuka elimboli kobuka — nzungu, nzete, elaka. Kobuka mibeko ezali kobuka boyokani ya bato; liloba moko elobi ndenge mibale ya kobuka.

examples.english: Climbing the mountain is hard.
examples.french: Gravir la montagne est difficile.

words.culturalNote:
To climb — the rising effort of foot and hand.

Kobuta is the infinitive "to climb or ascend." A tree, a hill, a long road, a life — to kobuta is to gain height by labour, and to know the breath the climb costs.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Monter — l'effort qui s'élève des pieds et des mains.

Kobuta est l'infinitif « grimper, monter ». Un arbre, une colline, une longue route, une vie — kobuta, c'est gagner de la hauteur par le labeur, et connaître le souffle que la montée coûte.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobuta — bopikiliki ya makolo na maboko oyo ezali komata.

Kobuta elimboli komata likolo. Nzete, ngomba, nzela molai, bomoyi — kobuta ezali kozwa likolo na mosala, mpe koyeba mopepe oyo komata epesi.

examples.english: I'm inviting friends to the party.
examples.french: J'invite des amis à la fête.

words.culturalNote:
To invite — opening the door to a guest.

Kobyanga is the infinitive "to invite." To byanga friends to a fete is to set the table wider; in Congolese hospitality, an invitation is warmly given and gladly answered.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Inviter — ouvrir la porte à l'invité.

Kobyanga est l'infinitif « inviter ». Byanga des amis à une fête, c'est élargir la table ; dans l'hospitalité congolaise, l'invitation se donne chaleureusement et se reçoit avec joie.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobyanga — kofungolela mopaya porte.

Kobyanga elimboli kobyanga. Kobyanga baninga na feti ezali kotanda mesa monene; na boyambi ya bato ya Congo, libyangi epesami na motema ya molunge mpe eyambami na esengo.

examples.english: I don't know how to borrow money.
examples.french: Je ne sais pas emprunter de l'argent.

words.culturalNote:
To borrow — a small trust between neighbours.

Kodefa is the infinitive "to borrow" (kodefisa is the related "to lend"). To defa salt, money or a tool — and to return it well — is the small currency of trust that holds a community together.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Emprunter — une petite confiance entre voisins.

Kodefa est l'infinitif « emprunter » (kodefisa étant « prêter »). Defa du sel, de l'argent ou un outil — et le rendre comme il faut — est la petite monnaie de confiance qui tient une communauté ensemble.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kodefa — kondima ya mokemoke kati na bazalani.

Kodefa elimboli kodefa (kodefisa elimboli kodefisa). Kodefa mungwa, mbongo, to esaleli — mpe kozongisa yango malamu — ezali mbongo ya mokemoke ya kondima oyo esimbi mboka esika moko.

examples.english: Insulting a friend is wrong.
examples.french: Insulter un ami, c'est mal.

words.culturalNote:
To insult — words flung to wound.

Kofinga is the infinitive "to insult or curse at someone." A culture that prizes respectful speech treats kofinga as a real offence — "kofinga moninga ezali mabe" is plain wisdom.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Insulter — des mots lancés pour blesser.

Kofinga est l'infinitif « insulter, injurier quelqu'un ». Une culture qui valorise la parole respectueuse traite le kofinga comme une vraie offense — « kofinga moninga ezali mabe » est une sagesse claire.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kofinga — maloba ya kobwakela mpo na kozokisa.

Kofinga elimboli kofinga to kotuka moto. Kati na kondima oyo ezali na lokumu ya maloba ya boboto, kofinga ezali libebi ya solo — « kofinga moninga ezali mabe » ezali bwanya ya polele.

examples.english: We want to rent a house.
examples.french: Nous voulons louer une maison.

words.culturalNote:
To rent — paying for the use of a thing.

Kofutela is the infinitive "to rent or hire" — a house, a car, a hand for the day. In the city most live in a futela home, the rent due like clockwork.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Louer — payer pour l'usage d'une chose.

Kofutela est l'infinitif « louer, prendre en location » — une maison, une voiture, une main pour la journée. En ville, la plupart vivent dans un foyer futela, le loyer tombant comme une horloge.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kofutela — kofuta mpo na kosalela eloko.

Kofutela elimboli kofutela — ndako, motuka, loboko ya mokolo. Na vile bato mingi bavandi na ndako ya futela, lofuti efutamaka lokola montre.

examples.english: Clothes dry in the sun.
examples.french: Les vêtements sèchent au soleil.

words.culturalNote:
To dry — the work of sun and wind.

Koka is to dry. Clothes on a line, fish split for the smokehouse, maize spread to harden — all wait for the heat to koka them through.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Sécher — l'œuvre du soleil et du vent.

Koka, c'est sécher. Les vêtements sur le fil, le poisson fendu pour le fumoir, le maïs étendu pour durcir — tous attendent que la chaleur les koka jusqu'au bout.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koka — mosala ya moi na mopepe.

Koka elimboli kokauka. Bilamba na nzela ya bilamba, mbisi efungwami mpo na ndako ya milinga, masangu epanzami mpo ekoma makasi — nyonso ezeli ete moi ekokauka yango.

examples.english: They know how to haggle at the market.
examples.french: Ils savent marchander au marché.

words.culturalNote:
To bargain — the friendly contest of the market.

Kokakola is the infinitive "to bargain or haggle." In the market no price is final; the dance of kakola — pushing, joking, settling — is half the business and half the fun.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Marchander — le combat amical du marché.

Kokakola est l'infinitif « marchander, négocier le prix ». Au marché, aucun prix n'est final ; la danse du kakola — pousser, plaisanter, conclure — est moitié l'affaire et moitié le plaisir.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokakola — etumba ya boboto ya zando.

Kokakola elimboli kokakola to kobongisa motuya. Na zando motuya moko te ezali ya nsuka; mabina ya kakola — kotinda, kosakana, koyokana — ezali kati-kati ya mombongo mpe kati-kati ya esengo.

examples.english: The fisherman can catch fish.
examples.french: Le pêcheur sait attraper du poisson.

words.culturalNote:
To catch — closing the hand on what moves.

Kokanga is to seize, catch, or close hold of. A fish in the net, a child mid-flight, a thief at the door — to kokanga is to hold what was free.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Attraper — refermer la main sur ce qui bouge.

Kokanga, c'est saisir, attraper, fermer la main sur. Un poisson dans le filet, un enfant en fuite, un voleur à la porte — kokanga, c'est tenir ce qui était libre.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokanga — kokanga loboko likolo ya oyo ezali kotambola.

Kokanga elimboli kosimba, kokanga. Mbisi na monyama, mwana na mbangu, moyibi na porte — kokanga ezali kosimba oyo ezalaki na bonsomi.

examples.english: He needs to cut the tree.
examples.french: Il doit couper l'arbre.

words.culturalNote:
To cut — dividing with the blade or the word.

Kokata is the infinitive "to cut." Bread, cloth, a tree, or the talk gone too long — the same word slices and decides.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Couper — partager avec la lame ou la parole.

Kokata est l'infinitif « couper ». Le pain, le tissu, un arbre, ou la conversation qui s'éternise — le même mot tranche et décide.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokata — kokabola na mbeli to na liloba.

Kokata elimboli kokata. Mampa, elamba, nzete, to lisolo oyo eumeli mingi — liloba moko ekati mpe ekata.

examples.english: Father decided the matter.
examples.french: Papa a tranché l'affaire.

words.culturalNote:
To decide — cutting the matter clean.

Kokata likambo — literally "to cut the matter" — is to give a verdict, settle a dispute. The elder who kati likambo brings a quarrel to its quiet end.

examples.english: We want to go to the market.
examples.french: Nous voulons aller au marché.

words.culturalNote:
To go — setting out from where you stand.

Kokende is the infinitive "to go." It starts the day's journey — to the school, the field, the city — and seals the parting at the door.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Aller — partir de là où l'on se tient.

Kokende est l'infinitif « aller ». Il ouvre le voyage du jour — à l'école, au champ, en ville — et scelle l'au-revoir à la porte.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokende — kobima na esika oyo otelemi.

Kokende elimboli kokende. Ebandisaka mobembo ya mokolo — na kelasi, na bilanga, na vile — mpe ekangaka liloba ya « kende malamu » na porte.

examples.english: This money suffices.
examples.french: Cet argent suffit.

words.culturalNote:
To suffice — when there is just enough.

Kokoka is to be able, to fit, or to suffice — not "to dry up" (kokauka). "Mbongo oyo ekoki" — this money suffices — is the host's relief and the worker's measure.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Suffire — quand il y a juste assez.

Kokoka, c'est pouvoir, convenir, ou suffire — pas « tarir » (kokauka). « Mbongo oyo ekoki » — cet argent suffit — est le soulagement de l'hôte et la mesure du travailleur.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokoka — ntango oyo ezali kaka oyo esengeli.

Kokoka elimboli kokoka, kobonga, to kotonda — kasi te « kokauka ». « Mbongo oyo ekoki » — mbongo oyo ekoki — ezali kopema ya moyambi mpe komeka ya mosali.

examples.english: Deceiving a friend is wrong.
examples.french: Tromper un ami, c'est mal.

words.culturalNote:
To deceive — bending the truth to a hidden end.

Kokosa is to fool, trick, or deceive. In a culture that prizes the straight word, kokosa is a wound to the bond; honesty heals what trickery breaks.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Tromper — courber la vérité vers un but caché.

Kokosa, c'est berner, duper, tromper. Dans une culture qui valorise la parole droite, kokosa est une blessure au lien ; l'honnêteté guérit ce que la tromperie brise.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokosa — kogumba bosolo mpo na mwango oyo ebombami.

Kokosa elimboli kokosa, kosakana na moto. Kati na kondima oyo ezali na lokumu ya liloba ya semba, kokosa ezali kozokisa boyokani; bosembo ebikisi oyo lokuta ebebisi.

examples.english: Enter the house.
examples.french: Entre dans la maison.

words.culturalNote:
To enter — crossing the threshold of a place.

Kokota is to enter, go in. To kokota a house is to be received; the welcome at the door turns a guest into a member of the room.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Entrer — franchir le seuil d'un lieu.

Kokota, c'est entrer, pénétrer. Kokota une maison, c'est être reçu ; l'accueil à la porte transforme un invité en membre de la pièce.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokota — koleka libungutu ya esika.

Kokota elimboli kokota, kokoma na kati. Kokota ndako ezali koyambama; boyambi na porte ebongoli mopaya na moto ya ndako.

examples.english: Coconut is a tasty fruit.
examples.french: La noix de coco est un fruit savoureux.

words.culturalNote:
Coconut — sweet milk inside a hard shell.

Kokoti is a coconut. Cracked open, it gives milk for cooking and meat for the chewing; on the coast and in the markets, it is a familiar small treasure.

examples.english: Smallpox is a severe disease.
examples.french: La variole est une maladie grave.

words.culturalNote:
Smallpox — the old, marked disease.

Kokoto is smallpox, a sickness elders remember with dread. Vaccination has tamed it; the word remains in the language as a memory of harder days.

examples.english: People die sooner or later.
examples.french: Les gens meurent tôt ou tard.

words.culturalNote:
To die — the journey every road meets.

Kokufa is the infinitive "to die." Spoken with respect, the word is not avoided; "bato bakokufa kala to nsima" frames every life within its limit.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Mourir — le voyage que toute route rencontre.

Kokufa est l'infinitif « mourir ». Prononcé avec respect, le mot ne s'évite pas ; « bato bakokufa kala to nsima » encadre toute vie dans sa limite.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokufa — mobembo oyo nzela nyonso ekutani na yango.

Kokufa elimboli kokufa. Elobamaki na lokumu, liloba liwendaka te; « bato bakokufa kala to nsima » epesi bomoyi nyonso ndelo na yango.

examples.english: They went to bury the body.
examples.french: Ils sont allés enterrer le corps.

words.culturalNote:
To bury — laying the body in the earth.

Kokunda is to bury. Death gathers the whole family; to kokunda an ebembe is a slow, sung ritual — the closing of one life and the gathering of those it touched.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Enterrer — poser le corps dans la terre.

Kokunda, c'est enterrer. La mort rassemble toute la famille ; kokunda un ebembe est un rituel lent, chanté — la fermeture d'une vie et le rassemblement de ceux qu'elle a touchés.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokunda — kotia nzoto na mabele.

Kokunda elimboli kokunda. Liwa esangisi libota mobimba; kokunda ebembe ezali eyenga ya malembe, ya boyembi — kokanga bomoyi moko mpe kosangisa bato oyo bayebanaki na yango.

examples.english: I went to find my father.
examples.french: Je suis allé trouver mon père.

words.culturalNote:
To find — coming upon what was sought.

Kokuta is to find or come upon. The child who was missing, the answer that was hiding, the friend at the corner — to kokuta is the small relief of arrival.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Trouver — tomber sur ce qu'on cherchait.

Kokuta, c'est trouver, rencontrer. L'enfant qu'on avait perdu, la réponse qui se cachait, l'ami au coin — kokuta est le petit soulagement de l'arrivée.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokuta — kokuta oyo ozalaki koluka.

Kokuta elimboli kokuta to kokutana na eloko. Mwana oyo abungaki, eyano oyo ebombamaki, moninga na nzela — kokuta ezali kopema ya mokemoke ya kokomi.

examples.english: Father is advising the child.
examples.french: Papa conseille l'enfant.

words.culturalNote:
To advise — guiding from older steps.

Kolaka is to counsel or advise. Elders kolaka the young with patience; the laka they give is meant to walk ahead and light the way.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Conseiller — guider depuis des pas plus anciens.

Kolaka, c'est conseiller. Les anciens kolaka les jeunes avec patience ; le laka qu'ils donnent doit marcher devant et éclairer la voie.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolaka — kotambwisa uta na matambe ya bampaka.

Kolaka elimboli kopesa toli. Bampaka bakolaka bilenge na motema molai; laka oyo bapesi ezali mpo na kotambola liboso mpe kongengisa nzela.

examples.english: Follow him, he knows the way.
examples.french: Suis-le, il connaît le chemin.

words.culturalNote:
To follow — keeping the leader's track.

Kolanda is to follow or accompany. To kolanda a guide is to trust their feet; the word also follows an idea, a rule, a road.

examples.english: The child is crying.
examples.french: L'enfant pleure.

words.culturalNote:
To cry — the heart's'outward water.

Kolela is to cry, weep, lament. From a child's bumped knee to a family's mourning, the word names every honest tear.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Pleurer — l'eau extérieure du cœur.

Kolela, c'est pleurer, sangloter, se lamenter. Du genou cogné de l'enfant au deuil d'une famille, le mot nomme toute larme honnête.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolela — mai ya motema oyo ebimi libanda.

Kolela elimboli kolela, kolela na mawa. Banda libolongo oyo mwana abeti kino matanga ya libota, liloba etangaka mpisoli nyonso ya solo.

examples.english: We want to eat food.
examples.french: Nous voulons manger.

words.culturalNote:
To eat — the most ordinary verb of hospitality.

Kolia is to eat. Around the shared plate the family gathers; to be invited to kolia is to be invited to belong.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Manger — le verbe le plus ordinaire de l'hospitalité.

Kolia, c'est manger. Autour du plat partagé la famille se rassemble ; être invité à kolia, c'est être invité à appartenir.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolia — liloba ya boyambi ya mikolo nyonso.

Kolia elimboli kolia. Zingazinga ya sani oyo bakaboli, libota esangani; kobengisama na kolia ezali kobengisama mpo na kozala moto ya esika.

examples.english: Children should love each other.
examples.french: Les enfants doivent s'aimer.

words.culturalNote:
To love one another — reciprocal kolinga.

Kolingana, the reciprocal of kolinga, is to love each other. Family, friends, neighbours — those who kolingana hold the simplest, sturdiest bond.
words.culturalNoteFr:
S'aimer mutuellement — réciproque de kolinga.

Kolingana, réciproque de kolinga, c'est s'aimer les uns les autres. Famille, amis, voisins — ceux qui kolingana tiennent le plus simple et le plus solide des liens.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolingana — kolingana moko na mosusu (réciproque ya kolinga).

Kolingana, ndenge ya réciproque ya kolinga, elimboli kolingana. Libota, baninga, bazalani — bato oyo balingani basimbi boyokani ya pete koleka mpe ya makasi koleka.

examples.english: I can allow him to go.
examples.french: Je peux le laisser partir.

words.culturalNote:
To give way — granting passage to another.

Kopesa nzela — literally "to give a path" — is the standard Lingala for "to allow." Kolingisa is rarer and more literal; the everyday phrase opens the way.

examples.english: We went to collect fruits.
examples.french: Nous sommes allés cueillir des fruits.

words.culturalNote:
To collect — gathering up what the ground gave.

Kolokota is to pick up or collect — fallen mangoes, scattered grain, money owed. The careful collector misses nothing the day has left lying.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Ramasser — recueillir ce que le sol a donné.

Kolokota, c'est ramasser ou recueillir — les mangues tombées, le grain éparpillé, l'argent dû. Le ramasseur attentif ne laisse rien de ce que la journée a laissé traîner.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolokota — kosangisa oyo mabele epesi.

Kolokota elimboli kolokota to kosangisa — mangoo oyo ekweyi, mbuma oyo epalanganaki, mbongo ya nyongo. Mosangisi ya bopembe atikaka eloko moko te oyo mokolo etiki na nse.

examples.english: Father went to shave his beard.
examples.french: Papa est allé se raser la barbe.

words.culturalNote:
To shave — the morning blade at the chin.

Kokolola is to shave hair or a beard. Before church or work, the careful man takes the blade to mandefu (beard) and steps out tidy.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Raser — la lame du matin au menton.

Kokolola, c'est raser les cheveux ou la barbe. Avant l'église ou le travail, l'homme soigneux porte la lame au mandefu (barbe) et sort net.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolola — mbeli ya tongo na mbanga.

Kokolola elimboli kokata nsuki to mandefu. Liboso ya kokende na ndako ya Nzambe to na mosala, mobali ya bopembe abendaka mbeli na mandefu mpe abimi peto.

examples.english: Remove it from the table.
examples.french: Enlève-le de la table.

words.culturalNote:
To remove — taking the thing out of the way.

Kolongola is to take away, remove, or extract. To kolongola a splinter, a name from a list, a stain from cloth — the gentle, decisive verb of clearing.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Retirer — ôter la chose du chemin.

Kolongola, c'est enlever, retirer, extraire. Kolongola une écharde, un nom d'une liste, une tache sur un tissu — verbe doux et décisif du nettoyage.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolongola — kolongola eloko na nzela.

Kolongola elimboli kolongola. Kolongola monzete, nkombo na lisi, salite na elamba — liloba ya boboto mpe ya bokati ya kopetola.

examples.english: Good health is good.
examples.french: La bonne santé, c'est précieux.

words.culturalNote:
Health — the body in good standing.

Kolongono is health or wellness. Proverbs place health above wealth; "kolongono ya nzoto ezali malamu" is the plain truth the elders teach.
words.culturalNoteFr:
La santé — le corps en bonne posture.

Kolongono, c'est la santé ou le bien-être. Les proverbes placent la santé au-dessus de la richesse ; « kolongono ya nzoto ezali malamu » est la vérité simple qu'enseignent les anciens.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolongono — nzoto oyo ezali malamu.

Kolongono elimboli kolongono ya nzoto. Masese etiaka kolongono likolo ya bomengo; « kolongono ya nzoto ezali malamu » ezali bosolo ya polele oyo bampaka bateyaka.

examples.english: Write your name.
examples.french: Écris ton nom.

words.culturalNote:
To write — turning thought into ink.

Koma is to write. The schoolchild's first koma name, the trader's koma figures, the friend's koma letter — paper kept for memory.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Écrire — transformer la pensée en encre.

Koma, c'est écrire. Le premier koma nkombo de l'écolier, les koma chiffres du commerçant, le koma mokanda de l'ami — papier gardé pour la mémoire.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koma — kobongola makanisi na encre.

Koma elimboli kokoma. Koma nkombo ya liboso ya mwana ya kelasi, koma motango ya motekisi, koma mokanda ya moninga — papier ebombami mpo na kondima.

examples.english: Climb up.
examples.french: Monte.

words.culturalNote:
To climb — the rising step.

Komata is to climb or go up. A tree, a hill, a higher rank — to komata is to gain height, and to feel the effort the climb costs.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Monter — le pas qui s'élève.

Komata, c'est grimper, monter. Un arbre, une colline, un rang plus haut — komata, c'est gagner de la hauteur, et sentir l'effort que la montée coûte.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Komata — litambe oyo ezali komata.

Komata elimboli komata. Nzete, ngomba, esika ya likolo — komata ezali kozwa likolo, mpe koyoka mosala oyo komata epesi.

examples.english: Sweep the yard.
examples.french: Balaye la cour.

words.culturalNote:
To sweep — the morning broom against the dust.

Kokomba is to sweep. Before the day begins the kokomba shapes the courtyard — the dust pushed out, the home set ready for what comes. (The headword "kombo" alone usually means "name"; the verb is kokomba.)
words.culturalNoteFr:
Balayer — le balai du matin contre la poussière.

Kokomba, c'est balayer. Avant que le jour commence, le kokomba façonne la cour — la poussière chassée, la maison prête pour ce qui vient. (Le mot seul « kombo » veut généralement dire « nom » ; le verbe est kokomba.)
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokomba — kombo ya tongo likolo ya putulu.

Kokomba elimboli kokombo. Liboso mokolo ebanda, kokomba esalaki lopango — putulu ebenganami, ndako etelemi mpo na oyo ezali koya. (Liloba « kombo » yango moko elimboli mingi « nkombo »; liloba ya kosala ezali kokomba.)

examples.lingala: Tata azali na kompani ya monene.
examples.english: Father has a big company.
examples.french: Papa a une grande entreprise.

words.culturalNote:
Company — an enterprise of business.

Kompani (from the French compagnie) is a company. From the small family firm to the big mining house, the kompani is where wages come from.

examples.english: I agree with your idea.
examples.french: Je suis d'accord avec ton idée.

words.culturalNote:
To accept — saying yes to the offered idea.

Kondima is to agree, accept, or believe. "Nandimi" — I agree — settles a plan; the same verb names the act of faith, of accepting a thing as so.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Accepter — dire oui à l'idée proposée.

Kondima, c'est consentir, accepter, croire. « Nandimi » — j'accepte — scelle un plan ; le même verbe nomme l'acte de foi, l'acceptation d'une chose comme vraie.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kondima — koloba iyo na likanisi oyo bapesi.

Kondima elimboli kondima, koyamba, kondimila. « Nandimi » — nandimi — esimbi mwango; liloba moko etangaka likambo ya kondima, koyamba eloko ndenge ezali.

examples.english: Congo is my country.
examples.french: Le Congo est mon pays.

words.culturalNote:
Congo — the river that names the nation.

Kongo is the country and the great river both. Vast, river-laced, music-rich — "Kongo ezali mboka na ngai" — Congo is my country — carries a particular pride.

examples.english: Mother forbids the children from going out.
examples.french: Maman interdit aux enfants de sortir.

words.culturalNote:
To forbid — closing a door to a behaviour.

Kopekisa is to forbid or prohibit. Parents kopekisa what is dangerous; the law kopekisa what would tear the social cloth — both keep the room safe.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Interdire — fermer une porte à un comportement.

Kopekisa, c'est interdire ou prohiber. Les parents kopekisa ce qui est dangereux ; la loi kopekisa ce qui déchirerait le tissu social — tous deux gardent la pièce en sécurité.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kopekisa — kokanga porte na ezaleli.

Kopekisa elimboli kopekisa. Baboti bapekisa oyo ezali likama; mibeko epekisaka oyo ekoki kobuka elamba ya bato — banso babateli ndako na bobateli.

examples.english: Give money to the children.
examples.french: Donne de l'argent aux enfants.

words.culturalNote:
To give — the open hand of the culture.

Kopesa is to give. The gift, the wage, the favour, the word of thanks — Congolese life turns on small giving. The base verb already carries "to give to"; the extended kopesela is largely redundant.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Donner — la main ouverte de la culture.

Kopesa, c'est donner. Le cadeau, le salaire, la faveur, le mot de merci — la vie congolaise tourne autour des petits dons. Le verbe de base porte déjà « donner à » ; le kopesela étendu est largement redondant.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kopesa — loboko ya kofungwama na kaba.

Kopesa elimboli kopesa. Likabo, lifuta, ngolu, liloba ya botondi — bomoyi ya bato ya Congo ebalukaka na bopesi ya mokemoke. Liloba oyo esili koloba « kopesa epai ya »; kopesela ya kobakisama ezali na ntina te mingi.

examples.english: The child is jumping.
examples.french: L'enfant saute.

words.culturalNote:
To jump — feet launched from the ground.

Kopumbwa is to leap, jump, or fly. The dancer at the fete, the child over a puddle, the bird at sudden lift — all are kopumbwa in their moment.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Sauter — les pieds lancés du sol.

Kopumbwa, c'est bondir, sauter, voler. Le danseur à la fête, l'enfant par-dessus la flaque, l'oiseau à l'envol soudain — tous sont en kopumbwa à leur instant.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kopumbwa — makolo ebimaki na nse.

Kopumbwa elimboli kopumbwa, kopumbwa likolo, kopumbwa lokola ndeke. Mobini na feti, mwana likolo ya mai, ndeke oyo epumbwi mbangu — banso bazali kopumbwa na ntango na bango.

examples.english: Water is in the cup.
examples.french: L'eau est dans la tasse.

words.culturalNote:
Cup — vessel for water, milk, and welcome.

Kopo is a cup or bowl. The first kopo of water set before a guest, the morning kopo of kawa — small vessels of daily kindness.

examples.english: Choose the good path.
examples.french: Choisis le bon chemin.

words.culturalNote:
To choose — weighing what to take.

Kopona is to choose, select, or elect. To kopona well is a small art — to look at many and rest the hand on the right one.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Choisir — peser ce qu'il faut prendre.

Kopona, c'est choisir, sélectionner, élire. Bien kopona est un petit art — regarder beaucoup et poser la main sur le bon.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kopona — komeka oyo esengeli kozwa.

Kopona elimboli kopona, kopona. Kopona malamu ezali mayele ya moke — kotala mingi mpe kosimba loboko likolo ya oyo ya solo.

examples.english: The mother will kiss the child.
examples.french: La mère embrassera l'enfant.

words.culturalNote:
To kiss — the cheek's quick greeting.

Kopesa bize — literally "to give a kiss" (from the French bise) — is the modern, standard way to say to kiss. Kopwepwa is older and regional; in current speech kopesa bize carries the moment.

examples.english: Wipe your hand.
examples.french: Essuie ta main.

words.culturalNote:
To wipe — the cloth that clears the surface.

Kopangusa is to wipe, rub, or polish. Hands after a meal, a table after spilling, a shoe before going out — the small motion that puts things right. (Kosa alone usually means to fry or to deceive.)
words.culturalNoteFr:
Essuyer — le tissu qui nettoie la surface.

Kopangusa, c'est essuyer, frotter, polir. Les mains après le repas, la table après une éclaboussure, la chaussure avant de sortir — le petit geste qui remet en ordre. (Kosa seul veut souvent dire frire ou tromper.)
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kopangusa — elamba oyo epetolaka esika.

Kopangusa elimboli kopangusa, kopangusa, kokomisa peto. Maboko na nsima ya kolia, mesa na nsima ya kosopa, sapato liboso ya kobima — mosala ya mokemoke oyo ezongisi makambo na esika.

examples.english: They will declare victory.
examples.french: Ils proclameront la victoire.

words.culturalNote:
To declare — speaking a thing publicly true.

Kosakola is to announce, declare, or proclaim. Independence is sakoli; victory is sakoli; the priest sakoli the blessing — public words that change the room.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Déclarer — dire publiquement qu'une chose est vraie.

Kosakola, c'est annoncer, déclarer, proclamer. L'indépendance est sakoli ; la victoire est sakoli ; le prêtre sakoli la bénédiction — paroles publiques qui changent la pièce.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosakola — koloba na miso ya bato ete eloko ezali solo.

Kosakola elimboli kosakola, kobimisa polele. Lipanda esakoli; elonga esakoli; nganga-Nzambe asakoli mapamboli — maloba ya polele oyo ebongoli ndako.

examples.english: We want to do the work.
examples.french: Nous voulons faire le travail.

words.culturalNote:
To do — and to work, the verb of effort.

Kosala is to do, make, or work. The day is shaped around mosala; to kosala well is honoured, and the diligent are those the village trusts.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Faire — et travailler, le verbe de l'effort.

Kosala, c'est faire, fabriquer, travailler. La journée se construit autour du mosala ; bien kosala est honoré, et les diligents sont ceux à qui le village fait confiance.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosala — kosala, mpe mosala, liloba ya mosala.

Kosala elimboli kosala, kobongisa, mpe komosala. Mokolo etongami zingazinga ya mosala; kosala malamu epesami lokumu, mpe bato ya etingya bazali bato oyo mboka eyebani na bango.

examples.english: We want to help the parents.
examples.french: Nous voulons aider les parents.

words.culturalNote:
To help — the hand offered for another's load.

Kosalisa is to help. From the small kosalisa with a basket to the deeper help in trouble, the word names the practical love that keeps the community knit.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Aider — la main offerte pour la charge d'autrui.

Kosalisa, c'est aider. Du petit kosalisa avec un panier à l'aide plus profonde dans la difficulté, le mot nomme l'amour pratique qui tient la communauté tricotée.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosalisa — loboko oyo epesami mpo na mokumba ya moto mosusu.

Kosalisa elimboli kosalisa. Banda kosalisa mokemoke na kitunga kino lisalisi ya mozindo na mpasi, liloba etangaka bolingo ya mosala oyo esimbi lisanga.

examples.english: The children are laughing.
examples.french: Les enfants rient.

words.culturalNote:
To laugh — joy released into the air.

Koseke is to laugh. Congolese gatherings are loud with seke; a good joke earns a roar, and the laughter is the proof that the company is well.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Rire — la joie libérée dans l'air.

Koseke, c'est rire. Les rassemblements congolais sont bruyants de seke ; une bonne blague gagne un rugissement, et le rire est la preuve que la compagnie est bonne.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koseke — esengo oyo ebimi na mopepe.

Koseke elimboli koseke. Mayangani ya bato ya Congo ezalaka na seke makasi; lisapo ya malamu ezwaka koganga, mpe koseke ezali elembo ete lisanga ezali malamu.

examples.english: They came to rejoice together.
examples.french: Ils sont venus se réjouir ensemble.

words.culturalNote:
To rejoice — gladness welling up.

Kosepela is to be glad or to enjoy. A song, a meeting, a meal — what you kosepela leaves a mark; the verb names every small lit moment.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Se réjouir — la joie qui monte.

Kosepela, c'est être heureux ou se réjouir. Un chant, une rencontre, un repas — ce que tu kosepela laisse une marque ; le verbe nomme chaque petit moment illuminé.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosepela — esengo oyo ezali komata.

Kosepela elimboli kozala na esengo to kosepela. Loyembo, bokutani, kolia — oyo osepeli etiki elembo; liloba etangaka ntango nyonso ya mokemoke ya kongenga.

examples.english: We will finish the work tomorrow.
examples.french: Nous finirons le travail demain.

words.culturalNote:
To finish — bringing the task to its end.

Kosilisa is to finish or complete. Mosala kosilisa lobi — the work to finish tomorrow — paces the next day's plans.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Terminer — mener la tâche jusqu'à sa fin.

Kosilisa, c'est terminer ou compléter. Mosala kosilisa lobi — le travail à finir demain — cadence les plans du lendemain.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosilisa — kokomisa mosala kino na suka.

Kosilisa elimboli kosilisa to kosukisa. Mosala kosilisa lobi — mosala mpo ya kosilisa lobi — etalisaka mibongisi ya mokolo oyo elandi.

examples.english: Hold my hand.
examples.french: Tiens-moi la main.

words.culturalNote:
To hold — the hand closed around what matters.

Kosimba is to hold or grasp. A child's'hand at a crossing, a wedding ring placed on a finger, a promise kept — to kosimba is to keep something close.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Tenir — la main refermée sur ce qui compte.

Kosimba, c'est tenir ou saisir. La main d'un enfant à la traversée, l'anneau de mariage glissé au doigt, une promesse tenue — kosimba, c'est garder quelque chose près de soi.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosimba — loboko ekangamaki na oyo ezali na ntina.

Kosimba elimboli kosimba. Loboko ya mwana na ntango ya koleka nzela, lopete ya libala etiami na mosapi, elaka esimbamaki — kosimba ezali kobomba eloko penepene.

examples.english: The child is washing.
examples.french: L'enfant se lave.

words.culturalNote:
To wash — water and soap against the day's dust.

Kosukola is to wash or bathe. The morning kosukola, the laundry on the line, the hands before the meal — the daily discipline of clean. (Kosola itself usually means to peel or clear brush.)
words.culturalNoteFr:
Laver — eau et savon contre la poussière du jour.

Kosukola, c'est laver ou se baigner. Le kosukola du matin, le linge sur le fil, les mains avant le repas — la discipline quotidienne du propre. (Kosola tout seul veut généralement dire éplucher ou défricher.)
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosukola — mai na sabolo likolo ya putulu ya mokolo.

Kosukola elimboli kosukola to kosukola nzoto. Kosukola ya tongo, bilamba na nzela ya bilamba, maboko liboso ya kolia — molongo ya mokolo na mokolo ya bopembe. (Kosola yango moko elimboli mingi koputola to kolongola matiti.)

examples.english: I'm going to buy bread.
examples.french: Je vais acheter du pain.

words.culturalNote:
To buy — the daily errand of the market.

Kosomba is the everyday market verb that runs through every Congolese household budget: kosomba mampa (buy bread), kosomba bilei (buy food), kosomba elamba (buy cloth). It pairs with koteka (to sell) in the rhythm of zando life. A mother sending a child on a market errand says "kende kosomba" — go buy — and the small mission begins.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Acheter — la course quotidienne au marché.

Kosomba est le verbe quotidien du marché qui traverse tout budget de ménage congolais : kosomba mampa (acheter du pain), kosomba bilei (acheter à manger), kosomba elamba (acheter du tissu). Il va de pair avec koteka (vendre) dans le rythme de la vie du zando. Une mère envoyant un enfant en course au marché dit « kende kosomba » — va acheter — et la petite mission commence.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosomba — mosala ya mokolo na mokolo ya zando.

Kosomba ezali liloba ya zando oyo eleki na budget ya libota nyonso ya bato ya Congo: kosomba mampa, kosomba bilei, kosomba elamba. Esangani na koteka na rythme ya bomoyi ya zando. Mama oyo atindi mwana na zando alobaka « kende kosomba » — mpe mosala ya mokemoke ebandi.

examples.english: We want to exchange things.
examples.french: Nous voulons échanger des affaires.

words.culturalNote:
To exchange — one thing given for another.

Kosombitinya is to swap or exchange. At the market, between neighbours, in trade — to kosombitinya is the friendly equality of even hands.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Échanger — une chose donnée pour une autre.

Kosombitinya, c'est troquer ou échanger. Au marché, entre voisins, dans le commerce — kosombitinya est l'égalité amicale des mains égales.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosombitinya — kopesa eloko mpe kozwa mosusu.

Kosombitinya elimboli kobongola eloko moko na mosusu. Na zando, kati ya bazalani, na mombongo — kosombitinya ezali bokokani ya boboto ya maboko bokokani.

examples.english: He has a cough.
examples.french: Il a une toux.

words.culturalNote:
Cough — the rough sound of irritated breath.

Kosukosu is a cough. In the dry season and the cool nights it goes round the compound; "azali na kosukosu" summons the herbs, the syrup, or the clinic.

examples.english: Enter the house.
examples.french: Entre dans la maison.

words.culturalNote:
To enter — the bare stem of kokota.

Kota is the stem of kokota, to enter. "Kota na ndako" — enter the house — is the welcome at the door, the verb that opens what was closed.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Entrer — la racine nue de kokota.

Kota est la racine de kokota, entrer. « Kota na ndako » — entre dans la maison — est l'accueil à la porte, le verbe qui ouvre ce qui était fermé.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kota — motó ya kokota.

Kota ezali motó ya kokota. « Kota na ndako » — kota na ndako — ezali boyambi na porte, liloba oyo efungoli oyo ekangami.

examples.english: Look after the child well.
examples.french: Prends bien soin de l'enfant.

words.culturalNote:
To look — eyes set on the thing that needs them.

Kotala is to look at, watch, or look after. The watchman, the doctor, the mother all kotala their charge — eyes that protect by paying attention.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Regarder — les yeux posés sur ce qui en a besoin.

Kotala, c'est regarder, observer, veiller. Le gardien, le médecin, la mère, tous kotala leur charge — des yeux qui protègent en faisant attention.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotala — miso etia likolo ya oyo esengeli na yango.

Kotala elimboli kotala, kobatela. Mokengeli, monganga, mama nyonso bakotala oyo babateli — miso oyo ebateli na kotya likebi.

examples.english: The children learned to read.
examples.french: Les enfants ont appris à lire.

words.culturalNote:
To read — eyes moving down the page.

Kotanga is to read and to count. Children learn to kotanga in school; merchants kotanga their figures; the same word covers letters and numbers both.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Lire — les yeux qui descendent la page.

Kotanga, c'est lire et compter. Les enfants apprennent à kotanga à l'école ; les commerçants kotanga leurs chiffres ; le même mot couvre lettres et nombres.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotanga — miso ezali kokita lokasa.

Kotanga elimboli kotanga mpe kotanga motango. Bana bayekolaka kotanga na kelasi; bamotekisi batangaka motango na bango; liloba moko ezipi makomi mpe motango.

examples.lingala: Elamba ya koto ezali ya petepete.
examples.english: Cotton cloth is soft.
examples.french: Le tissu en coton est doux.

words.culturalNote:
Cotton — the soft, breathable cloth.

Koto is cotton. Light to wear in the heat, easy to wash, it is the everyday fabric — the elamba ya koto carries through the day with comfort.

examples.english: He will fill the bottle.
examples.french: Il remplira la bouteille.

words.culturalNote:
To fill — turning empty into full.

Kotondisa is to fill — a katini with mai, a kopo with kawa, a sentence with sense. The verb finishes what emptiness only starts.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Remplir — passer du vide au plein.

Kotondisa, c'est remplir — une katini de mai, une kopo de kawa, une phrase de sens. Le verbe achève ce que le vide ne fait que commencer.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotondisa — kobongola kopanzana mpe kotondisa.

Kotondisa elimboli kotondisa — katini ya mai, kopo ya kawa, fraza ya ndimbola. Liloba esilisi oyo bopanzani ebandi kaka.

examples.english: They are building a house.
examples.french: Ils construisent une maison.

words.culturalNote:
To build — the slow rising of walls.

Kotonga is to build. From a single ndako to a whole engumba, kotonga is patient work — the mason, the carpenter, the family pooling for blocks.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Construire — la montée lente des murs.

Kotonga, c'est bâtir. D'une seule ndako à toute une engumba, kotonga est un travail patient — le maçon, le menuisier, la famille mettant ensemble pour les briques.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotonga — komata ya malembe ya bifelo.

Kotonga elimboli kotonga. Banda na ndako moko kino na engumba mobimba, kotonga ezali mosala ya bopembe — motongi, motongi ya banzete, libota oyo esangisi mbongo mpo na biteni.

examples.english: The doctor will give an injection.
examples.french: Le médecin va faire une piqûre.

words.culturalNote:
To inject — the needle's small bright pain.

Kotuba tonga — literally "to push a needle" — is to give an injection. At the clinic, the monganga's kotuba tonga is the door to many cures.

examples.english: The fire is burning.
examples.french: Le feu brûle.

words.culturalNote:
To burn — fire taking what it can hold.

Kotumba is to burn. The makala in the stove, the dry brush at the field's'edge, the bread left too long — moto kotumba whatever it reaches.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Brûler — le feu prenant ce qu'il peut tenir.

Kotumba, c'est brûler. Le makala dans le foyer, la brousse sèche au bord du champ, le pain laissé trop longtemps — moto kotumba ce qu'il atteint.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotumba — moto ezali kozwa oyo ekoki kosimba.

Kotumba elimboli kotumba. Makala na fulo, matiti ya kokauka na monoko ya elanga, mampa oyo etikalaki ntango molai — moto ekotumba oyo ekomi.

examples.english: He won't be long.
examples.french: Il ne sera pas long.

words.culturalNote:
To delay — making the wait longer.

Koumela is to delay or take a long time. "Akoumela mingi te" — he won't be long — is the small reassurance whispered at the door.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Tarder — rallonger l'attente.

Koumela, c'est tarder ou prendre du temps. « Akoumela mingi te » — il ne sera pas long — est la petite assurance murmurée à la porte.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koumela — kosala ete bozeli ezala molai.

Koumela elimboli koumela to kozwa ntango molai. « Akoumela mingi te » — akoumela mingi te — ezali kondimisa ya mokemoke oyo eyebisamaka na porte.

examples.english: I come from Kinshasa.
examples.french: Je viens de Kinshasa.

words.culturalNote:
To come from — naming the place left behind.

Kouta is to come from. "Nauti na Kinshasa" fixes a person in a story — where you kouta tells the listener something about who you are.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Venir de — nommer le lieu laissé derrière.

Kouta, c'est venir de. « Nauti na Kinshasa » fixe une personne dans une histoire — d'où tu kouta dit à l'auditeur quelque chose sur qui tu es.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kouta — kobimisa esika oyo otiki nsima.

Kouta elimboli kouta. « Nauti na Kinshasa » etii moto na lisapo — esika oyo outi eyebisi moyoki eloko mpo na nani ozali.

examples.english: Come here.
examples.french: Viens ici.

words.culturalNote:
To come — drawing near to the speaker.

Koya is to come. "Koya awa" — come here — pulls a person across the distance; the word is the warm invitation of arrival.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Venir — s'approcher de celui qui parle.

Koya, c'est venir. « Koya awa » — viens ici — tire une personne par-delà la distance ; le mot est l'invitation chaleureuse de l'arrivée.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koya — kobeleme na moto oyo azali koloba.

Koya elimboli koya. « Koya awa » — koya awa — ebenda moto na mosika; liloba ezali libyangi ya molunge ya boyei.

examples.english: We want to know the truth.
examples.french: Nous voulons connaître la vérité.

words.culturalNote:
To know — possessing a fact or a face.

Koyeba is to know. To koyeba someone is to recognise them; to koyeba a thing is to have it lit inside you — a word of both information and acquaintance.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Savoir — posséder un fait ou un visage.

Koyeba, c'est savoir. Koyeba quelqu'un, c'est le reconnaître ; koyeba une chose, c'est l'avoir éclairée en soi — un mot d'information et de connaissance ensemble.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyeba — kozala na likambo to elongi.

Koyeba elimboli koyeba. Koyeba moto ezali koyeba ye; koyeba eloko ezali kozala na yango ekongenga kati na yo — liloba ya boyebi mpe ya kondima.

examples.english: He will inform us tomorrow.
examples.french: Il nous informera demain.

words.culturalNote:
To inform — passing the news along.

Koyebisa is to inform or tell. From a quiet whisper to a public announcement, koyebisa carries what one person knows into the room of many.
