words.culturalNoteFr:
Informer — faire passer la nouvelle.

Koyebisa, c'est informer ou dire. Du chuchotement tranquille à l'annonce publique, koyebisa porte ce qu'une personne sait dans la pièce des autres.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyebisa — koleka nsango.

Koyebisa elimboli koyebisa to koyebisa. Banda kotanga ya nse kino kosakola ya polele, koyebisa ememi oyo moto moko ayebi na ndako ya bato mingi.

examples.english: I am learning Lingala.
examples.french: J'apprends le lingala.

words.culturalNote:
To learn — making the new thing one's'own.

Koyekola is to learn or study. The student koyekola in class; the apprentice koyekola at the bench; the elder, too, says "nazali koyekola" when the day teaches them something.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Apprendre — faire sienne la chose nouvelle.

Koyekola, c'est apprendre ou étudier. L'élève koyekola en classe ; l'apprenti koyekola à l'établi ; l'ancien aussi dit « nazali koyekola » quand le jour lui apprend quelque chose.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyekola — kokomisa ya yo eloko ya sika.

Koyekola elimboli koyekola to kotanga. Moyekoli akoyekola na kelasi; moyekoli ya mosala akoyekola na esika ya mosala; mopaka mpe alobaka « nazali koyekola » ntango mokolo eteyi ye eloko moko.

examples.english: Bring him something.
examples.french: Apporte-lui quelque chose.

words.culturalNote:
To bring to — carrying the thing to its asker.

Koyela specifically means "to bring to someone" (komema or koya na are the more general "to carry/bring"). The small errand that turns up at every visit and every meal.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Apporter à — porter la chose à celui qui l'a demandée.

Koyela signifie spécifiquement « apporter à quelqu'un » (komema ou koya na sont les « porter / amener » plus généraux). La petite course qui surgit à chaque visite et à chaque repas.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyela — komema eloko epai ya moto oyo asengi yango.

Koyela elimboli mingi « komema epai ya moto » (komema to koya na ezali « komema » ya bonene). Mosala ya mokemoke oyo ebimaka na bokutani nyonso mpe na kolia nyonso.

examples.english: Do not hate anyone.
examples.french: Ne hais personne.

words.culturalNote:
To hate — the verb the language warns against.

Koyina is to hate or strongly dislike. "Koyina moto te" — do not hate anyone — comes early and often from elders; the language places hate where it belongs, at the edge.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Haïr — le verbe contre lequel la langue met en garde.

Koyina, c'est haïr ou détester fortement. « Koyina moto te » — ne hais personne — vient tôt et souvent des anciens ; la langue place la haine là où elle doit être, à la marge.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyina — liloba oyo monoko ekebisi.

Koyina elimboli koyina to kotioka makasi. « Koyina moto te » — koyina moto te — eyaka noki mpe mbala mingi epai ya bampaka; monoko etii boyini esika oyo ebongi, na monoko.

examples.english: I heard his words.
examples.french: J'ai entendu ses paroles.

words.culturalNote:
To hear — and to feel, the same verb.

Koyoka covers hearing and feeling both. To koyoka a word and to koyoka a chill share the same root — the language treats perception as one act of receiving.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Entendre — et sentir, le même verbe.

Koyoka couvre à la fois l'ouïe et la sensation. Koyoka un mot et koyoka un frisson partagent la même racine — la langue traite la perception comme un seul acte de réception.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyoka — koyoka mpe koyoka, liloba moko.

Koyoka ezipi koyoka mpe koyoka na nzoto. Koyoka liloba mpe koyoka malili basangani na motó moko — monoko ezwi boyoki lokola mosala moko ya boyambi.

examples.english: To be wise is good.
examples.french: Être sage, c'est bon.

words.culturalNote:
To be — the verb beneath every state.

Kozala is the infinitive "to be." It seats every other word — "kozala na bwanya," to be wise; "kozala na esengo," to be glad — the simple, deep verb of presence.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Être — le verbe sous tout état.

Kozala est l'infinitif « être ». Il pose chaque autre mot — « kozala na bwanya », être sage ; « kozala na esengo », être joyeux — le verbe simple et profond de la présence.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kozala — liloba oyo ezali na nse ya nyonso.

Kozala elimboli kozala. Etyaka liloba mosusu nyonso na esika — « kozala na bwanya », kozala na bwanya; « kozala na esengo », kozala na esengo — liloba ya pete mpe ya mozindo ya kozala.

examples.lingala: Kozala na mbongo te ezali pasi.
examples.english: To have no money is hard.
examples.french: Ne pas avoir d'argent, c'est dur.

words.culturalNote:
To have — Lingala says it with "be with."

Kozala na — literally "to be with" — is how Lingala says to have. "Kozala na mbongo te" — to have no money — is the everyday economy made into grammar.

examples.english: The child got hurt in the yard.
examples.french: L'enfant s'est blessé dans la cour.

words.culturalNote:
To get hurt — the body taking the day's mishap.

Kozoka is to be wounded or hurt. The child who azoki in the yard, the worker on a sharp tool — to kozoka is the small or large damage life can deal.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Se blesser — le corps prenant l'accident du jour.

Kozoka, c'est être blessé. L'enfant qui azoki dans la cour, l'ouvrier sur un outil tranchant — kozoka est le dommage, petit ou grand, que la vie peut infliger.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kozoka — nzoto ezwi mpasi ya mokolo.

Kozoka elimboli kozoka to kozwa mpasi. Mwana oyo azoki na lopango, mosali na esaleli ya makasi — kozoka ezali libebi, ya mokemoke to ya monene, oyo bomoyi ekoki kopesa.

examples.english: I will get the victory.
examples.french: Je remporterai la victoire.

words.culturalNote:
To get — receiving what comes to the hand.

Kozwa is to get, take, or receive. A wage, a gift, a reward, an opportunity — "nakozwa" announces the moment a thing crosses over to you.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Obtenir — recevoir ce qui vient à la main.

Kozwa, c'est obtenir, prendre, recevoir. Un salaire, un cadeau, une récompense, une opportunité — « nakozwa » annonce le moment où une chose passe à toi.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kozwa — koyamba oyo eyei na loboko.

Kozwa elimboli kozwa, kozwa, koyamba. Lifuta, likabo, mbano, libaku — « nakozwa » esakolaka ntango oyo eloko eyei epai na yo.

examples.english: Christ is the Saviour.
examples.french: Le Christ est le Sauveur.

words.culturalNote:
Christ — the central figure of Congolese faith.

Kristo is Christ. In a deeply Christian country, the name shapes Sundays, songs, and the small daily prayers that bracket the day.

examples.english: Father's death brought sorrow.
examples.french: La mort du père a apporté du chagrin.

words.culturalNote:
Death — the word the language names plainly.

Kufa is death and dying. "Kufa ya tata epesi mawa" carries the same word for the event and its grief.

examples.english: Mother is in the kitchen.
examples.french: Maman est à la cuisine.

words.culturalNote:
Kitchen — the smoke-warmed room of meals.

Kuku is the kitchen. Of charcoal stove and shared pot, the kuku is where the family eats with its hands and the evening rests in the smell of the cooking.

examples.english: Carry this bag.
examples.french: Porte ce sac.

words.culturalNote:
To carry — the standard verb for bearing a load.

Komema is the gold-standard "to carry" across Lingala dialects (kumba is understood in some zones). A saki, a child, a message — what is komema is borne forward by the willing back, head, or hand.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Porter — le verbe standard pour porter une charge.

Komema est le « porter » étalon-or à travers les dialectes du lingala (kumba est compris dans certaines zones). Un saki, un enfant, un message — ce qui est komema est porté vers l'avant par le dos, la tête ou la main consentante.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Komema — liloba ya solo mpo na komema mokumba.

Komema ezali ebongiseli oyo eyebani na bisika nyonso na monoko ya Lingala (kumba eyebani na bisika mosusu). Saki, mwana, nsango — oyo ezali komema ememami liboso na mokongo, motó, to loboko ya kondima.

examples.english: There is my house.
examples.french: Là-bas se trouve ma maison.

words.culturalNote:
There — the place far enough to be pointed at.

Kuna is "there," a place at distance. "Kuna ezali ndako na ngai" sends the listener's'eye across the courtyard or the town.

examples.lingala: Kundola maloba ya tata na yo.
examples.english: Remember your father's words.
examples.french: Souviens-toi des paroles de ton père.

words.culturalNote:
To remember — drawing the past back into mind.

Kokundola is to remember or to remind. "Kundola maloba ya tata na yo" is the elder's quiet command to the young to carry the family forward.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Se souvenir — ramener le passé dans l'esprit.

Kokundola, c'est se rappeler ou rappeler à autrui. « Kundola maloba ya tata na yo » est le commandement tranquille de l'ancien au jeune pour porter la famille vers l'avant.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokundola — kobenda kala kati na makanisi.

Kokundola elimboli kokanisa kala to koyebisa moto akanisa. « Kundola maloba ya tata na yo » ezali mokano ya mopaya oyo apesi elenge mpo na kotambwisa libota liboso.

examples.english: This road is short.
examples.french: Ce chemin est court.

words.culturalNote:
Short — what does not take long.

Mokuse is short — a road, a story, a season. The stem -kuse takes the agreement of its noun: nzela mokuse, mbula mokuse, mokolo mokuse.

examples.english: Look for a good way.
examples.french: Cherche un bon chemin.

words.culturalNote:
To look for — the patient search.

Koluka is to seek, search, or look for (kuta means to physically encounter a thing already there). Children koluka a lost ball; elders koluka the right word for hard advice.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Chercher — la recherche patiente.

Koluka, c'est chercher (kuta veut dire rencontrer physiquement une chose déjà là). Les enfants koluka un ballon perdu ; les anciens koluka le bon mot pour un conseil difficile.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koluka — boluki ya bopembe.

Koluka elimboli koluka (kokuta elimboli kokutana na eloko oyo ezali bongo). Bana balukaka mondenge oyo ebungaki; bampaka balukaka liloba ya malamu mpo na toli ya makasi.

examples.english: We will meet tomorrow.
examples.french: Nous nous retrouverons demain.

words.culturalNote:
To meet — paths crossing at the agreed time.

Kutana is to meet, encounter, or come together. "Tokokutana lobi" — we'll meet tomorrow — sets the elaka that two people keep with their feet.

examples.english: The child fell.
examples.french: L'enfant est tombé.

words.culturalNote:
To fall — the body going down despite itself.

Kokweya is to fall. The child who kwei, the leaf from the branch, the price in the market — the verb covers every kind of going down.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Tomber — le corps qui descend malgré lui.

Kokweya, c'est tomber. L'enfant qui kwei, la feuille de la branche, le prix au marché — le verbe couvre toute forme de descente.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokweya — nzoto oyo ezali kokita ata bolingo na yango te.

Kokweya elimboli kokweya. Mwana oyo akwei, lokasa euti na etape, motuya na zando — liloba ezipi ndenge nyonso ya kokita.

examples.lingala: Sakosi ya mposo ya nyama ezali ya makasi.
examples.english: A leather bag is strong.
examples.french: Un sac en cuir est solide.

words.culturalNote:
Leather — the prepared skin of an animal.

Mposo ya nyama — literally "animal skin" — is leather. (Kwire is a direct French loan; the standard Lingala is descriptive.) A sakosi ya mposo ya nyama is built to last seasons, and pays in long use.

examples.lingala: Ebende ya motane ezali ebende ya kilo.
examples.english: Copper is a heavy metal.
examples.french: Le cuivre est un métal lourd.

words.culturalNote:
Copper — Lingala says it descriptively: the red metal.

Ebende ya motane — "red iron" — is copper. (Kwivre is a direct French loan.) The Congo's'earth holds famous copper; the word names the metal by the colour the eye sees in its glow.

examples.english: He is tall.
examples.french: Il est grand.

words.culturalNote:
Long — and tall, the same stem.

The stem -lai is long or tall. It takes the agreement of its noun: nzela molai (long road), moto molai (tall person), bolai (length/height). One stem, many heights.

examples.english: Advise the child with wisdom.
examples.french: Conseille l'enfant avec sagesse.

words.culturalNote:
To advise — counsel from the elder's chair.

Kolaka is the infinitive "to advise." Elders kolaka the young with patience; the laka they give is meant to walk ahead and light the way.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Conseiller — guider depuis des pas plus anciens.

Kolaka, c'est conseiller. Les anciens kolaka les jeunes avec patience ; le laka qu'ils donnent doit marcher devant et éclairer la voie.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolaka — kotambwisa uta na matambe ya bampaka.

Kolaka elimboli kopesa toli. Bampaka bakolaka bilenge na motema molai; laka oyo bapesi ezali mpo na kotambola liboso mpe kongengisa nzela.

examples.english: Show me the way.
examples.french: Montre-moi le chemin.

words.culturalNote:
To show — making a thing seen.

Lakisa is to show or display. To lakisa someone the way is to give them direction; to lakisa a thing is to set it before another's'eyes.

examples.english: Sleep well.
examples.french: Dors bien.

words.culturalNote:
To sleep — the body's nightly setting down.

Lala is to sleep. "Lala malamu" — sleep well — is the soft parting before the lamp is put out; rest is honoured, and good sleep blessed.

examples.english: Cook food.
examples.french: Cuisine la nourriture.

words.culturalNote:
To cook — the slow simmer of the home meal.

Lamba is to cook. From the morning rice to the evening pondu, lamba shapes the day's rhythm; the cook's'hands carry the household's well-being.

examples.english: This child is good.
examples.french: Cet enfant est bon.

words.culturalNote:
Good — the simple word for a thing well.

Malamu is good. "Mwana malamu" is a good child; "kozala malamu" is to be well. The stem -lamu takes the agreement: moto malamu, ndako malamu, biloko malamu.

examples.english: Follow him.
examples.french: Suis-le.

words.culturalNote:
To follow — keeping the path of another.

Landa is the stem of kolanda, to follow. "Landa ye" — follow him — points the feet behind a guide; the verb covers paths, leaders, and rules.

examples.lingala: Langi ya elamba na yo ezali kitoko.
examples.english: The color of your dress is beautiful.
examples.french: La couleur de ta robe est belle.

words.culturalNote:
Color in Lingala.

Langi covers any color you can name. Kongolese fabric — pagne, raffia, beadwork — is a riot of color, so this word lives in everyday speech.

examples.lingala: Akolata elamba ya kitoko na fete.
examples.english: She will wear a beautiful dress to the party.
examples.french: Elle portera une belle robe a la fete.

words.culturalNote:
To wear / to put on (clothes).

Kolata is the verb for putting clothing on yourself. Used for everyday dressing and for special occasions alike.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Porter / mettre (un vêtement).

Kolata est le verbe pour s'habiller. Utilisé pour la tenue de tous les jours comme pour les grandes occasions.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolata — kolata bilamba.

Kolata ezali liloba mpo na kolata bilamba. Basaleli yango mpo na bilamba ya mikolo nyonso mpe mpo na bafeti ya minene.

examples.lingala: Mama azali kolatisa mwana na ye.
examples.english: The mother is dressing her child.
examples.french: La mere habille son enfant.

words.culturalNote:
To dress someone (causative).

From kolata + -isa, the causative suffix. Used for dressing a child, an elder, or a sick person.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Habiller quelqu'un (causatif).

De kolata + -isa, le suffixe causatif. Utilisé pour habiller un enfant, un ancien, ou un malade.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolatisa — kolatisa moto (causatif).

Euti na kolata + -isa, suffixe ya causatif. Basaleli yango mpo na kolatisa mwana, mopaka, to mobeli.

examples.lingala: Sapatu oyo esalemi na mposo ya nyama.
examples.english: These shoes are made of leather.
examples.french: Ces chaussures sont faites en cuir.

words.culturalNote:
Leather, literally animal-skin.

Mposo = skin/peel, nyama = animal. Used for bags, shoes, drum heads. Quality leather goods are a mark of dignity.

examples.english: He left me at the house.
examples.french: Il m'a laisse a la maison.

words.culturalNote:
To leave (someone or something behind), to allow.

Kotika can mean physically depart or let-be. Context tells which.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Laisser (quelqu'un ou quelque chose), permettre.

Kotika peut signifier partir physiquement ou laisser-être. Le contexte dit lequel.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotika — kotika moto to eloko, kondima.

Kotika ekoki kolimbola kobima ya nzoto to kotika eloko. Esika ya likambo eyebisi nini ezali.

examples.lingala: Loboko na ngai ya mwasi ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My left hand hurts.
examples.french: Ma main gauche me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Left side, left hand.

Ya mwasi = of the woman; in Lingala the left side is called the woman side and the right ya mobali, the man side.

examples.lingala: Lokolo na ngai ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My leg hurts.
examples.french: Ma jambe me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Leg or foot.

Lokolo covers both leg and foot, distinguished by context. To walk far is to use makolo (plural) malamu.

examples.english: Today I feel better.
examples.french: Aujourd hui je me sens mieux.

words.culturalNote:
Better, literally good-surpassing.

Malamu = good, koleka = to surpass. The phrase compares: better than before, better than another.

examples.english: He will pass by this road.
examples.french: Il passera par ce chemin.

words.culturalNote:
To pass, to go past, to exceed.

Used for time passing, people passing by, and one thing surpassing another.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Passer, dépasser, s'écouler.

Utilisé pour le temps qui passe, les gens qui passent à côté, et une chose qui en surpasse une autre.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koleka — koleka, koleka liboso.

Basaleli yango mpo na ntango oyo eleki, bato oyo bazali koleka, mpe eloko oyo eleki mosusu.

examples.english: We went strolling at the market.
examples.french: Nous sommes alles nous promener au marche.

words.culturalNote:
To stroll, to walk about aimlessly.

Doubling the verb kotambola intensifies it into a leisurely-walk meaning. Common on cool Kinshasa evenings.

examples.english: My younger sibling goes to school.
examples.french: Mon cadet va a l'ecole.

words.culturalNote:
Younger sibling.

Used without specifying boy/girl. Pairs with kulutu (elder sibling). Birth order is socially meaningful.

examples.lingala: Mwana oyo akolekisa baninga na ye na kelasi.
examples.english: This child will surpass his classmates at school.
examples.french: Cet enfant depassera ses camarades a l'ecole.

words.culturalNote:
To make pass, to exceed, to outdo.

Causative of koleka. Used for achievement and overtaking.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Faire passer, dépasser, surpasser.

Causatif de koleka. Utilisé pour les exploits et le fait de devancer.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolekisa — kosala ete eleka, koleka liboso.

Causatif ya koleka. Basaleli yango mpo na elonga mpe kozwa esika ya liboso.

examples.english: Today has been a good day.
examples.french: Aujourd hui a ete une bonne journee.

words.culturalNote:
Today.

Lelo anchors planning and gratitude. Lelo ezali = today is. The greeting Boni lelo? = How is today going?

examples.english: I am very tired after work.
examples.french: Je suis tres fatigue apres le travail.

words.culturalNote:
To tire, to be exhausted.

Na-lembi (I am tired) is a common opener after a long day. Elders may answer Kasi tokoki = But we manage.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Se fatiguer, être épuisé.

Na-lembi (je suis fatigué) est une ouverture courante après une longue journée. Les anciens peuvent répondre : Kasi tokoki = mais on tient le coup.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolembe — kolemba, koyoka bopoli ya nzoto.

Na-lembi (nalembi) ezali liloba ya ebandeli na nsima ya mokolo molai. Bampaka bakoki kozongisa: Kasi tokoki = kasi tokoki kosala.

examples.english: This bed is very soft.
examples.french: Ce lit est tres doux.

words.culturalNote:
Soft, gentle, tender.

Used for textures, voices, and behaviour. A soft heart = motema ya pete.

examples.lingala: Napesi yo ndimo mpo na pona masanga.
examples.english: I give you a lemon for your drink.
examples.french: Je te donne un citron pour ta boisson.

words.culturalNote:
Lemon (corrected from libazi).

Ndimo is the standard word for lemon/lime in Lingala. Used to flavor sauces and water.

examples.english: The ground is shaking.
examples.french: La terre tremble.

words.culturalNote:
To shake, to tremble.

Used for trembling hands, an earthquake, or shivering from cold or fear.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Trembler, vibrer.

Utilisé pour les mains qui tremblent, un tremblement de terre, ou le frisson du froid ou de la peur.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kolenga — koningana, kolenga.

Basaleli yango mpo na maboko oyo ezali kolenga, mabele oyo eningani, to nzoto oyo ezali kolenga na malili to na bobangi.

examples.lingala: Nakomi nkanda mpo na mama na ngai.
examples.english: I wrote a letter to my mother.
examples.french: J'ai ecrit une lettre a ma mere.

words.culturalNote:
A written letter (corrected from letele).

Nkanda is the more authentic Lingala term; letele is a French loan (lettre). Both are heard.

examples.lingala: Liteya ya lelo ezali ya ntina.
examples.english: Today s lesson is important.
examples.french: La lecon d'aujourd hui est importante.

words.culturalNote:
Lesson, teaching.

Liteya is used in school and in the church for any teaching session.

examples.english: Mother sent me a letter.
examples.french: Maman m'a envoye une lettre.

words.culturalNote:
Letter, mail (alternate listing for letter; cf. #413).

In the diaspora, news from home once meant nkanda; now it means a phone call, but the word lives on.

examples.english: Their marriage will last forever.
examples.french: Leur mariage durera pour toujours.

words.culturalNote:
Marriage.

Libala joins two families, not only two people. Dowry, blessings, and elders presence are central.

examples.english: The children are playing in the courtyard.
examples.french: Les enfants jouent dans la cour.

words.culturalNote:
Courtyard, open ground outside the house.

Libanda is the social heart of the parcelle: meals, talk, and play happen there.

examples.english: My father has become bald.
examples.french: Mon pere est devenu chauve.

words.culturalNote:
Bald-headed (corrected from libata).

Libandi describes a bare crown. Often said affectionately of an elder.

examples.lingala: Lipeka na ngai ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My shoulder hurts.
examples.french: Mon epaule me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Shoulder (corrected from libeke).

Lipeka carries the load — children, baskets, sacks of charcoal. The body part of work.

examples.lingala: Bana basali libulu na nse ya nzete.
examples.english: The children dug a hole under the tree.
examples.french: Les enfants ont creuse un trou sous l'arbre.

words.culturalNote:
Hole, pit (corrected from libela).

Libulu is used for any dug-out cavity; the word for grave is the same root.

examples.english: The mother breastfed the child.
examples.french: La mere a allaite l'enfant.

words.culturalNote:
Breast.

Libele evokes mothering and feeding. Kopesa libele = to breastfeed, central to early childcare.

examples.english: He put the items in the bag.
examples.french: Il a mis les affaires dans le sac.

words.culturalNote:
Bag, sack, pouch.

Libenga is a general word for any carrying bag — market, school, or travel.

examples.lingala: Tolambi mbala mpo na bilei ya pokwa.
examples.english: We cooked sweet potatoes for dinner.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit des patates pour le diner.

words.culturalNote:
Sweet potato (corrected from libenge).

Mbala is the standard word for sweet potato. A staple food across Kongo households.

examples.english: Father wrapped a fish bundle.
examples.french: Pere a enveloppe un paquet de poisson.

words.culturalNote:
A wrapped bundle, often a leaf-wrapped steamed package.

Liboke ya mbisi (fish steamed in leaves) is a beloved DRC dish — banana leaves, fish, chilli, slow steam.

examples.lingala: Tokendaki libongo mpo na komona masuwa.
examples.english: We went to the port to see the boat.
examples.french: Nous sommes alles au port pour voir le bateau.

words.culturalNote:
Beach, riverbank, port.

Libongo evokes the Congo River life — pirogues arriving, fish landed, traders gathered.

examples.english: She gave me a beautiful gift.
examples.french: Elle m'a donne un beau cadeau.

words.culturalNote:
Gift, offering.

Libonza is also the word for an offering at church; the same root carries generosity and devotion.

examples.english: He is in front of the others.
examples.french: Il est devant les autres.

words.culturalNote: Liboso — front, ahead, before. Both a place and a time word: to stand liboso is to stand in front; to happen liboso is to happen earlier. Liboso ya = in front of / before. The shorter boso is the informal spoken contraction.

examples.english: Our family is large.
examples.french: Notre famille est grande.

words.culturalNote:
Family.

Libota in Kongo culture stretches wide — aunts, cousins, and elders all count. The family is the first community.

examples.english: Where is the toilet?
examples.french: Ou sont les toilettes?

words.culturalNote:
Toilet, literally body-hole/relief place.

In many households libulu is also the simple word for outhouse. Polite alternative: kabine.

examples.lingala: Libumu na ngai ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My stomach hurts.
examples.french: Mon ventre me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Stomach, belly.

Libumu is also used emotionally — a heavy libumu means worry.

examples.english: He is constipated.
examples.french: Il est constipe.

words.culturalNote:
Constipation, literally the belly is closed.

Likangani = is closed/blocked. A common everyday complaint, no shame attached.

examples.english: I have nine children.
examples.french: J'ai neuf enfants.

words.culturalNote:
Nine.

Libwa is the standard counting word for nine. Large families historically common, valued.

examples.english: Lying is bad.
examples.french: Mentir est mauvais.

words.culturalNote:
To lie / tell a lie.

Kobuka = to break, lokuta = lie — to break truth. Lying breaks community trust and is treated seriously.

examples.english: I have the house key.
examples.french: J'ai la cle de la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Key.

From kofungola (to open). One who holds the lifungola holds responsibility for the house.

examples.lingala: Lifungu ya simisi na ngai ekweyi.
examples.english: My shirt button fell off.
examples.french: Le bouton de ma chemise est tombe.

words.culturalNote:
Button (clothing or device).

From the same root as lifungola: a small thing that fastens or releases.

examples.english: The monthly pay has arrived.
examples.french: Le salaire du mois est arrive.

words.culturalNote:
Wage, payment.

Lifuta is what one earns for work. Lifuta malamu = a good wage; the dream of every worker.

examples.english: Many fish live in the swamp.
examples.french: Beaucoup de poissons vivent dans le marais.

words.culturalNote:
Swamp, marshy ground.

The Congo basin holds vast lobongo — a place of fishing and danger both.

examples.english: The light is on in the house.
examples.french: La lumiere est allumee dans la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Light, lamp.

In the days of frequent power cuts, mwinda also meant a kerosene lamp or candle — and warm gatherings around it.

examples.english: The lightning lit up the sky.
examples.french: L'eclair a illumine le ciel.

words.culturalNote:
Lightning.

Kongo storms are dramatic; monkalali ya makasi cracks across the river at the start of the rains.

examples.english: An accident happened on the road.
examples.french: Un accident est arrive sur la route.

words.culturalNote:
Danger, accident.

Likama covers both ongoing risk and the moment of a crash. Kala na likama = beware.

examples.english: This matter is important.
examples.french: Cette affaire est importante.

words.culturalNote:
Matter, affair, issue.

Likambo is broad — a topic of discussion, a problem, a court case, news of the day.

examples.lingala: Tata na ngai abolaka likaya te.
examples.english: My father does not smoke.
examples.french: Mon pere ne fume pas.

words.culturalNote:
Cigarette, tobacco.

Kobola likaya = to smoke. Tobacco is part of older social rituals, less common with the young.

examples.english: He has become like his father.
examples.french: Il est devenu comme son pere.

words.culturalNote:
Like, as, similar to.

Used in comparisons. Lokola also opens proverbs: lokola lobi = as yesterday.

examples.english: This egg is fresh.
examples.french: Cet oeuf est frais.

words.culturalNote:
Egg.

Likei (sing.) / makei (pl.). Eggs are everyday breakfast or a special treat for a sick child.

examples.english: The sacred enclosure is a place of respect.
examples.french: L'enclos sacre est un lieu de respect.

words.culturalNote:
A sacred or restricted enclosure (uncertain; gloss uncertain).

The dictionary glossed seminary; among the Mongo and some Kongo communities likindo refers to a sacred precinct. Verify locally.

examples.lingala: Ebele ya bato bayaki na fete.
examples.english: A crowd of people came to the party.
examples.french: Une foule de gens est venue a la fete.

words.culturalNote:
Crowd, lots of people (corrected from likita).

Ebele = many, bato = people. The natural Lingala phrase. Markets and weddings often draw an ebele ya bato.

examples.english: The bird is on top of the tree.
examples.french: L'oiseau est sur l'arbre.

words.culturalNote:
Sky, above, on top of.

Likolo serves both for the physical sky and for above as a preposition (likolo ya = on top of).

examples.english: He is still single.
examples.french: Il est encore celibataire.

words.culturalNote:
Single, unmarried (corrected from likombe).

Monzemba is the standard word for a single adult. In Kongo society marriage is a strong norm; monzemba carries gentle social weight.

examples.english: Mother is sweeping with the broom.
examples.french: Maman balaie avec le balai.

words.culturalNote:
Broom (corrected from likombo).

Komba is woven from palm midribs. Sweeping the libanda each morning is a daily Kongo rhythm.

examples.english: This orange is sweet.
examples.french: Cette orange est sucree.

words.culturalNote:
Orange (the fruit).

Lilala (sing.) / malala (pl.). Bright market piles of malala are a Kinshasa morning sight.

examples.english: The chief s word is strong.
examples.french: La parole du chef est forte.

words.culturalNote:
Word, speech.

A chief's liloba carries weight. Liloba na liloba = word for word.

examples.english: Some people believe in witchcraft.
examples.french: Certaines personnes croient a la sorcellerie.

words.culturalNote:
Witchcraft / occult power (corrected from liloki).

Kindoki names hidden harmful power; the topic is socially heavy and best handled with care.

examples.english: The palm tree produces palm nuts.
examples.french: Le palmier produit des noix de palme.

words.culturalNote:
Palm tree.

The oil palm provides cooking oil (mafuta ya mbila), wine (masanga ya mbila), and roofing. A pillar of Kongo life.

examples.english: Believers fear hell.
examples.french: Les croyants craignent l'enfer.

words.culturalNote:
Hell.

From Portuguese inferno via Kikongo. Used in church teaching; an everyday warning word, not a casual one.

examples.english: The end of the road is over there.
examples.french: La fin du chemin est la-bas.

words.culturalNote:
Limit, end, edge.

Nsuka closes a thing — end of journey, end of patience, end of a story.

examples.lingala: Bato bazali na mokoloto longwa na nzela.
examples.english: People are in a line from the road.
examples.french: Les gens sont en file depuis la route.

words.culturalNote:
Line, row, queue.

Mokoloto is the long line at the market, the bank, or the bus stop — a daily test of patience.

examples.english: I love you very much.
examples.french: Je t'aime beaucoup.

words.culturalNote:
To love, to like, to want.

The habitual -aka form (nalingaka) means I love / I like in general; nalingi means I love right now / I want.

examples.english: We cooked crab today.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit du crabe aujourd hui.

words.culturalNote:
Crab (corrected from lingalo).

Kanga appears in riverside and coastal Kongo cooking — served with rice or fufu.

examples.english: There is a crab at the riverbank.
examples.french: Il y a un crabe sur la rive.

words.culturalNote:
Crab (variant listing).

Same as #458 — the bank had this entry duplicated under lingato.

examples.english: The elder held his walking stick.
examples.french: L'aine a tenu son baton.

words.culturalNote:
Walking stick (corrected from lingenda).

Mwango is the elder's companion — a sign of dignity, a help on the road, sometimes a teaching tool.

examples.lingala: Tata apesi ngai nzela ya kokende.
examples.english: Father gave me permission to go.
examples.french: Pere m'a donne la permission de partir.

words.culturalNote:
To allow, to give way (corrected from lingisa).

Literally to give the path. Used for permission and for letting someone pass.

examples.english: The interpreter translated the chief s words.
examples.french: L'interprete a traduit les paroles du chef.

words.culturalNote:
Interpreter / translator (corrected from lingisi).

Mobongoli = one who turns/translates, maloba = words. Crucial in a country with many languages spoken side by side.

examples.english: The house window is open.
examples.french: La fenetre de la maison est ouverte.

words.culturalNote:
Window.

In many Kongo homes the lininisa is the social link — neighbours call through it, children watch the street from it.

examples.lingala: Lino na ngai ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My tooth hurts.
examples.french: Ma dent me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Tooth.

Lino (sing.) / mino (pl.). A bright laugh full of mino malamu is a sign of health.

examples.english: We ate bread in the evening.
examples.french: Nous avons mange du pain le soir.

words.culturalNote:
Bread (corrected from lipa).

Mampa is the everyday word. The local fresh baguette, sold warm at the kiosk, is a beloved morning ritual.

examples.english: This guava is very sweet.
examples.french: Cette goyave est tres sucree.

words.culturalNote:
Guava.

Lipela (sing.) / mapela (pl.). Children climb for them; markets pile them high.

examples.english: Mother went to the field today.
examples.french: Maman est allee au champ aujourd hui.

words.culturalNote:
Field, garden, plantation.

Lisala is the cultivated land that feeds the family — cassava, maize, peanuts, vegetables.

examples.english: Children s play is beautiful.
examples.french: Le jeu des enfants est beau.

words.culturalNote:
Play, entertainment, game.

Lisano covers games, performances, and any joyful diversion.

examples.lingala: Lisasi ya bondoki ezali na ntalo.
examples.english: A gun bullet is expensive.
examples.french: Une cartouche de fusil est chere.

words.culturalNote:
Bullet, cartridge.

Lisasi appears in news of conflict and in hunting talk. A heavy word.

examples.english: The cow s horns are long.
examples.french: Les cornes de la vache sont longues.

words.culturalNote:
Horn of an animal (corrected from mbongi / liseke).

Ngomolo refers to the keratin horn. Sometimes used for drinking-horns in older usage.

examples.lingala: Liso na ngai ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My eye hurts.
examples.french: Mon oeil me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Eye.

Liso (sing.) / miso (pl.). A child with miso ya kitoko — beautiful eyes — is a great compliment.

examples.lingala: Lisolo na biso eumeli ngonga ebele.
examples.english: Our conversation lasted many hours.
examples.french: Notre conversation a dure plusieurs heures.

words.culturalNote:
Conversation, story, talk.

Lisolo is the unhurried Kongo way of talking — relationships are built in long, looping conversations.

examples.english: Listen carefully to the elder s words.
examples.french: Ecoute bien les paroles de l'aine.

words.culturalNote:
To hear, to listen, to feel.

Koyoka covers hearing sounds and feeling (koyoka pasi = to feel pain). Listening to elders is a deep value.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Entendre — et sentir, le même verbe.

Koyoka couvre à la fois l'ouïe et la sensation. Koyoka un mot et koyoka un frisson partagent la même racine — la langue traite la perception comme un seul acte de réception.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyoka — koyoka mpe koyoka, liloba moko.

Koyoka ezipi koyoka mpe koyoka na nzoto. Koyoka liloba mpe koyoka malili basangani na motó moko — monoko ezwi boyoki lokola mosala moko ya boyambi.

examples.english: Give me a little more.
examples.french: Donne-moi encore un peu.

words.culturalNote:
Again, more, anew.

Used at table, in conversation, in song refrains. Lisusu lisusu! = Again! Again!

examples.lingala: Litama ya mwana ezali ya kovimba.
examples.english: The child s cheek is plump.
examples.french: La joue de l'enfant est rebondie.

words.culturalNote:
Cheek.

A child with full litama is praised — a sign of health and good feeding.

examples.lingala: Bakangi nyama ya mpoka na zamba.
examples.english: They caught a wild animal in the forest.
examples.french: Ils ont attrape un animal sauvage dans la foret.

words.culturalNote:
Wild animal / game (corrected from bibwele/lititi).

Nyama = animal, mpoka = wilderness. Hunting talk and forest stories run deep in Kongo culture.

examples.lingala: Litoi na ngai ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My ear hurts.
examples.french: Mon oreille me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Ear.

Litoi (sing.) / matoi (pl.). To open one's matoi = to listen well, to take advice.

examples.english: Give me a little bit.
examples.french: Donne-moi un peu.

words.culturalNote:
Little, small, a bit.

Moke is the standard adjective; -ke alone is the suffix form. Used for size, amount, age.

examples.english: He stood at the corner of the house.
examples.french: Il s'est tenu au coin de la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Corner, angle.

Litumu names a corner of a room, a building, a street. A quiet litumu can be a hiding place or a thinking place.

examples.lingala: Tozali na bomoi mpo na Nzambe.
examples.english: We live for God.
examples.french: Nous vivons pour Dieu.

words.culturalNote:
To live, to be alive.

Kozala = to be, bomoi = life. Kozala na bomoi = literally to be with life. A weighty phrase.

examples.lingala: Esika na ngai ya kovanda ezali Kinshasa.
examples.english: My residence is in Kinshasa.
examples.french: Ma residence est a Kinshasa.

words.culturalNote:
Residence / place to live (corrected from esika ya mosolo).

Literally place of dwelling. Kovanda = to sit / to dwell. Used for one's'home base.

examples.lingala: Liwa ya nkoko ezalaki mawa makasi.
examples.english: The elder s death was a great sorrow.
examples.french: La mort de l'aine fut une grande tristesse.

words.culturalNote:
Death.

Liwa is named directly but treated with weight. Wake (matanga) and burial gather the whole community.

examples.lingala: Lobanga na ngai ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My jaw hurts.
examples.french: Ma machoire me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Chin, jaw.

Lobanga also refers to the lower jawline. A strong lobanga is a feature of beauty in song.

examples.lingala: Loboko na ngai ya mobali ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My right hand hurts.
examples.french: Ma main droite me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Hand, arm.

Loboko covers both hand and arm. Kopesa loboko = to give a hand / to help. A gesture of solidarity.

examples.english: A leaf from the tree fell.
examples.french: Une feuille de l'arbre est tombee.

words.culturalNote:
Leaf.

Lokasa (sing.) / nkasa (pl.). Leaves wrap liboke, sweeten tea, treat fevers — useful in many ways.

examples.english: That old man cannot hear.
examples.french: Ce vieillard n'entend pas.

words.culturalNote:
Deaf, literally does not hear (corrected from loko).

A habitual negative of koyoka. The kinder phrasing among Kongo speakers.

examples.english: He speaks like his father.
examples.french: Il parle comme son pere.

words.culturalNote:
Like, as, similar to (variant entry; see #443).

Lokola opens proverbs and comparisons. A core small word.

examples.lingala: Lokolo na ngai ya mwasi ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My left foot hurts.
examples.french: Mon pied gauche me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Foot, leg (variant; see #402).

Lokolo carries the family across long walks to school, to the field, to church.

examples.english: Lying brings trouble.
examples.french: Le mensonge apporte des ennuis.

words.culturalNote:
A lie, falsehood.

Koloba lokuta = to tell a lie. Kongo morality places truthfulness very high; lokuta is a serious accusation.

examples.english: He must pay a fine.
examples.french: Il doit payer une amende.

words.culturalNote:
Fine, monetary penalty.

From French amende. Used for traffic fines, market fines, and customary fines paid to elders.

examples.english: The road is long.
examples.french: La route est longue.

words.culturalNote:
Long, tall.

Molai describes a long road, a tall person, a long-lasting matter. Pairs with mokuse (short).

examples.english: He looked at me with feeling.
examples.french: Il m'a regarde avec emotion.

words.culturalNote:
To look at, to watch.

Kotala is the deliberate gaze; kotala ngai = look at me. Used in greetings, attention, and care.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Regarder — les yeux posés sur ce qui en a besoin.

Kotala, c'est regarder, observer, veiller. Le gardien, le médecin, la mère, tous kotala leur charge — des yeux qui protègent en faisant attention.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotala — miso etia likolo ya oyo esengeli na yango.

Kotala elimboli kotala, kobatela. Mokengeli, monganga, mama nyonso bakotala oyo babateli — miso oyo ebateli na kotya likebi.

examples.english: They took the child to the hospital.
examples.french: Ils ont emmene l'enfant a l'hopital.

words.culturalNote:
Hospital.

From French hopital. Going to the lopitalo can mean a long wait and the gathering of family for vigil.

examples.english: The truck is full of goods.
examples.french: Le camion est plein de marchandises.

words.culturalNote:
Lorry, truck.

From French camion. Big kamio caravans cross the country with food, fuel, and traders.

examples.english: I lost my money.
examples.french: J'ai perdu mon argent.

words.culturalNote:
To lose.

Kobungisa = to make-be-lost, the causative. Used for objects, time, opportunities, and people.

examples.english: Many people came to the party.
examples.french: Beaucoup de gens sont venus a la fete.

words.culturalNote:
A lot, many, much.

Ebele is the everyday word for quantity. Kongo gatherings often draw ebele ya bato.

examples.english: They stayed at the hotel in the evening.
examples.french: Ils ont loge a l'hotel le soir.

words.culturalNote:
Hotel.

From French hotel. In Kinshasa, lotele also names guesthouses and small inns along the road.

examples.lingala: Bolingo ya mama ezali ya solo.
examples.english: A mother s love is true.
examples.french: L'amour d'une mere est vrai.

words.culturalNote: Bolingo — love. The word that anchors a hundred years of Congolese rumba: from Wendo Kolosoy to Franco, Tabu Ley, Papa Wemba, and the guitarists of the modern Kinshasa scene, "bolingo" is the chorus the whole hall sings back. It carries romantic love and the deeper sense of devotion — bolingo ya mama (a mother's love), bolingo ya mboka (love of country). When Congolese say "bolingo ekosila te" — love will not end — they mean something larger than any one person.

examples.lingala: Elamba na yo ezali kitoko mingi.
examples.english: Your dress is very lovely.
examples.french: Ta robe est tres jolie.

words.culturalNote:
Lovely, very beautiful.

Kitoko alone = beautiful; kitoko mingi adds the lovely warmth. A common compliment.

examples.english: You are lucky today.
examples.french: Tu as de la chance aujourd hui.

words.culturalNote:
Luck, chance.

From French chance. Sanse malamu = good luck; sanse mabe = bad luck.

examples.lingala: Biloko na ngai ezali na motuka.
examples.english: My luggage is in the car.
examples.french: Mes bagages sont dans la voiture.

words.culturalNote:
Luggage, belongings, things.

Biloko is broad — it can mean luggage, belongings, or simply stuff. Bagasi is also heard.

examples.english: Lunch is ready.
examples.french: Le dejeuner est pret.

words.culturalNote:
Lunch, midday meal (corrected from bilei na moi).

From French midi for noon. The big family meal of the day, often around 13h–14h.

examples.english: We cooked beef today.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit du boeuf aujourd hui.

words.culturalNote:
Beef (corrected from the bare ma listing).

Nyama = meat, ngombe = cow. Beef is a treat in many homes; chicken and fish are more common.

examples.lingala: Mabele na biso ezali ya solo malamu.
examples.english: Our land is truly good.
examples.french: Notre terre est vraiment bonne.

words.culturalNote:
Earth, soil, land.

Mabele evokes ancestry and belonging — the soil of one's village. Also breast (plural form) in some contexts.

examples.lingala: Mabongo ya nde ya bilamba ezali na Kinshasa.
examples.english: The textile factory is in Kinshasa.
examples.french: L'usine de textile est a Kinshasa.

words.culturalNote:
Factory, workshop (corrected from maboma).

The word covers small workshops and large factories. Industry in DRC has known many boom-and-bust cycles.

examples.english: Give me drinking water.
examples.french: Donne-moi de l'eau à boire.

words.culturalNote:
Water — the first thing offered to a guest who arrives.

Mai is water, and offering it is the oldest gesture of welcome there is. A guest who arrives tired and dusty is given water before anything else. The Congo River — Ebale, the great water that names the country itself — is never far from the Congolese sense of who they are.

examples.english: The cooking charcoal is finished.
examples.french: Le charbon de cuisine est epuise.

words.culturalNote:
Charcoal.

Makala is the dominant household fuel. Charcoal trade is a vast informal economy across Kongo cities.

examples.lingala: Likambo ya makango ezali ya nsoni.
examples.english: The matter of mistresses is shameful.
examples.french: L'affaire des maitresses est honteuse.

words.culturalNote:
Concubine, mistress.

Makango carries social tension; the word appears in songs and proverbs warning about secret relationships.

examples.english: His blood was flowing.
examples.french: Son sang coulait.

words.culturalNote:
Blood.

Makila ties to kinship — bandeko ya makila = blood relatives. Also figures in proverbs and ritual.

examples.lingala: Maladi na ye ezali ya makasi.
examples.english: His illness is serious.
examples.french: Sa maladie est grave.

words.culturalNote:
Illness, disease.

From French maladie. Bokono is the older Lingala word, still widely used alongside maladi.

examples.english: This man is a kind person.
examples.french: Cet homme est une bonne personne.

words.culturalNote:
Good, kind.

Malamu is the all-purpose word for good — good food, good road, good person. Pairs with mabe (bad).

examples.lingala: Asaleli malato mpo na kobakisa nzete.
examples.english: He used a hammer to fix the wood.
examples.french: Il a utilise un marteau pour fixer le bois.

words.culturalNote:
Hammer.

From French marteau (related). The tool of the carpenter and roof-fixer.

examples.lingala: Bakundi nkoko na malita ya mboka.
examples.english: They buried the elder at the village cemetery.
examples.french: Ils ont enterre l'aine au cimetiere du village.

words.culturalNote:
Cemetery.

Malita is treated with deep respect; visits during All Souls (1 November) draw families to remember and tend graves.

examples.lingala: Mama na ngai azali na bomengo monene.
examples.english: My mother has a great heart.
examples.french: Ma mere a un grand coeur.

words.culturalNote:
Mother; also respectful term for any woman.

Mama is used to address one's mother and as a respectful you addressed to any adult woman.

examples.lingala: Manaka ya mbula oyo ezali na ndako.
examples.english: This year s calendar is in the house.
examples.french: Le calendrier de cette annee est dans la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Calendar.

Manaka helps plan the year — feast days, school terms, market days. Often hung in the living room.

examples.english: The boat is arriving at the port.
examples.french: Le bateau arrive au port.

words.culturalNote:
Boat, ship.

Masuwa carries people and goods up and down the Congo River — a journey of days and many stories.

examples.lingala: Matondi mingi mpo na lisalisi na yo.
examples.english: Many thanks for your help.
examples.french: Merci beaucoup pour ton aide.

words.culturalNote:
Thanks.

Matondi is the warm reply to a gift or help. Matondi mingi = many thanks. Pairs with merci (from French).

examples.english: We woke up early today.
examples.french: Nous nous sommes leves tot aujourd hui.

words.culturalNote:
Early, quickly.

Mbangu describes both speed and earliness. Konzela mbangu = come quickly.

examples.english: Many houses are made of bamboo.
examples.french: Beaucoup de maisons sont faites en bambou.

words.culturalNote:
Bamboo.

Mbanzi is used for walls, fences, scaffolding, and fishing weirs. A renewable building staple.

examples.english: We are almost at the house.
examples.french: Nous sommes presque a la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Almost, nearly (corrected from mbele).

Mbele also means perhaps; pene pene is the cleaner almost. Used for arrival, finishing, and near-misses.

examples.lingala: Mbeli ya kokata nyama ezali makasi.
examples.english: The meat-cutting knife is sharp.
examples.french: Le couteau a viande est tranchant.

words.culturalNote:
Knife.

Mbeli is the kitchen knife, the field machete, and the symbol of cutting cleanly through a problem.

examples.lingala: Mbeto na ngai ezali ya pete.
examples.english: My bed is soft.
examples.french: Mon lit est doux.

words.culturalNote:
Bed.

Mbeto can mean a raised bed, a mattress, or a sleeping mat. Mbeto malamu = a good bed, a small comfort.

examples.english: We cooked Congo fish.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit du poisson du Congo.

words.culturalNote:
Fish.

The Congo River feeds Kinshasa with mbisi — capitaine, ngolo, malangwa. Liboke ya mbisi (steamed fish) is a regional treasure.

examples.english: Many siblings have gone abroad.
examples.french: Beaucoup de proches sont partis a l'etranger.

words.culturalNote:
Abroad, foreign lands (reinstated, owner gloss).

Mikili in everyday speech means abroad — Europe, the Americas. Going to mikili is a major family event.

examples.english: The antelope ran into the forest.
examples.french: L'antilope s'est enfuie dans la foret.

words.culturalNote:
Antelope.

Mboloko appears in old hunting tales and in stews where game is still served.

examples.english: The money is coming out of the bank.
examples.french: L'argent sort de la banque.

words.culturalNote:
Money.

Mbongo is the everyday word. The Congolese franc (FC) and the US dollar both circulate in daily life.

examples.english: Hello to you, mama!
examples.french: Bonjour a toi, maman!

words.culturalNote:
Hello.

Mbote is the standard Kinshasa greeting. Pairs with the warmer Losako reply in some traditions.

examples.english: We cooked fresh corn.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit du mais frais.

words.culturalNote:
Corn, maize.

Mboto (corn cob) is grilled, boiled, or ground. Maize flour goes into ugali-like fufu in some regions.

examples.lingala: Mbuma ya nzete oyo ezali kitoko.
examples.english: The fruit of this tree is beautiful.
examples.french: Le fruit de cet arbre est beau.

words.culturalNote:
Fruit; also a result.

Mbuma is used literally and figuratively — mbuma ya mosala = fruit of work.

examples.lingala: Mbwa na biso azali na libanda.
examples.english: Our dog is in the courtyard.
examples.french: Notre chien est dans la cour.

words.culturalNote:
Dog.

Mbwa is the household watcher. Kept for safety and as a quiet companion of the libanda.

examples.english: The elder s gray hair is plentiful.
examples.french: Les cheveux gris de l'aine sont nombreux.

words.culturalNote:
Gray hair / grayness of age.

Mbwi is a sign of years, wisdom, and respect. To carry mbwi well is praised.

examples.english: We are two children in the house.
examples.french: Nous sommes deux enfants dans la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Two.

Mibale is the standard counting word for two. Used with countable noun classes throughout.

examples.lingala: Mikili ya mpio ezali na pasi.
examples.english: Cold countries can be hard.
examples.french: Les pays froids peuvent etre durs.

words.culturalNote:
Countries (and by extension climate/region).

Mikili is the plural of mokili = country/world. Diaspora speak: mikili ya mpio = cold countries (Europe, Canada).

examples.english: I think of you always.
examples.french: Je pense a toi tous les jours.

words.culturalNote:
Always, literally all days.

Mikolo = days, minso = all. Used in songs, prayers, and warm everyday speech.

examples.english: I work every day.
examples.french: Je travaille tous les jours.

words.culturalNote:
Every day.

Very close to mikolo minso, sometimes interchangeable. Nyonso = every/all, with a slightly broader feel.

examples.english: The child is drinking milk.
examples.french: L'enfant boit du lait.

words.culturalNote:
Milk.

From English milk via colonial trade routes. Mabele = breast milk in older speech; miliki = the everyday word now.

examples.english: He must repent.
examples.french: Il doit se repentir.

words.culturalNote:
To repent, literally to change one's'heart (replacing mima).

Used widely in church language; a deep moral pivot.

examples.lingala: Tozali na bandako minei na lopango.
examples.english: We have four buildings in the compound.
examples.french: Nous avons quatre batiments dans la parcelle.

words.culturalNote:
Four.

Standard counting word. Often heard in fours: bana minei = four children.

examples.english: Many people came to the party.
examples.french: Beaucoup de gens sont venus a la fete.

words.culturalNote:
Many, much, very.

Mingi is the all-purpose intensifier. Malamu mingi = very good; matondi mingi = many thanks.

examples.english: The child went to urinate.
examples.french: L'enfant est alle uriner.

words.culturalNote:
Urine (corrected from minya).

Kosuba = to urinate; masuba = urine. A normal everyday word, used without embarrassment.

examples.english: We can attend the evening mass.
examples.french: Nous pouvons aller a la messe du soir.

words.culturalNote:
Mass (Catholic church service).

From French messe. Sunday misa is a major weekly rhythm in Kinshasa Catholic life.

examples.english: We are three siblings.
examples.french: Nous sommes trois freres et soeurs.

words.culturalNote:
Three.

Standard counting word. Misato also names the Trinity in church (basato — Three Persons).

examples.english: This item is cheap.
examples.french: Cet article est bon marche.

words.culturalNote:
Cheap, low price (reinstated, owner: mobobe → ntalo moke).

Ntalo = price, moke = small. The natural everyday phrase for cheap.

examples.english: We fed five children today.
examples.french: Nous avons nourri cinq enfants aujourd hui.

words.culturalNote:
Five.

Standard counting word. Mitano often appears in proverbs and groupings.

examples.lingala: Miziki ya Congo eyebani na mokili mobimba.
examples.english: Congolese music is known across the whole world.
examples.french: La musique congolaise est connue dans le monde entier.

words.culturalNote:
Music.

From French musique. Rumba, soukous, sebene, ndombolo — the Congo has shaped African music for generations.

examples.english: My husband goes to work.
examples.french: Mon mari va au travail.

words.culturalNote:
Man, husband.

Mobali is the everyday word. Pairs with mwasi (woman/wife). The right side is ya mobali = the male side.

examples.english: The country s law must be obeyed.
examples.french: La loi du pays doit etre respectee.

words.culturalNote:
Law.

Mobeko covers civil law and traditional custom alike. Bambuta = elders are the keepers of older mibeko.

examples.english: Much water gathers in the marsh.
examples.french: Beaucoup d'eau s'accumule dans le marais.

words.culturalNote:
Marsh, swamp.

Close in meaning to lobongo. Mobela is the lower, water-logged land near rivers and streams.

examples.english: The children are playing in the street.
examples.french: Les enfants jouent dans la rue.

words.culturalNote:
Street, road (reinstated, owner: mofembo → balabala).

Balabala is the everyday street — site of football, gossip, vendors, and life.

examples.english: This guava is still unripe.
examples.french: Cette goyave est encore verte.

words.culturalNote:
Green / unripe / raw.

Mobesu describes a green leaf, an unripe fruit, or uncooked food. Pairs with -teli (ripe).

examples.lingala: Mokili mobimba eyebani na miziki na biso.
examples.english: The whole world knows our music.
examples.french: Le monde entier connait notre musique.

words.culturalNote:
Whole, entire.

Mobimba is the adjective for entire — mokili mobimba = the whole world. A favorite word in songs of pride.

examples.lingala: Eloko oyo ezali ntalo moke na zando.
examples.english: This item is cheap at the market.
examples.french: Cet article est bon marche au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Cheap (corrected from mobobe).

Ntalo = price, moke = small. The natural phrase. Pairs with ntalo makasi = expensive.

examples.english: Poverty is a sorrowful matter.
examples.french: La pauvrete est une affaire triste.

words.culturalNote:
Poor; a poor person.

Mobola is treated with dignity in Lingala. Lisalisi na bobola = helping the poor, a central value.

examples.lingala: Mobomi-mbisi azali na libongo na ntongo.
examples.english: The fisherman is at the riverbank in the morning.
examples.french: Le pecheur est a la rive le matin.

words.culturalNote:
Fisherman, literally fish-catcher.

Fishing communities along the Congo River keep deep knowledge of the water — currents, fish, and seasons.

examples.english: The midwife helped the mother in giving birth.
examples.french: La sage-femme a aide la mere a accoucher.

words.culturalNote:
Midwife.

From kobota = to give birth + -isi (causative/agent). A revered role in village and city alike.

examples.english: This year is a good one.
examples.french: Cette annee est belle.

words.culturalNote:
Year.

Mobu marks age, harvest cycles, and remembrance. Mibu mingi! is a long-life wish at celebrations.

examples.english: This day was turbulent.
examples.french: Cette journee a ete agitee.

words.culturalNote:
Turbulent, troubled, riotous.

Mobulu names disorder — political unrest, a stormy day, a chaotic crowd. Used in news and proverbs.

examples.english: The Kinshasa road has been newly built.
examples.french: La route de Kinshasa a ete nouvellement construite.

words.culturalNote:
Road (corrected from mofali).

Balabala covers both street and main road. The everyday word.

examples.english: In the evening the courtyard becomes dark.
examples.french: Le soir, la cour devient sombre.

words.culturalNote:
Dark, darkness; also black.

Moindo describes night-darkness; also used for the deep-black color and for dark skin in songs of beauty.

examples.lingala: Atindeli ngai mokanda longwa na Europe.
examples.english: He sent me a letter from Europe.
examples.french: Il m'a envoye une lettre d'Europe.

words.culturalNote:
Paper, document, written letter.

Mokanda is the broad word — schoolbook, certificate, formal letter. Owners often keep mikanda in a tin box, treasured.

examples.lingala: Mongongo ezali kosalisa na lopitalo te.
examples.english: A fly does not help in the hospital.
examples.french: Une mouche n'aide pas a l'hopital.

words.culturalNote:
Fly, insect (corrected from mokangi).

Mongongo is the everyday insect; nzinzi is also heard. A pest in markets and a sign of poor hygiene.

examples.lingala: Mokati-nsuki asili kokata nsuki na ngai.
examples.english: The barber has cut my hair.
examples.french: Le coiffeur a fini de couper mes cheveux.

words.culturalNote:
Barber, literally hair-cutter.

Kokata = to cut, nsuki = hair. The neighborhood salon is a male social hub.

examples.english: The widow is asking for help.
examples.french: La veuve demande de l'aide.

words.culturalNote:
Widow (corrected from mokbya OCR junk).

Literally a woman whose has died. The community is expected to care for widows and orphans.

examples.lingala: Mokengeli azali na ekuke ya ndako.
examples.english: The watchman is at the gate of the house.
examples.french: Le gardien est a la porte de la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Watchman, guard.

From kokenga = to watch over. The mokengeli is part of nearly every Kinshasa parcelle — a quiet trusted presence.

examples.lingala: Mokengeli-mwana akeleli mwana na ye malamu.
examples.english: The babysitter watched the child well.
examples.french: La nounou a bien garde l'enfant.

words.culturalNote:
Babysitter, child minder.

Kokenga + mwana = to watch over a child. Often a young relative or trusted neighbor; rarely a paid stranger.

examples.english: Our country is beautiful.
examples.french: Notre pays est beau.

words.culturalNote:
World, country, land.

Mokili stretches from one's village to the whole world. Mokili mobimba = the whole world.

examples.english: Many refugees came to the country.
examples.french: Beaucoup de refugies sont venus au pays.

words.culturalNote:
Refugee, one who has fled.

From kokima = to flee. A heavy word in a region marked by displacement; treated with compassion.

examples.english: Give me one thing.
examples.french: Donne-moi une chose.

words.culturalNote:
One, a, a single.

Moko is the basic numeral. Also used as an indefinite article: moto moko = a person.

examples.lingala: Mokobo ya ndako ezali ya bule.
examples.english: The house paint is blue.
examples.french: La peinture de la maison est bleue.

words.culturalNote:
Paint, pigment.

Mokobo names paint or any coloring pigment. Painting the front of a Kinshasa house is a small celebration.

examples.english: This day is beautiful.
examples.french: Cette journee est belle.

words.culturalNote:
Day; also an elder/respected person.

Mokolo can mean both day and elder (an old person, weighty with years). Context decides.

examples.english: People are standing in line.
examples.french: Les gens sont debout en file.

words.culturalNote:
Line, queue, row (variant; see #456).

Mokoloto: the waiting line for bread, bank, or bureau.

examples.english: The dog s tail is wagging.
examples.french: La queue du chien remue.

words.culturalNote:
Tail.

Mokila (mokondo is a variant). The dog's tail tells its mood; the proverb mokila bobele moko = one and the same warns of repeated harm.

examples.lingala: Mokongo na ngai ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My back hurts.
examples.french: Mon dos me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Back (the body part).

Mokongo carries the burden — a sack, a child, a year of work. Mokongo malamu = a strong back.

examples.english: The sick one cannot go out.
examples.french: Le malade ne peut pas sortir.

words.culturalNote:
Disabled or sick person.

A dignified word for someone living with disability or chronic illness. Community care is expected.

examples.english: The village chief has arrived.
examples.french: Le chef du village est arrive.

words.culturalNote:
Chief, boss, leader.

Mokonzi covers traditional chiefs, employers, and presidents. Respect is shown through greetings and gesture.

examples.lingala: Mokonzi mobali ya mboka asengeli kosolola.
examples.english: The king of the land must speak.
examples.french: Le roi du pays doit parler.

words.culturalNote:
King.

Literally male chief. Used for kings in stories and history, alongside the French roi.

examples.english: My skin is itching.
examples.french: Ma peau me demange.

words.culturalNote:
To itch (correction for mokosa).

Kosakwa describes the prickly skin sensation. Heat, insect bites, and dust make it a common complaint.

examples.english: The fishbone is straight.
examples.french: L'arete du poisson est droite.

words.culturalNote:
Bone.

Mokuwa is also used figuratively for the structural backbone of a thing or group.

examples.english: We stayed at the camp for two days.
examples.french: Nous sommes restes au camp pendant deux jours.

words.culturalNote:
Camp, camping ground, lodging.

Molako names a temporary lodging — a hunters camp, a worker's site, a transit point.

examples.lingala: Molangi ya mai ezali ya polele.
examples.english: The water bottle is open.
examples.french: La bouteille d'eau est ouverte.

words.culturalNote:
Bottle.

Molangi can hold water, palm wine, or palm oil. Reused for everything in Kinshasa kitchens.

examples.english: This work is easy.
examples.french: Ce travail est facile.

words.culturalNote:
Easy, soft (corrected from molembu).

Pete describes ease and softness. Pairs with makasi (hard, strong).

examples.english: My true friend.
examples.french: Mon vrai ami.

words.culturalNote:
Friend, companion (corrected from molingami).

Moninga is the everyday warm word. Pairs with baninga (plural). Moninga ya motema = friend of the heart.

examples.english: The blind person reads with the hands.
examples.french: L'aveugle lit avec les mains.

words.culturalNote:
Blind (corrected from mololanda).

Literally one whose eyes have died. The kinder modern phrasing in Lingala speech.

examples.lingala: Moluka ya mai ezali pene na ndako.
examples.english: A small stream is near the house.
examples.french: Un ruisseau est pres de la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Brook, small stream.

Moluka names the small water of village life — washing clothes, fetching, children playing.

examples.english: Kinshasa s heat is strong.
examples.french: La chaleur de Kinshasa est forte.

words.culturalNote:
Heat.

Molunge of Kinshasa shapes daily rhythms — early mornings, long afternoon rests, cool late evenings on the libanda.

examples.english: The frog is calling in the evening.
examples.french: La grenouille coasse le soir.

words.culturalNote:
Frog.

Frog songs at dusk are the soundtrack of the rainy season in many villages.

examples.lingala: Mombongo na ye ezali kotambola malamu.
examples.english: His business is going well.
examples.french: Son commerce marche bien.

words.culturalNote:
Business, trade, commerce.

Kongo trade culture is vibrant — small kiosks, large markets, traders crisscrossing borders.

examples.english: The country s custom must be preserved.
examples.french: La coutume du pays doit etre preservee.

words.culturalNote:
Custom, habit, tradition.

Momeseno covers cultural custom and personal habit alike. Carrying old momeseno is a form of belonging.

examples.english: People made a bet in the game.
examples.french: Les gens ont fait un pari dans le jeu.

words.culturalNote:
Bet, wager.

Mondenge appears around football, card games, and contests. Gambling can be a social hazard, often discussed.

examples.english: This house is very big.
examples.french: Cette maison est tres grande.

words.culturalNote:
Big, great, large.

Monene describes size, importance, and significance. Mokonzi monene = a great chief.

examples.english: The doctor gave me medicine.
examples.french: Le medecin m'a donne des medicaments.

words.culturalNote:
Doctor.

From an old term for healer/medicine person; now used for medical doctors and traditional healers alike.

examples.english: An enemy should not become great.
examples.french: L'ennemi ne doit pas devenir grand.

words.culturalNote:
Enemy.

Monguna is named directly but rarely used lightly. Proverbs warn of secret enemies and hasty conflict.

examples.english: The electricity was cut in the neighborhood today.
examples.french: L'electricite a ete coupee dans le quartier aujourd hui.

words.culturalNote:
Electricity (correction for monili).

Monini = the current; bakati monini = they cut the power. A familiar refrain in Kinshasa.

examples.english: The Lingala language is beautiful.
examples.french: La langue lingala est belle.

words.culturalNote:
Mouth; also language, tongue.

Monoko = mouth, by extension a language. Monoko ya Lingala = the Lingala tongue.

examples.english: We sat on the riverside.
examples.french: Nous nous sommes assis au bord du fleuve.

words.culturalNote:
Side, edge, coast.

Mopanzi names any side or edge — riverbank, roadside, side of the body.

examples.english: A stranger has arrived in the village.
examples.french: Un etranger est arrive au village.

words.culturalNote:
Foreigner, stranger.

Mopaya is treated with hospitality; Kongo culture holds that a visitor brings news and blessing.

examples.lingala: Mosala na ngai ezali makasi lelo.
examples.english: My work is hard today.
examples.french: Mon travail est dur aujourd hui.

words.culturalNote:
Work, job, task.

Mosala is daily work and honor alike. Mosala malamu = good work; the praise an elder gives.

examples.lingala: Mosapi na ngai ezali na pasi.
examples.english: My finger hurts.
examples.french: Mon doigt me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Finger.

Mosapi (sing.) / misapi (pl.). Misapi mitano = five fingers; the everyday measure for a small amount.

examples.english: Our village is far.
examples.french: Notre village est loin.

words.culturalNote:
Far, distant.

Mosika is a word the diaspora knows well — far from home, far from the river. Pairs with pene = near.

examples.lingala: Fisye ya mosala ezali na biro.
examples.english: The work file is in the office.
examples.french: Le dossier de travail est au bureau.

words.culturalNote:
File, folder (correction for mosiyo, OCR/loan word).

From French fiche/fichier. Used in offices, schools, and administration.

examples.lingala: Mosolo ya libala epesami na libota.
examples.english: The dowry was given to the family.
examples.french: La dot a ete donnee a la famille.

words.culturalNote:
Dowry, bride-price.

Mosolo (or mosolo ya libala) is the gift the groom’s family brings to the bride’s — a sign of seriousness and respect. Negotiated openly between elders.

examples.english: The buyer came to the market.
examples.french: L'acheteur est venu au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Buyer, purchaser.

From kosomba (to buy). The market relationship between moteki (seller) and mosombi is a daily Kongo ritual of greeting, haggling, and trust.

examples.english: The butcher cut the cow.
examples.french: Le boucher a decoupe la vache.

words.culturalNote:
Butcher, literally meat-seller.

Moteki = seller, nyama = meat/animal. The neighborhood butcher is a known figure, his stall a gathering point.

examples.english: The car engine broke down.
examples.french: Le moteur de la voiture est tombe en panne.

words.culturalNote:
Engine, motor.

From French moteur. Used for car engines, generators, and small machines. Motele ebebi = the engine is dead, a common Kinshasa lament.

examples.lingala: Motema na ngai ezali na esengo.
examples.english: My heart is full of joy.
examples.french: Mon coeur est rempli de joie.

words.culturalNote:
Heart.

Motema is the physical organ and the seat of feeling. Motema malamu = good-hearted; motema ya pete = a tender heart.

examples.english: This carving is beautiful.
examples.french: Cette sculpture est belle.

words.culturalNote:
Carving, sculpture (corrected from motende, which means stripe/streak).

Loyembo (or ekeko) is a carved wooden figure. Kongo and Luba sculpture is renowned worldwide.

examples.lingala: Kiyungulu atambolaka na nzela ya malembe.
examples.english: The lame one walks slowly.
examples.french: Le boiteux marche lentement.

words.culturalNote:
Lame person (corrected from motengoli; alternate moto ya kotengama).

The community is expected to walk patiently alongside the kiyungulu, never to leave them behind.

examples.english: The fire is burning in the stove.
examples.french: Le feu brule dans le fourneau.

words.culturalNote:
Fire.

Moto warms food, light, and gathering. The cooking fire burns in a fulo (stove, from French fourneau) or a mbabula (open charcoal brazier).

examples.english: We are six children.
examples.french: Nous sommes six enfants.

words.culturalNote:
Six.

Standard counting word. Often heard in family counts: bana motoba = six children, a sign of family abundance.

examples.english: The builder finished the work.
examples.french: Le macon a fini le travail.

words.culturalNote:
Builder, mason.

From kotonga (to build) + ndako (house). The motongi-ndako is a respected trade; cement-block houses define new Kinshasa neighborhoods.

examples.english: The bottle is empty.
examples.french: La bouteille est vide.

words.culturalNote:
Empty, vain.

Mpamba is the bottle without water and the promise without substance. Maloba ya mpamba = empty words.

examples.lingala: Mosala ya lelo ezali na mpasi.
examples.english: Today’s work is difficult.
examples.french: Le travail d'aujourd hui est difficile.

words.culturalNote:
Difficulty, suffering, pain.

Mpasi covers physical pain and life hardship. To koyoka mpasi = to feel pain or hurt.

examples.english: I am going too.
examples.french: Moi aussi je pars.

words.culturalNote:
Also, and, too.

A small connector word doing big work. Pairs subjects, joins phrases, adds a person to a plan.

examples.english: The morning air is soft.
examples.french: L'air du matin est doux.

words.culturalNote:
Air, breath.

Mpema also = a moment to breathe; kopema = to rest. The cool early morning air on the libanda is one of Kongo’s small daily blessings.

examples.lingala: Mpembe ya nzoku ezali na ntalo.
examples.english: Elephant ivory is expensive.
examples.french: L'ivoire d'elephant est cher.

words.culturalNote:
Ivory; also white.

Mpembe historically meant ivory; today it commonly serves as the color white. Ivory trade is now restricted to protect elephants.

examples.lingala: Mpete na matoi ezali ya wolo.
examples.english: The earring is made of gold.
examples.french: La boucle d'oreille est en or.

words.culturalNote:
Earring or finger ring.

Mpete is shared between earrings (mpete ya litoi) and finger rings (mpete ya mosapi). Jewelry marks both adornment and milestones.

examples.english: I am happy because of you.
examples.french: Je suis heureux a cause de toi.

words.culturalNote:
Because, for.

Mpo opens reason-clauses. Pairs with mpo na (for / in order to) and mpo nini? (why?).

examples.english: I bought bread for the children.
examples.french: J'ai achete du pain pour les enfants.

words.culturalNote:
For, in order to, on behalf of.

Mpo na binds purpose and beneficiary. Mpo na nini = why? Mpo na yo = for you.

examples.english: We will meet in the afternoon.
examples.french: Nous nous retrouverons l'apres-midi.

words.culturalNote:
Afternoon, evening.

Mpokwa names the cool of the day after the heat, when work eases and people gather.

examples.english: We cooked cassava leaves with meat.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit du saka-saka avec de la viande.

words.culturalNote:
Pounded cassava leaves — saka-saka.

Mpondu is a soul dish of the Congo: pounded young leaves of the cassava plant, simmered slowly with palm oil, fish, or meat.

examples.english: I am thirsty (have desire for water).
examples.french: J'ai soif (envie d'eau).

words.culturalNote:
Appetite, desire, thirst.

Mposa names any strong wanting — hunger, thirst, longing. Mposa ya mai = thirst.

examples.english: The donkey walked the road.
examples.french: L'ane a marche sur le chemin.

words.culturalNote:
Donkey; sometimes horse.

Less common in central Kongo, mpunda appears more in eastern DRC trade routes and in proverbs.

examples.lingala: Mwana ya mpata azali na lopango.
examples.english: The lamb is in the pen.
examples.french: L'agneau est dans l'enclos.

words.culturalNote:
Lamb — literally child of a sheep (corrected from mwa mpata).

The standard genitive: mwana ya mpata. Lambs carry Easter and Christmas associations in Christian Kongo households.

examples.english: We have eight relatives.
examples.french: Nous avons huit proches.

words.culturalNote:
Eight.

Standard counting word. Mwambe often closes a counted set in proverbs.

examples.english: The child is sleeping.
examples.french: L'enfant dort.

words.culturalNote:
Child, baby; offspring.

Mwana (sing.) / bana (pl.). Used widely — mwana ya mboka = child of the country (citizen), mwana mwasi = daughter.

examples.english: A citizen must obey the laws.
examples.french: Un citoyen doit respecter les lois.

words.culturalNote:
Citizen, literally child of the country.

Mwana = child, ekolo = country / nation. The phrase appears in civic talk and national speeches.

examples.lingala: Mwana mwasi na ngai akoyaka kelasi.
examples.english: My daughter goes to school.
examples.french: Ma fille va a l'ecole.

words.culturalNote:
Daughter, girl.

Mwana = child, mwasi = female. Pairs with mwana mobali = son. Girls’ education is a growing priority across DRC.

examples.english: The morning lamp is lit.
examples.french: La lampe du matin est allumee.

words.culturalNote:
Lamp, light.

Mwinda once meant a kerosene lamp; now it covers light bulbs and any source of light. Kopelisa mwinda = to light a lamp; passive epelisami = is lit.

examples.lingala: Mobange azali na pasi ya rumatisimo.
examples.english: The elder suffers from rheumatism.
examples.french: L'aine souffre de rhumatisme.

words.culturalNote:
Rheumatism (cleaned from OCR junk).

From French rhumatisme. A common complaint among elders, joints aching with the weather.

examples.english: You and I will go.
examples.french: Toi et moi nous irons.

words.culturalNote:
And, with, by.

The small word na binds many roles — with someone, at a place, to have something. A core particle of Lingala grammar.

examples.english: The elder is still alive.
examples.french: L'aine est encore en vie.

words.culturalNote:
Alive, living.

Literally with life. Bomoi = life. A reassuring phrase in news from home.

examples.lingala: Biloko ezali na kati ya sanduku.
examples.english: The items are inside the box.
examples.french: Les affaires sont dans la boite.

words.culturalNote:
Inside, within.

Na kati ya = inside of. A common preposition phrase used for containers, rooms, and groups.

examples.lingala: Ndeke ezali na likolo ya nzete.
examples.english: The bird is above the tree.
examples.french: L'oiseau est au-dessus de l'arbre.

words.culturalNote:
Above, on top.

Likolo on its own = sky / above; na likolo ya = on top of.

examples.lingala: Mbwa ezali na nse ya mesa.
examples.english: The dog is under the table.
examples.french: Le chien est sous la table.

words.culturalNote:
Below, under, at the bottom.

Nse = bottom; na nse ya = under. Pairs with na likolo (above).

examples.english: This book is his.
examples.french: Ce livre est a lui.

words.culturalNote:
His / hers / theirs (singular).

Literally to/of him-her. Lingala has no gender split; ya ye covers both.

examples.english: I got lost in the forest.
examples.french: Je me suis perdu dans la foret.

words.culturalNote:
To get lost, to lose the way (cleaned from OCR nabungise).

Kobunga = to lose, nzela = path. Used physically and figuratively: kobunga nzela ya bomoi = to lose one’s way in life.

examples.english: He is still at the house.
examples.french: Il est encore a la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Still, yet.

Naino marks ongoing state. Naino te = not yet; naino mingi = for a long time still.

examples.english: Our house is big.
examples.french: Notre maison est grande.

words.culturalNote:
House, building.

Ndako covers any built dwelling — hut, family home, office. Kongo culture treats the ndako as a sacred social center.
