examples.english: We went to church in the evening.
examples.french: Nous sommes alles a l'eglise le soir.

words.culturalNote:
Church, literally God’s'house.

Kinshasa’s Sunday rhythm centers on the ndako-nzambe — Catholic, Protestant, Kimbanguist, charismatic. Music and dance fill the services.

examples.english: Give me a bit of bread.
examples.french: Donne-moi un peu de pain.

words.culturalNote:
A portion, a bit, a piece.

Ndambo also names half (cf. #710). Used to ask for a small share of food, money, or time.

examples.english: The bird is flying.
examples.french: L'oiseau vole.

words.culturalNote:
Bird.

Ndeke (sing.) / bandeke (pl.). Also an old term for airplane: ndeke ya bisalelo = mechanical bird.

examples.english: My sibling has arrived.
examples.french: Mon frere/soeur est arrive.

words.culturalNote:
Sibling, kin, brother/sister (gloss corrected from broom).

Ndeko stretches beyond same-mother siblings to cousins and close relatives. Bandeko na biso = our people.

examples.english: The country border is near.
examples.french: La frontiere du pays est proche.

words.culturalNote:
Border, limit, boundary.

Ndelo applies to country borders and to personal limits. Crossing ndelo is always a weighted act.

examples.english: The lemon is sharp/sweet.
examples.french: Le citron est acidule.

words.culturalNote:
Lemon, citrus (variant; cf. #411).

Ndimo squeezes brighten sauces and water; also a folk remedy for colds.

examples.english: Father grew a long beard.
examples.french: Pere a fait pousser une longue barbe.

words.culturalNote:
Beard (corrected: only used in the plural mandefu).

The root ndefu becomes mandefu when speaking of a person’s beard — a sign of years, dignity, and patience.

examples.english: I had a beautiful dream last night.
examples.french: J'ai fait un beau reve hier soir.

words.culturalNote:
Dream.

Dreams are taken seriously in Kongo culture — they may carry warnings, blessings, or news from the ancestors.

examples.english: The wedding ceremony will be held tomorrow.
examples.french: La fete du mariage aura lieu demain.

words.culturalNote:
Ceremony, party, feast (corrected from ndulu, which is a small trumpet).

From French fete. Feti covers weddings, baptisms, birthdays — large family-and-friends celebrations.

examples.english: We cooked greens in oil.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit des legumes a l'huile.

words.culturalNote:
Vegetables, leafy greens.

Ndunda covers leafy greens — amaranth, cassava leaves, spinach. A core part of every Kongo meal.

examples.english: This house is big.
examples.french: Cette maison est grande.

words.culturalNote:
Big, great, large (standard form of "nene"; cf. #590).

Monene takes class agreement with nouns. Mokonzi monene = a great chief.

examples.english: I am going home.
examples.french: Moi je vais a la maison.

words.culturalNote:
I, me.

Ngai is the emphatic pronoun. Subject prefix na- is usually enough; ngai is added for emphasis or contrast.

examples.english: The old tower still stands.
examples.french: La vieille tour est encore debout.

words.culturalNote:
Tower, fortress (corrected from ngala which means turn/shift).

From French tour. Kongo elders also speak of ndako ya nzombo (fortified houses) in historical contexts.

examples.lingala: Nganda ya quartier etondi na bato.
examples.english: The neighborhood bar is full of people.
examples.french: Le bar du quartier est plein de monde.

words.culturalNote:
Small bar, drinking hangout (sometimes camp).

In Kinshasa, the nganda is the open-air neighborhood bar — music, beer, talk. A central social place.

examples.lingala: Nganga-nkisi azali na nkisi ya mboka.
examples.english: The traditional healer has village medicine.
examples.french: Le guerisseur traditionnel possede des remedes du village.

words.culturalNote:
Traditional healer.

Nganga = ritual expert, nkisi = medicine/charm. The nganga-nkisi works with herbs, prayer, and inherited knowledge.

examples.english: The priest finished mass.
examples.french: Le pretre a fini la messe.

words.culturalNote:
Priest, literally God’s ritual-keeper.

Used in Catholic and Kimbanguist contexts. Sango is also commonly heard for Catholic priest.

examples.english: Poison is a great danger.
examples.french: Le poison est un grand danger.

words.culturalNote:
Poison.

Ngenge appears in proverbs about hidden harm. Strongly avoided in conversation as a word of bad omen.

examples.english: The red cloth is beautiful.
examples.french: L'etoffe rouge est belle.

words.culturalNote:
Red.

Ngola names the red of laterite earth, the DRC flag, and ripe peppers. A color tied to land and pride.

examples.english: We climbed the hill to the top.
examples.french: Nous avons gravi la colline jusqu'en haut.

words.culturalNote:
Hill, mountain.

Ngomba covers both gentle hills and steep mountains. Eastern DRC is full of them.

examples.lingala: Ngomba-moto ya Nyiragongo ezali na Goma.
examples.english: The Nyiragongo volcano is in Goma.
examples.french: Le volcan Nyiragongo est a Goma.

words.culturalNote:
Volcano, literally fire-mountain.

Nyiragongo above Goma is a defining national landmark; its eruptions have reshaped Goma’s'history.

examples.english: The cow is eating grass.
examples.french: La vache mange de l'herbe.

words.culturalNote:
Cow, cattle.

Ngombe symbolizes wealth in many Kongo communities. Cattle gifts feature in marriages and ceremonies.

examples.lingala: Feti ya miziki ya pokwa ekosalema.
examples.english: The evening concert will happen.
examples.french: Le concert du soir aura lieu.

words.culturalNote:
Concert, music gathering (corrected from ngombi, which is an archaic harp).

Kongo music nights pack stadiums and yards alike — rumba, soukous, gospel, ndombolo. The feti ya miziki is a communal pulse.

examples.english: The church bell rang.
examples.french: La cloche de l'eglise a sonne.

words.culturalNote:
Bell; also clock hour.

Ngonga marks time — the church bell, the school bell, the noon hour. Ngonga ekoki = the hour has come.

examples.english: We cooked peanuts in the soup.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit des arachides dans la soupe.

words.culturalNote:
Peanut, groundnut.

Nguba is ground into the rich peanut sauce poured over meat or fish, beloved across central Africa.

examples.english: The pig is in the pen.
examples.french: Le porc est dans l'enclos.

words.culturalNote:
Pig, pork.

Nyama ya ngulu = pork. Raised in many compounds for meat and trade.

examples.english: A boa is in the forest.
examples.french: Un boa est dans la foret.

words.culturalNote:
Boa, very large snake.

Nguma fills both forest stories and folklore. Sightings command quick, careful response.

examples.lingala: Tolambi ngungutu na mafuta ya mbila.
examples.english: We cooked eggplant in palm oil.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit l'aubergine a l'huile de palme.

words.culturalNote:
Eggplant, aubergine.

A staple of Kongo cooking, often stewed slowly with palm oil and dried fish.

examples.english: The market peanuts are tasty.
examples.french: Les arachides du marche sont savoureuses.

words.culturalNote:
Roasted groundnuts.

Sold in paper cones at every Kinshasa stop — schools, taxis, churches. A pocket-money snack.

examples.english: We paid one hundred francs.
examples.french: Nous avons paye cent francs.

words.culturalNote:
One hundred.

Falanga = Congolese franc. Daily transactions hop between nkama, nkoto, and dollars.

examples.english: The book costs two hundred.
examples.french: Le livre coute deux cents.

words.culturalNote:
Two hundred.

Literally one-hundred two. Counting is additive: nkama mibale na ntuku mitano = 250.

examples.english: He gave me five hundred.
examples.french: Il m'a donne cinq cents.

words.culturalNote:
Five hundred.

A common Kinshasa price point — fish, bread, transport fares.

examples.english: His anger is over.
examples.french: Sa colere est passee.

words.culturalNote:
Anger, wrath.

Nkanda is treated as a fire to be cooled. Elders mediate quickly; long-held nkanda is seen as harmful to the heart.

examples.lingala: Pesa ngai nkanya mpo na kolia.
examples.english: Give me a fork to eat.
examples.french: Donne-moi une fourchette pour manger.

words.culturalNote:
Fork (utensil).

Kongo meals often use the hand for fufu and saka-saka; the nkanya appears for rice and meat dishes.

examples.english: He has sorrow in his heart.
examples.french: Il porte du chagrin dans le coeur.

words.culturalNote:
Grief, sorrow, regret (gloss corrected; the OCR’d'one-million was wrong).

Nkese names heart-pain, often after loss. Pairs with mawa (sorrow) in laments and prayers.

examples.english: The child rode a bicycle.
examples.french: L'enfant a roule a velo.

words.culturalNote:
Bicycle.

Nkinga is the rural Congo workhorse — hauling charcoal sacks, water cans, and people across long distances.

examples.english: My neck hurts.
examples.french: Mon cou me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Neck.

Esali pasi = is doing pain, the standard active phrasing across the anatomy entries.

examples.english: The doctor gave me medicine.
examples.french: Le medecin m'a donne des medicaments.

words.culturalNote:
Medicine, remedy, charm.

Nkisi covers modern pills, traditional herbs, and ritual charms. Context names which.

examples.english: The tortoise walks slowly.
examples.french: La tortue marche lentement.

words.culturalNote:
Tortoise, turtle.

Nkoba is a frequent figure in Kongo folktales — patient, clever, sometimes a trickster.

examples.english: The leopard ran into the forest.
examples.french: Le leopard a fui dans la foret.

words.culturalNote:
Leopard.

The leopard is a symbol of royal Kongo power; chiefs once wore leopard skin as a mark of authority.

examples.english: The children ate sugar cane.
examples.french: Les enfants ont mange de la canne a sucre.

words.culturalNote:
Sugar cane.

A cheap, beloved sweet — stalks sold by the meter and chewed at roadside.

examples.english: The owner of the house arrived.
examples.french: Le proprietaire de la maison est venu.

words.culturalNote:
Owner, master, lord.

Nkolo signals rightful holding — of a house, a business, or a domain. Also used in religious speech: Nkolo Nzambe = Lord God.

examples.english: My name is Kongolo.
examples.french: Je m'appelle Kongolo.

words.culturalNote:
Name.

A Kongo name carries meaning, lineage, and often a circumstance of birth. Names open doors and tell stories.

examples.english: The cat is playing.
examples.french: Le chat joue.

words.culturalNote:
Cat — domestic (corrected: nkondoko is a wild genet/civet).

Niau (or pusi) is the household cat. Cats are common in Kongo homes as quiet companions and mouse-keepers.

examples.lingala: Mama akei na lisala na nkongo.
examples.english: Mother went to the field with a hoe.
examples.french: Maman est allee au champ avec la houe.

words.culturalNote:
Hoe.

The nkongo is the central farming tool, often passed between generations. Field work begins and ends with it.

examples.english: We gathered firewood to cook.
examples.french: Nous avons ramasse du bois pour cuisiner.

words.culturalNote:
Firewood.

Gathering nkoni is daily work in many villages; in cities makala (charcoal) plays the cooking role.

examples.lingala: Nkoko na ngai abandi koyebisa lisapo.
examples.english: My grandparent began to tell a story.
examples.french: Mon grand-parent a commence a raconter une histoire.

words.culturalNote:
Grandparent (corrected from OCR nkonko).

Nkoko covers grandmother and grandfather alike. Stories from a nkoko shape every Kongo childhood.

examples.english: The lion is the king of animals.
examples.french: Le lion est le roi des animaux.

words.culturalNote:
Lion.

Lions appear in proverbs about courage and authority, even though they no longer roam DRC’s forests.

examples.english: The parrot is speaking.
examples.french: Le perroquet parle.

words.culturalNote:
Parrot.

The African grey parrot (nkoso) is native to the Congo basin and famed for its intelligence and mimicry.

examples.english: We paid a thousand francs.
examples.french: Nous avons paye mille francs.

words.culturalNote:
One thousand.

Nkoto is the everyday Kongo unit at the market and the bus stop. Multiples (nkoto mibale = two thousand) keep the day moving.

examples.lingala: Nkulutu na ngai ayebi makambo mingi.
examples.english: My elder knows many things.
examples.french: Mon aine connait beaucoup de choses.

words.culturalNote:
Elder, older sibling (pairs with leki = younger sibling).

Birth order shapes social life — nkulutu is consulted first, eats first, speaks first.

examples.english: We cooked beans in the morning.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit des haricots le matin.

words.culturalNote:
Beans.

Nkunde simmer slowly with palm oil, onions, and dried fish. A patient, nourishing daily dish.

examples.lingala: Nkungi ezali kotungisa biso na butu.
examples.english: Mosquitoes torment us at night.
examples.french: Les moustiques nous tourmentent la nuit.

words.culturalNote:
Mosquito.

Nkungi carry malaria; mosquito nets (moustikere) are part of every household’s defense.

examples.english: It rained heavily today.
examples.french: Il a beaucoup plu aujourd hui.

words.culturalNote:
Rain (cleaned from OCR no-noko).

Mvula times planting, school visits, and travel. Mvula makasi = a storm. The rainy season transforms the country.

examples.english: Come quickly!
examples.french: Viens vite!

words.culturalNote:
Quickly, immediately.

Noki adds urgency without sharpness. Sala noki = do it quickly; common in households with errands to send.

examples.english: My uncle goes to work.
examples.french: Mon oncle va au travail.

words.culturalNote:
Maternal uncle.

In Kongo kinship the mother’s brother is socially central — counselor, ceremonial witness, often a second father.

examples.english: The northern country is far.
examples.french: Le pays du nord est loin.

words.culturalNote:
North.

From French nord. Older Lingala also uses epai ya likolo for north — the upper side.

examples.lingala: Nsai ya pokwa ezali ya solo.
examples.english: The evening joy is real.
examples.french: La joie du soir est vraie.

words.culturalNote:
Joy.

Nsai pairs with esengo (gladness). The end-of-day relief on the libanda, surrounded by family, is nsai itself.

examples.english: The elders drank palm wine.
examples.french: Les anciens ont bu du vin de palme.

words.culturalNote:
Palm wine.

Tapped fresh from oil-palm trees and shared communally. Strong cultural drink for ceremonies and gatherings of elders.

examples.english: We are seven siblings.
examples.french: Nous sommes sept freres et soeurs.

words.culturalNote:
Seven.

Standard counting word. Often appears in proverbs and biblical counts (the seven days, seven sons).

examples.english: We stayed seven days.
examples.french: Nous sommes restes sept jours.

words.culturalNote:
Seven — duplicate listing kept per "do not drop any words."

Same meaning as #697. The bank had a duplicate; we preserve it.

examples.english: News from the country arrived.
examples.french: Des nouvelles du pays sont arrivees.

words.culturalNote:
News, information.

Nsango from home is precious to the diaspora. Kobeta nsango = to spread news; Mbote, nsango? = Hello, what’s the news?

examples.english: The item fell to the bottom.
examples.french: L'objet est tombe au fond.

words.culturalNote:
Bottom, under, beneath.

Nse contrasts with likolo (top). Used spatially and metaphorically — bana ya nse = the people of the lowlands.

examples.english: The boat arrived at the harbor.
examples.french: Le bateau est arrive au port.

words.culturalNote:
Harbor, port (corrected from nsele).

Libongo is the everyday Lingala word; the Congo and Ubangi rivers carry boats to many libongo.

examples.english: An awful thing happened.
examples.french: Une chose effroyable est arrivee.

words.culturalNote:
Awful, terrifying, horror-inducing.

Nsomo names things that strike fear and silence. Used carefully, often in news of tragedy.

examples.english: The cassava in the field has grown.
examples.french: Le manioc dans le champ a pousse.

words.culturalNote:
Cassava (uncertain regional term; the everyday word is sambala / manioc).

Kept per "do not drop"; verify locally — nsongo may be a regional or dialectal name.

examples.english: We cooked chicken with cassava leaves.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit du poulet aux feuilles de manioc.

words.culturalNote:
Chicken.

Nsoso is the staple meat of celebrations — weddings, baptisms, Sundays. Often combined with mpondu.

examples.english: The hen laid eight eggs.
examples.french: La poule a pondu huit oeufs.

words.culturalNote:
Hen, literally female chicken.

Mwasi = female. Pairs with nsoso mobali = rooster. Hens scratch in every Kongo courtyard.

examples.english: The end of the story has come.
examples.french: La fin du conte est arrivee.

words.culturalNote:
End, limit, conclusion.

Nsuka closes a story, a journey, or patience itself. Te na nsuka = without end.

examples.english: Her hair is long.
examples.french: Ses cheveux sont longs.

words.culturalNote:
Hair (head hair).

Nsuki sing./pl. used the same. Hair styling — braids, plaits, cuts — is a major Kinshasa salon culture.

examples.lingala: Ntaka kati na mboka mibale ezali milai.
examples.english: The distance between the two villages is long.
examples.french: La distance entre les deux villages est grande.

words.culturalNote:
Distance, span.

Ntaka measures physical and emotional distance — between villages, between hearts.

examples.english: This item is expensive.
examples.french: Cet article coute cher.

words.culturalNote:
Expensive, high-priced.

Ntalo = price, mingi = much. The market haggle revolves around this phrase — and its opposite, ntalo moke (cheap).

examples.english: Give me half of the bread.
examples.french: Donne-moi la moitie du pain.

words.culturalNote:
Half, middle (corrected: ndambo means a portion/piece; the standard word for mathematical half is katikati or ntei).

Katikati also means middle/center. Useful at table, market, and in directions.

examples.lingala: Lipela mpe ntela ezali na zando.
examples.english: Guavas and bananas are at the market.
examples.french: Goyaves et bananes sont au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Banana.

Ntela (sing.) / mantela (pl.). Cooking bananas (makemba) are a staple alongside dessert bananas.

examples.lingala: Ntoki ya kosalela maboko ezali ya kitoko.
examples.english: Handcraft art is beautiful.
examples.french: L'art manuel est beau.

words.culturalNote:
Art, skill, craft.

Ntoki names both fine art and practiced skill. Mwana ntoki = a skilled child / apprentice.

examples.english: Every morning I go to work.
examples.french: Chaque matin je vais au travail.

words.culturalNote:
Every morning, daily.

Ntongo = morning, nyonso = every. Shapes the rhythm of work, prayer, and school.

examples.english: The elder reached ninety years.
examples.french: L'aine a atteint quatre-vingt-dix ans.

words.culturalNote:
Ninety, literally nine tens.

A milestone age, celebrated with feasts and blessings — ntuku libwa is rare and revered.

examples.english: We paid twenty francs.
examples.french: Nous avons paye vingt francs.

words.culturalNote:
Twenty, literally two tens.

Decades in Lingala build by ntuku + number. Simple, regular, and very old in the language.

examples.english: Forty years have passed.
examples.french: Quarante ans ont passe.

words.culturalNote:
Forty.

A marker of full adulthood. Many proverbs anchor at forty years.

examples.english: Thirty people came.
examples.french: Trente personnes sont venues.

words.culturalNote:
Thirty.

A modest gathering size for a small family fete.

examples.english: We paid fifty dollars.
examples.french: Nous avons paye cinquante dollars.

words.culturalNote:
Fifty.

A common Kinshasa transaction size; the dollar is in everyday use alongside the franc.

examples.english: Mother reached sixty years.
examples.french: Maman a atteint soixante ans.

words.culturalNote:
Sixty.

A much-honored birthday — children gather, gifts and prayers flow.

examples.english: Eighty elders sat down.
examples.french: Quatre-vingts anciens se sont assis.

words.culturalNote:
Eighty.

A full assembly of elders — rare and reverent.

examples.english: We stayed seventy days.
examples.french: Nous sommes restes soixante-dix jours.

words.culturalNote:
Seventy.

Used in counting longer stays — pilgrimages, mourning periods, extended travel.

examples.english: We cooked beef.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit du boeuf.

words.culturalNote:
Animal, meat.

Nyama covers both — animals in the wild and the meat we eat. Context decides which.

examples.english: I am hungry.
examples.french: J'ai faim.

words.culturalNote:
Hunger.

Nzala is named openly. Hospitality demands that no visitor leave hungry — sharing is sacred.

examples.english: God is with us.
examples.french: Dieu est avec nous.

words.culturalNote:
God.

Nzambe centers Kongo life — in greetings (Nzambe apambola yo = God bless you), prayer, and music. Both Christian and ancestral religious life invoke Nzambe.

examples.english: Many flies are at the market.
examples.french: Beaucoup de mouches sont au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Fly (insect).

Nzinzi gather at markets and uncovered food. A reminder for the washbasin and the lid.

examples.english: My body aches.
examples.french: Mon corps me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Body.

Nzoto is the whole body. Esali pasi = is doing pain, the standard active phrasing across anatomy.

examples.english: He is at the house.
examples.french: Il est a la maison.

words.culturalNote:
At, in — older locative particle (modern usage prefers na).

Still heard in song, prayer, and formal speech; less common in everyday Kinshasa conversation.

examples.english: He stood between the siblings.
examples.french: Il s'est tenu entre les freres.

words.culturalNote:
Between, among, in the midst of.

O ntaka ya = between two. A spatial and relational phrase used in proverbs.

examples.lingala: Sanza ya ogusiti ezali ya mopepe.
examples.english: August is the windy month.
examples.french: Aout est le mois venteux.

words.culturalNote:
August.

From French aout. Marks the end of the dry season in Kinshasa, when winds pick up and skies stay clear.

examples.english: Give me another one.
examples.french: Donne-moi un autre.

words.culturalNote:
Other, another, different (corrected from the gloss-direction error).

Mosusu takes class agreement: eloko mosusu = another thing; bato basusu = other people.

examples.english: The bus arrived at the market.
examples.french: Le bus est arrive au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Bus, autobus.

From French autobus. Kinshasa transport includes otobisi, taxi, and the famous esprit-de-mort minibuses.

examples.lingala: Pamplemousse ezali na ntalo na zando.
examples.english: Grapefruit is expensive at the market.
examples.french: Le pamplemousse coute cher au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Grapefruit.

Kept as the French loanword; Lingala has no separate native term.

examples.english: Easter is a great feast.
examples.french: Paques est une grande fete.

words.culturalNote:
Easter.

From Portuguese pascoa via Kikongo. A major Christian celebration across DRC, with church services and family gatherings.

examples.english: The airplane arrived at the airport.
examples.french: L'avion est arrive a l'aeroport.

words.culturalNote:
Airplane.

From Swahili / French. In older Lingala, ndeke ya bisalelo (mechanical bird) was used.

examples.lingala: Pipa ya mafuta ezali na zando.
examples.english: The oil barrel is at the market.
examples.french: Le baril d'huile est au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Barrel.

From French pipe (cask). Kept as a market staple — oil and fuel sold by the pipa.

examples.english: We bought kerosene for the lamp.
examples.french: Nous avons achete du petrole pour la lampe.

words.culturalNote:
Kerosene, petrol.

From French petrole. In rural areas pitolo still fuels lamps and stoves.

examples.english: His words are clear.
examples.french: Ses paroles sont claires.

words.culturalNote:
Clear, open, plainly visible.

Polele is one of the warmest Lingala adjectives — clear weather, clear speech, an open heart.

examples.english: The house door is closed.
examples.french: La porte de la maison est fermee.

words.culturalNote:
Door (cleaned from OCR polte; passive ekangami = is closed).

Ekuke is the standard word for door. Kanga is the verb stem to close; ekangami is the perfect passive state.

examples.english: Those (people) are near me.
examples.french: Ceux-la sont pres de moi.

words.culturalNote:
Those (people) — cleaned from OCR pron.

Baoyo / boye = those, used demonstratively. Class agreement chooses the right form.

examples.english: The cat is sleeping.
examples.french: Le chat dort.

words.culturalNote:
Cat (domestic).

Pusi is the standard cat word; niau is also used. Both are heard side by side.

examples.english: The dust on the road is heavy.
examples.french: La poussiere de la route est abondante.

words.culturalNote:
Dust.

The dry season layers Kinshasa in putulu; the rains wash it away.

examples.lingala: Rido ya lininisa ezali ya bule.
examples.english: The window curtain is blue.
examples.french: Le rideau de la fenetre est bleu.

words.culturalNote:
Curtain.

From French rideau. Hung on doorways and windows; chosen with care for the front room.

examples.english: My watch broke.
examples.french: Ma montre est cassee.

words.culturalNote:
Watch, clock; also hour (corrected example: kopasuka = to split/break).

From French. Sa shows the hour and the wristwatch; ngonga is also used for the bell-marked hour.

examples.english: On Saturday we will go to the market.
examples.french: Samedi nous irons au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Saturday.

From Portuguese sabado via Kikongo. Market day in many Kinshasa quarters.

examples.english: We bought soap for washing.
examples.french: Nous avons achete du savon pour laver.

words.culturalNote:
Soap.

From French savon. Brown bar soap (saboni mokembo) is the everyday staple for clothes and dishes.

examples.english: The children are playing in the courtyard.
examples.french: Les enfants jouent dans la cour.

words.culturalNote:
To play, to joke.

Kosakana with bana = play with children; kosakana na maloba = to joke with words.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Jouer, plaisanter.

Kosakana na bana = jouer avec les enfants ; kosakana na maloba = plaisanter avec les mots.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosakana — kosakana, kosakana na maloba.

Kosakana na bana = kosakana na bana; kosakana na maloba = kosakana na maloba.

examples.lingala: Saki ya manioc ezali ya kilo zomi.
examples.english: The sack of cassava is ten kilos.
examples.french: Le sac de manioc fait dix kilos.

words.culturalNote:
Sack, large bag.

From French sac. Saki holds the family’s rice, cassava, charcoal — bought by weight.

examples.english: The chief proclaimed the news.
examples.french: Le chef a proclame la nouvelle.

words.culturalNote:
To declare, proclaim, announce.

Kosakola has weight — used for chiefs’ declarations and preachers’ messages.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Déclarer — dire publiquement qu'une chose est vraie.

Kosakola, c'est annoncer, déclarer, proclamer. L'indépendance est sakoli ; la victoire est sakoli ; le prêtre sakoli la bénédiction — paroles publiques qui changent la pièce.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosakola — koloba na miso ya bato ete eloko ezali solo.

Kosakola elimboli kosakola, kobimisa polele. Lipanda esakoli; elonga esakoli; nganga-Nzambe asakoli mapamboli — maloba ya polele oyo ebongoli ndako.

examples.english: My work is done.
examples.french: Mon travail est fini.

words.culturalNote:
Work (variant; cf. #597).

Mosala is daily labor and honor alike. Mosala malamu = good work.

examples.english: I used the money well.
examples.french: J'ai bien utilise l'argent.

words.culturalNote:
To use, to work for, to serve (corrected past tense: nasalelaki = I used).

Kosalela carries the everyday use-of-things and the deeper service-to-someone meaning.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Utiliser, travailler pour, servir (passé correct : nasalelaki = j'ai utilisé).

Kosalela porte à la fois l'usage quotidien des choses et le sens plus profond du service à quelqu'un.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosalela — kosalela eloko, kosalela mpo na moto, kosalisa.

Kosalela ememi bosaleli ya mokolo na mokolo ya biloko mpe ndimbola ya kosalisa moto.

examples.english: I helped you with my heart.
examples.french: Je t'ai aide avec coeur.

words.culturalNote:
To help (corrected verb form: nasalisi, not nasaleli).

Kosalisa = to make-work, the causative of kosala. The everyday verb of helping a neighbor or family.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Aider — la main offerte pour la charge d'autrui.

Kosalisa, c'est aider. Du petit kosalisa avec un panier à l'aide plus profonde dans la difficulté, le mot nomme l'amour pratique qui tient la communauté tricotée.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosalisa — loboko oyo epesami mpo na mokumba ya moto mosusu.

Kosalisa elimboli kosalisa. Banda kosalisa mokemoke na kitunga kino lisalisi ya mozindo na mpasi, liloba etangaka bolingo ya mosala oyo esimbi lisanga.

examples.english: His words are true.
examples.french: Ses paroles sont vraies.

words.culturalNote:
Correct, true, straight (corrected: samba means to plead a legal case; standard truth is solo or sembo).

Solo = truth; sembo = straight/just. Both carry moral weight.

examples.english: We prayed for the country.
examples.french: Nous avons prie pour le pays.

words.culturalNote:
To pray.

Kosambela centers Kinshasa Sunday life and morning household prayer alike.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Prier.

Kosambela est au centre de la vie dominicale à Kinshasa comme de la prière matinale à la maison.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosambela — kosambela.

Kosambela ezali na motó ya bomoyi ya eyenga na Kinshasa mpe ya losambo ya tongo na ndako.

examples.english: Seven days passed.
examples.french: Sept jours ont passe.

words.culturalNote:
Seven — variant of nsambo (cf. #697-698).

Kept per "do not drop any words."

examples.english: The children played in the yard.
examples.french: Les enfants ont joue dans la cour.

words.culturalNote:
To play (variant of kosakana, cf. #746).

Shorter form heard in some regions and songs.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Jouer (variante de kosakana).

Forme plus courte entendue dans certaines régions et chansons.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosana — kosakana (ndenge mosusu ya kosakana).

Ndenge ya mokuse oyo eyokami na bisika mosusu mpe na banzembo.

examples.english: This tree is very tall.
examples.french: Cet arbre est tres grand.

words.culturalNote:
High, tall (corrected from sanda).

Molai pairs with mokuse (short). Used for trees, people, and journeys.

examples.english: We put the items in the box.
examples.french: Nous avons range les affaires dans la boite.

words.culturalNote:
Box, chest, trunk.

From Swahili sanduku. The family sanduku keeps documents, mementos, and quietly held treasures.

examples.english: The priest prayed at the church.
examples.french: Le pretre a prie a l'eglise.

words.culturalNote:
Catholic priest; also news.

Sango pere = Father (priest). The same word also means news in informal greetings: sango? = what’s the news?

examples.lingala: Sani ya bilei ezali na mesa.
examples.english: The food plate is on the table.
examples.french: L'assiette de nourriture est sur la table.

words.culturalNote:
Plate, dish.

Sani holds the meal; in many Kongo homes a shared sani gathers everyone around it.

examples.english: Mother used a comb.
examples.french: Maman a utilise un peigne.

words.culturalNote:
Comb (corrected: kisanola is the universal grammatical standard; bisanola pl.).

A daily tool — natural-hair styling is a major cultural ritual in Kinshasa salons.

examples.english: The month of July passed.
examples.french: Le mois de juillet est passe.

words.culturalNote:
Month, moon.

Sanza counts months and names the moon. The lunar calendar lives in proverbs and farming sayings.

examples.english: My shoes are torn.
examples.french: Mes chaussures sont dechirees.

words.culturalNote:
Shoes, slippers (corrected verb: epasuki = are torn/split).

From Portuguese sapato via Kikongo. Kept polished for church and special occasions.

examples.english: Mother prays the rosary in the morning.
examples.french: Maman recite le chapelet le matin.

words.culturalNote:
Rosary.

From French chapelet. The morning rosary is a Catholic Kinshasa rhythm in many households.

examples.english: Come right now!
examples.french: Viens tout de suite!

words.culturalNote:
Now, right now, immediately.

Sasapi is the most urgent of the now-words (cf. sikawa, sikoyo). Used when waiting is over.

examples.english: We are the same.
examples.french: Nous sommes pareils.

words.culturalNote:
Same, only, just.

Se carries a small-but-firm emphasis. Se moko = the very same one.

examples.english: My tooth hurts.
examples.french: Ma dent me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Toothache (corrected sentence: tooth-as-subject pattern).

Lino na ngai esali pasi = literally my tooth is doing pain; standard Kongo phrasing for body afflictions.

examples.english: The office boss arrived.
examples.french: Le chef du bureau est arrive.

words.culturalNote:
Chief, boss.

From French chef. Used for workplace bosses; mokonzi remains the deeper word for chief/leader.

examples.english: This bed is comfortable.
examples.french: Ce lit est confortable.

words.culturalNote:
Comfortable, soft (corrected from OCR sei).

Pete is the everyday word for soft surfaces, gentle voices, and easy work.

examples.english: A century passed in a hundred years.
examples.french: Un siecle est passe en cent ans.

words.culturalNote:
Century.

From Portuguese seculo via Kikongo. Used in history and church readings.

examples.english: The direct road is near.
examples.french: Le chemin droit est proche.

words.culturalNote:
Straight, direct, honest (corrected spelling: sembo, not semba).

Sembo applies to roads and to character. Moto ya sembo = an honest person.

examples.lingala: Semeki na ngai ayei na fete.
examples.english: My in-law came to the party.
examples.french: Mon beau-frere est venu a la fete.

words.culturalNote:
In-law (brother- or sister-in-law).

Semeki names the new kin gained through marriage. The relationship carries warm but careful respect.

examples.lingala: Semisi ya tata ezali ya pembe.
examples.english: Father s shirt is white.
examples.french: La chemise de pere est blanche.

words.culturalNote:
Shirt.

From French chemise. Pressed semisi for church and special occasions; everyday t-shirts go by maillot.

examples.english: He asked me for help.
examples.french: Il m'a demande de l'aide.

words.culturalNote:
To ask, to request, to beg.

Kosenga is a polite request, not a demand. Asking elders is a careful art in Kongo etiquette.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Demander, solliciter, prier.

Kosenga est une demande polie, pas une exigence. Demander aux anciens est un art prudent dans l'étiquette du Kongo.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosenga — kosenga na boboto.

Kosenga ezali bosengeli ya boboto, ezali kosenga makasi te. Kosenga bampaka ezali mosala ya bopembe na mibeko ya bonkonde ya Kongo.

examples.english: You must go.
examples.french: Tu dois partir.

words.culturalNote:
Must, ought to.

Sengeli expresses obligation gently — duty owed to family, country, or God.

examples.english: I am pleased with you.
examples.french: Je suis content de toi.

words.culturalNote:
To be pleased, glad, happy with.

Kosepela na = to be pleased with. Used freely to express warm satisfaction.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Se réjouir — la joie qui monte.

Kosepela, c'est être heureux ou se réjouir. Un chant, une rencontre, un repas — ce que tu kosepela laisse une marque ; le verbe nomme chaque petit moment illuminé.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosepela — esengo oyo ezali komata.

Kosepela elimboli kozala na esengo to kosepela. Loyembo, bokutani, kolia — oyo osepeli etiki elembo; liloba etangaka ntango nyonso ya mokemoke ya kongenga.

examples.lingala: Sanza ya setembele ezali ya mvula.
examples.english: September is a rainy month.
examples.french: Septembre est un mois pluvieux.

words.culturalNote:
September.

From French septembre. School re-opens in setembele across DRC.

examples.english: I cut the meat with a knife.
examples.french: J'ai coupe la viande avec un couteau.

words.culturalNote:
To cut, to slice (corrected from sesa).

Kokata names the kitchen cut and the field machete cut. The clean separation of one thing into two.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Couper — partager avec la lame ou la parole.

Kokata est l'infinitif « couper ». Le pain, le tissu, un arbre, ou la conversation qui s'éternise — le même mot tranche et décide.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokata — kokabola na mbeli to na liloba.

Kokata elimboli kokata. Mampa, elamba, nzete, to lisolo oyo eumeli mingi — liloba moko ekati mpe ekata.

examples.english: The new cloth is beautiful.
examples.french: L'etoffe neuve est belle.

words.culturalNote:
New.

Sika takes class agreement. A new cloth, a new road, a new beginning — all marked with sika.

examples.english: Come now!
examples.french: Viens maintenant!

words.culturalNote:
Now.

Sikawa is the immediate now (paired with sikoyo, sasapi). Tense and a little urgent.

examples.english: Now I am done.
examples.french: Maintenant j'ai fini.

words.culturalNote:
Now, right now.

Sikoyo is the everyday now — the present moment, what is happening.

examples.english: I finished the work.
examples.french: J'ai fini le travail.

words.culturalNote:
To finish, to complete.

Kosilisa is to bring something to its end, by your own action — a project, a meal, a debt.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Terminer — mener la tâche jusqu'à sa fin.

Kosilisa, c'est terminer ou compléter. Mosala kosilisa lobi — le travail à finir demain — cadence les plans du lendemain.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosilisa — kokomisa mosala kino na suka.

Kosilisa elimboli kosilisa to kosukisa. Mosala kosilisa lobi — mosala mpo ya kosilisa lobi — etalisaka mibongisi ya mokolo oyo elandi.

examples.english: He arrived after me.
examples.french: Il est arrive apres moi.

words.culturalNote:
After, behind, later.

Sima ya = after / behind. Used in time and space alike.

examples.english: He held my hand.
examples.french: Il a tenu ma main.

words.culturalNote:
To touch, hold, grasp.

Kosimba carries physical and emotional weight — to hold a hand, to keep a promise (kosimba elaka).
words.culturalNoteFr:
Tenir — la main refermée sur ce qui compte.

Kosimba, c'est tenir ou saisir. La main d'un enfant à la traversée, l'anneau de mariage glissé au doigt, une promesse tenue — kosimba, c'est garder quelque chose près de soi.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosimba — loboko ekangamaki na oyo ezali na ntina.

Kosimba elimboli kosimba. Loboko ya mwana na ntango ya koleka nzela, lopete ya libala etiami na mosapi, elaka esimbamaki — kosimba ezali kobomba eloko penepene.

examples.english: We went to the cinema in the evening.
examples.french: Nous sommes alles au cinema le soir.

words.culturalNote:
Cinema, movies.

From French cinema. Kinshasa cinema culture is now mostly home-based, with films watched on phones and small TVs.

examples.english: The watchman is at the gate.
examples.french: Le gardien est a la porte.

words.culturalNote:
Watchman, guard (variant of mokengeli).

Many parcelle have a sinzili at the ekuke — known by name, trusted by the family.

examples.english: The soldier is at the camp.
examples.french: Le soldat est au camp.

words.culturalNote:
Soldier.

From French soldat. Soda are familiar at checkpoints and parade grounds in DRC cities.

examples.english: The car driver arrived.
examples.french: Le chauffeur de la voiture est arrive.

words.culturalNote:
Driver, chauffeur.

From French chauffeur. The sofele is part of the daily Kinshasa scene — taxis, buses, family cars.

examples.english: Father cut the tree with an axe.
examples.french: Pere a abattu l'arbre avec une hache.

words.culturalNote:
Axe.

The soka clears land, cuts firewood, and shapes timber. Often kept by the kitchen door.

examples.english: If you come, we go.
examples.french: Si tu viens, nous partons.

words.culturalNote:
If, when (conditional).

Soki opens conditional clauses. Soki + verb sets the condition for the rest of the sentence.

examples.english: About thirty people came.
examples.french: Environ trente personnes sont venues.

words.culturalNote:
About, approximately.

Soko softens a count or a time. Soko mokolo moko = about one day.

examples.english: Your words are true.
examples.french: Tes paroles sont vraies.

words.culturalNote:
Truth, really, for real.

Solo is the heart of Kongo testimony — koloba solo = to speak truth. Pairs with sembo.

examples.english: I bought bread at the market.
examples.french: J'ai achete du pain au marche.

words.culturalNote:
To buy — the daily errand of the market.

Kosomba is the everyday market verb that runs through every Congolese household budget: kosomba mampa (buy bread), kosomba bilei (buy food), kosomba elamba (buy cloth). It pairs with koteka (to sell) in the rhythm of zando life. A mother sending a child on a market errand says "kende kosomba" — go buy — and the small mission begins.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Acheter — la course quotidienne au marché.

Kosomba est le verbe quotidien du marché qui traverse tout budget de ménage congolais : kosomba mampa (acheter du pain), kosomba bilei (acheter à manger), kosomba elamba (acheter du tissu). Il va de pair avec koteka (vendre) dans le rythme de la vie du zando. Une mère envoyant un enfant en course au marché dit « kende kosomba » — va acheter — et la petite mission commence.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosomba — mosala ya mokolo na mokolo ya zando.

Kosomba ezali liloba ya zando oyo eleki na budget ya libota nyonso ya bato ya Congo: kosomba mampa, kosomba bilei, kosomba elamba. Esangani na koteka na rythme ya bomoyi ya zando. Mama oyo atindi mwana na zando alobaka « kende kosomba » — mpe mosala ya mokemoke ebandi.

examples.english: We exchanged our items.
examples.french: Nous avons echange nos affaires.

words.culturalNote:
To exchange, change, convert (corrected from sombitinya).

Kobongola also means to translate (kobongola maloba = to translate words).
words.culturalNoteFr:
Changer — transformer une forme en une autre.

Kobongola est l'infinitif « changer » ou « traduire ». Des vêtements, de l'argent, un esprit, une langue — kobongola, c'est faire passer une chose d'un état à un autre, pour le prochain usage.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobongola — kobongola ndenge moko na ndenge mosusu.

Kobongola elimboli kobongola to koloba na monoko mosusu. Bilamba, mbongo, makanisi, monoko — kobongola ezali kosala ete eloko ekoma ndenge mosusu, ekoki na bosaleli ya sika.

examples.english: The shame is strong.
examples.french: La honte est forte.

words.culturalNote:
Shame.

Nsoni in Kongo culture is a serious social weight. Avoiding nsoni shapes much daily behavior — modesty, respect, restraint.

examples.english: Mother sewed cloth.
examples.french: Maman a cousu une etoffe.

words.culturalNote:
To sew (also to build).

Kotonga covers stitching cloth and constructing a house — the verb of building things together piece by piece.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Construire — la montée lente des murs.

Kotonga, c'est bâtir. D'une seule ndako à toute une engumba, kotonga est un travail patient — le maçon, le menuisier, la famille mettant ensemble pour les briques.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotonga — komata ya malembe ya bifelo.

Kotonga elimboli kotonga. Banda na ndako moko kino na engumba mobimba, kotonga ezali mosala ya bopembe — motongi, motongi ya banzete, libota oyo esangisi mbongo mpo na biteni.

examples.english: My sock is torn.
examples.french: Ma chaussette est dechiree.

words.culturalNote:
Sock (corrected verb: epasuki = is torn).

From French chaussette. Worn for school uniforms and church visits.

examples.lingala: Mboka ya sudi ezali na molunge.
examples.english: The southern country is hot.
examples.french: Le pays du sud est chaud.

words.culturalNote:
South.

From French sud. Older Lingala uses epai ya nse = the lower side.

examples.english: We added sugar to the tea.
examples.french: Nous avons ajoute du sucre au the.

words.culturalNote:
Sugar.

From Arabic via Swahili sukari. Sweet tea and sweetened porridge are Kongo morning staples.

examples.english: I finished the work.
examples.french: J'ai termine le travail.

words.culturalNote:
To finish off, to end.

Close cousin of kosilisa; carries a slightly stronger sense of ending fully.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Achever, mettre fin.

Proche cousin de kosilisa ; porte un sens légèrement plus fort de fin complète.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosukisa — kokomisa na nsuka, kosukisa mobimba.

Ndeko ya kosilisa; ezali na ndimbola ya nsuka oyo eleki makasi mwa moke.

examples.english: Mother washed clothes.
examples.french: Maman a lave les habits.

words.culturalNote:
To wash.

Kosukola is the everyday verb — clothes, dishes, body. Saturday morning is wash day in many homes.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Laver — eau et savon contre la poussière du jour.

Kosukola, c'est laver ou se baigner. Le kosukola du matin, le linge sur le fil, les mains avant le repas — la discipline quotidienne du propre. (Kosola tout seul veut généralement dire éplucher ou défricher.)
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosukola — mai na sabolo likolo ya putulu ya mokolo.

Kosukola elimboli kosukola to kosukola nzoto. Kosukola ya tongo, bilamba na nzela ya bilamba, maboko liboso ya kolia — molongo ya mokolo na mokolo ya bopembe. (Kosola yango moko elimboli mingi koputola to kolongola matiti.)

examples.english: My room is small.
examples.french: Ma chambre est petite.

words.culturalNote:
Room.

Suku names a room within the ndako (house). Suku ya kolala = bedroom; suku ya kolia = dining room.

examples.english: Sin is not desired.
examples.french: Le peche ne doit pas etre.

words.culturalNote:
Sin (standard noun form of sumuki).

A weighty word in Christian Kongo speech; lisumu is named openly in prayer and confession.

examples.english: The meat soup is tasty.
examples.french: La soupe de viande est savoureuse.

words.culturalNote:
Soup.

From French soupe. Supu ya nguba (peanut soup) is one of central Africa's most beloved dishes.

examples.english: Another item is at the market.
examples.french: Un autre article est au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Other, another (variant; cf. #730).

Mosusu / basusu (pl.) takes class agreement.

examples.english: The dog bit the child.
examples.french: Le chien a mordu l'enfant.

words.culturalNote:
To bite.

Koswa names the bite of dogs, snakes, mosquitoes, and sharp words.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Mordre.

Koswa nomme la morsure des chiens, des serpents, des moustiques, et des paroles tranchantes.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koswa — koswa.

Koswa etangaka koswa ya mbwa, ya bantoka, ya bangungi, mpe ya maloba ya makasi.

examples.english: The siblings are quarreling.
examples.french: Les freres se disputent.

words.culturalNote:
To quarrel, argue.

Koswana is the open, voiced disagreement. Elders step in to cool it before it becomes lasting nkanda.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Se quereller, se disputer.

Koswana est le désaccord ouvert et vocal. Les anciens interviennent pour le refroidir avant qu'il ne devienne nkanda durable.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koswana — koswana, kotunisana.

Koswana ezali boboyani ya polele mpe ya mongongo makasi. Bampaka bakotaka mpo na kokitisa yango liboso ekoma nkanda ya kala.

examples.english: The goat is in the pen.
examples.french: La chevre est dans l'enclos.

words.culturalNote:
Goat.

Goats are central to Kongo households — meat, milk, and ceremonial sacrifice. A wedding gift may include taba.

examples.english: I went to visit grandma.
examples.french: Je suis alle rendre visite a grand-mere.

words.culturalNote:
To visit, to look at (variant; cf. #492).

Kotala carries warmth — visiting an elder, looking after a child.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Regarder — les yeux posés sur ce qui en a besoin.

Kotala, c'est regarder, observer, veiller. Le gardien, le médecin, la mère, tous kotala leur charge — des yeux qui protègent en faisant attention.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotala — miso etia likolo ya oyo esengeli na yango.

Kotala elimboli kotala, kobatela. Mokengeli, monganga, mama nyonso bakotala oyo babateli — miso oyo ebateli na kotya likebi.

examples.english: The mirror is on the wall.
examples.french: Le miroir est sur le mur.

words.culturalNote:
Mirror (corrected example: efelo = wall, not lopango).

Talatala is the household mirror. Efelo is the inside wall of a room.

examples.english: We walked far.
examples.french: Nous avons marche longtemps.

words.culturalNote:
To walk, to travel on foot.

Kotambola covers walking, traveling, and managing — kotambola malamu = it is going well.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Marcher, voyager à pied.

Kotambola couvre la marche, le voyage, et la gestion — kotambola malamu = ça se passe bien.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotambola — kotambola na makolo.

Kotambola ezipi kotambola, mobembo, mpe bobongisi — kotambola malamu = ezali kotambola malamu.

examples.english: The child read the book.
examples.french: L'enfant a lu le livre.

words.culturalNote:
To read, to count, to recite.

Kotanga makei = to count eggs; kotanga buku = to read a book. The same verb for both. Universally recognised across Central Africa; the spicy warmth of fresh tangawisi root is a standard household remedy for colds, coughs, and stomach trouble.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Lire — les yeux qui descendent la page.

Kotanga, c'est lire et compter. Les enfants apprennent à kotanga à l'école ; les commerçants kotanga leurs chiffres ; le même mot couvre lettres et nombres.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotanga — miso ezali kokita lokasa.

Kotanga elimboli kotanga mpe kotanga motango. Bana bayekolaka kotanga na kelasi; bamotekisi batangaka motango na bango; liloba moko ezipi makomi mpe motango.

examples.english: We added ginger to the tea.
examples.french: Nous avons ajoute du gingembre au the.

words.culturalNote:
Ginger.

A staple seasoning and home remedy — ginger tea for colds is widely trusted.

examples.english: Time is important.
examples.french: Le temps est important.

words.culturalNote:
Time, hour, moment.

Tango carries patience in Kongo culture; relationships take tango, and rushing risks shallowness.

examples.english: Father went to work.
examples.french: Pere est alle au travail.

words.culturalNote:
Father (corrected verb: akende = went).

Tata is also a respectful address for any older man. Tata Nkoko = grandfather.

examples.english: Grandfather knows many things.
examples.french: Grand-pere connait beaucoup de choses.

words.culturalNote:
Grandfather.

The tata nkoko anchors family memory and lineage. His blessing is sought before major decisions.

examples.english: I was surprised by that news.
examples.french: J'ai ete surpris par cette nouvelle.

words.culturalNote:
To be surprised, amazed (corrected from tatabana).

Kokamwa names wonder, astonishment, and shock alike.

examples.english: This bed is soft.
examples.french: Ce lit est doux.

words.culturalNote:
Soft (corrected from tatu, which is non-standard).

Pete is the universal Lingala word for soft, pliable, and comfortable.

examples.english: No, I am not coming.
examples.french: Non, je ne viens pas.

words.culturalNote:
No, not.

Te is the negative particle placed after the verb. Yes is iyo or ee.

examples.english: We stayed until evening.
examples.french: Nous sommes restes jusqu'au soir.

words.culturalNote:
Until, till.

Tii na = until. Used for time and distance — tii Kinshasa = all the way to Kinshasa.

examples.english: Mother sold vegetables at the market.
examples.french: Maman a vendu des legumes au marche.

words.culturalNote:
To sell.

Koteka pairs with kosomba (to buy). The market is a daily Kongo economic and social hub.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Vendre.

Koteka va de pair avec kosomba (acheter). Le marché est un centre économique et social quotidien du Kongo.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koteka — koteka.

Koteka esangani na kosomba. Zando ezali esika ya motó ya mombongo mpe ya lisanga ya mokolo na mokolo ya Kongo.

examples.english: He resold the items at a high price.
examples.french: Il a revendu les marchandises a un prix eleve.

words.culturalNote:
To resell, to cause to sell (causative of koteka).

Middle-traders (batekisi) are essential to the Kinshasa supply chain.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Revendre, faire vendre (causatif de koteka).

Les intermédiaires (batekisi) sont essentiels à la chaîne d'approvisionnement de Kinshasa.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotekisa — koteka lisusu, kosala ete moto ateka (causatif ya koteka).

Batekisi bazali na ntina mingi na molongo ya bozwi biloko ya Kinshasa.

examples.english: The fruit has ripened.
examples.french: Le fruit est mur.

words.culturalNote:
To ripen, to become ripe.

Kotela names natural maturing — fruit, an idea, a child growing up.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Mûrir, devenir mûr.

Kotela nomme la maturation naturelle — un fruit, une idée, un enfant qui grandit.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotela — kotela, kokoma na ntango.

Kotela etangaka bokoli ya bomoyi — mbuma, likanisi, mwana oyo azali kokola.

examples.english: He stood in front of the house.
examples.french: Il s'est tenu devant la maison.

words.culturalNote:
To stand, to stop.

Kotelema also means to halt; a chief stands first when speaking, signaling attention.

examples.english: The children are watching television this evening.
examples.french: Les enfants regardent la television ce soir.

words.culturalNote:
Television.

From French television. Family evenings often center on televizyo — football matches, news, telenovelas.

examples.english: We drank morning tea.
examples.french: Nous avons bu le the du matin.

words.culturalNote: Ti — informal/truncated spelling of tii (tea); a French loan (the). Both spellings are heard in Kinshasa speech. See also tii (#ti-tea in bank).

examples.english: He abandoned his work.
examples.french: Il a abandonne son travail.

words.culturalNote:
To abandon, leave, allow (variant; cf. #400).

Kotika carries lighter (allow) and heavier (abandon) meanings; context decides.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Laisser (quelqu'un ou quelque chose), permettre.

Kotika peut signifier partir physiquement ou laisser-être. Le contexte dit lequel.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotika — kotika moto to eloko, kondima.

Kotika ekoki kolimbola kobima ya nzoto to kotika eloko. Esika ya likambo eyebisi nini ezali.

examples.english: I stayed at the house.
examples.french: Je suis reste a la maison.

words.culturalNote:
To remain, to stay behind.

Kotikala is to be left/staying — etikali = remains; natikali = I am left.

examples.english: I bought a plane ticket.
examples.french: J'ai achete un billet d'avion.

words.culturalNote:
Ticket.

From English. Tike ya pepo (plane ticket) is the diaspora’s most longed-after purchase.

examples.english: He sent a letter to mother.
examples.french: Il a envoye une lettre a maman.

words.culturalNote:
To send (corrected example: mokanda = letter, not nkanda = anger).

Kotinda is sending — letters, money, messages, news.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Envoyer (exemple corrigé : mokanda = lettre, pas nkanda = colère).

Kotinda, c'est envoyer — lettres, argent, messages, nouvelles.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotinda — kotinda eloko to nsango.

Kotinda elimboli kotinda — mikanda, mbongo, nsango, nsango ya sika.

examples.english: He sent me a letter.
examples.french: Il m'a envoye une lettre.

words.culturalNote:
To send to / for someone (applicative of kotinda).

The -el- suffix marks the recipient — the standard Bantu applicative.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Envoyer à / pour quelqu'un (applicatif de kotinda).

Le suffixe -el- marque le destinataire — applicatif bantou standard.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotindela — kotinda epai ya moto (applicatif ya kotinda).

Suffixe -el- emonisi moto oyo azwi — applicatif ya solo ya Bantou.

examples.english: He pushed the car.
examples.french: Il a pousse la voiture.

words.culturalNote:
To push, to drive forward.

Causative of kotinda. Used physically and figuratively — kotindisa mosala = to push the work forward.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Pousser, faire avancer.

Causatif de kotinda. Utilisé physiquement et figurativement — kotindisa mosala = pousser le travail vers l'avant.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotindisa — kotinda, kotindisa liboso.

Causatif ya kotinda. Basaleli yango na nzoto mpe na ndimbola — kotindisa mosala = kotindisa mosala liboso.

examples.english: He put the items on the table.
examples.french: Il a pose les affaires sur la table.

words.culturalNote:
To put, to place, to set down.

A core action verb. Kotiya motema = to set one’s'heart on something.

examples.english: Do you want tea or coffee?
examples.french: Veux-tu du the ou du cafe?

words.culturalNote: To — two overlapping uses: (1) CONJUNCTION: "or" in alternative questions: Olingi tii to kafe? = Tea or coffee? (2) SUBJECT PREFIX: "we" — to- is attached to a verb to mark first-person plural: tokei = we went (to + kei).

examples.english: We went to the market.
examples.french: Nous sommes alles au marche.

words.culturalNote:
We (subject prefix).

To- attaches to verbs as the 1st-person plural marker. Tokei = we went; tolambi = we cooked.

examples.english: He sent the child to the market.
examples.french: Il a envoye l'enfant au marche.

words.culturalNote:
To send, dispatch.

Used for sending a person on an errand; cousin to kotinda (sending things and messages).

examples.english: We bought tomatoes at the market.
examples.french: Nous avons achete des tomates au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Tomato.

From French tomate. The base of Kongo sauces, simmered with onion, garlic, and chili.

examples.english: The bottle is full of water.
examples.french: La bouteille est pleine d'eau.

words.culturalNote:
To fill, to be full.

Kotonda + na = to be filled with. Kotonda na esengo = to be full of joy.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Remplir, être plein.

Kotonda + na = être rempli de. Kotonda na esengo = être plein de joie.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotonda — kotonda, kotonda mobimba.

Kotonda + na = kotonda na. Kotonda na esengo = kotonda na esengo.

examples.english: I thank you very much.
examples.french: Je te remercie beaucoup.

words.culturalNote:
Thanks (noun) — the act of thanking.

Botondi pairs with the verb kotondo. Kopesa botondi = to give thanks. Matondi mingi is also a common phrase.

examples.english: They built a new house.
examples.french: Ils ont construit une nouvelle maison.

words.culturalNote:
To build (variant; cf. #795 for sewing sense).

The same verb sews cloth and builds a house — a craft of assembling pieces.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Construire — la montée lente des murs.

Kotonga, c'est bâtir. D'une seule ndako à toute une engumba, kotonga est un travail patient — le maçon, le menuisier, la famille mettant ensemble pour les briques.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotonga — komata ya malembe ya bifelo.

Kotonga elimboli kotonga. Banda na ndako moko kino na engumba mobimba, kotonga ezali mosala ya bopembe — motongi, motongi ya banzete, libota oyo esangisi mbongo mpo na biteni.

examples.english: The child obeyed his father.
examples.french: L'enfant a obei a son pere.

words.culturalNote:
To obey, to respect.

Kotosa carries the weight of Kongo respect — for parents, elders, and tradition.

examples.english: We worked with difficulty.
examples.french: Nous avons travaille avec peine.

words.culturalNote:
With difficulty, painfully.

Na mpasi is a phrase modifier — softens or sharpens a verb to mean it was hard.

examples.english: The case went to court.
examples.french: L'affaire est allee au tribunal.

words.culturalNote:
Court of law, tribunal.

From French tribunal. Both state and customary courts handle disputes; elders often mediate before going formal.

examples.english: The fire burned the tree.
examples.french: Le feu a brule l'arbre.

words.culturalNote:
To burn.

Kotumba names cooking-fires, brush-clearing, and emotional burning (kotumba motema).
words.culturalNoteFr:
Brûler — le feu prenant ce qu'il peut tenir.

Kotumba, c'est brûler. Le makala dans le foyer, la brousse sèche au bord du champ, le pain laissé trop longtemps — moto kotumba ce qu'il atteint.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotumba — moto ezali kozwa oyo ekoki kosimba.

Kotumba elimboli kotumba. Makala na fulo, matiti ya kokauka na monoko ya elanga, mampa oyo etikalaki ntango molai — moto ekotumba oyo ekomi.

examples.english: Father does not smoke tobacco.
examples.french: Pere ne fume pas le tabac.

words.culturalNote:
To smoke tobacco (corrected: komela = to drink; the standard verb for smoking is to "drink" the smoke).

In Lingala one melaka likaya or melaka tumbako — drinks the cigarette or tobacco.

examples.english: He asked me a question.
examples.french: Il m'a pose une question.

words.culturalNote:
To ask a question.

Kotuna is to ask for information (vs. kosenga = to ask for a thing/favor).
words.culturalNoteFr:
Poser une question.

Kotuna, c'est demander une information (vs. kosenga = demander une chose ou une faveur).
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotuna — kotuna motuna.

Kotuna elimboli kotuna mpo na koyeba (vs. kosenga = kosenga eloko to ngolu).

examples.english: Mosquitoes troubled us at night.
examples.french: Les moustiques nous ont tourmentes la nuit.

words.culturalNote:
To annoy, to trouble.

Used for pests, persistent worries, and trying people. Pairs with the calmer kotungisa te = do not trouble.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Ennuyer, troubler.

Utilisé pour les nuisibles, les soucis tenaces, et les gens éprouvants. Va de pair avec le plus calme kotungisa te = ne dérange pas.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotungisa — kotungisa, kotia mokakatano.

Basaleli yango mpo na biloko oyo etungisaka, makambo oyo eumeli, mpe bato oyo bayoki moto. Esangani na kotungisa te = kotungisa te.

examples.english: Mother pounded cassava leaves.
examples.french: Maman a pile le saka-saka.

words.culturalNote:
To pound, crush (with mortar and pestle).

Kotuta is the rhythmic kitchen labor that turns leaves and grains into food. A sound of Kongo courtyards.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Piler, écraser (au mortier et au pilon).

Kotuta est le labeur rythmé de la cuisine qui transforme les feuilles et les grains en nourriture. Un son des cours du Kongo.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotuta — kotuta na liboka mpe na motó ya liboka.

Kotuta ezali mosala ya rythme ya cuisine oyo ebongoli matiti mpe mbuma na bilei. Lokito ya mapango ya Kongo.

examples.english: He spat on the ground.
examples.french: Il a crache par terre.

words.culturalNote:
To spit.

Kotwa is the literal action; figuratively it can show contempt — kotwa na elongi = to spit in the face.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Cracher.

Kotwa est l'action littérale ; au figuré, il peut marquer le mépris — kotwa na elongi = cracher au visage.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotwa — kotwa nsoi.

Kotwa ezali mosala ya solo; na ndimbola ya likolo, ekoki komonisa botioli — kotwa na elongi = kotwa nsoi na elongi.

examples.english: He delayed on the road.
examples.french: Il a tarde sur le chemin.

words.culturalNote:
To delay, to take long.

The traffic of Kinshasa makes kowumela a daily reality — taxis, fuel queues, school runs.

examples.english: I come from the village.
examples.french: Je viens du village.

words.culturalNote:
To come from, to originate from.

Kouta na = to come from. A self-introduction phrase carrying both pride and homesickness.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Venir de — nommer le lieu laissé derrière.

Kouta, c'est venir de. « Nauti na Kinshasa » fixe une personne dans une histoire — d'où tu kouta dit à l'auditeur quelque chose sur qui tu es.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kouta — kobimisa esika oyo otiki nsima.

Kouta elimboli kouta. « Nauti na Kinshasa » etii moto na lisapo — esika oyo outi eyebisi moyoki eloko mpo na nani ozali.

examples.english: They dug a pit.
examples.french: Ils ont creuse un trou.

words.culturalNote:
To dig up (cleaned from OCR v.).

Kotimola is for digging — wells, pits, foundations, graves. A long-arc Bantu verb.

examples.english: My suitcase is full.
examples.french: Ma valise est pleine.

words.culturalNote:
Suitcase.

From French valise. The diaspora’s valizi packs gifts and memories on every trip home.

examples.english: Father s car is new.
examples.french: La voiture de pere est neuve.

words.culturalNote:
Car (variant of motuka).

From French voiture. Both vatiri and motuka are heard daily; ndako-motambwisi for fancier vehicles.

examples.english: The child rode a bicycle.
examples.french: L'enfant a roule a velo.

words.culturalNote:
Bicycle.

From French velo. Velo is universal in DRC towns — cheap, durable, the workhorse of small trade.

examples.english: My leg swelled.
examples.french: Ma jambe a enfle.

words.culturalNote:
To swell.

Kovimba names the body swelling — bites, sprains, infections. A monganga is consulted when it persists.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Enfler.

Kovimba nomme le corps qui gonfle — piqûres, foulures, infections. On consulte un monganga quand cela persiste.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kovimba — kovimba ya nzoto.

Kovimba etangaka nzoto oyo evimbi — mwingi, mokuwa oyo etyemi, makono. Batunaka monganga ntango eumeli.

examples.english: The elder died.
examples.french: L'aine est mort.

words.culturalNote:
To die.

A heavy word, named directly. Awei = he/she has died. The community gathers immediately at the matanga (wake).

examples.english: Whose item is that?
examples.french: A qui appartient cet objet la?

words.culturalNote:
There; that one.

Wana points to a specific thing or place at a distance — a demonstrative of place and identity.

examples.english: Where are you going?
examples.french: Ou vas-tu?

words.culturalNote:
Where (question).

Wapi opens location questions. Ozali wapi = where are you?

examples.english: He hurried on the road.
examples.french: Il s'est presse sur la route.

words.culturalNote:
To hurry, rush, scramble.

Kowela is more urgent than kotambola noki — it carries pushing, scrambling, getting there fast.

examples.english: The morning small-market is nearby.
examples.french: Le petit marche du matin est tout pres.

words.culturalNote:
Small neighborhood market.

Kinshasa quarters all have their wenze — the small daily market, distinct from the larger zando.

examples.english: The gold ring is valuable.
examples.french: La bague en or est precieuse.

words.culturalNote:
Gold.

From Portuguese ouro via Kikongo. DRC gold mining is a major industry, much of it informal.

examples.english: A dear friend has come.
examples.french: Un cher ami est venu.

words.culturalNote:
Dear, precious, valued.

Motuya = value/worth. Used for people, relationships, and treasured things.

examples.english: The last day of the month.
examples.french: Le dernier jour du mois.

words.culturalNote:
Last, final, ending.

Nsuka = end; ya nsuka = of-the-end. Often pairs with ya yambo (first).

examples.english: We welcomed the visitors with joy.
examples.french: Nous avons accueilli les visiteurs avec joie.

words.culturalNote:
To receive, welcome.

Koyamba carries Kongo hospitality — water for the visitor, a place to sit, food shared.

examples.english: First, we pray.
examples.french: D'abord, nous prions.

words.culturalNote:
First, before, in the beginning.

Used to open a sequence; yambo na = before. A storytelling and prayer opener.

examples.english: That is a big matter.
examples.french: C'est une grande affaire.

words.culturalNote:
It, that.

Yango refers back to a thing or matter already named. Yango wana = therefore (lit. that there).

examples.english: The matter itself is over.
examples.french: L'affaire elle-meme est terminee.

words.culturalNote:
Itself, the very thing.

Yango moko emphasizes self-reference. Used to underline a person or matter without further explanation.

examples.english: He answered my question.
examples.french: Il a repondu a ma question.

words.culturalNote:
To answer, respond.

Koyanola pairs with kotuna (to ask). Answering elders well is taught early.

examples.lingala: Sanza ya yanuari ezali ya malili.
examples.english: January is a cool month.
examples.french: Janvier est un mois frais.

words.culturalNote:
January.

From French janvier. Marks the start of the new year and school’s second term in DRC.

examples.lingala: Yaya na ngai akende na mosala.
examples.english: My elder sibling went to work.
examples.french: Mon aine est alle au travail.

words.culturalNote:
Elder sibling (corrected verb: akende = went, simple past).

Yaya is the warm, affectionate term for an elder brother or sister. Birth order shapes daily respect.

examples.english: He gave him money.
examples.french: Il lui a donne de l'argent.

words.culturalNote:
Him, her (no gender split in Lingala).

The 3rd-person object pronoun. Ye covers both he/she/him/her.

examples.english: He did it himself.
examples.french: Il l'a fait lui-meme.

words.culturalNote:
Himself, herself.

Ye moko emphasizes the actor. Asali ye moko = he himself did it.

examples.english: I know you.
examples.french: Je te connais.

words.culturalNote:
To know (a person, fact, or how to do something).

Koyeba covers knowing people, things, languages, and skills. Nayebi Lingala = I know Lingala.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Savoir — posséder un fait ou un visage.

Koyeba, c'est savoir. Koyeba quelqu'un, c'est le reconnaître ; koyeba une chose, c'est l'avoir éclairée en soi — un mot d'information et de connaissance ensemble.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyeba — kozala na likambo to elongi.

Koyeba elimboli koyeba. Koyeba moto ezali koyeba ye; koyeba eloko ezali kozala na yango ekongenga kati na yo — liloba ya boyebi mpe ya kondima.

examples.english: He told me the news.
examples.french: Il m'a annonce la nouvelle.

words.culturalNote:
To tell, inform, announce (causative of koyeba).

Koyebisa = to make-know — to share news, pass on information.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Informer — faire passer la nouvelle.

Koyebisa, c'est informer ou dire. Du chuchotement tranquille à l'annonce publique, koyebisa porte ce qu'une personne sait dans la pièce des autres.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyebisa — koleka nsango.

Koyebisa elimboli koyebisa to koyebisa. Banda kotanga ya nse kino kosakola ya polele, koyebisa ememi oyo moto moko ayebi na ndako ya bato mingi.

examples.english: The child learned Lingala.
examples.french: L'enfant a appris le lingala.

words.culturalNote:
To learn, study.

Koyekola is the lifelong verb of learning — language, trade, faith, life.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Apprendre — faire sienne la chose nouvelle.

Koyekola, c'est apprendre ou étudier. L'élève koyekola en classe ; l'apprenti koyekola à l'établi ; l'ancien aussi dit « nazali koyekola » quand le jour lui apprend quelque chose.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyekola — kokomisa ya yo eloko ya sika.

Koyekola elimboli koyekola to kotanga. Moyekoli akoyekola na kelasi; moyekoli ya mosala akoyekola na esika ya mosala; mopaka mpe alobaka « nazali koyekola » ntango mokolo eteyi ye eloko moko.

examples.english: He brought me bread.
examples.french: Il m'a apporte du pain.

words.culturalNote:
To bring, to bring to (applicative of koya).

The -el- applicative adds the recipient. Pairs with koya (to come).
words.culturalNoteFr:
Apporter à — porter la chose à celui qui l'a demandée.

Koyela signifie spécifiquement « apporter à quelqu'un » (komema ou koya na sont les « porter / amener » plus généraux). La petite course qui surgit à chaque visite et à chaque repas.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyela — komema eloko epai ya moto oyo asengi yango.

Koyela elimboli mingi « komema epai ya moto » (komema to koya na ezali « komema » ya bonene). Mosala ya mokemoke oyo ebimaka na bokutani nyonso mpe na kolia nyonso.

examples.english: Mother sang a song.
examples.french: Maman a chante une chanson.

words.culturalNote:
To sing (corrected from the bank gloss "sign").

Koyemba shapes every Kongo Sunday morning. Church choirs are legendary across DRC.

examples.english: Jesus is Savior.
examples.french: Jesus est le Sauveur.

words.culturalNote:
Jesus.

Yesu (or Yezu) anchors Christian DRC. Songs, prayers, and daily greetings invoke His name.

examples.english: We pray to Jesus.
examples.french: Nous prions Jesus.

words.culturalNote:
Jesus — variant spelling of Yesu.

Both Yesu and Yezu are heard in churches and Bibles; preserved per "do not drop any words."

examples.english: The thief stole money.
examples.french: Le voleur a vole de l'argent.

words.culturalNote:
To steal.

Koyiba is a serious accusation; moyibi (thief) names the doer. Markets and crowds raise constant vigilance.

examples.english: The car tire popped.
examples.french: Le pneu de la voiture a eclate.

words.culturalNote:
Tire, tyre (from French pneu).

A car tire pops or bursts — the verb is kopasuka (epasuki = has burst). Spare tires are a daily Kinshasa road necessity.

examples.english: We multiplied the fruit among the children.
examples.french: Nous avons multiplie les fruits parmi les enfants.

words.culturalNote:
To multiply, to increase (corrected from koyikinya, which is non-standard).

Kokolisa = to cause to grow; kobakisa = to add to. The natural Lingala way to express multiplying or increasing abundance.

examples.english: I hate lies.
examples.french: Je deteste le mensonge.

words.culturalNote:
To hate, dislike strongly.

Koyina is named carefully — long-held hatred is treated as harmful to the soul in Kongo moral teaching.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Haïr — le verbe contre lequel la langue met en garde.

Koyina, c'est haïr ou détester fortement. « Koyina moto te » — ne hais personne — vient tôt et souvent des anciens ; la langue place la haine là où elle doit être, à la marge.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyina — liloba oyo monoko ekebisi.

Koyina elimboli koyina to kotioka makasi. « Koyina moto te » — koyina moto te — eyaka noki mpe mbala mingi epai ya bampaka; monoko etii boyini esika oyo ebongi, na monoko.

examples.english: The black cloth is beautiful.
examples.french: L'etoffe noire est belle.

words.culturalNote:
Black, dark.

Yindo names the color. In songs it also names beautiful dark skin.

examples.english: Where are you?
examples.french: Toi, ou es-tu?

words.culturalNote:
You (singular).

Yo is the emphatic singular you. The subject prefix o- carries the basic meaning.

examples.lingala: Biloko ezali na kati ya sanduku.
examples.english: The items are inside the box.
examples.french: Les affaires sont dans la boite.

words.culturalNote:
Inside (variant; cf. #632; bank had OCR junk "yoh").

Na kati ya = inside of. The standard Lingala locative phrase.

examples.english: Listen to my words.
examples.french: Ecoute mes paroles.

words.culturalNote:
To hear, listen, feel.

Koyoka covers ear-listening and emotional feeling (koyoka pasi = to feel pain). Deep listening is a Kongo virtue.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Entendre — et sentir, le même verbe.

Koyoka couvre à la fois l'ouïe et la sensation. Koyoka un mot et koyoka un frisson partagent la même racine — la langue traite la perception comme un seul acte de réception.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyoka — koyoka mpe koyoka, liloba moko.

Koyoka ezipi koyoka mpe koyoka na nzoto. Koyoka liloba mpe koyoka malili basangani na motó moko — monoko ezwi boyoki lokola mosala moko ya boyambi.

examples.english: We agree with your words.
examples.french: Nous sommes d'accord avec tes paroles.

words.culturalNote:
To agree, to be in accord.

Koyokana = to hear-with-one-another. The reciprocal -an- suffix carries the mutual sense.

examples.english: All the people came.
examples.french: Toutes les personnes sont venues.

words.culturalNote:
All, every, whole.

Nyonso adds totality to a noun. Mikolo nyonso = every day; bato nyonso = all people.

examples.english: Do it yourself.
examples.french: Fais-le toi-meme.

words.culturalNote:
Yourself (singular).

Moko adds the self-emphasis. Yo moko = you yourself; ye moko = he/she him/herself.

examples.lingala: Sanza ya yuli ezali ya malili.
examples.english: July is a cool month.
examples.french: Juillet est un mois frais.

words.culturalNote:
July.

From French juillet. The heart of Kinshasa’s dry season — cool mornings, dry afternoons.

examples.english: June has passed.
examples.french: Juin est passe.

words.culturalNote:
June.

From French juin. Independence Day (Mokolo ya lipanda, June 30) is the year’s biggest national feast.

examples.english: The devil tempts people.
examples.french: Le diable tente les gens.

words.culturalNote:
Devil.

From Portuguese diabo via Kikongo. Named in church teaching and in proverbs about temptation.

examples.english: Believers fear the devil.
examples.french: Les croyants craignent le diable.

words.culturalNote:
Devil — standard secondary terms (corrected from zabulu).

Diabolo (French) and satana (biblical) are the universal Lingala alternatives heard alongside zabolo.

examples.english: I am at the house.
examples.french: Je suis a la maison.

words.culturalNote:
To be, to exist.

The core verb of being. Nazali = I am; tozali = we are. Kozala na = to have (be with).
words.culturalNoteFr:
Être — le verbe sous tout état.

Kozala est l'infinitif « être ». Il pose chaque autre mot — « kozala na bwanya », être sage ; « kozala na esengo », être joyeux — le verbe simple et profond de la présence.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kozala — liloba oyo ezali na nse ya nyonso.

Kozala elimboli kozala. Etyaka liloba mosusu nyonso na esika — « kozala na bwanya », kozala na bwanya; « kozala na esengo », kozala na esengo — liloba ya pete mpe ya mozindo ya kozala.

examples.english: Animals live in the forest.
examples.french: Les animaux vivent dans la foret.

words.culturalNote:
Forest, bush.

Zamba is the great Congo forest — home, hunt, mystery. A foundational Kongo word.

examples.english: Mother went to the market.
examples.french: Maman est allee au marche.

words.culturalNote:
Market.

Zando is the great Kongo institution — Kinshasa’s zando like Gambela and Marche Central pulse daily with traders, food, music, and life.

examples.english: We lack money.
examples.french: Nous manquons d'argent.

words.culturalNote:
To miss, to lack, to be without.

Kozanga names what is missing — money, food, family, peace. A heavy verb of need.

examples.lingala: Zelo ya libongo ezali ya pembe.
examples.english: The riverbank sand is white.
examples.french: Le sable de la rive est blanc.

words.culturalNote:
Sand.

Zelo lines the Congo and Ubangi riverbanks — the long pale beaches where boats land and children play. A familiar texture of river life.

examples.english: Mother is pregnant.
examples.french: Maman est enceinte.

words.culturalNote:
Pregnancy.

Zemi is named with warmth and care. A pregnant woman is treated with extra gentleness — bilei ya zemi (food for pregnancy) and elders’ blessings surround her.

examples.english: I am waiting for you at the door.
examples.french: Je t'attends a la porte.

words.culturalNote:
To wait, to await (cleaned headword from bare "zila").

Kozila is patient waiting — for someone, for news, for the right moment. A daily Kongo virtue, taught early.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Attendre, patienter (entrée nettoyée du nu « zila »).

Kozila est l'attente patiente — d'une personne, d'une nouvelle, du bon moment. Une vertu quotidienne du Kongo, enseignée tôt.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kozila — kozela.

Kozila ezali kozela ya bopembe — mpo na moto, mpo na nsango, mpo na ntango ya malamu. Bonkonde ya mokolo na mokolo ya Kongo, eteyami banda mokemoke.

examples.english: This sack is very heavy.
examples.french: Ce sac est tres lourd.

words.culturalNote:
Heavy (corrected from kilo, which is the loanword noun for weight/kilograms).

Zito is the standard adjective for heavy — used for physical weight (a sack, a load) and emotional weight (zito ya motema = a heavy heart).
