examples.english: A fool does not listen.
examples.french: Un sot n'ecoute pas.

words.culturalNote:
Idiot, fool.

Zoba is a direct word, used in proverbs more often than as a personal insult. The teaching: the wise listen; the zoba does not.

examples.english: The accident injured his leg.
examples.french: L'accident l'a blesse a la jambe.

words.culturalNote:
To injure, wound (corrected headword: causative of kozoka).

Kozokisa names the act of causing a wound; the wound itself = mpota. A heavy verb of road accidents and fights.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Blesser (causatif de kozoka).

Kozokisa nomme l'acte de causer une blessure ; la blessure elle-même = mpota. Verbe lourd des accidents de la route et des bagarres.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kozokisa — kozokisa moto (causatif ya kozoka).

Kozokisa elimboli mosala ya kozokisa; mpota yango moko = mpota. Liloba ya kilo ya makama ya nzela mpe ya bitumba.

examples.english: My nose hurts.
examples.french: Mon nez me fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Nose.

Zolo is the body part; the standard esali pasi pattern says it hurts. Colds and dust make zolo a common everyday complaint.

examples.english: The children stood in a circle.
examples.french: Les enfants se sont tenus en cercle.

words.culturalNote:
Circle, round formation.

Zolongano shapes children’s games, dance circles, and the village council. A round circle invites everyone equally to face one another.

examples.english: We paid ten francs.
examples.french: Nous avons paye dix francs.

words.culturalNote:
Ten.

The base for counting beyond ten in Lingala — zomi na moko = eleven; ntuku mibale = twenty (lit. two tens). A foundational number word.

examples.lingala: Mwana akokisi mibu zomi na moko.
examples.english: The child reached eleven years.
examples.french: L'enfant a atteint onze ans.

words.culturalNote:
Eleven, literally ten and one.

Lingala builds compound numbers transparently: zomi na moko, zomi na mibale, zomi na misato. A clear and gentle counting logic.

examples.english: Father returned to the house.
examples.french: Pere est rentre a la maison.

words.culturalNote:
To return, to come back (cleaned headword from bare "zonga"; example typo Atata → Tata fixed).

Kozonga carries warmth — the return of a traveler, the prayer that those who leave for mikili (abroad) one day kozonga na mboka.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Rentrer, revenir (entrée nettoyée du nu « zonga » ; typo Atata → Tata corrigée).

Kozonga porte une chaleur — le retour du voyageur, la prière que ceux qui partent pour les mikili (l'étranger) kozonga un jour na mboka.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kozonga — kozonga.

Kozonga ememi molunge — kozonga ya mobembi, libondeli ete bato oyo bakei na mikili bakozonga mokolo moko na mboka.

examples.english: We sat around the fire.
examples.french: Nous nous sommes assis autour du feu.

words.culturalNote:
Around, surrounding.

Reduplication of zonga adds the encircling sense. Zongazonga na moto = around the fire — the deepest image of Kongo gathering, story, and song.

examples.english: Jealousy destroys friendship.
examples.french: La jalousie detruit l'amitie.

words.culturalNote:
Jealousy.

Zuwa is treated as a hidden poison in Kongo moral teaching — between siblings, friends, co-workers. Proverbs warn against it gently and often.

examples.english: I received father’s letter.
examples.french: J'ai recu la lettre de pere.

words.culturalNote:
To get, receive, obtain (cleaned headword from bare "zwa").

Kozwa is the everyday verb of getting hold of something — a letter, a job, news, an opportunity. Foundational and warm.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Obtenir — recevoir ce qui vient à la main.

Kozwa, c'est obtenir, prendre, recevoir. Un salaire, un cadeau, une récompense, une opportunité — « nakozwa » annonce le moment où une chose passe à toi.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kozwa — koyamba oyo eyei na loboko.

Kozwa elimboli kozwa, kozwa, koyamba. Lifuta, likabo, mbano, libaku — « nakozwa » esakolaka ntango oyo eloko eyei epai na yo.

examples.english: We met at the market.
examples.french: Nous nous sommes rencontres au marche.

words.culturalNote:
To meet, encounter one another (reciprocal -an- of kozwa).

Kozwana closes the bank with a fitting verb — the Kongo gift of finding one another, in markets, in church, in life. A warm last word.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Se rencontrer (réciproque -an- de kozwa).

Kozwana clôt la banque par un verbe approprié — le don congolais de se trouver les uns les autres, au marché, à l'église, dans la vie. Une dernière parole chaleureuse.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kozwana — kokutana, kozwana (réciproque -an- ya kozwa).

Kozwana ekangi banque na liloba oyo ebongi — likabo ya Kongo ya kokutana, na zando, na ndako ya Nzambe, na bomoyi. Liloba ya nsuka ya molunge.

examples.english: We cooked fried horse mackerel this evening.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit du chinchard frit ce soir.

words.culturalNote:
Tomson — fried horse mackerel.

From the brand "Thomson," tomson is one of the cheapest, most beloved street fish in Kinshasa: fried whole and eaten with kwanga, fufu, or cassava bread. A working-class Sunday plate.

examples.lingala: Pesa ngai kwanga mpo na kolia na tomson.
examples.english: Give me cassava bread to eat with the mackerel.
examples.french: Donne-moi du chikwangue pour manger avec le chinchard.

words.culturalNote:
Kwanga (chikuwange) — fermented cassava bread wrapped in marantaceae leaves.

A defining Kongo staple. Dense, slightly sour, kwanga keeps for days, travels well, and pairs with fried fish, mpondu, or palm-oil sauces. The food of the river and the road.

examples.lingala: Bana bazali kolia kamundele na libanda.
examples.english: The children are eating beef skewers outside.
examples.french: Les enfants mangent des brochettes dehors.

words.culturalNote:
Kamundele — grilled beef skewers.

The night-time street food of Kinshasa: marinated cubes of beef threaded on bamboo, grilled over charcoal at the kiosk, eaten with pilipili. A whole social ritual gathers around the kamundele grill.

examples.english: Mother fried ripe plantains.
examples.french: Maman a frit des bananes plantains mures.

words.culturalNote:
Makemba — cooking plantains.

Green makemba boil into fufu-like sides; ripe makemba fry into sweet golden discs (makemba ya kokalinga). One of the most beloved daily carbohydrates across DRC.

examples.lingala: Mpiodi ya kotumba ezali elengi mingi.
examples.english: Grilled mackerel is very tasty.
examples.french: Le chinchard grille est tres savoureux.

words.culturalNote:
Mpiodi — jack mackerel, sister fish to tomson.

Grilled or fried, mpiodi is a household staple. Salted-and-dried mpiodi (libata) lasts the rainy season in inland villages.

examples.lingala: Tolambi bilolo na mafuta ya mbila.
examples.english: We cooked bitter greens in palm oil.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit le ndole a l'huile de palme.

words.culturalNote:
Bilolo — bitter leaf (the West/Central African ndole leaf).

Washed and pounded to soften the bitterness, then simmered slowly with palm oil and smoked fish. A medicinal green said to "clean the blood."

examples.lingala: Molunge makasi, nzoto ezali kobima nkute.
examples.english: The heat is intense, the body is sweating.
examples.french: La chaleur est intense, le corps transpire.

words.culturalNote:
Nkute — sweat, steam, the rising heat from the body or a pot.

Kinshasa's'heavy molunge (heat) makes nkute a constant companion. To "kobima nkute" is literally "to bring out sweat."

examples.english: Put a little chili pepper in the soup.
examples.french: Mets un peu de piment dans la soupe.

words.culturalNote:
Pilipili — hot chili pepper.

From Swahili. Ground fresh into sauces or set on the table as a fiery condiment, pilipili is the heat of Kongo cooking. A small jar is on every kamundele stand.

examples.english: Give me a tiny little portion.
examples.french: Donne-moi une toute petite portion.

words.culturalNote:
Mfioti — tiny, very small (modern Kinshasa street slang).

Heard everywhere among the young — "mwa moke mfioti" for an even-smaller-than-small bit. The flavor is affectionate and joking.

examples.lingala: Liboke ya mbisi ezali na moto.
examples.english: The fish packet is cooking over the fire.
examples.french: Le paquet de poisson cuit sur le feu.

words.culturalNote:
Liboke — a leaf-wrapped steamed parcel (food-specific sense; cf. #424).

Fish, spices, and palm oil tied tightly in banana leaves and slow-cooked over coals. Liboke ya mbisi is one of the iconic dishes of the Congo.

examples.lingala: Supu oyo ezali na mayi ya banyama mingi.
examples.english: This soup has a lot of meat broth.
examples.french: Cette soupe a beaucoup de bouillon de viande.

words.culturalNote:
Mayi ya banyama — meat broth, savoury cooking liquor.

Literally "water of the animals." The deep, slow stock that finishes a Kongo sauce and gets poured generously over fufu or rice.

examples.lingala: Bana batuka bazali kosiba na wenze.
examples.english: The young guys are chilling at the small market.
examples.french: Les jeunes flanent au petit marche.

words.culturalNote:
Kosiba — to hang out, to chill (modern Kinshasa street slang).

The verb of unhurried social loitering: at the wenze, on a stoop, at a nganda. A core verb of urban youth culture.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kosiba — traîner, se la couler douce (argot moderne de Kinshasa).

Le verbe de la flânerie sociale sans hâte : au wenze, sur un perron, dans une nganda. Verbe central de la culture urbaine des jeunes.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosiba — kotambola na bopembe, kopema (liloba ya argot ya Kinshasa ya sika).

Liloba ya kotambola-tambola ya lisanga kozanga koswana: na wenze, na esika ya kovanda liboso ya ndako, na nganda. Liloba ya motó ya bonkoko ya bilenge ya vile.

examples.english: He needs to tear that cloth apart.
examples.french: Il doit dechirer cette etoffe.

words.culturalNote:
Kopasola — to rip, tear apart (active causative of kopasuka).

Used for cloth, paper, and figuratively for breaking apart a group or relationship. Stronger than kokata (to cut).
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kopasola — déchirer (causatif actif de kopasuka).

Utilisé pour le tissu, le papier, et figurativement pour briser un groupe ou une relation. Plus fort que kokata (couper).
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kopasola — kopasola (causatif ya kopasuka).

Basaleli yango mpo na elamba, papier, mpe na ndimbola ya kobuka lisanga to boyokani. Makasi koleka kokata.

examples.english: Throw these things away in the pit.
examples.french: Jette ces affaires dans la fosse.

words.culturalNote:
Kobwaka — to throw away, discard.

Used for trash, but also for abandoning something dear (kobwaka libala = to throw away the marriage). A weighted verb.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kobwaka — jeter, abandonner.

Utilisé pour les ordures, mais aussi pour abandonner quelque chose de cher (kobwaka libala = jeter le mariage). Un verbe lourd de sens.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobwaka — kobwaka, kotika.

Basaleli yango mpo na bosoto, kasi mpe mpo na kotika eloko ya motuya (kobwaka libala = kobwaka libala). Liloba ya kilo.

examples.lingala: Mosala na ye nyonso ezali mpamba.
examples.english: All his work is in vain.
examples.french: Tout son travail est vain.

words.culturalNote:
Mpamba — useless, vain, for nothing (extended sense of #611 mpamba = empty).

Likambo ya mpamba = an empty matter; maloba ya mpamba = empty words. A pointed word used to call out wasted effort.

examples.english: His insult started the quarrel.
examples.french: Son insulte a declenche la dispute.

words.culturalNote:
Fingo — an insult, an offensive word.

Kopesa fingo = to insult. In Kongo culture insults carry social weight; reconciliation often requires elders to step in and "cool" the fingo.

examples.lingala: Mwana oyo azali na mayele mingi.
examples.english: This child has a lot of intelligence.
examples.french: Cet enfant a beaucoup d'intelligence.

words.culturalNote:
Mayele — intelligence, cleverness, practical wisdom.

A prized Kongo trait. Mayele covers book-smarts, street-smarts, and the social wit to read a room. Pairs with bwanya (deeper wisdom).

examples.lingala: Kiboko azali na kati ya mai.
examples.english: The hippopotamus is inside the water.
examples.french: L'hippopotame est dans l'eau.

words.culturalNote:
Kiboko — hippopotamus (from Swahili).

Kiboko inhabit the Congo and Ubangi rivers; encounters with them are a real river danger. The word also entered English via colonial Swahili.

examples.english: The jackal ran into the forest.
examples.french: Le chacal s'est enfui dans la foret.

words.culturalNote:
Mbulu — jackal or fox, a trickster of folktales.

In Kongo stories mbulu often plays the clever-but-greedy role, outsmarting bigger animals and sometimes himself.

examples.lingala: Tosombi ntaba ya kotumba na nganda.
examples.english: We bought grilled goat at the bar.
examples.french: Nous avons achete de la chevre grillee au bar.

words.culturalNote:
Ntaba ya kotumba — grilled goat meat, a kamundele variant.

Goat marinated in pilipili, garlic, and onion, then slow-grilled over coals at the nganda. A weekend evening staple.

examples.english: Catfish is a muddy water fish.
examples.french: Le poisson-chat est un poisson des eaux boueuses.

words.culturalNote:
Ngolu — catfish.

A muddy-water river fish, smoked or stewed. Strong, rich flavour; central to many riverside Kongo dishes.

examples.english: Mother came to visit us.
examples.french: Mere est venue nous rendre visite.

words.culturalNote:
Nyango — a respectful, older-feeling word for mother.

Warmer and weightier than the everyday mama; used in songs, prayers, and when invoking maternal authority. Tata pairs with mama; nkoko or nyango honor the elder mother.

examples.lingala: Mwana akoti na kelasi ya sika.
examples.english: The child entered the new grade.
examples.french: L'enfant est entre dans la nouvelle classe.

words.culturalNote:
Kelasi — classroom, school grade.

From French classe. The school year and its kelasi progression are central to family planning and pride. Kelasi ya yambo = first grade.

examples.lingala: Balabala etondi na potopoto mpo na mvula.
examples.english: The street is full of mud because of the rain.
examples.french: La rue est pleine de boue a cause de la pluie.

words.culturalNote:
Potopoto — mud, sticky wet ground.

Reduplicated for the sploshy feel. Kinshasa rainy-season streets become a sea of potopoto; navigating them is its own daily skill.

examples.english: Mother cooked corn fufu.
examples.french: Maman a cuit du fufu de mais.

words.culturalNote:
Fufu — pounded cassava (or maize) porridge.

The defining starch of central Africa. Soft, springy, pinched off with the right hand and dipped into soups and sauces. Fufu ya masango = corn fufu; fufu ya manioc = cassava fufu. The food of family meals.
words.french: fufu / pate (de manioc ou de mais)

words.english: nape of the neck / back of the head

examples.english: He held the child by the nape of the neck.
examples.french: Il a tenu l'enfant par la nuque.

words.culturalNote:
Likosi — the nape of the neck, the back of the head.

Distinct from kingo / nkingo (whole neck). A mother lifts a kitten or steadies a fussy child gently by the likosi.

examples.english: He hit him with a punch to the face.
examples.french: Il lui a donne un coup de poing au visage.

words.culturalNote:
Likofi — the closed fist, and by extension a punch.

Kobeta likofi = to throw a punch. Heard in news of street fights and in proverbs warning that the open hand is wiser than the fist.

examples.english: His jaw hurts.
examples.french: Sa machoire lui fait mal.

words.culturalNote:
Ebanga — the jaw, the chin line.

Close in meaning to lobanga (cf. #483). A strong ebanga is praised in song; a sore ebanga is a common everyday complaint.

examples.lingala: Tosombi monzombo ya sika na wenze.
examples.english: We bought fresh eel at the small market.
examples.french: Nous avons achete de l'anguille fraiche au petit marche.

words.culturalNote:
Monzombo — eel, river mudfish.

A prized river fish in central African cooking — long, slippery, rich in fat. Grilled or stewed slowly with palm oil.

examples.lingala: Likundu na ye etondi na bilei.
examples.english: His belly is full of food.
examples.french: Son ventre est plein de nourriture.

words.culturalNote:
Likundu — the belly, the inner organ, and in Kongo traditional belief, the seat of hidden power said to underlie kindoki (witchcraft).

Used literally for the full stomach and figuratively for the inner source of moral or occult force. Treated with care in conversation.

examples.english: He needs to trim his fingernails.
examples.french: Il doit couper les ongles.

words.culturalNote:
Linzaka — fingernail, toenail, or animal claw.

Linzaka (sing.) / manzaka (pl.). Clean, trimmed nails are part of everyday Kongo presentation; weekly clipping is a small household ritual.

examples.english: The child has a prominent belly button.
examples.french: L'enfant a un nombril proeminent.

words.culturalNote:
Mutolo (also mutolu) — the navel, the belly button.

In Kongo culture the mutolo is symbolically tied to ancestry and the bond with the mother. The umbilical cord is sometimes ritually buried at home.

examples.lingala: Monganga apesi nkisi mpo na ebolo.
examples.english: The doctor gave medicine for the vaginal area.
examples.french: Le medecin a donne des medicaments pour la zone vaginale.

words.culturalNote:
Ebolo — vagina (the direct anatomical term, used in clinical and medical contexts).

Not a casual conversational word; used by health workers, in church teaching, and in modesty-conscious medical settings.

examples.lingala: Nyama mobali azali na makata manene.
examples.english: The male animal has large testicles.
examples.french: L'animal male a de gros testicules.

words.culturalNote:
Likata — testicle (likata sing., makata pl.).

Used in livestock and medical contexts. In casual speech the topic is approached with humour or euphemism.

examples.english: He got hurt in the groin area this evening.
examples.french: Il s'est blesse a l'aine ce soir.

words.culturalNote:
Mofati — the groin, the hip crease (variant mosiyo).

A common site of football injuries (kobeta mupira) and lifting strains. Worth noting: mosiyo as "groin" is distinct from the OCR "mosiyo = file" we corrected at #600.

examples.lingala: Lobebu na ye ezali kobima makila.
examples.english: His lip is bleeding.
examples.french: Sa levre saigne.

words.culturalNote:
Lobebu (also lobebo) — the lip.

Mabebu (pl.) = the lips. Used in everyday descriptions of beauty, expression, and minor injuries.

examples.lingala: Atiye loboko na ebeku mpo na kokanisa.
examples.english: He put his hand on his chin to think.
examples.french: Il a mis sa main au menton pour reflechir.

words.culturalNote:
Ebeku — the chin, especially as the resting-place of a thinking hand.

Used for the thoughtful gesture: hand to ebeku, eyes far away. A common pose in Kongo elders pondering a matter.

examples.lingala: Ebelo na ngai esali pasi mpo na kotambola.
examples.english: My thigh hurts from walking.
examples.french: Ma cuisse me fait mal a force de marcher.

words.culturalNote:
Ebelo — the thigh.

The long thigh muscle does the work of carrying loads up Kinshasa's'hills and across long village walks. A common site of strain.

examples.lingala: Azali na ebobo makasi mpo na mosala.
examples.english: He has strong biceps from the physical work.
examples.french: Il a de gros biceps grace au travail physique.

words.culturalNote:
Ebobo — biceps, the rounded muscle bulge of the upper arm.

A mark of a hard worker — the porter at the libongo, the mason on the building site, the rower on the river. Pride and labor combined.

examples.lingala: Libata ezali na edada mpo na kobina na mai.
examples.english: The duck has webbed feet to swim in the water.
examples.french: Le canard a des pieds palmes pour nager dans l'eau.

words.culturalNote:
Edada — webbed feet (of waterbirds), or by extension flat-footedness in people.

Used in animal description and in gentle teasing about gait.

examples.lingala: Mokuwa oyo ezali na esongo ya kitoko.
examples.english: This bone has delicious marrow.
examples.french: Cet os a une moelle delicieuse.

words.culturalNote:
Esongo — bone marrow, or a sharp bone point.

The marrow inside a slow-cooked beef bone is a treasured bite, scooped out and savoured. Esongo also names sharp bone shards to watch for.

examples.lingala: Sapato ya sika esali lifuni pasi.
examples.english: The new shoe hurts the back of the heel.
examples.french: La chaussure neuve fait mal au talon.

words.culturalNote:
Lifuni — the back of the heel, the Achilles area.

New shoes famously bite the lifuni; a Kongo grandmother's remedy is shea butter and patience.

examples.english: He hit his knee on the ground.
examples.french: Il s'est cogne le genou par terre.

words.culturalNote:
Libolongo — the knee.

A recurring site of childhood scrapes, football injuries, and old-age aches. Mabolongo (pl.) bear the weight of life.

examples.lingala: Lisasamba na ye ezali kosala mosala malamu.
examples.english: His lungs are functioning well.
examples.french: Ses poumons fonctionnent bien.

words.culturalNote:
Lisasamba — the lungs, the chest cavity.

Used in health contexts and in talking about breath, singing, and stamina. Strong lisasamba supports the long Kongo rumba vocals.

examples.lingala: Putulu etondi na mbunzu na ye.
examples.english: Dust filled his forehead.
examples.french: La poussiere recouvrait son front.

words.culturalNote:
Mbunzu — the forehead, the brow.

A high, smooth mbunzu is praised in songs. The forehead also bears the day's sweat and the elder's thoughtful furrow.

examples.english: The child has a runny nose today.
examples.french: L'enfant a le nez qui coule aujourd hui.

words.culturalNote:
Moyoyo — nasal mucus, runny nose.

A universal childhood scene: the toddler with moyoyo and mama wiping with the corner of her wrapper. Cold-season universal.

examples.lingala: Mongongo na ye ezali kitoko soki azali koyemba.
examples.english: Her voice is beautiful when she sings.
examples.french: Sa voix est belle quand elle chante.

words.culturalNote:
Mongongo — voice, throat (homonym of #561 mongongo "fly"; this is the body / sound sense).

The Kongo musical tradition treasures a strong mongongo. Choir leaders, preachers, and rumba singers shape their entire art around it.

examples.lingala: Mupende na ye ezoki na nzela.
examples.english: His shin got injured on the road.
examples.french: Son tibia s'est blesse sur la route.

words.culturalNote:
Mupende (also mopende) — the shin, the front edge of the lower leg.

The sore spot of every football match and bicycle scrape. A tender body part with little padding.

examples.lingala: Tia nkisi na pota mpo ebika.
examples.english: Put medicine on the wound so it heals.
examples.french: Mets du medicament sur la plaie pour qu'elle guerisse.

words.culturalNote:
Pota — a wound, a sore, an open injury.

Cleaning a pota with water and saboni, then applying nkisi (medicine), is a daily Kongo first-aid ritual. Pota ekobika = the wound will heal.

examples.english: Sit next to me.
examples.french: Assieds-toi a cote de moi.

words.culturalNote:
Pembeni (variant pambeni) — beside, near, next to.

One of the most-used spatial words in Lingala. Pembeni ya = next to / beside. The everyday word for closeness, both physical and relational.

examples.lingala: Vanda na mopenzi ya moninga na yo.
examples.english: Sit at your friend s side.
examples.french: Assieds-toi au cote de ton ami.

words.culturalNote:
Mopenzi — side, flank (variant of mopanzi at #595).

Used for the side of the body, of a road, or of a group. Mopenzi na mopenzi = side by side.

examples.english: Be careful at the edge of the river.
examples.french: Fais attention au bord du fleuve.

words.culturalNote:
Pembele — edge, rim, margin.

Used for riverbanks, cliff edges, and the rim of a cup or pot. A word of caution and of careful balance.

examples.english: The church is near the market.
examples.french: L'eglise est pres du marche.

words.culturalNote:
Pene — near, close.

Pairs with mosika (far). Pene na = near to. A daily word in directions and family talk.

examples.lingala: Benda singa mpo na kotonga efelo.
examples.english: Pull a string line to build the wall.
examples.french: Tire une ficelle pour construire le mur.

words.culturalNote:
Singa — line, string, cord, rope.

Used for building lines, fishing lines, washing lines, and the binding cord on bundles. A foundational tool of the household.

examples.english: Where is the exit of the small market?
examples.french: Ou est la sortie du petit marche?

words.culturalNote:
Ebimelo — exit, way out.

From kobima (to come out / exit). Used for doors, market gates, and figuratively for finding a way out of trouble.

examples.english: The entrance of the yard is here.
examples.french: L'entree de la cour est ici.

words.culturalNote:
Ekotelo — entrance, way in.

From kokota (to enter). The ekotelo of a Kongo parcelle is the social threshold — greetings begin there.

examples.lingala: Mwana oyo azali kasa na kelasi.
examples.english: This child is very energetic in class.
examples.french: Cet enfant est tres dynamique en classe.

words.culturalNote:
Kasa — fast, energetic, lively.

Used for spirited children, quick workers, and brisk activity. A warm word of praise for energy.

examples.english: I thank you for the help.
examples.french: Je te remercie pour l'aide.

words.culturalNote:
Kotondo — the verb of giving thanks (noun form botondi at #838).

Natondi (I thank) opens every formal gathering and many warm phone calls home.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kotondo — le verbe du remerciement (forme nominale botondi).

Natondi (je remercie) ouvre chaque rassemblement formel et bien des chauds appels téléphoniques au pays.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotondo — liloba ya botondi.

Natondi epesi botondi ezali ebandeli ya mayangani nyonso ya boboto mpe ya babiluki ya telefone ya mboka.

examples.english: The morning prayer brings peace.
examples.french: La priere du matin apporte la paix.

words.culturalNote:
Losambo — prayer (noun form of the verb kosambela at #753).

Morning losambo and evening losambo bookend Kongo days for many families. The word also names the original brand greeting that gave the project its old codename.

examples.lingala: Tia mpiko mpo na kosilisa mosala.
examples.english: Have courage to finish the work.
examples.french: Aie du courage pour terminer le travail.

words.culturalNote:
Mpiko — courage, endurance, fortitude.

Kotia mpiko = to put on courage. A core Kongo virtue, especially in stories of long roads, hard labor, and exile.

examples.english: The evening breeze is cool.
examples.french: La brise du soir est fraiche.

words.culturalNote:
Mopepe — wind, breeze, air in motion.

The cool mopepe of Kinshasa evenings is one of the city's daily blessings — drying clothes, easing the heat, carrying music from the libanda.

examples.english: This tree has borne a lot of fruit.
examples.french: Cet arbre a porte beaucoup de fruits.

words.culturalNote:
Nzete — tree, wood, stick.

A foundational nature word. The Kongo forest is built of mabuta ma nzete. Used also for cut wood and walking sticks.

examples.lingala: Nzambe apesi biso ngolu na ye.
examples.english: God has given us his grace.
examples.french: Dieu nous a donne sa grace.

words.culturalNote:
Ngolu — grace, mercy (homonym of #936 ngolu "catfish"; this is the theological sense).

The central church word for divine grace, sung in countless Kongo hymns. Ngolu ya Nzambe = the grace of God.

examples.english: Open the can of beans.
examples.french: Ouvre la boite de haricots.

words.culturalNote:
Kofungola — to open, to unlock.

The verb behind lifungola (key, #434) and lifungu (button, #435). Used for doors, containers, books, and possibilities.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kofungola — ouvrir, déverrouiller.

Le verbe derrière lifungola (clé) et lifungu (bouton). Utilisé pour les portes, les récipients, les livres, et les possibilités.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kofungola — kofungola, kolongola libungutu.

Liloba oyo ezali na motó ya lifungola (fungola) na lifungu (bouton). Basaleli yango mpo na baporte, biloko ya kobomba, mikanda, mpe makoki.

examples.lingala: Mobali oyo azali na maboko makasi.
examples.english: This man has strong arms.
examples.french: Cet homme a des bras forts.

words.culturalNote:
Makasi — strong, hard, forceful, loud.

Used for strength, intensity, and difficulty. Mosala ya makasi = hard work; nzela ya makasi = a tough road. Pairs with pete (soft, easy).

examples.english: An elder must speak with wisdom.
examples.french: Un aine doit parler avec sagesse.

words.culturalNote:
Bwanya — wisdom, deep intelligence, good judgment.

Distinct from mayele (cleverness/skill). Bwanya is the deeper, slower wisdom of elders, proverbs, and prayer.

examples.lingala: Asombi kazaka ya mai ya mpondu.
examples.english: He bought a dark green jacket.
examples.french: Il a achete une veste vert fonce.

words.culturalNote:
Mai ya mpondu — dark green, the deep color of cassava-leaf water.

Literally "water of mpondu." A wonderfully Kongo way to name a color — by the dish that produces it.

examples.lingala: Nzete oyo ezali na minoi mingi.
examples.english: This tree has many thorns.
examples.french: Cet arbre a beaucoup d'epines.

words.culturalNote:
Minoi — thorns (plural; sing. monoi).

Thorny trees and bushes line many village paths; minoi are a daily caution and a familiar proverb image for hidden dangers.

examples.english: The elders are sitting on the porch.
examples.french: Les anciens sont assis sur la veranda.

words.culturalNote:
Mbalasa — porch, covered veranda.

The mbalasa is where elders sit through the heat, where stories are told in the evening, where guests are received before entering the inner house.

examples.english: We cooked roasted corn.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit du mais grille.

words.culturalNote:
Masango — corn / maize, especially in the cooked and ground form (cf. #528 mboto for the cob).

Fufu ya masango (corn fufu) is a staple in many regions. Roasted masango cobs are sold along Kinshasa roads.

examples.lingala: Sofele atemisi motuka pembeni ya zando.
examples.english: The driver stopped the car next to the market.
examples.french: Le chauffeur a arrete la voiture pres du marche.

words.culturalNote:
Motuka — car, automobile (variants mutuka, vatiri at #853).

The everyday word; motuka enters the cultural notes of dozens of bank entries. The Kongo car culture is large — old Mercedes, minibuses, motorcycle taxis.

examples.lingala: Tia nkoni na kati ya fulo.
examples.english: Put firewood inside the stove.
examples.french: Mets du bois dans le foyer.

words.culturalNote:
Fulo — stove, hearth, cooking fire (from French fourneau).

The fulo is the heart of the Kongo kitchen — charcoal or wood, with pots stacked above. Pairs with mbabula (charcoal brazier).

examples.english: The children are playing in the yard.
examples.french: Les enfants jouent dans la parcelle.

words.culturalNote:
Lopango — yard, plot of land, the family compound (the parcelle).

The lopango holds the ndako, the libanda (open courtyard), the fulo, the chickens, and the daily life of the household.

examples.lingala: Akalingi mbisi na mafuta ya mbila.
examples.english: She fried fish in palm oil.
examples.french: Elle a frit du poisson a l'huile de palme.

words.culturalNote:
Mafuta — oil, fat, butter.

Mafuta ya mbila (palm oil) is the deep-red Kongo cooking oil — flavor, color, and tradition all in one. Mafuta also names body oil and ointments.

examples.english: Remove the peel of the orange.
examples.french: Enleve la peau de l'orange.

words.culturalNote:
Mposo — skin, peel, bark.

The shared word for human skin, fruit peel, and tree bark. Mposo ya nyama = leather (cf. #399); mposo ya nzete = tree bark.

examples.english: Light the charcoal in the brazier.
examples.french: Allume le charbon dans le brasero.

words.culturalNote:
Mbabula — open charcoal brazier, the everyday Kongo cooking stove.

Made of recycled metal, the mbabula holds makala (charcoal) under a pot or a grill. The smoky symbol of Kongo home cooking.

examples.english: You removed hairs from the eyebrow.
examples.french: Tu as enleve les poils du sourcil.

words.culturalNote:
Nkongi — eyebrow.

Used in beauty talk and in expressions about emotion — raised nkongi signals surprise, furrowed nkongi marks concern.

examples.lingala: Bato ya bikolo ndenge na ndenge bayei.
examples.english: People of different nations came.
examples.french: Des gens de differentes nations sont venus.

words.culturalNote:
Ekolo — tribe, nation, ethnic group (pl. bikolo).

DRC holds over 200 bikolo — Mongo, Luba, Kongo, Yaka, Tetela, and many more. Ekolo names belonging, language, and tradition.

examples.english: Our ancestors used to live here.
examples.french: Nos ancetres vivaient ici.

words.culturalNote:
Nkondo — ancestor, founding lineage head (pl. bankondo).

Ancestors are honored across Kongo culture — their names are invoked in prayers, libations, and decisions of weight.

examples.english: The watchman is patrolling the yard.
examples.french: Le gardien patrouille la parcelle.

words.culturalNote:
Koyengela — to patrol, watch over carefully, stand guard.

The verb of a mokengeli or sinzili at the gate, of soldiers on a road, of a mother watching over a sleeping child.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Koyengela — patrouiller, surveiller attentivement, monter la garde.

Le verbe d'un mokengeli ou sinzili à la porte, des soldats sur une route, d'une mère veillant sur un enfant qui dort.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Koyengela — kotambola na bokengi, kobatela makasi.

Liloba ya mokengeli to sinzili na porte, ya basoda na nzela, ya mama oyo azali kokengela mwana oyo azali kolala.

examples.english: A white person came to visit the factory.
examples.french: Un blanc est venu visiter l'usine.

words.culturalNote:
Mondele — white person, European (pl. bandele).

A common everyday word, used neutrally in most contexts. Carries colonial-era weight; its connotation shifts with tone and intent.

examples.english: His wound has started to heal.
examples.french: Sa plaie commence a guerir.

words.culturalNote:
Kobika — to heal, recover, be saved, survive.

The root behind kobikisa (#298, to heal someone). Kobika also carries the church meaning of being saved (Mobikisi = Savior).
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kobika — guérir, se rétablir, être sauvé, survivre.

La racine derrière kobikisa (guérir quelqu'un). Kobika porte aussi le sens chrétien d'être sauvé (Mobikisi = Sauveur).
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kobika — kobika maladi, kozonga na nzoto, kobikisama, koumela na bomoyi.

Motó ya kobikisa (kobikisa moto mosusu). Kobika ememi mpe ndimbola ya kondima ya kobikisama (Mobikisi = oyo abikisi).

examples.english: Give me your left hand.
examples.french: Donne-moi ta main gauche.

words.culturalNote:
Lomoso — left side, left hand (alternative to loboko ya mwasi at #401).

Kongo etiquette favors the right hand for greetings and giving; the lomoso is for daily tasks and balance.

examples.lingala: Tika lobobo wana, tia mpiko na mosala.
examples.english: Stop that chatter, focus energy on the work.
examples.french: Arrete ce bavardage, mets ton energie au travail.

words.culturalNote:
Lobobo — empty chatter, idle talk, gossip.

Elders use this word to redirect young people from time-wasting conversation back to mosala or to listening. Pairs gently with lokutu (lies).

examples.lingala: Nzete ya mai ekolaka pembele ya ebale.
examples.english: The water-reed grows by the edge of the river.
examples.french: Le saule pousse au bord du fleuve.

words.culturalNote:
Nzete ya mai — water-loving trees and reeds, literally "tree of water."

Found along Congo riverbanks — providing fishing-rod stems, basket reeds, and bird habitat.

examples.english: This gate is made of iron.
examples.french: Ce portail est fait en fer.

words.culturalNote:
Ebende — iron, metal, steel.

The base word behind ebende ya motane = copper (#388). Used for fences, tools, machinery — the material of Kinshasa's'endless welding workshops.

examples.english: Children, stop the noise in the room!
examples.french: Les enfants, arretez le bruit dans la chambre!

words.culturalNote:
Makelele — noise, racket, loud commotion.

Kinshasa is rich in makelele — markets, weddings, street music, prayer. The word can name joyful sound or unwelcome disturbance.

examples.lingala: Bato batelemi na molongo mpo na tike.
examples.english: People stood in a line for tickets.
examples.french: Les gens ont fait la queue pour les billets.

words.culturalNote:
Molongo — queue, ordered line; figuratively the world order.

Close cousin to mokoloto (#456). Molongo also names the way of the world — bomoi na molongo = life in order.

examples.english: Think well before speaking.
examples.french: Reflechis bien avant de parler.

words.culturalNote:
Kokanisa — to think, ponder, reflect (imperative kanisa).

A core verb of Kongo decision-making — elders insist on kokanisa malamu before any major step. Pairs with bwanya.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kokanisa — penser, réfléchir, méditer (impératif : kanisa).

Verbe central de la décision congolaise — les anciens insistent pour kokanisa malamu avant tout pas important. Va de pair avec bwanya.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kokanisa — kokanisa, komitungisa na makanisi (komandi: kanisa).

Liloba ya motó ya kozwa makanisi ya bato ya Kongo — bampaka basengaki ete kokanisa malamu liboso ya litambe nyonso ya monene. Esangani na bwanya.

examples.lingala: Mwasi na ye azali kosala na lopitalo.
examples.english: His wife works at the hospital.
examples.french: Sa femme travaille a l'hopital.

words.culturalNote:
Mwasi — woman, wife, female (basi pl.).

The core counterpart to mobali (#546). Mwasi na ngai = my wife. The word appears in countless compounds: mwana mwasi (daughter), mokonzi mwasi (queen).

examples.english: The soldier held a gun in his hand.
examples.french: Le soldat a tenu un fusil a la main.

words.culturalNote:
Bondoki — gun, rifle, firearm.

A heavy word, named carefully. Appears in news of conflict and in hunting talk. The same root carries lisasi (bullet, #469).

examples.english: Fill the bottle with water.
examples.french: Remplis la bouteille d'eau.

words.culturalNote:
Kotondisa — to fill up, saturate (causative of kotonda, #837 "to be full").

The -is- suffix marks the causative — to make-full. Used for bottles, buckets, hearts, and tanks.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Remplir — passer du vide au plein.

Kotondisa, c'est remplir — une katini de mai, une kopo de kawa, une phrase de sens. Le verbe achève ce que le vide ne fait que commencer.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kotondisa — kobongola kopanzana mpe kotondisa.

Kotondisa elimboli kotondisa — katini ya mai, kopo ya kawa, fraza ya ndimbola. Liloba esilisi oyo bopanzani ebandi kaka.

examples.lingala: Monganga apesi nkisi mpo na maladi ya libolo.
examples.english: The doctor gave medicine for the vaginal disease.
examples.french: Le medecin a donne des medicaments pour la maladie vaginale.

words.culturalNote:
Libolo — direct anatomical term for the vagina, flagged VULGAR / TABOO.

While lexicographically the singular term for the body part, libolo is highly taboo in public and functions as a severe profanity in casual speech. Polite alternatives: esika ya mwasi (a woman's place), nzoto (body), ebolo (clinical, cf. #948). Recorded here for completeness — a dictionary documents the language as it is actually spoken, including taboo registers, with clear social warnings.

examples.english: They should stop talking about semen.
examples.french: Qu'ils arretent de parler du sperme.

words.culturalNote:
Libidi — VULGAR SLANG for semen / reproductive fluid.

A crude street-language term, extremely vulgar in public dialogue. Polite/medical contexts use mai ya mobali or French sperme.

examples.english: He kicked him in the ass.
examples.french: Il lui a donne un coup au derriere.

words.culturalNote:
Lisoko — VULGAR singular form for buttock / arse.

The plural masoko is the cover term for profanity / insults in Lingala — masoko literally = "the rude words." Polite alternative for the body part: misuni ya nse / nzoto ya nsima.

examples.lingala: Liloba wana ezali liyende, tika koyoka yango.
examples.english: That word is clitoris, stop listening to it.
examples.french: Ce mot est clitoris, cesse de l'ecouter.

words.culturalNote:
Liyende — heavily TABOO anatomical term, almost exclusively used as a sharp, aggressive insult.

Recorded for lexicographic completeness with strong social warning. Not for general use; no neutral conversational equivalent.

examples.lingala: Basungili nzoto mpo na soka te.
examples.english: They do not speak publicly about the penis.
examples.french: On ne parle pas en public du sexe masculin.

words.culturalNote:
Soka — VULGAR / TABOO term for the penis. Not to be confused with the noun soka = axe (cf. #788).

Used in street-fight insults; severe register. Clinical / polite alternatives: nzoto ya mobali, French sexe.

examples.english: Insulting someone as uncircumcised is bad.
examples.french: Insulter quelqu un en le traitant de non-circoncis est mauvais.

words.culturalNote:
Mongele — VULGAR slang for an uncircumcised penis / foreskin; a deeply offensive cultural insult in the Congos attacking a man's maturity, hygiene, or initiation status.

Circumcision is a strong cultural marker across most DRC communities; this word weaponizes that.

examples.english: Pre-cum comes out first.
examples.french: Le liquide pre-seminal sort en premier.

words.culturalNote:
Mundende — CRUDE street slang for pre-ejaculatory fluid.

Highly explicit; used in vulgar sexual banter. No polite Lingala equivalent; medical contexts use French.

examples.lingala: Elongi na ye etondi na mafuta ya nsoko.
examples.english: His face is covered in ass juices.
examples.french: Son visage est couvert de fluides anaux.

words.culturalNote:
Mafuta ya nsoko — literally "oil of the buttocks." A VILE, graphic street insult used to degrade an opponent during arguments.

Among the strongest insults in Kinshasa street-quarrel vocabulary; recorded with extreme social warning.

examples.lingala: Tika koloba ete olingi kosiba ye.
examples.english: Stop saying you want to fuck her.
examples.french: Arrete de dire que tu veux la baiser.

words.culturalNote:
Kosiba (low tone) — VULGAR verb for sexual intercourse. Not to be confused with the modern slang kosiba (high tone) at #976 meaning "to chill / hang out."

The tonal difference is critical: kosiba (low) = sexual; kosiba (high) = chill. Mixing them publicly causes serious misunderstanding.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kosiba — traîner, se la couler douce (argot moderne de Kinshasa).

Le verbe de la flânerie sociale sans hâte : au wenze, sur un perron, dans une nganda. Verbe central de la culture urbaine des jeunes.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosiba — kotambola na bopembe, kopema (liloba ya argot ya Kinshasa ya sika).

Liloba ya kotambola-tambola ya lisanga kozanga koswana: na wenze, na esika ya kovanda liboso ya ndako, na nganda. Liloba ya motó ya bonkoko ya bilenge ya vile.

examples.lingala: Tamboli na ye ezali ya kilobolobo.
examples.english: Her lifestyle is slutty.
examples.french: Son comportement est devergonde.

words.culturalNote:
Kilobolobo — STREET DEROGATORY term attacking a person's sexual promiscuity.

Used almost exclusively as a slur; recorded for completeness with strong slur-warning. No neutral synonym.

examples.lingala: Bameki kobenga ye mwasi ya mamba.
examples.english: They tried calling her a hooker.
examples.french: Ils ont essaye de la traiter de prostituee.

words.culturalNote:
Mwasi ya mamba — literally "woman of the water/crocodile"; STREET SLANG / DEROGATORY for a sex worker.

A slur, not a neutral term; the modern neutral term is mosali ya nzoto (literally "body worker") or French travailleuse du sexe.

examples.lingala: Boyokani mpo na nzela ya sima te.
examples.english: Do not agree to anal sex.
examples.french: N'accepte pas la sodomie.

words.culturalNote:
Nzela ya sima — literally "the road behind." Euphemistic-but-crude VULGAR slang for anal intercourse.

Used in street talk and explicit conversation; clinical contexts use French sodomie.

examples.lingala: Abwaki ye fingo ya zolo ya libolo.
examples.english: He threw a vile "vagina-nose" insult at him.
examples.french: Il lui a lance l'insulte vile "nez de vagin".

words.culturalNote:
Zolo ya libolo — literally "nose of the vagina." A SEVERE, nonsensical compound insult designed purely to shock and degrade.

No literal meaning; the form is the offense. Recorded as a documented Kinshasa street-fight epithet.
words.french: insulte vile composee (litt. nez de vagin)

examples.english: That woman is an easy target.
examples.french: Cette femme est une fille facile.

words.culturalNote:
Mwaye — KINSHASA STREET SLANG for a woman perceived as promiscuous or as an "easy target."

A slur; recorded with derogatory-label warning.

examples.lingala: Sofele amoni ngai zoba lokola muga.
examples.english: The driver saw me as a fool, like a sucker.
examples.french: Le chauffeur m'a pris pour un pigeon.

words.culturalNote:
Muga — STREET SLANG used by hustlers and shrewd traders for a "mark" — someone easily ripped off or cheated.

Derogatory but not as severe as the sexual vulgarities; the hustler's vocabulary of the Kinshasa zando.

examples.english: Come here, you animal!
examples.french: Viens ici, sale bete!

words.culturalNote:
Niama — INSULT form (tonal homonym of #722 nyama = meat/animal, which is neutral).

When nyama is leveled directly at a person as "niama," it carries deep offense — implying the person lacks a soul or human decency. The change in tone marks the change in register.

examples.english: This man is a shameless degenerate.
examples.french: Cet homme n'a aucune honte.

words.culturalNote:
Soni te — literally "no shame." DEROGATORY label for someone who breaks heavy cultural taboos without showing remorse.

Nsoni (shame, #794) carries enormous weight in Kongo culture; saying someone has soni te is to mark them as outside the social order.

examples.english: Your shit! / Fuck you!
examples.french: Ta merde! / Va te faire foutre!

words.culturalNote:
Tufi — VULGAR street expletive for shit/feces; one of the most common Kinshasa swear words.

Used as a freestanding insult ("Tufi na yo!") to show absolute contempt. Polite reference for excrement: nyei (medical) or French selles.

examples.lingala: Likambo oyo ezali tufi ya mbwa.
examples.english: This whole matter is dog shit.
examples.french: Toute cette affaire est de la merde de chien.

words.culturalNote:
Tufi ya mbwa — literally "dog shit." VULGAR insult for something worthless, disgusting, or a total mess.

Applied to ideas, situations, or projects perceived as utterly broken.

examples.lingala: Kofinga moto "mama na yo" ebimisaka bitumba.
examples.english: Insulting someone with "your mother" triggers physical fights.
examples.french: Lancer "ta mere" a quelqu un provoque des bagarres.

words.culturalNote:
Mama na yo — literally "your mother." A SEVERE standalone exclamation in Kongo culture; explicitly hurling someone's mother at them as an insult is an extreme verbal assault that triggers immediate physical confrontation.

The mother is sacred; this weaponizes that. Reserved for when a fight is intended.

examples.lingala: Mbanda na ngai ayei kotumola ngai.
examples.english: My rival came to provoke me.
examples.french: Ma rivale est venue me provoquer.

words.culturalNote:
Mbanda — technically the co-wife in polygamous structures; in modern street slang weaponized to label any rival, hater, or romantic competitor.

Flexible insult-context word; the tone of voice colors whether it sits as a neutral kinship term or an attack.

examples.lingala: Tika kosala lokola moto ya kizengi.
examples.english: Stop acting like a crazy person.
examples.french: Arrete de faire le fou.

words.culturalNote:
Kizengi — INSULT attacking mental capacity or rational behavior.

A harsh slur in Lingala street speech. Polite/clinical: moto na maladi ya makanisi.

examples.lingala: Mobali wana azali yuma, akoki kobunda te.
examples.english: That man is a coward, he cannot fight.
examples.french: Cet homme est un lache, il ne sait pas se battre.

words.culturalNote:
Yuma — HEAVY street insult targeted at a male's masculinity or bravery.

A fighting word — used to publicly shame a man for backing down. Carries social weight in Kongo male-honor codes.

examples.english: Look at your ugly kitchen-soot face!
examples.french: Regarde ta face de suie de cuisine!

words.culturalNote:
Elongi kuku — literally "kitchen-pot-bottom face." INSULT mocking someone's'appearance, comparing it to the black soot caked on the underside of cooking pots.

Kitchen-pot insults are a long Kinshasa tradition of cooking-imagery slurs.

examples.english: This blockhead does not listen.
examples.french: Cette tete vide n'ecoute pas.

words.culturalNote:
Mutu gbagba — literally "head [+ ideophone for clumsy/bulky]." INSULT mocking stubbornness or lack of intelligence.

Gbagba is a Kinshasa street ideophone for something heavy, dull, and unresponsive.

examples.lingala: Kanga mbanga, munoko solo na yo!
examples.english: Shut your mouth, you stinky breath!
examples.french: Ferme ta gueule, espece de mauvaise haleine!

words.culturalNote:
Munoko solo — literally "stinky mouth." STREET INSULT used in arguments to humiliate an opponent.

A classic Kinshasa quarrel weapon — attacks both hygiene and the words coming out.

examples.english: This deaf blockhead won t hear.
examples.french: Cette tete dure aux oreilles bouchees n'ecoutera pas.

words.culturalNote:
Matoi ganda — literally "dead/blocked ears." INSULT for someone who ignores warnings or refuses to listen.

Family and elder context: used in exasperation toward stubbornly disobedient youth.

examples.english: A gossiping woman ruins the community.
examples.french: Une femme medisante detruit la communaute.

words.culturalNote:
Songi-songi — DEROGATORY label for a toxic gossip / rumormonger.

Less vulgar than the body-part insults; carries a deep moral sting in tightly-woven Kongo community life where gossip can fracture families.

examples.lingala: Kotika zoba wana ateka yo lokola ekeke.
examples.english: Don t let that fool sell you out like a dummy.
examples.french: Ne laisse pas ce sot te tromper comme un imbecile.

words.culturalNote:
Ekeke — Kinshasa STREET SLANG for someone naive or easy to manipulate.

Tonal homonym of #151 ekeke (yam, neutral). The slur sense is distinguished by tone and context.

examples.lingala: Eloko oyo ezali mosala ya zoba mabe.
examples.english: This thing is the work of an absolute idiot.
examples.french: Cette chose est l'oeuvre d'un imbecile total.

words.culturalNote:
Zoba mabe — INTENSIFIED zoba (#905 fool) + mabe (bad/evil). A sharper, fully aggressive insult.

Used to mock incompetent work, foolish decisions, or visible self-sabotage.

examples.english: Shut your trap right now!
examples.french: Ferme ta gueule tout de suite!

words.culturalNote:
Kanga mbanga — literally "close [your] jaw/trap." HIGHLY AGGRESSIVE command to silence someone.

Kanga = the imperative of kokanga (to close); mbanga = the jaw apparatus, here a crude term for mouth.

examples.lingala: Lofendo na yo ekokitisa yo na nse.
examples.english: Your extreme arrogance will bring you down.
examples.french: Ton arrogance excessive te fera tomber.

words.culturalNote:
Lofendo — DEROGATORY label for a younger or lower-status person acting disrespectfully toward elders.

In Kongo culture respect for elders is a load-bearing value; lofendo names a serious social breach.

examples.english: Go away, you stray beast!
examples.french: Va-t'en, sale bete errante!

words.culturalNote:
Nyama bamba — INTENSIFIED nyama (animal, #722) with bamba indicating feral, masterless, or unwanted.

INSULT implying the target has no lineage, no home, no human standing. Severe register.

examples.lingala: Mwana oyo akoti na nzela mbeba.
examples.english: This child entered a criminal lifestyle.
examples.french: Cet enfant est entre dans une voie criminelle.

words.culturalNote:
Nzela mbeba — literally "the destroyed road / corrupt path." DEROGATORY phrase used by parents or authorities for someone in gang life, sex work, or heavy street trouble.

A word of grief as much as judgment.
words.french: voie de la perdition / vie criminelle

examples.english: I will kick you in the asshole.
examples.french: Je vais te frapper au cul.

words.culturalNote:
Mono — VULGAR anatomical term for the anus, used colloquially in raw street arguments.

Clinical/polite: libulu ya nse / French anus. The vulgar register is the street-fight register.

examples.english: He went to take a shit in the bush.
examples.french: Il est alle chier dans la brousse.

words.culturalNote:
Kosumba — VULGAR verb for defecating.

Highly improper in polite company; speakers use euphemisms such as kokende kosala moke (literally "to go do a small thing") or kosala bizalele (to handle bathroom business).
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kosumba — verbe VULGAIRE pour déféquer.

Totalement inapproprié en compagnie polie ; les locuteurs utilisent des euphémismes comme kokende kosala moke (littéralement « aller faire une petite chose ») ou kosala bizalele (s'occuper d'une affaire de toilettes).
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kosumba — liloba ya mbindo mpo na kobimisa nyei.

Ebongi te na lisanga ya boboto; bato basaleli maloba ya bopembe lokola kokende kosala moke (kokende kosala likambo ya mokemoke) to kosala bizalele.

examples.english: They should stop this mindless street brawling.
examples.french: Qu'ils arretent ces bagarres absurdes.

words.culturalNote:
Bitumba mpamba — literally "empty fights." STREET PHRASE used to criticize pointless neighborhood violence.

Elders use it to redirect young men away from rivalries that lead nowhere.

examples.english: Do you see me as stale bread?
examples.french: Tu me prends pour du pain rassis?

words.culturalNote:
Lipa golo — literally "cheap/stale bread." STREET IDIOM thrown back at someone who is underestimating your worth.

A defiant slur-comeback, asserting that the speaker is being treated as worthless when they are not.

examples.english: That thing rotted away long ago.
examples.french: Ce truc est pourri depuis longtemps.

words.culturalNote:
Kofwama — STREET SLANG verb for rotting away, expiring, being completely finished.

Applied aggressively to broken items, dead projects, or a person whose reputation is gone. Sharper than just kobeba (to spoil).
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kofwama — verbe d'ARGOT pour pourrir, expirer, être complètement fini.

Appliqué avec force aux objets cassés, aux projets morts, ou à une personne dont la réputation s'est effondrée. Plus tranchant que kobeba (gâter).
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kofwama — liloba ya argot ya rue mpo na kopola, kosila, kobeba mobimba.

Basaleli yango makasi mpo na biloko ya kobukana, mosala ya kokufa, to moto oyo lokumu na ye esili. Makasi koleka kobeba.

examples.lingala: Maloba na yo ezali liyebisi mpamba.
examples.english: Your words are absolute bullshit.
examples.french: Tes paroles sont des sornettes.

words.culturalNote:
Liyebisi mpamba — literally "empty announcement." SLANG rejection of a claim as fake or useless.

A verbal kill-shot in marketplace and barbershop arguments: marks the other person's talk as worthless.

examples.english: Right now I am completely broke, the money is gone.
examples.french: Maintenant je suis fauche, l'argent est fini.

words.culturalNote:
Lofele — UNIVERSAL KINSHASA SLANG for being completely broke, having zero funds.

Mild slang, not offensive — heard at the market, the nganda, the kiosk. A daily Kinshasa condition recognized with humor.

examples.lingala: Batika kobenga ye ekbele na nzela.
examples.english: They should stop calling her a low-tier prostitute on the street.
examples.french: Qu'ils arretent de la traiter de prostituee bas-de-gamme dans la rue.

words.culturalNote:
Ekbele — CRUDE Kinshasa street slur targeting a woman's'appearance and promiscuity.

A severe slur; recorded for completeness with strong derogatory warning.

examples.english: They are drinking heavy moonshine this evening.
examples.french: Ils boivent du fort alcool de quartier ce soir.

words.culturalNote:
Zola — STREET SLANG for low-quality, highly intoxicating locally brewed alcohol.

In many Kinshasa quarters zola is a known social hazard; the word appears in songs and warnings.

examples.lingala: Tala ebolo moto oyo, ayebi mosala te.
examples.english: Look at this dumb beast — he doesn t know how to work.
examples.french: Regarde cet abruti, il ne sait pas travailler.

words.culturalNote:
Ebolo moto — AGGRESSIVE compound combining anatomy-vulgarity with moto (person) to strip away someone's'intellect.

Severe register; used at peak frustration in arguments.

words.english: dog s testicle / absolute zero (vulgar insult)

examples.lingala: Mosala na yo ezali likato ya mbwa.
examples.english: Your work is completely worthless dog shit.
examples.french: Ton travail est de la merde de chien.

words.culturalNote:
Likato ya mbwa — literally "dog's testicle." HIGHLY OFFENSIVE marketplace term used to tell someone their effort or product is utter garbage.

Reserved for sharp commercial rebukes.

examples.lingala: Afwamisi mbongo nyonso na biloko mpamba.
examples.english: He completely wasted all the money on useless things.
examples.french: Il a totalement gaspille tout l'argent en futilites.

words.culturalNote:
Kofwamisa — STREET SLANG causative of kofwama (to rot, #1046). To make-rot, i.e., to ruin entirely.

Applied to budgets, projects, careers, reputations.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kofwamisa — causatif d'ARGOT de kofwama (pourrir). « Faire pourrir », c'est-à-dire ruiner entièrement.

Appliqué aux budgets, aux projets, aux carrières, aux réputations.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kofwamisa — causatif ya argot ya kofwama. Kosala ete eloko epola, elingi koloba kobebisa mobimba.

Basaleli yango mpo na mbongo, misala, bomoyi ya mosala, lokumu.

examples.lingala: Likambo wana ezali solo lokola mayi ya soko.
examples.english: That matter stinks like ass fluids.
examples.french: Cette affaire pue comme des fluides anaux.

words.culturalNote:
Mayi ya soko — literally "water of buttocks." VULGAR street epithet for a disgusting situation or a lie.

Used in escalated arguments to label something as foul beyond repair.

examples.lingala: Kende kosukola elongi potopoto na yo.
examples.english: Go wash your muddy trash face.
examples.french: Va laver ta sale gueule boueuse.

words.culturalNote:
Elongi potopoto — literally "mud face." STREET INSULT mocking unkempt appearance or poor hygiene.

A mud-as-metaphor insult, sister to elongi kuku (#1031 soot-face).

examples.lingala: Mata na mutuka, motengoli zoba oyo!
examples.english: Get in the car, you limping idiot!
examples.french: Monte dans la voiture, espece de boiteux imbecile!

words.culturalNote:
Motengoli zoba — combines a physical-impairment slur with zoba (fool, #905).

Aggressively mocks both physical coordination and intelligence. Severe register.

examples.lingala: Sikoyo azali lofele mabe, azangi ndako.
examples.english: Right now he is completely flat broke and lacks a house.
examples.french: En ce moment il est completement fauche et sans abri.

words.culturalNote:
Lofele mabe — INTENSIFIED lofele (#1048 broke) + mabe (bad).

Describes total destitution with no backup or family fallback. A worried elder's phrase about a struggling youth.

examples.lingala: Koyoka ye te, azali munoko mpamba.
examples.english: Do not listen to him — he is an empty talker.
examples.french: Ne l'ecoute pas, il est un beau parleur.

words.culturalNote:
Munoko mpamba — literally "empty mouth." DEROGATORY for someone who promises big and delivers nothing.

A classic marketplace warning about smooth talkers.

examples.english: He cursed me out explicitly in front of people.
examples.french: Il m'a insulte publiquement devant tout le monde.

words.culturalNote:
Kofingela — APPLICATIVE form of kofinga (#305 to insult). Marks the verbal abuse as directed at a specific person.

The -el- applicative suffix focuses the action on a recipient.
words.culturalNoteFr:
Kofingela — forme APPLICATIVE de kofinga (insulter). Marque l'injure verbale dirigée vers une personne précise.

Le suffixe applicatif -el- recentre l'action sur un destinataire.
words.culturalNoteLn:
Kofingela — ndenge ya APPLICATIVE ya kofinga. Emonisi kofinga oyo etalisami na moto moko ya sikisiki.

Suffixe -el- atalisaki mosala likolo ya moto oyo azwi yango.

examples.english: Shut up, you stinky asshole!
examples.french: Ferme-la, sale trou-du-cul!

words.culturalNote:
Mono solo — compound of mono (anus, #1043) + solo (stinky/rot).

VILE, raw street profanity for shutting down an opponent during a screaming match.

examples.english: He fled the fight like a spineless coward.
examples.french: Il a fui la bagarre comme un lache traitre.

words.culturalNote:
Yuma mabe — INTENSIFIED yuma (#1030 coward) + mabe (bad/evil).

Degrades a male's character on two fronts: cowardice + treachery.

examples.lingala: Elengi na ye ekomi lokola mwasi ya zando.
examples.english: Her behavior has become like a loud, unrefined market woman.
examples.french: Son comportement est devenu celui d'une marchande criarde.

words.culturalNote:
Mwasi ya zando — STREET STEREOTYPE used to insult a woman's manners or volume.

The zando (market) is a place of strong personalities; the slur unfairly weaponizes that into a class/refinement attack.

examples.lingala: Somba biloko na ye, azali muga zoba.
examples.english: Buy his things — he is a prime sucker.
examples.french: Achete-lui ses affaires, c'est un pigeon parfait.

words.culturalNote:
Muga zoba — INTENSIFIED muga (#995 sucker) + zoba (fool).

Hustler vocabulary for a victim who is exceptionally easy to overcharge or cheat.

examples.lingala: Olingi mosala te, ozali se niama ndako.
examples.english: You don t want to work — you are just a lazy house beast.
examples.french: Tu ne veux pas travailler, tu n'es qu'une bete de maison.

words.culturalNote:
Niama ndako — combines niama (animal-as-insult, #1023) with ndako (house).

A family-level slur for a dependent who eats but contributes nothing. Cuts deep in households where everyone is expected to pull weight.

examples.english: This shit-head forgot the key.
examples.french: Cette tete de merde a oublie la cle.

words.culturalNote:
Mutu tufi — literally "shit-head." GRAPHIC compound insult mocking memory or common sense.

Direct Lingala parallel to the English shit-head, used in similar contexts.

examples.lingala: Mobali wana azali mofati mpamba na mosala.
examples.english: That man is physically useless at manual labor.
examples.french: Cet homme est nul physiquement au travail manuel.

words.culturalNote:
Mofati mpamba — combines mofati (hip/groin, #950) with mpamba (empty/useless).

STREET SLUR targeting physical weakness or stamina; can be a fighting word among day-laborers.

examples.lingala: Atamboli na lisoko monene na balabala.
examples.english: She walked down the street with a prominent rear end.
examples.french: Elle marche dans la rue avec un gros derriere.

words.culturalNote:
Lisoko monene — VULGAR descriptor / catcall pairing lisoko (vulgar buttock, #1010) with monene (big).

Depending on tone, functions as crude street catcalling or direct body insult.

examples.lingala: Lofendo mabe na ye ebebisi boninga.
examples.english: His toxic arrogance ruined the friendship.
examples.french: Son arrogance toxique a detruit l'amitie.

words.culturalNote:
Lofendo mabe — INTENSIFIED lofendo (#1039 arrogance) + mabe (bad).

Calls out arrogance that has crossed from off-putting into actively destructive.

examples.lingala: Bakoti na kati ya bitumba zoba.
examples.english: They got tangled up in a stupid street brawl.
examples.french: Ils se sont embarques dans une bagarre stupide.

words.culturalNote:
Bitumba zoba — bitumba (fights) + zoba (fool).

Elders use this to criticize chaotic, disorganized neighborhood violence that produces only injuries.

examples.lingala: Tika ye, azali lipa fwama sikoyo.
examples.english: Leave him alone, he is a total write-off right now.
examples.french: Laisse-le, c'est un cas perdu maintenant.

words.culturalNote:
Lipa fwama — bread-imagery compound combining lipa (#1045 cheap bread) with fwama (rotten).

Slang for a person whose chances, career, or life have collapsed past recovery.

examples.english: That entire matter is a malicious lie.
examples.french: Toute cette histoire est un mensonge calomnieux.

words.culturalNote:
Liyebisi lokuta — liyebisi (announcement / news) + lokuta (#489 lie).

Aggressive rejection of a rumor or report as fake. Politics and gossip alike.

examples.lingala: Azali koluka bitumba mpo azali na soka moke.
examples.english: He is looking for fights because he has a small penis.
examples.french: Il cherche la bagarre parce qu'il a un petit penis.

words.culturalNote:
Soka moke — soka (#1012 vulgar penis) + moke (small). SEVERE blow to male ego in verbal confrontations.

A fighting word; reserved for moments meant to provoke physical retaliation.

examples.lingala: Bomoi na bango etondi na kilobolobo mabe.
examples.english: Their lifestyle is full of extreme promiscuity.
examples.french: Leur mode de vie est rempli de devergondage extreme.

words.culturalNote:
Kilobolobo mabe — INTENSIFIED kilobolobo (#1017 slutty behavior) + mabe (bad).

Vile street label for socially ostracizing a person or group's sexual conduct.

examples.lingala: Mpese ezali kotambola na kati ya kuku.
examples.english: A cockroach is walking inside the kitchen.
examples.french: Un cafard marche dans la cuisine.

words.culturalNote:
Mpese — the common cockroach, ubiquitous in Kinshasa kitchens and markets.

Robust survivors; mpese is often used figuratively for someone impossibly hard to get rid of.

examples.lingala: Lipekapeka ya kitoko epumbwa pembeni ya nzete.
examples.english: A beautiful butterfly flew next to the tree.
examples.french: Un beau papillon a volé près de l'arbre.

words.culturalNote:
Lipekapeka — butterfly or moth; the reduplication mirrors the fluttering of wings.

In Congolese proverbs, the butterfly symbolises transformation and the fleeting nature of beauty.

examples.lingala: Liyoyo ezali koyemba na zamba na butu.
examples.english: The cricket is singing in the forest at night.
examples.french: Le grillon chante dans la forêt la nuit.

words.culturalNote:
Liyoyo — the chirping cricket or cicada whose song fills the equatorial night.

The sound of liyoyo is the acoustic backdrop of village evenings across the Congo Basin.

examples.lingala: Keba na kanga-nkando, eswaka na makasi.
examples.english: Careful with the scorpion, it stings fiercely.
examples.french: Fais attention au scorpion, il pique férocement.

words.culturalNote:
Kanga-nkando — literally "holder of the stinger / tail." The scorpion; found in rocky crevices and under bark.

Its curved tail (nkando) gives it the name; greatly feared in rural communities.

examples.lingala: Nsingo eswi mwana mwasi na litama.
examples.english: A wasp stung the girl on the cheek.
examples.french: Une guêpe a piqué la fille sur la joue.

words.culturalNote:
Nsingo — wasp or hornet; nests are found under eaves and in hollow trees.

Distinct from nzoi (honeybee) — nsingo produces no honey and attacks unprovoked if disturbed.

examples.lingala: Mafundo ezali kotambola malembe na mabele.
examples.english: A centipede is walking slowly on the ground.
examples.french: Un mille-pattes marche lentement sur le sol.

words.culturalNote:
Mafundo — multi-legged crawler; the centipede (fast, venomous) or millipede (slow, harmless).

Children are taught to avoid the red centipede whose bite causes intense pain.

examples.lingala: Monguna-ya-nzinzi asali singa na litumu ya suku.
examples.english: The spider made a web in the corner of the room.
examples.french: L'araignée a fait une toile dans le coin de la pièce.

words.culturalNote:
Monguna-ya-nzinzi — literally "enemy of the fly." The spider; its Lingala name already tells its ecological role.

Large orb-weaver spiders are common across the Congo Basin and respected for their intricate webs.

examples.english: A snake bit the goat in the field.
examples.french: Un serpent a mordu la chèvre dans le champ.

words.culturalNote:
Nioka — the generic Lingala word for snake.

The Congo Basin hosts hundreds of species including the Gaboon viper and green mamba. Nioka carries deep symbolic weight: in oral tradition, the python ancestor-spirit appears as a great serpent.

examples.english: The monkey is jumping across the trees.
examples.french: Le singe saute à travers les arbres.

words.culturalNote:
Makaku — monkey or ape; used broadly for primates.

The DRC is home to bonobos (the closest living relatives to humans) and gorillas. Makaku in everyday speech usually means the smaller, common forest monkey.

examples.lingala: Ngando azali kozila banyama na kati ya ebale.
examples.english: The crocodile is waiting for animals inside the river.
examples.french: Le crocodile attend des animaux au fond de la rivière.

words.culturalNote:
Ngando — the Nile crocodile, apex ambush predator of the Congo River.

Ngando appears in Kongo cosmology as a creature bridging the worlds of the living and the ancestors who dwell beneath the water.

examples.english: The wild buffalo has strong bones.
examples.french: Le buffle des forêts a des os solides.

words.culturalNote:
Nzamba — the African forest buffalo (Syncerus caffer nanus), smaller and darker than the savanna cape buffalo.

Hunted across DRC; its tough hide is used for drums and shields in traditional communities.

examples.lingala: Nzoku amemi nzete monene na molai.
examples.english: The elephant carried a huge, tall tree.
examples.french: L'éléphant a porté un grand arbre immense.

words.culturalNote:
Nzoku — the elephant; among the most culturally revered animals in Congo.

Once prolific across the Basin, forest elephants are now endangered from ivory poaching. In proverbs, nzoku represents power, memory, and the weight of tradition.

examples.lingala: Pakasa azali kotambola na makasi na kati ya esobe.
examples.english: The forest buffalo is walking powerfully inside the marshy plain.
examples.french: Le buffle de forêt marche puissamment dans la plaine marécageuse.

words.culturalNote: Pakasa — the African forest buffalo, the smaller, reddish-coated cousin of the savanna buffalo. Lives in small herds in the equatorial deep wood; unpredictable when surprised and capable of a fast charge. Hunters walk wide of fresh tracks. (Bushbuck/antelope is mboloko, not pakasa.)
words.french: buffle de forêt d'Afrique (Syncerus caffer nanus)

examples.lingala: Mobali amati na mpunda mpo na kokende mosika.
examples.english: The man rode a horse to go far away.
examples.french: L'homme est monté sur le cheval pour aller loin.

words.culturalNote:
Mpunda — horse or donkey; not native to equatorial Africa but present through trade and colonial introduction.

In the DRC, horses are associated with wealth and colonial administration; donkeys with heavy rural labour.

examples.lingala: Ligbanga amati na efelo ya ndako.
examples.english: The lizard climbed up the house wall.
examples.french: Le lézard a grimpé sur le mur de la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Ligbanga — the common wall lizard or gecko; a familiar companion in every Congolese home.

Geckos are welcomed for eating mosquitoes; in some communities they are considered luck-bringers near the hearth.

examples.lingala: Makanga balei nkoni nyonso na sima ya ndako.
examples.english: Termites ate all the firewood behind the house.
examples.french: Les termites ont mangé tout le bois de chauffage derrière la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Makanga — termites; their mounds (termitieres) are a defining feature of the Congolese landscape, some rising over 3 metres.

Termite alates (flying termites) are caught and eaten as a crunchy protein snack during their swarming season.

examples.english: The dragonfly flew over the water.
examples.french: La libellule a volé au-dessus de l'eau.

words.culturalNote:
Ndongondongo — the dragonfly; its reduplicated name imitates the rapid wing-beats.

Found hovering over streams and rice paddies; children try to catch them. Symbol of summer rains and the river life.

examples.english: The tsetse fly causes sleeping sickness.
examples.french: La mouche tsé-tsé provoque la maladie du sommeil.

words.culturalNote:
Nzinzi-ya-lolemo — literally "fly of the tongue / sleeping." The tsetse fly, vector of trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), one of the most feared diseases in rural DRC.

Control campaigns have dramatically reduced cases, but nzinzi-ya-lolemo remains a feared name in the forest regions.

examples.lingala: Kimbwa azali koluka nyama ya kowa na zamba.
examples.english: The jackal is looking for a dead animal in the forest.
examples.french: Le chacal cherche une bête morte dans la forêt.

words.culturalNote:
Kimbwa — the jackal or wild dog; a scavenger of the savanna and forest edge.

Distinct from mbwa (domestic dog), kimbwa carries a connotation of cunning and opportunism in Lingala proverbs.

examples.lingala: Esele abombi mbuma ya nzete na libulu.
examples.english: The squirrel hid the tree fruit in the hole.
examples.french: L'écureuil a caché le fruit de l'arbre dans le trou.

words.culturalNote:
Esele — the tree squirrel; quick, cheeky climbers of the forest canopy.

Children delight in watching squirrels; esele is also slang for someone nimble and hard to catch.

examples.lingala: Elulu ayembaka na butu na likolo ya ndako.
examples.english: The owl sings at night on top of the house.
examples.french: Le hibou chante la nuit sur le toit de la maison.

words.culturalNote:
Elulu — the owl; its nocturnal call carries deep cultural weight in many Congolese communities.

Elulu is widely associated with omens and witchcraft; hearing it hoot near a home at night is considered a warning of misfortune in many villages.

examples.lingala: Mpongo akangi nsoso mwasi kowuta na likolo.
examples.english: The eagle caught a hen from up above.
examples.french: L'aigle a attrapé une poule depuis les hauteurs.

words.culturalNote:
Mpongo — the eagle or large hawk; the king of the sky in Congolese oral tradition.

The African crowned eagle preys on monkeys and small antelopes. Mpongo feathers are used in ceremonial headdresses for chiefs.

examples.lingala: Ganga azali na mposo ya moindo na pembe.
examples.english: The crow has a coat of black and white.
examples.french: Le corbeau a un plumage noir et blanc.

words.culturalNote: Ganga — broad term for the family of dark scavenging birds: pied crow, vulture, raven. Used colloquially across all of them; context (the rubbish heap, the carcass on the road, the roof at dawn) tells you which. In folk reading, a perched ganga can carry an omen.

examples.english: The toad is jumping in the mud.
examples.french: Le crapaud saute dans la boue.

words.culturalNote:
Elondo — the large toad or bullfrog; its booming call announces the rains.

In Congo, toads are associated with rain season. Some communities use toad skins in traditional medicine.

examples.lingala: Limfumbe azali kotimola na nse ya mabele.
examples.english: The earthworm is digging beneath the soil.
examples.french: Le ver de terre creuse sous la terre.

words.culturalNote:
Limfumbe — the earthworm; unseen aerator of the soil, essential to farmland health.

Farmers across the DRC know a field with many limfumbe is fertile soil. Also used as fishing bait.

examples.lingala: Kigwa azali koyemba tango mvula ebandi konoka.
examples.english: The green tree frog sings when the rain starts falling.
examples.french: La petite grenouille verte chante quand la pluie commence à tomber.

words.culturalNote:
Kigwa — the small green tree frog; its piercing chirp is the opening note of every rainstorm.

Distinct from elondo (toad); kigwa lives in trees and is rarely seen but always heard before rain.

examples.lingala: Mwasi asukoli nsuki mpo na longola nsili.
examples.english: The woman washed her hair to remove lice.
examples.french: La femme a lavé ses cheveux pour enlever les poux.

words.culturalNote:
Nsili — head louse; grooming to remove nsili (delousing) has been a community bonding ritual across Central Africa for centuries.

Parents routinely check children's'hair; "bali nsili" (removing lice) also describes the act of careful communal care.

examples.lingala: Ndamba abongolaka langi na ye na nzete.
examples.english: The chameleon changes its color on the tree.
examples.french: Le caméléon change de couleur sur l'arbre.

words.culturalNote:
Ndamba — the chameleon; one of the most symbolically rich animals in Kongo cosmology.

The chameleon's colour change is a metaphor for hypocrisy or adaptability depending on context. In some traditions, ndamba is a messenger between realms because it moves between light and shadow.

examples.lingala: Bana balokoti liyebe ebele pembeni ya ebale.
examples.english: The children collected many snails by the edge of the river.
examples.french: Les enfants ont ramassé beaucoup d'escargots au bord de la rivière.

words.culturalNote:
Liyebe — the snail; collected by children along river banks and in the forest after rain.

Snails are eaten as a protein source in many Congolese communities; their shells are also used as musical instruments and in decorative crafts.

examples.lingala: Linyongo azali kolia lokasa ya nzete.
examples.english: The caterpillar is eating the tree leaf.
examples.french: La chenille mange la feuille de l'arbre.

words.culturalNote:
Linyongo — the caterpillar; caterpillars of several species are dried and eaten as a crunchy, protein-rich delicacy across the DRC.

The edible caterpillar harvest is an important seasonal food source in forest communities — not to be confused with the inedible varieties.

examples.lingala: Bambwa batondi na mpilo mpo na potopoto.
examples.english: The dogs are full of fleas because of the mud.
examples.french: Les chiens sont pleins de puces à cause de la boue.

words.culturalNote:
Mpilo — the flea; a pest of domestic animals and occasionally humans.

Distinct from nsili (head louse), mpilo jumps and infests bedding. Controlling mpilo in livestock is an ongoing rural concern.

examples.lingala: Mwasi-ya-nzoi azali na kati ya ndako-nzoi.
examples.english: The queen bee is inside the beehive.
examples.french: La reine des abeilles est à l'intérieur de la ruche.

words.culturalNote:
Mwasi-ya-nzoi — literally "woman of the bee / wife of the bee." The queen bee.

Beekeeping is practised across DRC; honey is both a food and medicine. The queen's role as the hive's mother is directly reflected in her Lingala name.

examples.lingala: Nkungi ebele ezali kotungisa biso na mbalasa.
examples.english: Many gnats are bothering us on the porch.
examples.french: De nombreux moucherons nous importunent sur la véranda.

words.culturalNote:
Nkungi — the tiny biting gnat or midge; different from the larger nzinzi (housefly) and the feared nzinzi-ya-lolemo (tsetse).

Nkungi swarms are a nuisance at dusk near standing water; they are small enough to pass through standard mosquito nets.

examples.english: The rotting meat has bred maggots.
examples.french: La viande pourrie a produit des asticots.

words.culturalNote:
Mofoti — maggot or grub; the larval form of flies found in decaying organic matter.
