In traditional medicine, some healers use cleaned fly larvae to debride wounds — a practice known in many cultures. In everyday speech, calling food "mofoti" is a severe insult.

examples.lingala: Mongongoliko atelemi na singa ya lopango.
examples.english: The horned lizard stood on the yard wire.
examples.french: Le lézard cornu s'est arrêté sur le fil de la clôture.

words.culturalNote:
Mongongoliko — a horned or spiny variant lizard; distinct from the common ligbanga (wall gecko).

Less common than geckos; its distinctive spines and colours make it memorable. In some communities it is considered a luck charm.

examples.english: The water snake is swimming in the river.
examples.french: Le serpent d'eau nage dans la rivière.

words.culturalNote:
Ngando-ya-mai — literally "crocodile of the water" or water snake; refers to semi-aquatic snakes of the Congo River basin.

Some species are venomous; fishermen on dugout canoes learn to spot them by the V-wake they leave crossing the current.

examples.lingala: Ngulu-ya-zamba azali koluka masango na elanga.
examples.english: The wild boar is looking for corn in the field.
examples.french: Le sanglier cherche du maïs dans le champ.

words.culturalNote:
Ngulu-ya-zamba — literally "pig of the forest." The warthog or forest wild boar.

Distinct from ngulu (domestic pig); the warthog's tusks make it dangerous. It raids crops and is hunted for its tough, flavourful meat.

examples.english: The otter caught a fish in the stream.
examples.french: La loutre a attrapé un poisson dans le ruisseau.

words.culturalNote:
Nkoi-ya-mai — literally "leopard of the water." The otter; its agility and hunting skill earn it this powerful name.

Spotted-necked and Congo clawless otters inhabit the river systems; they are shy and rarely seen despite living near fishing communities.

words.english: wild hunting dog / African wild dog

examples.english: The wild hunting dogs are tracking a dwarf antelope.
examples.french: Les chiens sauvages traquent une petite antilope.

words.culturalNote:
Mbwa-ya-zamba — literally "dog of the forest." The African painted hunting dog (Lycaon pictus); highly endangered.

Known for their co-operative pack hunting, they are among the most efficient predators in Africa. Rarely seen in the DRC today.

examples.lingala: Mboloko-mwasi akimi tango ayoki mongongo ya nkosi.
examples.english: The female antelope fled when she heard the lion's voice.
examples.french: La femelle antilope s'est enfuie quand elle a entendu la voix du lion.

words.culturalNote:
Mboloko-mwasi — literally "female dwarf antelope." The doe; distinguished from the male (with horns) by this compound.

The -mwasi (female/woman) suffix is the standard Lingala way to mark the female of a species.

examples.lingala: Ebenga azali kolokoti nguba na mabele.
examples.english: The pigeon is picking up peanuts on the ground.
examples.french: Le pigeon ramasse des arachides sur le sol.

words.culturalNote:
Ebenga — the pigeon or dove; one of the most common birds of Kinshasa's'urban landscape.

African green pigeons and speckled pigeons nest in mango and palm trees. The dove is a symbol of peace in Congolese Christian communities.

examples.lingala: Tata aboti nsoso-ya-zamba mibale na soka.
examples.english: Father caught two wild guinea fowls in the field.
examples.french: Père a attrapé deux pintades sauvages dans le champ.

words.culturalNote:
Nsoso-ya-zamba — literally "chicken of the forest." The helmeted guinea fowl, distinct from nsoso (domestic chicken).

Highly prized for its meat; hunters pursue it at dawn when it calls loudly. Its spotted feathers are used in traditional dress.

examples.lingala: Nkoo azali koloba maloba ya bato na mayele.
examples.english: The grey parrot is intelligently mimicking human words.
examples.french: Le perroquet gris imite intelligemment les mots humains.

words.culturalNote:
Nkoo — the African grey parrot (Psittacus erithacus); native to the Congo Basin rainforest and renowned as the world's most intelligent talking bird.

Illegal trafficking has devastated wild populations; DRC is a major source country. Owning nkoo was once a mark of prestige among chiefs.

examples.lingala: Mpongo-moke akiti mbangu mpo na kokanga mpese.
examples.english: The falcon swooped down fast to catch a cockroach.
examples.french: Le faucon a plongé vite pour attraper un cafard.

words.culturalNote:
Mpongo-moke — literally "small eagle." The kestrel or small falcon; agile aerial hunter that hovers before diving.

Distinct from the larger mpongo (eagle/hawk). Common around open fields and urban edges where it preys on insects and lizards.

examples.lingala: Mbila-ndeke avandi na likolo ya limbila.
examples.english: The hornbill sat on top of the oil palm tree.
examples.french: Le calao s'est posé au sommet du palmier à huile.

words.culturalNote:
Mbila-ndeke — literally "palm tree bird." The hornbill; recognisable by its massive, curved bill and casque.

The great hornbill is a keystone species, dispersing large seeds across the forest. Its beak is used in some ceremonial masks.

examples.lingala: Nsinga-mayi akangami na lokolo na ngai na ebale.
examples.english: A leech latched onto my leg in the river.
examples.french: Une sangsue s'est accrochée à ma jambe dans la rivière.

words.culturalNote:
Nsinga-mayi — literally "rope of the water." The leech; blood-sucking aquatic worm that clings to waders in slow-moving water.

Feared by children swimming in rivers; in some traditional healing practices, leeches are used for bloodletting.

examples.english: Mother fried fresh tilapia.
examples.french: Maman a frit du tilapia frais.

words.culturalNote:
Mbisi-mumpende — tilapia; the most important freshwater food fish of the Congo River and its tributaries.

A protein staple for millions of Congolese families; sold fresh, dried, and smoked at every riverside market. Farming tilapia in ponds is an expanding livelihood.

examples.lingala: Kanga-ya-mai azali na kati ya potopoto.
examples.english: The river crab is inside the mud.
examples.french: Le crabe de rivière est dans la boue.

words.culturalNote:
Kanga-ya-mai — literally "holder of the water." The freshwater / river crab.

River crabs are harvested from the banks of the Congo and its tributaries; they are boiled or grilled and are a popular street food in riverside towns.

examples.lingala: Nkisi oyo elongoli limfumbe-monene na libumu.
examples.english: This medicine removed the tapeworm from the stomach.
examples.french: Ce médicament a éliminé le ténia de l'estomac.

words.culturalNote:
Limfumbe-monene — literally "large earthworm." The tapeworm or intestinal worm; distinct from limfumbe (common earthworm) by the -monene (large/great) qualifier.

Intestinal parasites are a significant health issue in areas without clean water; anti-worm medicines are widely distributed in DRC health campaigns.

examples.lingala: Mumpulu ezali koswa mwana na mbeto na butu.
examples.english: Bedbugs are biting the child in bed at night.
examples.french: Les punaises de lit piquent l'enfant au lit la nuit.

words.culturalNote:
Mumpulu — the bedbug; a flat, blood-sucking insect that hides in mattress seams and wooden furniture.

A household pest across urban Congo; their bites cause intense itching. Controlling mumpulu is a persistent challenge in densely packed urban housing.

examples.lingala: Liyoyo-ya-elanga balei matiti nyonso na lisala.
examples.english: The locusts ate all the grass in the field.
examples.french: Les criquets ont mangé toute l'herbe dans le champ.

words.culturalNote:
Liyoyo-ya-elanga — literally "cricket of the field." The grasshopper or migratory locust.

Locust swarms historically devastated crops across Central Africa; today, a single swarm can still strip a field in hours. Grasshoppers are also fried and eaten as a crunchy snack.

examples.english: The black horsefly bit the cow on the flank.
examples.french: Le taon noir a piqué la vache sur le flanc.

words.culturalNote:
Ndongondongo-moindo — literally "black dragonfly." The large biting horsefly; distinct from the hovering dragonfly (ndongondongo) by the -moindo (black/dark) qualifier.

Bites are painful and bleed; livestock suffer greatly from horsefly attacks during the rainy season.

examples.lingala: Nzinzi-mabe azali kopumbwa likolo ya nyama ya kofwama.
examples.english: The blowfly is buzzing over the rotting meat.
examples.french: La mouche à viande bourdonne au-dessus de la viande pourrie.

words.culturalNote:
Nzinzi-mabe — literally "bad fly." The blowfly or bluebottle; attracted to rotting meat and open wounds where it lays eggs.

Its metallic sheen and loud buzz signal decay; nzinzi-mabe is a health hazard around outdoor markets in hot weather.

examples.lingala: Longola nzoloko na mposo ya mbwa.
examples.english: Remove the tick from the dog's skin.
examples.french: Enlève la tique de la peau du chien.

words.culturalNote:
Nzoloko — the tick; a blood-sucking arachnid parasite of livestock and dogs.

Cattle ticks spread East Coast Fever, a deadly cattle disease; tick control is critical for Congolese pastoralists. Removing nzoloko from mbwa (dogs) is a daily task for children in rural households.

examples.english: The house rat ate the bread on the table.
examples.french: Le rat domestique a mangé le pain sur la table.

words.culturalNote:
Esele-ya-ndako — literally "squirrel of the house." The domestic rat or house mouse.

Distinct from the wild esele (squirrel); the compound signals this animal has moved into human spaces. A pantry pest across all of urban Congo; also associated with the spread of leptospirosis.

examples.lingala: Lokonga atelemi na lokolo moko pembele ya mayi.
examples.english: The heron stood on one leg at the water's edge.
examples.french: Le héron s'est tenu sur une jambe au bord de l'eau.

words.culturalNote:
Lokonga — the heron or stork; a tall, elegant wading bird of river banks and wetlands.

The grey heron's patient single-leg stance while fishing is well known. Flocks of open-billed storks are a common sight over the Congo River's floodplains.

examples.english: The pied crow flew over the market.
examples.french: La corneille pie a volé au-dessus du marché.

words.culturalNote:
Ganga-pembe — literally "white crow." The pied crow (Corvus albus); the most common large corvid across sub-Saharan Africa.

Its black and white pattern makes it unmistakable over Kinshasa's markets, where it scavenges relentlessly. Highly intelligent like all crows.
words.french: corneille pie / corbeau à cou blanc

examples.english: The children caught a small mud eel in the swamp.
examples.french: Les enfants ont attrapé une petite anguille de vase dans le marécage.

words.culturalNote:
Monzombo-moke — literally "small swamp eel." A small mud eel found in marshy ground and river-edge mud.

Children catch these with their hands in the swamp mud; they are grilled whole and eaten as a snack.

examples.lingala: Liyebe-ya-nzete ezali kotambola na mposo ya nzete.
examples.english: The slug is crawling on the tree bark.
examples.french: La limace rampe sur l'écorce de l'arbre.

words.culturalNote:
Liyebe-ya-nzete — literally "snail of the tree." The tree snail or slug; found on bark and leaves in the forest.

Distinct from liyebe (river snail); the -ya-nzete (of the tree) qualifier places it in its forest habitat. Some species are eaten; others avoided.

examples.english: Give me a tiny portion.
examples.french: Donne-moi une toute petite portion.

words.culturalNote: Nga — rapid Kinshasa street shorthand for ngai (me / I). Universally used in marketplace bargaining and fast speech. Not formal.

examples.english: Child of a woman (daughter).
examples.french: Enfant d'une femme (fille).

words.culturalNote: Wa — older variant of ya (of); still found in traditional proverbs and western dialects tied to Kikongo.

examples.english: Yeah, I agree with your idea.
examples.french: Oui, je suis d'accord avec ton idée.

words.culturalNote: Ou — casual street affirmative borrowed directly from French oui. Common in urban Kinshasa conversation.

words.english: all / completely (street short form of nyonso/tuku)

examples.english: All the people fled into the forest.
examples.french: Tous les gens se sont enfuis dans la forêt.

words.culturalNote: Tu — Kinshasa street contraction of nyonso (all) or tuku (wholesale); marks complete inclusion of a group.

examples.english: I came to visit you.
examples.french: Je suis venu te rendre visite.

words.culturalNote: Mu — first-person pronoun found in western dialects closely related to Kikongo/Kituba. Standard Kinshasa uses ngai.

words.english: lo- (noun class prefix, singular abstract/elongated nouns)

examples.english: The leaf fell to the ground.
examples.french: La feuille est tombée par terre.

words.culturalNote: Lo- — singular noun class prefix for abstract or elongated items (leaves, streets, paths). Its plural is ma-.

examples.english: Leaves are many on the tree.
examples.french: Les feuilles sont nombreuses sur l'arbre.

words.culturalNote: Ma- — plural noun class prefix paired with lo- singular. Also appears in many food/liquid words (mai, mafuta, mampa).

examples.english: A pit is in the street.
examples.french: Il y a un trou dans la rue.

words.culturalNote: Li- — singular noun class prefix for round objects, body parts, and enclosed spaces. Its plural is bi-.

words.english: bi- (noun class prefix, plural of li-)

examples.english: Pits are many on the road.
examples.french: Les trous sont nombreux sur le chemin.

words.culturalNote: Bi- — plural of the li- noun class.

words.english: a little / slightly / a bit of

examples.lingala: Pesa ngai mwa ndambo moke ya mampa.
examples.english: Give me a little small portion of bread.
examples.french: Donne-moi une toute petite portion de pain.

words.culturalNote: Mwa — softening particle placed before a noun or adjective meaning a little, somewhat, or a bit of. Essential in polite requests.

examples.lingala: Mama asombi ton ya tini na zando.
examples.english: Mother bought a can of tuna at the market.
examples.french: Maman a acheté une boite de thon au marché.

words.culturalNote: Ton — from French thon (tuna). A common affordable protein in urban households; eaten with fufu or rice.

examples.lingala: Bilamba ekoki noki mpo moi ezali makasi.
examples.english: The clothes dried quickly because the sun is strong.
examples.french: Les vêtements ont séché vite parce que le soleil est fort.

words.culturalNote: Moi — the sun or daytime; also used for the concept of daylight heat. The suffix -moi appears in moindo (dark, sunless).

examples.lingala: Mopepe ezali koya fuu na lininisa.
examples.english: The wind is coming whoosh through the window.
examples.french: Le vent entre en sifflant par la fenêtre.

words.culturalNote: Fuu — an imitative word (ideophone) that mimics rushing air or a hard blow. Used after mopepe (wind) to intensify its force.

examples.lingala: Elamba na ye ezali pembe puu.
examples.english: His cloth is spotlessly white.
examples.french: Son tissu est d'un blanc immaculé.

words.culturalNote: Puu — ideophone reinforcing the color white (pembe); means completely or brilliantly white. Placed after the color adjective it modifies.

examples.english: What do you want to buy at the market?
examples.french: Qu'est-ce que tu veux acheter au marché?

words.culturalNote: Nii — rapid street truncation of nini (what). Common in quick Kinshasa questions and text messages.

examples.english: Boss, give me a little help.
examples.french: Grand, donne-moi un peu d'aide.

words.culturalNote: Yaa — street truncation of yaya (older sibling); used as a respectful but informal address to a peer or vendor. Conveys both respect and familiarity.

examples.english: We extract oil from palm nuts.
examples.french: Nous extrayons de l'huile des noix de palme.

words.culturalNote: Maba — palm nuts (Elaeis guineensis); the source of mafuta ya mabe (palm oil), the cornerstone cooking fat of Congolese cuisine. Whole maba are also boiled and eaten directly.
words.french: noix de palme / fruits de palme

examples.lingala: Mai ya bololo ezali na kati ya baso.
examples.english: The sour juice is in the glass.
examples.french: Le jus aigre est dans le verre.

words.culturalNote: Baso — specifically a glass for drinking (taller than kopo); often used for beer or juice at social gatherings.

examples.lingala: Latisa mwana koti mpo malili ezali makasi.
examples.english: Dress the child in a coat because the cold is intense.
examples.french: Habille l'enfant d'un manteau car le froid est intense.

words.culturalNote: Koti — from French coat; a jacket or overcoat. In Kinshasa where temperatures rarely drop, wearing a koti is a status symbol as much as a warmth strategy.

examples.lingala: Ndeko na ngai akei kovanda na Poto.
examples.english: My relative went to live in Europe.
examples.french: Mon parent est allé vivre en Europe.

words.culturalNote: Poto — from Portuguese or colonial usage; means Europe or abroad. Going to Poto is the Congolese diaspora dream. People who return from Poto carry special social prestige.

examples.lingala: Pesa ngai mola na ngai sikoyo.
examples.english: Give me my cash right now.
examples.french: Donne-moi mon argent maintenant.

words.culturalNote: Mola — Kinshasa street slang for money/cash; more urgent and street-level than the formal mbongo (money). Heard constantly in markets and taxi parks.

words.english: wake up / rise / get up (also a Congolese political rallying cry)
words.french: reveille-toi / leve-toi (aussi un cri politique congolais)

examples.english: Wake up, morning has come.
examples.french: Reveille-toi, le matin est arrive.

words.culturalNote:
Lamuka — the imperative "wake up" or "rise." Said by a mother at dawn to a sleeping child, by a friend nudging another out of a daze.

But Lamuka also carries a national weight no Congolese forgets: in 2018 the opposition coalition that united Martin Fayulu, Moise Katumbi, Jean-Pierre Bemba and others took this single word as its name. "Lamuka!" became the cry painted on walls, chanted in stadiums, and whispered between strangers — "wake up, Congo." For the diaspora it is a word with two mornings inside it: the one that ends the night, and the one a country is still waiting for.

words.english: to wake up / to rise / to get up

examples.english: I want to wake up early tomorrow.
examples.french: Je veux me reveiller tot demain.

words.culturalNote: Kolamuka — the infinitive form of lamuka. The everyday verb for waking up or getting on your feet. See the entry for lamuka for the deeper cultural weight the bare stem now carries.
words.culturalNoteFr: Kolamuka — forme infinitive de lamuka. Le verbe quotidien pour se réveiller ou se mettre sur ses pieds. Voir l'entrée lamuka pour le poids culturel plus profond que la racine nue porte aujourd'hui.
words.culturalNoteLn: Kolamuka — ndenge ya kosalela ya lamuka. Liloba ya mokolo na mokolo mpo na kolamuka to kotelema na makolo. Tala lamuka mpo na kilo ya bonkoko oyo motó moko ya liloba ezali na yango lelo.

examples.lingala: Yaka awa noki mpo na kolia bilei.
examples.english: Come here quickly to eat food.
examples.french: Viens ici vite pour manger.

words.culturalNote: Yaka — the everyday "come!" Said by a mother at the cooking fire, a friend at a doorway. In Lingala the singular imperative is formed by dropping the ko- infinitive prefix and keeping the final -a: koya (to come) → yaka. Almost every command in this dictionary follows the same pattern.

examples.lingala: Vanda na kiti oyo pembeni na ngai.
examples.english: Sit on this chair next to me.
examples.french: Assieds-toi sur cette chaise à côté de moi.

words.culturalNote: Vanda — sit, or stay. Offered to a visitor before any conversation begins. To refuse the chair is to refuse the welcome.

examples.lingala: Loba na bwanya liboso ya kopesa sango.
examples.english: Speak with wisdom before giving information.
examples.french: Parle avec sagesse avant de transmettre une nouvelle.

words.culturalNote: Loba — speak. Carries the weight of being asked to give your version of something. Elders use it to call a child to account; friends use it to ask for the real story behind a quiet face.

examples.lingala: Yoka maloba ya tata na yo tango nyonso.
examples.english: Listen to your father's words all the time.
examples.french: Écoute les paroles de ton père en tout temps.

words.culturalNote: Yoka — listen. Closer to "take in" than to "hear." A grandparent saying yoka is asking the child to hold what comes next as guidance, not noise.

examples.lingala: Tala ndeke oyo azali kopumbwa na likolo.
examples.english: Look at this bird flying up above.
examples.french: Regarde cet oiseau qui vole en haut.

words.culturalNote: Tala — look. Used to share what the speaker is seeing right now: a sunset, a child taking a first step, an injustice. A way of pulling someone into the same moment.

examples.lingala: Pesa ngai mampa moke mpo na ntongo.
examples.english: Give me a little bread for the morning.
examples.french: Donne-moi un peu de pain pour le matin.

words.culturalNote: Pesa — give. The verb of small daily requests across every Kinshasa household and market stall; said to a sibling, a vendor, a friend without apology, because in Congolese sharing is presumed, not negotiated.

examples.lingala: Mema biloko oyo na kati ya suku na ngai.
examples.english: Carry these items inside my room.
examples.french: Porte ces affaires dans ma chambre.

words.culturalNote: Mema — to carry, to bring along. The verb of helping a load reach the next place. Distinct from yela (bring TO someone), which adds a direction.

examples.lingala: Yela ngai baso ya mai noki.
examples.english: Bring me a glass of water quickly.
examples.french: Apporte-moi un verre d'eau vite.

words.culturalNote: Yela — bring (to me / to someone). The directional cousin of mema: yela always implies a destination, usually the speaker.

examples.lingala: Somba mbisi mpe tomati na wenze lelo.
examples.english: Buy fish and tomatoes at the small market today.
examples.french: Achète du poisson et des tomates au marché aujourd'hui.

words.culturalNote: Somba — buy. The verb of the wenze (small market) and the zando (big market). Said by a mother sending a child for the evening meal: a small mission entrusted, money counted into a folded hand.

examples.lingala: Teka nguba oyo nyonso mpo na kozwa mola.
examples.english: Sell all these peanuts to get cash.
examples.french: Vends toutes ces arachides pour avoir de l'argent.

words.culturalNote: Teka — sell. The pair to somba. A Kinshasa pavement vendor calling out teka teka! is announcing not just goods but the work of converting them into the day's needs.

examples.lingala: Lia bilei na yo noki liboso ekoma malili.
examples.english: Eat your food quickly before it becomes cold.
examples.french: Mange ta nourriture vite avant qu'elle ne devienne froide.

words.culturalNote: Lia — eat. The shorter, common form used in conversation; the longer kolia is the infinitive. Spoken across every Congolese table at every meal.

examples.lingala: Mela mai ya kitoko kowuta na molangi.
examples.english: Drink clean water coming from the bottle.
examples.french: Bois de l'eau propre venant de la bouteille.

words.culturalNote: Mela — drink, also smoke (one "drinks" tobacco in Lingala). Context separates them: mela mai = drink water, mela likaya = smoke a cigarette.

examples.lingala: Zila ngai pene na zando, nakoya noki.
examples.english: Wait for me near the market, I will come quickly.
examples.french: Attends-moi près du marché, je viendrai vite.

words.culturalNote: Zila — wait. A word of patience in a culture where appointments are approximate and arrival is when the heart is ready. Zila moke — wait a little — is the apology and the request in one.

examples.lingala: Longola koti na yo mpo molunge ezali makasi.
examples.english: Take off your coat because the heat is intense.
examples.french: Retire ton manteau car la chaleur est intense.

words.culturalNote: Longola — remove, take off, take away. From clothes (longola koti) to obstacles (longola mabe — take away the bad). The verb of clearing space.

examples.lingala: Zwa nkanda oyo kowuta epai ya yaya na yo.
examples.english: Receive this letter coming from your older sibling.
examples.french: Reçois cette lettre venant de ton aîné.

words.culturalNote: Zwa — receive, take, find. A versatile single-syllable verb. Zwa mbongo (find money), zwa nzela (find the way), zwa eloko (take a thing) — the same root for the lucky and the practical.

examples.lingala: Tika lobobo wana sikoyo, sala mosala!
examples.english: Stop that chatter right now, do the work!
examples.french: Arrête ce bavardage maintenant, fais le travail!

words.culturalNote: Tika — stop, let go, leave alone. A firm word from a parent or an exhausted friend. Carries both "stop doing that" and "let it go" depending on tone.

words.english: do not fear / do not be afraid (negative imperative)

examples.lingala: Kobanga te, nkoi akimi mosika na zamba.
examples.english: Do not fear, the leopard ran far into the forest.
examples.french: N'aie pas peur, le léopard a fui loin dans la forêt.

words.culturalNote: Kobanga te — do not fear. The negative imperative in Lingala is formed by sandwiching the verb between its infinitive ko- prefix and the negation particle te: ko[verb] te. Almost every prohibition in this dictionary follows the same rule. A parent speaking kobanga te to a child at night is offering both the verb and the calm to back it up.

examples.lingala: Kolala te, sinzili asengeli koyengela ndako pokwa.
examples.english: Do not sleep, the watchman must guard the house this evening.
examples.french: Ne dors pas, le veilleur doit garder la maison ce soir.

words.culturalNote: Kolala te — do not sleep. Said to a friend dozing during a long taxi ride, or to a watchman fighting the late hours.

examples.lingala: Kofinga te, kosuka zoba mabe lokola muga ezali mabe.
examples.english: Do not insult, treating a malicious idiot like a sucker is bad.
examples.french: N'insulte pas, traiter un imbécile comme un naïf est mauvais.

words.culturalNote: Kofinga te — do not insult. Spoken by elders to children before any street walk; the reminder that words carry weight long after they are said.

words.english: do not lie / don't deceive (negative imperative)

examples.lingala: Kokosa te, loba solo liboso ya mfumu ya mboka.
examples.english: Do not lie, speak the truth before the village chief.
examples.french: Ne mens pas, dis la vérité devant le chef du village.

words.culturalNote: Kokosa te — do not lie. In Congolese family discipline this is the heaviest verbal warning a parent gives. The truth is owed first to elders, the chief, and ancestors.

examples.lingala: Kobosana te, yela ngai sako ya fufu kowuta na wenze.
examples.english: Do not forget, bring me the sack of fufu coming from the small market.
examples.french: N'oublie pas, apporte-moi le sac de fufu venant du petit marché.

words.culturalNote: Kobosana te — do not forget. Often the last word a Congolese mother says as a child walks out the door for an errand. The phrase asks for memory the way other languages ask for love.

examples.lingala: Kobwaka te, biloko oyo ezali naino na mosala.
examples.english: Do not throw away, these items are still useful.
examples.french: Ne jette pas, ces choses sont encore utiles.

words.culturalNote: Kobwaka te — do not throw away. The verb of careful households where every piece of cloth, every bottle, every nail still has a future use.

words.english: do not upset / don't anger (negative imperative)

examples.lingala: Kosilikisa te, mama azali na mawa lelo mpo na maladi.
examples.english: Do not upset her, mother is in sorrow today because of sickness.
examples.french: Ne la fâche pas, maman est dans la tristesse aujourd'hui à cause de la maladie.

words.culturalNote: Kosilikisa te — do not anger / do not upset. The causative form (the -sa suffix) of kosilika (to be angry). To upset someone is, in Lingala, to make their anger happen.

words.english: do not abandon / don't let go (negative imperative)
words.french: ne laisse pas / ne lâche pas (impératif négatif)

examples.lingala: Kotika te, simba loboko na ngai makasi tango totambolaka.
examples.english: Do not let go, hold my hand tightly when we walk.
examples.french: Ne lâche pas, tiens ma main fortement quand nous marchons.

words.culturalNote: Kotika te — do not let go, do not leave behind. The opposite plea of tika (let go). Said by a child to a parent in a crowded market, or by a friend at a hospital bedside.

examples.lingala: Kofungola te, mpepe makasi mpe potopoto ezali na libanda.
examples.english: Do not open, a strong wind and mud are outside.
examples.french: N'ouvre pas, un vent fort et de la boue sont dehors.

words.culturalNote: Kofungola te — do not open. Said to the door of the house in storm season, to the lid of a cooking pot too soon, to a letter not yet ready to be read.

words.english: do not close / don't lock (negative imperative)

examples.lingala: Kokanga te, leki na ngai azali naino na libanda ya lopango.
examples.english: Do not close it, my younger sibling is still outside the yard.
examples.french: Ne le ferme pas, mon petit frère est encore dehors dans la cour.

words.culturalNote: Kokanga te — do not close, do not lock. The verb of inclusion: an older sibling reminding the household that someone is still outside, still on their way home.

words.english: do not drink / don't smoke (negative imperative)
words.french: ne bois pas / ne fume pas (impératif négatif)

examples.lingala: Komela te, mai oyo ezali na solo lokola tufi.
examples.english: Do not drink it, this water smells like waste.
examples.french: Ne le bois pas, cette eau sent les ordures.

words.culturalNote: Komela te — do not drink (also: do not smoke). Health warnings, parental warnings, the warning of a friend who has already smelled the bad water.

examples.lingala: Kolia te, nyama oyo efwami mpe ebotisi mofoti ebele.
examples.english: Do not eat it, this meat has rotted and bred many maggots.
examples.french: Ne le mange pas, cette viande a pourri et a produit beaucoup d'asticots.

words.culturalNote: Kolia te — do not eat. The first negative imperative a child hears, often about food on the ground, food at a stranger's'house, food that has been out too long in the heat.

words.english: do not quarrel / don't argue (negative imperative)

examples.lingala: Koswana te, tika lobobo wana sikoyo mpo na kimia.
examples.english: Do not argue, stop that loud chatter right now for the sake of peace.
examples.french: Ne te dispute pas, arrête ce bavardage maintenant pour la paix.

words.culturalNote: Koswana te — do not quarrel. An elder's phrase. In Congolese households peace is not the absence of disagreement, it is what you choose to protect over your need to be right.

examples.lingala: Kobima te, mvula enoki makasi mpe nkuba ebeti na likolo.
examples.english: Do not go out, the rain is falling heavily and lightning is striking up above.
examples.french: Ne sors pas, la pluie tombe fortement et la foudre frappe en haut.

words.culturalNote: Kobima te — do not go out. Said during the dry-season storms that hit Kinshasa fast and hard, when the streets flood faster than a child can run home.

examples.lingala: Kokota te na kati ya suku ya tata noki.
examples.english: Do not enter father's room quickly.
examples.french: N'entre pas dans la chambre de papa rapidement.

words.culturalNote: Kokota te — do not enter. The room of an elder, the room of someone resting, the kitchen during a delicate cooking moment. Boundaries spoken aloud.

words.english: do not play / don't mess around (negative imperative)

examples.lingala: Kosakana te, mosala oyo ezali zito mpe mfumu azali kotala.
examples.english: Do not mess around, this work is serious and the boss is watching.
examples.french: Ne joue pas, ce travail est sérieux et le chef regarde.

words.culturalNote: Kosakana te — do not play, do not joke. The phrase that turns a Congolese workplace from light to focused in one breath.

examples.lingala: Kosukola te, baso oyo ezali sika.
examples.english: Do not wash it, this glass is new.
examples.french: Ne le lave pas, ce verre est neuf.

words.culturalNote: Kosukola te — do not wash. Said about a fragile object, or about clothing that should be hand-cleaned, or about a wound that needs air.

examples.lingala: Kotuna te sango oyo epesi bandeko bitumba-zoba.
examples.english: Do not ask for this information that gave the relatives a stupid brawl.
examples.french: Ne demande pas cette information qui a provoqué une dispute idiote entre les proches.

words.culturalNote: Kotuna te — do not ask. Sometimes the kindest thing a family member can say. Some questions reopen what time was finally closing.

words.english: do not beat / don't strike (negative imperative)

examples.lingala: Kobeta te mbwa oyo, azali kobatela lopango na biso.
examples.english: Do not beat this dog, he is guarding our yard.
examples.french: Ne frappe pas ce chien, il garde notre cour.

words.culturalNote: Kobeta te — do not beat, do not strike. The verb of restraint, taught to children early about animals, younger siblings, and one day, anger itself.

words.english: do not burn / don't grill (negative imperative)
words.french: ne brûle pas / ne grille pas (impératif négatif)

examples.lingala: Kotumba te ntaba na fulo sikoyo.
examples.english: Do not grill the goat on the stove right now.
examples.french: Ne grille pas la chèvre sur le feu maintenant.

words.culturalNote: Kotumba te — do not burn, do not grill. Heard around every Congolese kitchen and every charcoal stove. A timing instruction, often said with a hand already reaching for the meat.

words.english: do not annoy / don't bother (negative imperative)

examples.lingala: Kotungisa te, mwana mwasi azali koyekola Lingala na suku.
examples.english: Do not bother her, the girl is learning Lingala in the room.
examples.french: Ne la dérange pas, la fille apprend le lingala dans la chambre.

words.culturalNote: Kotungisa te — do not annoy, do not disturb. The household boundary phrase. Children memorize this before they know what their own concentration feels like.

examples.lingala: Kokata te nzete oyo ebotani mbuma ebele.
examples.english: Do not cut this tree that has borne a lot of fruit.
examples.french: Ne coupe pas cet arbre qui a porté beaucoup de fruits.

words.culturalNote: Kokata te — do not cut. About a fruiting tree, a friendship, a conversation just becoming honest. The verb of preservation.

words.english: do not turn back / don't retreat (negative imperative)
words.french: ne recule pas / ne fais pas demi-tour (impératif négatif)

examples.lingala: Kobutwa te, nzela-mbeba ezali na sima na biso.
examples.english: Do not turn back, the path of destruction is behind us.
examples.french: Ne recule pas, le chemin de la destruction est derrière nous.

words.culturalNote: Kobutwa te — do not turn back. A line that fits both the literal road and the figurative one. The path behind is rarely safer than the path ahead.

examples.lingala: Kimia ezali malamu mpo na kobongisa mboka na biso.
examples.english: Peace is good for developing our country.
examples.french: La paix est bonne pour développer notre pays.

words.culturalNote: Kimia — peace, the kind that lets a country build and a household sleep. The word Congolese elders ask for in evening prayers and political speeches alike. In a region marked by long conflict, kimia is never abstract; it is the day no bad news arrives.

examples.lingala: Liwa ya nkoko epesi libota mawa monene.
examples.english: Grandparent's death brought great sorrow to the family.
examples.french: La mort du grand-parent a apporté un grand chagrin à la famille.

words.culturalNote:
Sorrow — and the tenderness of feeling it alongside someone.

Mawa is sorrow, but also the pity and compassion you feel for another's pain — "nazali na mawa" can mean I am sad, or I feel for you. In times of loss it is the word that names the room. To sit in mawa with a grieving family, saying little, is itself a Congolese way of offering comfort.

examples.lingala: Longola kanda na motema liboso ya koloba na bandeko.
examples.english: Remove anger from your heart before speaking to relatives.
examples.french: Enlève la colère du cœur avant de parler aux proches.

words.culturalNote: Kanda — anger, wrath. Distinct from frustration; this is the deeper heat that elders warn the young to set down before family conversations. The phrase "longola kanda" (remove the anger) is a counsel of self-mastery before speech.

examples.lingala: Tozali naino na elikia ya kozwa mosala sika.
examples.english: We still have hope of getting a new job.
examples.french: Nous avons encore l'espoir d'obtenir un nouveau travail.

words.culturalNote: Elikia — hope, expectation. A working word, not a sentimental one. In the diaspora, elikia is what you keep packed alongside the documents, the savings, the promise to send something home each month.

examples.lingala: Mpepe ya ntongo amemi malili na mbalasa.
examples.english: The morning breeze brought chill to the porch.
examples.french: La brise du matin a apporté du froid à la véranda.

words.culturalNote: Malili — cold, the kind that lifts the goosebumps on a Kinshasa morning or settles into a diaspora apartment in winter. Used as both noun and adjective. The opposite pair to molunge (heat).

examples.lingala: Mbula enoki makasi mpe ebebi nzela ya zando.
examples.english: Heavy rain fell and ruined the market road.
examples.french: Une pluie forte est tombée et a abîmé la route du marché.

words.culturalNote: Mbula — rain, and also year. The two meanings share one word because Congolese reckoning of years counts the rainy seasons: how many mbula has a child seen, how many mbula since you came home. The same word for the weather that defines the year and the year itself.

examples.lingala: Tomeli ti ya sukali na ntongo liboso ya kokende kelasi.
examples.english: We drank sweet tea in the morning before going to school.
examples.french: Nous avons bu du thé sucré le matin avant d'aller à l'école.

words.culturalNote: Ntongo — morning, dawn. The opening of the Congolese day, marked by ti ya sukali (sweet tea), the brushing sound of a yard being swept, and a parent's voice calling children to wash before school.

examples.lingala: Tokokutana na wenze na pokwa mpo na kosomba tomson.
examples.english: We will meet at the small market in the evening to buy horse mackerel.
examples.french: Nous nous retrouverons au petit marché le soir pour acheter du chinchard.

words.culturalNote: Pokwa — late afternoon into evening. The visiting hour in Congolese life, when neighbors stop by, dinner cooks, and the day's'heat finally breaks. Distinct from butu (night).

examples.lingala: Bana balei loso na mpondu pokwa lelo.
examples.english: The children ate rice with cassava leaves this evening.
examples.french: Les enfants ont mangé du riz avec des feuilles de manioc ce soir.

words.culturalNote: Loso — rice. The cheap, filling staple of urban DRC households alongside fufu. Loso na mpondu (rice with cassava leaves) is a national comfort plate, eaten in homes from Matete to Lubumbashi.

examples.lingala: Fungola tini ya madesu mpo na kolamba bilei.
examples.english: Open the can of beans to cook food.
examples.french: Ouvre la boîte de haricots pour préparer à manger.

words.culturalNote: Madesu — beans. Across the Congos, madesu na loso (beans and rice) is the everyday workman's plate at the maquis (small restaurant). Affordable protein, served by women who have served the same plate for thirty years.

examples.lingala: Bilei oyo ezangi mungwa, ezali na elengi te.
examples.english: This food lacks salt, it is not delicious.
examples.french: Cette nourriture manque de sel, elle n'est pas délicieuse.

words.culturalNote: Mungwa — salt. The first word for taste in a Congolese kitchen. Asking a cook "ezali na mungwa?" (does it have salt?) is asking whether the dish has been brought to life yet.

examples.lingala: Batia bakopo mpe basani likolo ya mesa.
examples.english: They put the cups and plates on top of the table.
examples.french: Ils ont mis les tasses et les assiettes sur la table.

words.culturalNote: Mesa — table. From the Portuguese mesa, one of the oldest loanwords in Lingala from the Atlantic trade era. The center of the Congolese meal: every plate eventually finds the mesa, and so does every long evening conversation.

examples.lingala: Kasanola oyo epasuki tango mwasi akataki nsuki.
examples.english: This comb broke when the woman trimmed her hair.
examples.french: Ce peigne s'est cassé quand la femme a coupé ses cheveux.

words.culturalNote: Kasanola — comb. A regional/dialect variant of kisanola. The everyday wide-toothed comb used on African hair in Congolese households, often passed between sisters at the start of any salon evening at home.

examples.lingala: Sukola mpota na mai ya kitoko mpo ebika noki.
examples.english: Wash the wound with clean water so it heals quickly.
examples.french: Lave la blessure avec de l'eau propre pour qu'elle guérisse vite.

words.culturalNote: Mpota — wound, cut, injury. The first noun any Congolese mother knows in both directions: the one she binds and the one she explains. Sukola mpota (wash the wound) is the universal first-aid sentence across DRC homes.

examples.lingala: Mwana ya mwasi azali na ndako.
examples.english: The daughter (child of woman) is in the house.
examples.french: La fille (enfant de femme) est dans la maison.

words.culturalNote: Ya — the bridge word of Lingala. The genitive particle that links one thing to another: mwana ya mwasi (child of woman = daughter), mai ya mbila (water of palm = palm wine), nzela ya ndako (road to the house). Every Lingala speaker uses ya a hundred times a day without thinking, the way English speakers use "of." If you only ever learned one Lingala particle, this is the one that opens the most sentences.

examples.lingala: Akei te zambi azali na maladi.
examples.english: He did not go because he is sick.
examples.french: Il n'est pas parti parce qu'il est malade.

words.culturalNote: Zambi — the archaic form of mpo, meaning "because." Heard from older speakers, in proverbs, and in lyrics by the elders of Congolese rumba; modern conversation has settled on mpo. When a grandparent says zambi instead of mpo, you are hearing the Lingala of an earlier generation speak through them.

words.english: front / before (informal short form of liboso)
words.french: devant / avant (forme courte informelle de liboso)

examples.english: Go ahead, I will follow you.
examples.french: Va devant, je vais te suivre.

words.culturalNote: Boso — the informal, fast-speech contraction of liboso (front, ahead, before). Heard constantly in Kinshasa street talk: "kende boso" (go ahead), "boso ya ndako" (in front of the house). The full liboso stays in writing and formal speech.

words.english: trash can / rubbish bin / garbage dump

examples.lingala: Bwaka bosoto oyo na kati ya fulu.
examples.english: Throw this trash inside the garbage dump.
examples.french: Jette ces ordures dans la poubelle.

words.culturalNote:
Fulu — the household bin or the open dump on the edge of a Kinshasa quartier where everyone's bosoto ends up. Distinct from fulo (FU-lo, stove) — one extra vowel changes the whole meaning.

Street slang sense: fulu is also used as an adjective for someone in an intense state of sexual arousal ("mobali wana azali fulu"). Vulgar; use only among peers, never in mixed or formal company.

examples.lingala: Mayi ya sabuni eboti fulufulu ebele.
examples.english: The soapy water made a lot of foam.
examples.french: L'eau savonneuse a fait beaucoup de mousse.

words.culturalNote:
Fulufulu — the foam on soapy laundry water, the head on a beer, the froth of breaking waves. A doubled, onomatopoeic word — the repetition itself sounds like bubbles piling up.

Street slang sense: also used to dismiss someone's words or behaviour as messy, chaotic, total garbage ("tika koloba na ndenge ya fulufulu" — stop talking that nonsense). Pejorative; reserved for dispute or insult, never neutral description.

examples.lingala: Sapato oyo ezali ya fululu, ekopasuka noki.
examples.english: These shoes are cheap imitations, they will tear quickly.
examples.french: Ces chaussures sont de la pacotille, elles vont vite se déchirer.

words.culturalNote: Fululu — Kinshasa marketplace shorthand for anything cheap, counterfeit, or low-grade: knock-off shoes, fake phones, materials that fall apart the first week. A hustler's tag for goods not worth your money. Heard in the negotiation phrase "eza ya fululu" (it's junk) used to push the price down.

examples.lingala: Nzoi ebele basali mafuta ya nzoi ya elengi na nzete.
examples.english: Many bees made delicious honey on the tree.
examples.french: Beaucoup d'abeilles ont fait un miel délicieux sur l'arbre.

words.culturalNote: Nzoi — the honeybee. The same word names the maker and what comes from her: "mafuta ya nzoi" (oil of the bee) is honey. Forest honey hunted in hollow trees is treasured across the Congo basin.

examples.lingala: Ndonzi balei matiti nyonso na elanga mbala moko.
examples.english: Locusts ate all the grass in the field at once.
examples.french: Les criquets ont mangé toute l'herbe du champ d'un seul coup.

words.culturalNote: Ndonzi — the swarming locust that strips a field in a morning. Both feared (the swarm wipes out a harvest) and eaten (roasted, salted — a dry-season delicacy).

examples.lingala: Lingbongbolo ezali kotambola malembe na putulu ya lopango.
examples.english: The millipede is crawling slowly in the yard dust.
examples.french: Le mille-pattes rampe lentement dans la poussière de la cour.

words.culturalNote: Lingbongbolo — the long, slow forest millipede that curls into a coil when touched. Harmless but unsettling; not to be confused with likongoli (centipede), which bites.

examples.lingala: Ntonzi ekoti mwana na mosapi ya lokolo.
examples.english: A jigger got into the child's toe.
examples.french: Une chique est entrée dans l'orteil de l'enfant.

words.culturalNote: Ntonzi — the jigger flea that burrows under the skin of bare feet, usually a toe. Removed carefully with a clean needle; a part of life for anyone who walks barefoot in the dry season.

examples.lingala: Mpasá ezali kopumbwa zingazinga ya mwinda na butu.
examples.english: The moth is flying around the lamp at night.
examples.french: Le papillon de nuit vole autour de la lampe la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Mpasá — the night moth drawn to lamps, sometimes large enough to startle. Distinct from the day butterfly; arrives with kerosene-lamp evenings and the smell of woodsmoke.

examples.lingala: Ekongolo azali kotindisa tufi ya maba na nzela.
examples.english: The dung beetle is pushing palm-nut waste on the road.
examples.french: Le bousier pousse des restes de noix de palme sur la route.

words.culturalNote: Ekongolo — the rolling dung beetle, patient labourer of the bush path. Watched by children with fascination; an everyday lesson in steady, unglamorous work.

examples.lingala: Nkusu alei mokanda mobimba na kati ya sanduku.
examples.english: The bookworm ate the entire document inside the trunk.
examples.french: Le ver des livres a mangé tout un document dans la malle.

words.culturalNote: Nkusu — the small grub that hollows out papers, school notebooks, and old documents left too long in a damp trunk. The reason families wrap important papers in plastic.

examples.lingala: Esunzu akangami na loboko tango totambolaki na potopoto.
examples.english: A leech attached to my arm when we walked in the mud.
examples.french: Une sangsue s'est accrochée à mon bras quand nous marchions dans la boue.

words.culturalNote: Esunzu — the leech that finds bare skin in flooded rice fields and forest mud. Removed with salt or a hot ember; the bite bleeds long because of the leech's natural anticoagulant.

examples.lingala: Mpesemone azali kobina na nse ya mai ya ebale.
examples.english: The giant water bug is swimming under the river water.
examples.french: La punaise d'eau géante nage sous l'eau de la rivière.

words.culturalNote: Mpesemone — the heavy aquatic bug that lurks in slow river pools. Eaten in some regions; respected for the painful pinch of its forelegs.

examples.lingala: Nzinzimbenga azali kongenga na kati ya zamba na butu.
examples.english: The firefly is shining inside the forest at night.
examples.french: La luciole brille dans la forêt la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Nzinzimbenga — the firefly. On still nights in the village they drift over banana groves like floating embers; in stories they carry the spirits of small children watching the living.

examples.lingala: Mofotiya mampa asili kopanza fufu ya masango.
examples.english: The weevil has completely ruined the corn flour.
examples.french: Le charançon a complètement gâté la farine de maïs.

words.culturalNote: Mofotiya mampa — literally "the bread-piercer." The weevil that turns up in flour, rice, and dried corn sacks left too long. The reason staples are kept in sealed metal tins.

examples.lingala: Mumpulukuku ezali koswa bato na mbeto tango butu eyi.
examples.english: Bedbugs are biting people in bed when night comes.
examples.french: Les punaises de lit piquent les gens au lit quand vient la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Mumpulukuku — the bedbug or soft tick that emerges after dark to feed on whoever is asleep. Mattresses are sunned in the courtyard to drive them out; a hidden plague of crowded rooms.

examples.lingala: Mpeseya zamba ezali kotambola na nse ya banzete ekweya.
examples.english: The wood roach is walking under fallen trees.
examples.french: La blatte des bois marche sous les arbres tombés.

words.culturalNote: Mpeseya zamba — the forest cousin of the kitchen cockroach, found under fallen logs and rotting bark. Larger and slower than its city counterpart; part of the constant turnover of the forest floor.

examples.lingala: Likalinganyama abimisaki makelele makasi na tongo lelo.
examples.english: The cicada made a loud racket this morning.
examples.french: La cigale a fait beaucoup de bruit ce matin.

words.culturalNote: Likalinganyama — the cicada whose long buzzing call marks the hottest hour of the dry season. Its sound is so woven into the bush that elders say it "calls the rain."

examples.lingala: Ndundumbasi azali kotuba nzete mpo na kosala ndako.
examples.english: The carpenter bee is boring into the wood to make a home.
examples.french: L'abeille charpentière perce le bois pour faire son nid.

words.culturalNote: Ndundumbasi — the large, low-humming bee that drills perfect round holes in roof beams and old furniture. Not aggressive, but the steady tunnelling weakens wood over years.

examples.lingala: Ekandandeke ezali kotungisa soso mwasi na lopango.
examples.english: Feather mites are bothering the hen in the yard.
examples.french: Les poux des plumes embêtent la poule dans la cour.

words.culturalNote: Ekandandeke — the tiny mite that infests chicken feathers and bedding. Hens given dust baths in wood ash to drive them out; a everyday small-farm pest.

examples.lingala: Keba na singayambangya, esalaka mpota ya pasi na mposo.
examples.english: Careful with the stinging caterpillar, it makes a painful sore on the skin.
examples.french: Attention à la chenille urticante, elle fait une plaie douloureuse sur la peau.

words.culturalNote: Singayambangya — the fuzzy caterpillar whose bristles leave a burning rash on bare skin. Children are warned never to touch one, no matter how soft it looks.

examples.lingala: Nzinziya ngombe azali kotungisa banyama ya mpoka na molunge.
examples.english: The cattle fly is bothering the livestock in the heat.
examples.french: La mouche du bétail embête le bétail dans la chaleur.

words.culturalNote: Nzinziya ngombe — literally "fly of the cow." The biting fly that torments cattle and goats in the heat of the day. Herds gather under shade trees to escape it.

examples.lingala: Likongoli eswi mwana na mosapi mpe evimbi.
examples.english: A centipede bit the child on the finger and it swelled.
examples.french: Une scolopendre a mordu l'enfant au doigt et c'est enflé.

words.culturalNote: Likongoli — the fast, biting centipede. Distinguished from the harmless lingbongbolo (millipede) by its flat body and venomous pincers. The bite is painful but rarely dangerous.

examples.lingala: Makangaya mabele batongi ndako ya makasi na elanga.
examples.english: Subterranean termites built a strong mound in the field.
examples.french: Les termites souterrains ont construit une grande termitière dans le champ.

words.culturalNote: Makangaya mabele — the soil termites whose tall, hardened mounds dot the savanna. Their tunnels enrich the soil; their winged forms (nswa) emerge after the first rains and are caught, roasted, and eaten as a delicacy.

examples.lingala: Kingungwasi azali kobangisa bangungi na mbalasa.
examples.english: The hornet is scaring the mosquitoes off the porch.
examples.french: Le frelon fait fuir les moustiques sous la véranda.

words.culturalNote: Kingungwasi — the large predatory hornet that hunts smaller insects mid-air. Feared for its sting, but useful: a nest near the house quietly keeps the mosquito population down.

examples.lingala: Likwanga abimisaki solo mabe tango asimbi elamba.
examples.english: The stink bug emitted a bad smell when it touched the cloth.
examples.french: La punaise puante a dégagé une mauvaise odeur quand elle a touché le tissu.

words.culturalNote: Likwanga — the shield-shaped bug that releases a foul, lingering smell when crushed or threatened. The reason no one swats it directly; brushed off gently instead. Distinct from the food kwanga (cassava loaf) — same syllables, different worlds.

examples.lingala: Mpesemoke ezali kokota na kati ya bakopo na kuku.
examples.english: Small roaches are entering inside the cups in the kitchen.
examples.french: Les petites blattes entrent dans les tasses dans la cuisine.

words.culturalNote: Mpesemoke — the small kitchen cockroach ("mpese" + "-moke" little) that turns up in cabinets and crockery. The everyday battle of city kitchens; lemon peels and bay leaves in the cupboards are the household defence.

examples.lingala: Nkungiya mai ezali kotungisa bato pene na ebale.
examples.english: River midges are troubling people near the river.
examples.french: Les moucherons de rivière embêtent les gens près de la rivière.

words.culturalNote: Nkungiya mai — literally "the fly of water." The tiny biting blackfly that hangs in clouds over fast-flowing streams. Worst at dawn and dusk; the reason fishermen smear themselves with palm oil.

examples.lingala: Limfumbeya mai ekoki kokota na banyama soki bameli mai mabe.
examples.english: Aquatic flatworms can enter animals if they drink bad water.
examples.french: Les vers plats aquatiques peuvent entrer chez les animaux s'ils boivent de l'eau souillée.

words.culturalNote: Limfumbeya mai — literally "the flat one of water." The waterborne worm that enters livestock and people through unfiltered drinking water. The reason elders insist water from streams be boiled.

examples.lingala: Nzoinene amati na lokasa mpo na kozela mwasi-ya-nzoi.
examples.english: The drone bee climbed onto the leaf to wait for the queen bee.
examples.french: Le faux bourdon est monté sur la feuille pour attendre la reine.

words.culturalNote: Nzoinene — literally "the big bee." The male drone in the hive; larger than the workers but stingless. Lives only to fertilise the queen; turned out of the hive when the cold season comes.

examples.lingala: Esunzuya ebale ekangami na sapato ya soda.
examples.english: A water leech attached itself to the soldier's shoe.
examples.french: Une sangsue d'eau s'est accrochée à la chaussure du soldat.

words.culturalNote: Esunzuya ebale — the river leech, larger and faster than the swamp esunzu. Fishermen know to check their legs after wading; pulled off with salt or a steady, slow grip.

examples.lingala: Likelele azali koyemba na nse ya mabele na butu.
examples.english: The cricket is singing underground at night.
examples.french: Le grillon chante sous terre la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Likelele — the foundational word for the burrowing cricket whose night-song fills village evenings. The plural-flavoured makelele (noise, racket, the chaos of a busy market) is built on this root: literally, "a chorus of crickets."

examples.lingala: Ekonda alei mposo ya nzete na zamba.
examples.english: The forest beetle ate the tree bark in the forest.
examples.french: Le scarabée des bois a mangé l'écorce de l'arbre.

words.culturalNote: Ekonda — the deep-forest beetle (or marching ant, depending on region) that lives in the thick brush. The name literally ties the insect to its habitat: "eloko ya ekonda" — a thing of the thick forest. Not to be confused with the Ekonda people, an Equatorial Mongo subgroup.

examples.lingala: Lokotá mayebo ya kitoko na nse ya banzete mpo na kolamba.
examples.english: Collect beautiful wild mushrooms under the trees to cook.
examples.french: Ramassez de beaux champignons sauvages sous les arbres pour cuisiner.

words.culturalNote: Mayebo — the wild mushrooms that flush after the first heavy rains and are gathered in baskets at the forest's edge. A seasonal staple across rural and forest regions; stewed with palm oil and dried fish, they carry the taste of the rainy season itself.

examples.lingala: Tika kotika biloko na yo ndenge ya bulubulu na kati ya suku.
examples.english: Stop leaving your things in a chaotic, disorganised way inside the room.
examples.french: Arrête de laisser tes affaires en pagaille dans la chambre.

words.culturalNote: Bulubulu — the doubled, onomatopoeic word for everything out of place: a messy room, a tangled argument, a market on a chaotic morning. Used as adjective or adverb; the repetition itself sounds like things tumbling over each other.

examples.lingala: Mbuta na biso ayebisi biso toli ya bwanya lelo.
examples.english: Our elder gave us wise advice today.
examples.french: Notre ancien nous a donné un conseil sage aujourd'hui.

words.culturalNote: Mbuta — the elder; used both as a respectful noun ("the senior") and as an honorific prefix before a name (Mbuta Joseph) to mark experience, age, and standing. To address someone as mbuta is to acknowledge their place in the community.

examples.lingala: Kolia te mayebo ya zamba oyo ezali na langi ya mabe.
examples.english: Do not eat forest mushrooms that have a bad colour.
examples.french: Ne mange pas de champignons de forêt à la couleur suspecte.

words.culturalNote: Mayebo ya zamba — literally "mushrooms of the deep forest." The wild fungi away from the village edge — some prized delicacies, others deadly. The teaching passed down with the baskets: bright colour means leave it; ask an elder before you cook anything you don't know.

examples.lingala: Bakoti na kati ya likambo ya bulubulu pembeni ya zando.
examples.english: They got tangled up in a messy situation next to the market.
examples.french: Ils se sont retrouvés mêlés à une affaire chaotique près du marché.

words.culturalNote: Likambo ya bulubulu — "an affair gone bulubulu." The phrase for a dispute, deal, or quarrel that has spiralled into pure confusion — no clear right or wrong, everyone shouting over each other. What you warn a younger sibling to stay far away from.

examples.lingala: Singamboka azali kolia mayebo na kati ya zamba.
examples.english: The bonobo is eating mushrooms inside the forest.
examples.french: Le bonobo mange des champignons dans la forêt.

words.culturalNote: Singamboka — the bonobo and close-chimp varieties of the equatorial forests. Found only in the DRC; treated in many regions as a near-relative, with strong taboos against hunting them.

examples.lingala: Pongo monene avandi na nse ya nzete mpo na kokengela libota na ye.
examples.english: The big gorilla sat under the tree to watch over his family.
examples.french: Le grand gorille s'est assis sous l'arbre pour veiller sur sa famille.

words.culturalNote: Pongo — the gorilla. Adult males are called "silverback" for the saddle of grey across the back; pongo monene is the family elder, head of the troop. Sacred in forest cosmology, rarely named directly when hunting.

examples.lingala: Mbengi azali koboma taba na zamba na butu.
examples.english: The hyena is killing a goat in the forest at night.
examples.french: L'hyène tue une chèvre dans la forêt la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Mbengi — the spotted hyena whose laugh-like call carries far across savanna nights. Feared for taking livestock; in some traditions linked to witchcraft because of its night activity.

examples.lingala: Nsimba akangi mpesemoke pembeni ya kuku.
examples.english: The civet caught a small cockroach near the kitchen.
examples.french: La civette a attrapé un petit cafard près de la cuisine.

words.culturalNote: Nsimba — the civet or genet, slender night hunter of small prey around villages. The scent gland under the tail is historically harvested for traditional perfumes.

examples.lingala: Punda ya milongo azali na mposo ya pembe mpe moindo.
examples.english: The zebra has a coat of white and black stripes.
examples.french: Le zèbre a un pelage à rayures blanches et noires.

words.culturalNote: Punda ya milongo — literally "horse of stripes." The zebra of the eastern savannas. Not native to the deep Congo forest but well known from southern Katanga rangelands.

examples.lingala: Ngubu monene azali kopema na kati ya mai ya ebale.
examples.english: The huge hippopotamus is resting inside the river water.
examples.french: L'énorme hippopotame se repose dans l'eau du fleuve.

words.culturalNote: Ngubu — regional variant for the hippopotamus alongside the standard kiboko. Most dangerous of the river animals; canoe paddlers steer wide of their pools.

examples.lingala: Nsoko amati na likolo ya nzete mpo na kolokota mbuma.
examples.english: The chimpanzee climbed on top of the tree to gather fruit.
examples.french: Le chimpanzé est monté sur l'arbre pour cueillir des fruits.

words.culturalNote: Nsoko — the common chimpanzee. Distinct from singamboka (bonobo); chimps tend to the savanna edges and northern forest, while bonobos are deep-forest exclusive to the south of the Congo bend.

examples.lingala: Ndeke ya mafuta azali kotambola na nse ya malili makasi.
examples.english: The penguin is walking under the intense cold.
examples.french: Le manchot marche sous le froid intense.

words.culturalNote: Ndeke ya mafuta — literally "bird of fat / oil-feather bird," the descriptive name for the penguin. Not native to Africa; the word entered Lingala via picture books and school texts.

examples.lingala: Esende akangi nioka na kati ya matiti.
examples.english: The mongoose caught a snake inside the grass.
examples.french: La mangouste a attrapé un serpent dans l'herbe.

words.culturalNote: Esende — the slender, fast-moving mongoose of villages and forest edges. Famous as a snake-killer; its sharp reflexes let it dodge a strike that would catch any other small animal. Welcomed around homes for keeping the courtyard snake-free. (Squirrel is esele or esele ya nzete.)

examples.lingala: Koikoi atalami na makolo mibale pene na potopoto.
examples.english: The heron watched with both legs near the mud.
examples.french: Le héron observait sur ses deux pattes près de la boue.

words.culturalNote: Koikoi — the long-legged heron of marshes and river edges. Stands motionless for long minutes before striking; the name imitates its call.

examples.lingala: Mbelekete amati na efelo sika ya ndako.
examples.english: The lizard climbed the new wall of the house.
examples.french: Le lézard a grimpé sur le mur neuf de la maison.

words.culturalNote: Mbelekete — general term covering the family of large, rough-skinned lizards: the small colourful agama doing push-ups on courtyard walls, and the much larger Nile monitor (varan) that raids henhouses for eggs. Both share the name; context tells which one.

examples.lingala: Limfunda atambolaka bulubulu te, atambolaka malembe.
examples.english: The tortoise does not walk chaotically; it walks slowly.
examples.french: La tortue ne marche pas n'importe comment, elle marche lentement.

words.culturalNote: Limfunda — the slow forest tortoise. A figure of patience in Lingala storytelling; appears in many fables outsmarting faster animals through steadiness.

examples.lingala: Ngando ya moke azali kobatela makei na ye na pembele ya mai.
examples.english: The dwarf crocodile is guarding its eggs at the water's edge.
examples.french: Le crocodile nain garde ses œufs au bord de l'eau.

words.culturalNote: Ngando ya moke — the small forest crocodile (Osteolaemus), barely the length of a man. Lives in the streams of the equatorial forest; hunted for meat in some villages despite its conservation status.

examples.lingala: Mbisi ya mikuwa evimbi tango asimbi sani.
examples.english: The pufferfish swelled when it touched the plate.
examples.french: Le poisson-globe a gonflé quand il a touché l'assiette.

words.culturalNote: Mbisi ya mikuwa — literally "fish of bones / spines." The pufferfish that swells when threatened. Coastal more than river; the inland word enters via market traders and seaside relatives.

examples.lingala: Tolambi mompende na mungwa mpe tomati lelo.
examples.english: We cooked tilapia with salt and tomatoes today.
examples.french: Nous avons cuit le tilapia avec sel et tomates aujourd'hui.

words.culturalNote: Mompende — regional variant of tilapia, one of the great staple fishes of Congo basin kitchens. Grilled whole, served with fufu or rice; the everyday Sunday fish.

examples.lingala: Likonzi alei nzete oyo esimbi motondo ya ndako.
examples.english: The wood-borer larva ate the wood supporting the house roof.
examples.french: La larve xylophage a mangé le bois qui soutenait le toit.

words.culturalNote: Likonzi — the wood-boring grub that quietly hollows roof beams and door frames from the inside. The reason new construction is treated with diesel or smoke.

examples.lingala: Nioka ya pembe akoti na kati ya sanduku ya mbongo.
examples.english: The white snake entered inside the money box.
examples.french: Le serpent blanc est entré dans la boîte d'argent.

words.culturalNote: Nioka ya pembe — literally "snake of white." The pale or albino serpent, charged with strong symbolism: in some traditions a guardian, in others a warning. Treated with extreme caution either way.

examples.lingala: Mbwampoka azali koyengela lopango mpo na moyibi.
examples.english: The village dog is patrolling the yard because of a thief.
examples.french: Le chien du village fait le tour de la cour à cause d'un voleur.

words.culturalNote: Mbwampoka — regional name for the village dog (mbwa + mpoka, the country/yard dog). Lean, watchful, sleeps in the doorway; the family's first warning system.

examples.lingala: Niau ya zamba akangi mboloko ya moke na zamba.
examples.english: The wildcat caught a small dwarf antelope in the forest.
examples.french: Le chat sauvage a attrapé une petite antilope dans la forêt.

words.culturalNote: Niau ya zamba — literally "cat of the forest." The wildcat or serval, larger than the village niau, with long legs and big ears. Rarely seen; mostly known by the prints it leaves around small-game traps.

examples.lingala: Ndeke ya mpongo apumbwa makasi mpo na kokanga pusi ya moke.
examples.english: The hawk flew powerfully to catch a small cat.
examples.french: Le faucon a volé puissamment pour attraper un petit chat.

words.culturalNote: Ndeke ya mpongo — "the bird of the eagle line," the everyday hawk or falcon. Smaller than the true mpongo (eagle); takes chicks from the yard if the hens stray too far.

examples.lingala: Ngulu ya mai azali kobina pene na kanga na kati ya ebale.
examples.english: The river pig is swimming near the crab inside the river.
examples.french: Le cochon de rivière nage près du crabe dans la fleuve.

words.culturalNote: Ngulu ya mai — literally "pig of water." Regional descriptor for the river-dwelling wild pig (and used in some areas for the hippopotamus). Largely nocturnal; seen at dusk drinking at the riverbank.

examples.lingala: Mbisi ya kazaka atambolaka na nse ya potopoto makasi.
examples.english: The armoured catfish crawls under the thick mud.
examples.french: Le poisson-chat cuirassé rampe sous la boue épaisse.

words.culturalNote: Mbisi ya kazaka — the armoured, mud-burrowing catfish or lungfish that can survive dry-season pools. Fishermen dig them out of caked mud at the end of the dry — flesh tough but nourishing.

examples.lingala: Nkosi ya mai apumbwa likolo ya mabanga mpo na kotala mai.
examples.english: The sea lion jumped on top of the rocks to look at the water.
examples.french: Le lion de mer a sauté sur les rochers pour regarder l'eau.

words.culturalNote: Nkosi ya mai — literally "lion of the sea." The seal or sea lion, named by descriptive analogy. Not native; the word lives in textbooks and ocean documentaries more than everyday speech.

examples.lingala: Nkoo ya moke avandi na lokasa mpe azali koyemba na tongo.
examples.english: The parakeet sat on the leaf and is singing in the morning.
examples.french: La perruche s'est posée sur la feuille et chante au matin.

words.culturalNote: Nkoo ya moke — the smaller cousin of the nkoo (grey parrot). Bright green, often kept in cages in cities; in the forest they fly in noisy pairs.

examples.lingala: Limfunda monene aboti makei ebele na zelo ya libongo.
examples.english: The giant sea turtle laid many eggs in the riverbank sand.
examples.french: La grande tortue marine a pondu beaucoup d'œufs dans le sable de la rive.

words.culturalNote: Limfunda monene — the sea turtle, named as "the big tortoise." Coastal more than inland; protected by law but eggs still poached on remote beaches.

examples.lingala: Esele ya nzete amatili mbuma mpo na komema yango na libulu.
examples.english: The tree squirrel climbed for fruit to carry it to its hole.
examples.french: L'écureuil arboricole est monté chercher des fruits pour les rapporter au trou.

words.culturalNote: Esele ya nzete — the canopy squirrel of the forest, distinct from esele on the ground. Caches palm nuts and fig fruits in trunk hollows; its scattering of half-eaten fruit feeds birds below.

examples.lingala: Mpongo monene akangi makaku likolo ya nzete ya molai.
examples.english: The crowned eagle caught a monkey on top of the tall tree.
examples.french: L'aigle couronné a attrapé un singe sur l'arbre haut.

words.culturalNote: Mpongo monene — the great forest eagle, large enough to take a monkey. One of the apex predators of the canopy; nests reused for generations.

examples.lingala: Ganga moindo avandi na motondo ya ndako ebebi.
examples.english: The black vulture sat on the roof of the ruined house.
examples.french: Le vautour noir s'est posé sur le toit de la maison en ruine.

words.culturalNote: Ganga moindo — the black vulture or raven; the silhouette on the roof or the rubbish pile. In folk reading, a perched ganga moindo near a sick person's house is read as an omen.

examples.lingala: Koikoi ya pembe alandaka ngombe mpo na kolia banyama moke.
examples.english: The white egret follows the cow to eat small bugs.
examples.french: L'aigrette blanche suit la vache pour manger les petits insectes.

words.culturalNote: Koikoi ya pembe — the pure-white egret that walks beside grazing cattle, picking off the ticks and flies the hooves stir up. A symbol of dry-season pastures.

examples.lingala: Esunzu ya mposo eswaka bato mpe ebimisaka makila ebele.
examples.english: The ringed leech bites people and draws a lot of blood.
examples.french: La sangsue annelée mord les gens et fait sortir beaucoup de sang.

words.culturalNote: Esunzu ya mposo — the ringed skin leech, larger than the swamp esunzu, with visible bands across its body. Found in wet undergrowth and bath pools; removed slowly so the jaws release whole.

examples.lingala: Menga apumbwa noki tango tata abetaki loboko.
examples.english: The green pigeon flew quickly when father clapped his hands.
examples.french: Le pigeon vert s'est envolé vite quand papa a tapé des mains.

words.culturalNote: Menga — the green pigeon of the forest fruit trees. Hunted with slingshots by children; the soft cooing call is the soundtrack of fig-ripening season.

examples.lingala: Tosombi mbisi ya fufu na zando mpo na kolamba na madesu.
examples.english: We bought dried saltfish at the market to cook with beans.
examples.french: Nous avons acheté du poisson séché au marché pour cuire avec des haricots.

words.culturalNote: Mbisi ya fufu — the smoked or salt-dried fish that travels well from river to inland markets. Backbone of many dry-season stews; soaked first to soften, then cooked into madesu (beans) or pondu.

examples.lingala: Niau ya ndako alingi kolala na nse ya mbeto ya mwana.
examples.english: The house cat wants to sleep under the child's bed.
examples.french: Le chat domestique veut dormir sous le lit de l'enfant.

words.culturalNote: Niau ya ndako — the house cat as opposed to niau ya zamba (wildcat). Kept for the same reason everywhere: rats in the food stores.

examples.lingala: Mbuta ya nyama atamboli liboso mpo na kotalisa nzela.
examples.english: The alpha animal walked in front to show the way.
examples.french: Le chef de meute marchait devant pour montrer le chemin.

words.culturalNote: Mbuta ya nyama — "the elder of the animals." The dominant male or female that leads a troop or pack. The same mbuta honourific (used for human elders) reaches across into the animal world.

examples.lingala: Pongo mobali azali na makasi makasi mpo na kobatela bikonda.
examples.english: The silverback has intense strength to protect the forest zones.
examples.french: Le dos argenté a une force redoutable pour défendre les zones forestières.

words.culturalNote: Pongo mobali — the adult male silverback gorilla. Head of a troop of females and juveniles; the silver saddle on his back develops with age, marking his rank.

examples.lingala: Taba ya zamba amati na mabanga ya molai mpo na kolia matiti.
examples.english: The wild bushgoat climbed high rocks to eat grass.
examples.french: La chèvre sauvage est montée sur les hauts rochers pour brouter.

words.culturalNote: Taba ya zamba — "goat of the forest," general term for the wild bushgoat or any of the smaller hill antelopes. Distinct from the everyday taba (domestic goat in the yard).

examples.lingala: Soso ya zamba abombi makei na ye na nse ya banzete.
examples.english: The wild guinea fowl hid its eggs under the trees.
examples.french: La pintade sauvage a caché ses œufs sous les arbres.

words.culturalNote: Soso ya zamba — the wild guinea fowl or francolin, prized for its dark, gamey meat. Hunted with traps along forest edges; eggs are a windfall for whoever finds the nest first.

examples.lingala: Punda ya zelo atamboli kilomitiri ebele kozanga komela mai.
examples.english: The desert donkey walked many kilometres without drinking water.
examples.french: L'âne sauvage a marché des kilomètres sans boire d'eau.

words.culturalNote: Punda ya zelo — "donkey of the sand," the wild desert ass of the Sahel and northern dry zones. Not Congo native; word travels south through Sahel-trade and school books.

examples.lingala: Pakasa ya moke azali na mposo te ya langi ya mai ya mpondu.
examples.english: The dwarf forest buffalo does not have a dark-green coat.
examples.french: Le buffle nain de forêt n'a pas une robe vert foncé.

words.culturalNote: Pakasa ya moke — the smaller, reddish-coated forest buffalo of the equatorial deep wood. More elusive than its savanna cousin; charge if cornered, so hunters walk wide of fresh tracks.

examples.lingala: Singamboka monene alei mayebo ebele na kati ya zamba.
examples.english: The large chimpanzee ate many mushrooms inside the forest.
examples.french: Le grand chimpanzé a mangé beaucoup de champignons dans la forêt.

words.culturalNote: Singamboka monene — the adult dominant chimpanzee or bonobo. Holds the troop together; younger males defer until age and politics let one of them take over.

examples.lingala: Ngandu ya mai azali kozila mbisi na nse ya mai ya ebale.
examples.english: The water crocodile is waiting for fish under the river water.
examples.french: Le crocodile d'eau attend le poisson sous l'eau du fleuve.

words.culturalNote: Ngandu ya mai — regional variant of ngando, the water-dwelling crocodile. Speed-strike from beneath the surface; reason riverbank washing is done from the bank, not knee-deep.

examples.lingala: Kigwa ya kitoko avandi na lokasa sika mpe azali kolenga te.
examples.english: The ornate tree frog sat on a new leaf and is not trembling.
examples.french: La rainette ornée s'est posée sur une feuille neuve et ne tremble pas.

words.culturalNote: Kigwa ya kitoko — "the pretty frog." The brightly patterned tree frog of the rainforest understorey; bright colour often warns of toxin in the skin.

examples.lingala: Bana balokoti liyebe monene na potopoto nsima ya mbula.
examples.english: The children picked up a giant land snail in the mud after the rain.
examples.french: Les enfants ont ramassé un escargot géant dans la boue après la pluie.

words.culturalNote: Liyebe monene — the African giant land snail, palm-sized after a wet season. Eaten roasted in some regions; the empty shells are collected by children for play.

examples.lingala: Nioka ya moindo akimi noki na kati ya matiti ya molai.
examples.english: The black cobra escaped quickly inside the tall grass.
examples.french: Le cobra noir s'est enfui vite dans les hautes herbes.

words.culturalNote: Nioka ya moindo — "the snake of darkness." The black cobra or mamba; one of the deadliest snakes in Africa. The advice is the same everywhere: do not chase it, do not corner it, give it the path.

examples.lingala: Likwanga nzala avandi pamba likolo ya lokasa ya mobesu.
examples.english: The praying mantis is just sitting on top of the green leaf.
examples.french: La mante religieuse est posée sur une feuille verte.

words.culturalNote: Likwanga nzala — literally "the insect of hunger" or "the hungry insect." The praying mantis, named for its still, waiting posture: always seeming to lie in ambush for its next meal. Not to be confused with likwanga (the stink bug) — same first word, different second.

words.french: scarabée noir / scarabée à carapace dure

examples.lingala: Kingongolo azali kokota na kati ya mampa ya ntongo.
examples.english: The black beetle is entering inside the morning bread.
examples.french: Le scarabée noir entre dans le pain du matin.

words.culturalNote: Kingongolo — the hard-shelled black beetle that turns up in kitchen sacks and bread tins. Squashed underfoot it leaves a faint smear; the reason flour and bread are kept in sealed containers.

examples.lingala: Longola likongolambwa na mposo ya mbwa na yo noki.
examples.english: Remove the dog tick from your dog's skin quickly.
examples.french: Enlève la tique du chien sur la peau de ton chien rapidement.

words.culturalNote: Likongolambwa — the dog tick that swells round and shiny as it fills with blood. Pulled out whole with a hot needle or tweezer; left in, the jaws can fester.

words.french: frelon géant de forêt / sphex tueur de cigales

examples.lingala: Linzambalakata apumbwi makasi mpo na kotuba nzete.
examples.english: The giant forest hornet flew powerfully to sting the tree.
examples.french: Le frelon géant a volé puissamment pour piquer l'arbre.
