words.culturalNote: Linzambalakata — the large solitary hornet of the deep forest that paralyses cicadas to feed its young. The sting is severe; villagers learn to read its low droning hum and step wide.

examples.lingala: Mpeseyamabele azali kotimola libulu na nse ya potopoto.
examples.english: The mole cricket is digging a hole under the mud.
examples.french: La courtilière creuse un trou sous la boue.

words.culturalNote: Mpeseyamabele — literally "the roach of the earth." The burrowing mole cricket whose tunnels honeycomb garden soil. Rarely seen above ground; betrayed by the soft chirring rising from the dirt at dusk.

examples.lingala: Ntonzimoke eswi mwana na makolo mpe esali mpota ya mokosa.
examples.english: The harvest mite bit the child on the feet and made an itchy sore.
examples.french: L'aoûtat a piqué l'enfant aux pieds et fait une plaie qui démange.

words.culturalNote: Ntonzimoke — "the little ntonzi." The microscopic harvest mite that drops from tall grass onto bare ankles in the dry season. The itch comes on hours later; lemon juice and lard are the village remedy.

examples.lingala: Nzoiyazamba abimisaki fulufulu ebele na monoko ya ndako na bango.
examples.english: The wild bee produced a lot of froth at the entrance of their hive.
examples.french: L'abeille sauvage a produit beaucoup de mousse à l'entrée de leur ruche.

words.culturalNote: Nzoiyazamba — the wild forest cousin of the kept nzoi. Aggressive when disturbed; honey hunters smoke them out at dusk and take the comb whole. The killer-bee strain travels in dense clouds.

examples.lingala: Ndonzimoke avandi kimya likolo ya lokasa ya nzete.
examples.english: The small green grasshopper sat quietly on top of the tree leaf.
examples.french: La petite sauterelle verte s'est posée tranquillement sur la feuille.

words.culturalNote: Ndonzimoke — the small green grasshopper or katydid whose body shape mimics a leaf so closely it disappears against the foliage. Sings in the cool of evening; harmless to crops.

examples.lingala: Lingbongboloyamai azali kobina na potopoto ya moluka.
examples.english: The water centipede is swimming in the mud of the stream.
examples.french: Le mille-pattes aquatique nage dans la boue du ruisseau.

words.culturalNote: Lingbongboloyamai — "the millipede of water." The amphibious cousin of the forest lingbongbolo, found in slow-moving stream mud. Eaten by fish and waterfowl; mostly noticed only when stirred up by wading feet.

words.french: papillon du palmier / charançon du palmier

examples.lingala: Mpasayambila akweyi kowuta na likolo ya limbila lelo.
examples.english: The palm-moth fell from the top of the palm tree today.
examples.french: Le papillon du palmier est tombé du sommet du palmier aujourd'hui.

words.culturalNote: Mpasayambila — "the moth of the palm." The adult palm weevil that lives in the crown of oil palms. Its grub (mbinzo, the fat palm-grub) is a treasured delicacy; the adult itself is mostly a quiet pollinator at dusk.

examples.lingala: Ndongondongoyamai atambolaka likolo ya mai kozanga kozinda.
examples.english: The water strider walks on top of the water without sinking.
examples.french: Le gerris marche sur l'eau sans couler.

words.culturalNote: Ndongondongoyamai — the water strider whose legs spread the weight so it skates across still pools. Children try to catch them in cupped hands; they always slip away in a flicker.

examples.lingala: Nyamankasimoke abombi nzoto na ye na nse ya banzete ekauka.
examples.english: The stick insect hid its body beneath the dry branches.
examples.french: Le phasme a caché son corps sous les branches sèches.

words.culturalNote: Nyamankasimoke — the slender stick insect that disguises itself as a twig, sometimes for hours without moving. Spotted only when it shifts position; the children's game is to count how many you can find on one dry branch.

examples.lingala: Nsongoyamabele akoti na nse ya mabele ya lisala sika.
examples.english: The burrowing bug entered beneath the soil of the new field.
examples.french: La punaise fouisseuse est entrée sous la terre du nouveau champ.

words.culturalNote: Nsongoyamabele — the soil-dwelling bug that attacks roots of new plantings. Farmers turn the soil and let chickens through to clear them before sowing.

examples.lingala: Ekongoloyazamba asimbi nzete na makuwa makasi na mutu.
examples.english: The stag beetle gripped the wood with the strong horns on its head.
examples.french: Le lucane a saisi le bois avec ses fortes cornes sur la tête.

words.culturalNote: Ekongoloyazamba — the large stag beetle whose powerful jaws can pinch a finger. Males joust over fallen logs; children pick them up by the back to feel the surprising grip.

words.french: charançon des grains / larve de teigne

examples.lingala: Nkusuya mampa alei fufu ya masango mobimba na kati ya saki.
examples.english: The grain moth larva ate the whole corn flour inside the sack.
examples.french: La larve de la teigne a mangé toute la farine de maïs dans le sac.

words.culturalNote: Nkusuya mampa — the grub that turns up living in corn flour, rice, and dry-bread sacks left too long. Distinct from the document-eating nkusu; same family, different appetite.

examples.lingala: Esunzuya ngombe akangami na mposo ya ngombe na esobe.
examples.english: The cattle leech attached to the cow's skin in the marshy plain.
examples.french: La sangsue du bétail s'est fixée à la peau de la vache dans la plaine marécageuse.

words.culturalNote: Esunzuya ngombe — the swamp leech that targets cattle and goats wading through wet pasture. Cattle herders check legs and bellies at the end of the day and pull them off with salt or hot ash.

words.french: blatte américaine / grosse blatte de cuisine

examples.lingala: Mpesemone ya kuku ezali kotambola na nse ya mesa ya bilei.
examples.english: The large kitchen cockroach is walking under the food table.
examples.french: La grosse blatte de cuisine marche sous la table à manger.

words.culturalNote: Mpesemone ya kuku — the big reddish-brown cockroach that takes over warm kitchens and pipes. Faster than mpesemoke; emerges at night, vanishes when the light goes on.

examples.lingala: Nzinzimbengamoke ezali kopumbwa pene na rido ya suku na butu.
examples.english: The click beetle is flying near the room curtain at night.
examples.french: Le taupin vole près du rideau de la chambre la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Nzinzimbengamoke — the smaller relative of the firefly that gives off a faint glow on warm nights. Lands on curtains and walls inside lit rooms; harmless and short-lived.

examples.lingala: Mofotiya mbisi abimi ebele likolo ya mbisi ya kofwama.
examples.english: Many blowfly maggots emerged on top of the rotting fish.
examples.french: De nombreux asticots ont émergé sur le poisson en décomposition.

words.culturalNote: Mofotiya mbisi — "the piercer of fish." The blowfly maggot that hatches in unsmoked, unsalted fish left in the heat. Fishmongers race the sun: catch, salt, smoke before the maggots win.

words.french: tique du poulailler / punaise molle du lit

examples.lingala: Mumpulukukuya mbeto azali koswa bana noki na butu.
examples.english: The soft bedbug is biting the children quickly at night.
examples.french: La punaise molle du lit pique les enfants vite la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Mumpulukukuya mbeto — "the soft tick of the bed." Variant of mumpulukuku that infests poultry coops and human bedding both. Mattresses sunned, bedframes scrubbed with kerosene to drive them out.

examples.lingala: Likalinganyamaya zamba ebandisi makelele makasi na zamba mobimba.
examples.english: The forest cicada started a loud racket in the entire woods.
examples.french: La cigale de forêt a commencé un grand vacarme dans toute la forêt.

words.culturalNote: Likalinganyamaya zamba — the deep-forest cicada whose collective drone in the heat of mid-afternoon can drown out conversation. Each generation emerges on its own multi-year cycle.

examples.lingala: Ndundumbasiya efelo atongi ndako ya potopoto na efelo ya lopango.
examples.english: The mason wasp built a mud nest on the yard wall.
examples.french: La guêpe maçonne a construit un nid en boue sur le mur de la cour.

words.culturalNote: Ndundumbasiya efelo — "the carpenter-bee of walls." Builds tube nests of dried mud on shaded courtyard walls; stocks each cell with a paralysed spider for the grub. Aggressive only if the nest is struck.

examples.lingala: Ekandandekeya soso ezali kotungisa nsoso mwasi na mbalasa.
examples.english: The chicken mite is troubling the hen on the porch.
examples.french: Le pou rouge embête la poule sur la véranda.

words.culturalNote: Ekandandekeya soso — "the feather-mite of chickens." The red mite that infests hen feathers and coop straw. Coops dusted with wood ash; hens given dust baths in the courtyard.

examples.lingala: Singayambangyamoke ezali kotambola malembe likolo ya lokasa ya lilala.
examples.english: The inchworm is crawling slowly on top of the orange leaf.
examples.french: L'arpenteuse rampe lentement sur la feuille d'orange.

words.culturalNote: Singayambangyamoke — the small looper caterpillar that moves by arching its body forward, drawing the rear feet up to meet the front. Pace of a patient measuring; a familiar sight on citrus leaves.

examples.lingala: Nzinziya mbwa ezali koswa mbwa na matoi mikolo nyonso.
examples.english: The dog fly is biting the dog on the ears every day.
examples.french: La mouche du chien mord le chien aux oreilles tous les jours.

words.culturalNote: Nzinziya mbwa — the biting fly that tortures dogs around the ears and belly. Smaller than nzinziya ngombe; the constant ear-flicking and head-shaking of village dogs in the heat is its work.

examples.lingala: Likongoli ya potopoto abimi kowuta na nse ya mabele nsima ya mbula.
examples.english: The soil centipede emerged from under the earth after the rain.
examples.french: La scolopendre du sol est sortie de sous la terre après la pluie.

words.culturalNote: Likongoli ya potopoto — the soil-dwelling centipede that surfaces after heavy rain pushes it out of its tunnels. Faster and more visible than the dry-soil likongoli; same painful bite.

examples.lingala: Simba abimisaki mongongo makasi mpo na kobangisa banyama.
examples.english: The lion made a loud roar to scare the animals.
examples.french: Le lion a poussé un rugissement puissant pour effrayer les animaux.

words.culturalNote: Simba — the lion, widely used across eastern Lingala under Swahili influence (Swahili simba = lion). The standard western Lingala word is nkosi; both are heard depending on the region. Homonym of the verb root meaning "hold" (which appears in koSIMBa).

examples.lingala: Kanga apasoli monyama ya mobomi-mbisi na mai.
examples.english: The crab tore the fisherman's net in the water.
examples.french: Le crabe a déchiré le filet du pêcheur dans l'eau.

words.culturalNote: Kanga — the freshwater crab of rivers, swamps, and flooded rice fields. Sharp claws strong enough to cut a fishing net; caught by hand or in baited traps. Homonym of the verb kanga / kokanga (to close, to catch).

examples.lingala: Likwaga abombi nzoto na ye tango amoni bakolo na nzela.
examples.english: The pangolin curled its body up when it saw the elders on the road.
examples.french: Le pangolin a roulé son corps en boule en voyant les aînés sur la route.

words.culturalNote: Likwaga (also ikwaga) — the scaly anteater. Solitary, nocturnal, rolls into an armoured ball when threatened. Sacred in many forest traditions and a treasured bushmeat in others; heavily trafficked, critically endangered. Distinct from likwanga (stink bug — note the 'n').

examples.lingala: Nkoso ya zamba ebele bazali kosakana likolo ya banzete.
examples.english: Many bonobos are playing on top of the trees.
examples.french: De nombreux bonobos jouent sur les arbres.

words.culturalNote: Nkoso ya zamba — "the parrot of the forest" used regionally for the bonobo's bright social calling. Compound form alongside singamboka (the more common bonobo word) and nsoko (chimpanzee). Found only in the DRC, south of the Congo River bend.

examples.lingala: Mboka ya nzete abimisaki mongongo makasi na zamba na butu.
examples.english: The tree hyrax made a loud noise in the forest at night.
examples.french: Le daman des arbres a poussé un cri puissant dans la forêt la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Mboka ya nzete — the small tree-dwelling hyrax whose sudden, piercing night-call carries across the canopy. Surprisingly loud for such a small animal; often the first thing a visitor to the deep forest notices after dark.

examples.lingala: Mboloko mobali akimi mbangu tango amoni nkoi.
examples.english: The male antelope ran fast when it saw the leopard.
examples.french: Le mâle de céphalophe a couru vite en voyant le léopard.

words.culturalNote: Mboloko mobali — the male of the small forest antelope, counterpart to mboloko mwasi (female). Hunters who track a single buck respect the same restraint as with a doe: not all are taken in any one season.

examples.lingala: Mbenge azali koluka nyama ya kokufa pembeni ya moluka.
examples.english: The jackal is looking for a dead animal near the stream.
examples.french: Le chacal cherche un animal mort près du ruisseau.

words.culturalNote: Mbenge — the jackal, lean scavenger of dawn and dusk along forest streams. Cleans the carrion no other predator finishes; in folktales, the trickster who outwits stronger animals through patience.

examples.lingala: Pongo mwasi azali kobatela mwana na ye na motema molai.
examples.english: The female gorilla is guarding her child with patience.
examples.french: La femelle gorille protège son enfant avec patience.

words.culturalNote: Pongo mwasi — the female gorilla; counterpart to pongo mobali (silverback). The bond between mother and infant in a gorilla troop is one of the longest in any wild mammal — years of close-carried care.

examples.lingala: Simba moindo abombi nzoto na nse ya banzete ebebi.
examples.english: The black panther hid its body beneath the thick trees.
examples.french: La panthère noire a caché son corps sous les arbres épais.

words.culturalNote: Simba moindo — "the dark lion," descriptive name for the melanistic leopard (black panther). Same species as nkoi, but the rare dark coat carries strong symbolism in many forest traditions — a sign for those who know how to read it.

examples.lingala: Mobali amati na punda ya makasi mpo na kokende mosika.
examples.english: The man rode the strong horse to go far away.
examples.french: L'homme est monté sur le cheval puissant pour aller loin.

words.culturalNote: Punda ya makasi — the strong, full-grown horse, usually the stallion. Punda by itself is the everyday horse; the qualifier makasi marks it as the working or riding animal of the household.

examples.lingala: Ngubu monene azali kobina na nse ya mai ya ebale.
examples.english: The giant hippopotamus is swimming under the river water.
examples.french: Le grand hippopotame nage sous l'eau du fleuve.

words.culturalNote: Ngubu monene — the full-grown hippo, the largest of the river's residents. Canoes detour widely; ngubu monene are responsible for more human deaths than any other African mammal.

examples.lingala: Nsoko mobali akamati lilala mpe alei yango na kiese.
examples.english: The male chimpanzee took the orange and ate it with joy.
examples.french: Le chimpanzé mâle a pris l'orange et l'a mangée avec joie.

words.culturalNote: Nsoko mobali — the male chimpanzee. The alpha holds the troop together through complex politics — alliances built and broken across years; the rise of a new dominant male is a community event.

examples.lingala: Esende monene abombi mbuma ebele na kati ya libulu.
examples.english: The giant forest squirrel hid many fruits inside the hole.
examples.french: Le grand écureuil de forêt a caché beaucoup de fruits dans le trou.

words.culturalNote: Esende monene — the large canopy squirrel of the deep forest, distinct from the everyday esende. Caches palm nuts and figs in trunk hollows; its scattered leftovers feed the birds of the understory.

examples.lingala: Ngulu ya sika azali kosakana na potopoto ya lopango.
examples.english: The young piglet is playing in the yard mud.
examples.french: Le porcelet joue dans la boue de la cour.

words.culturalNote: Ngulu ya sika — literally "the new pig." The piglet kept in the family yard, fed on kitchen scraps until ready for sale. Children name them and grow attached before market day.

examples.lingala: Mbwampoka moke azali koningisa mokila tango amoni tata.
examples.english: The puppy is wagging its tail when it sees father.
examples.french: Le chiot remue la queue en voyant papa.

words.culturalNote: Mbwampoka moke — the village puppy. Raised loose around the courtyard, learns its place in the household pack by watching the older mbwampoka. The bond with the family forms in those first months.

examples.lingala: Niau moke alingi komela miliki na kati ya kopo.
examples.english: The kitten wants to drink milk inside the cup.
examples.french: Le chaton veut boire du lait dans la tasse.

words.culturalNote: Niau moke — the kitten. Small, curious, the first month a constant tangle around the cook's feet. Kept for what they will grow into: the household's silent rat-hunter.

examples.lingala: Ngulube azali kotimola mabele mpo na koluka bilei.
examples.english: The bush-pig is digging the soil to look for food.
examples.french: Le potamochère creuse le sol pour chercher de la nourriture.

words.culturalNote: Ngulube — the bush-pig or red river hog; the wild cousin of the yard pig. Bright reddish coat, tufted ears; lives in forest edges and clearings. Crop-raider; farmers near the forest line build watch platforms against them.

examples.lingala: Likaku ya zamba abangisi bana na balabala na makelele.
examples.english: The baboon scared the children on the road with its noise.
examples.french: Le babouin a effrayé les enfants sur la route avec son vacarme.

words.culturalNote: Likaku ya zamba — "the monkey of the forest," the baboon. Larger and bolder than tree monkeys; travels in noisy troops. Children warned to keep distance — a dominant male's bared canines are no bluff.

examples.lingala: Ndoki ya nyama apumbwaka kaka na kati ya butu.
examples.english: The fruit bat flies only inside the night.
examples.french: La chauve-souris frugivore ne vole que la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Ndoki ya nyama — literally "the animal-witch." Regional marketplace and riverine nickname for the large fruit bat, capturing the night-flying mystery of the species. NOT the standard taxonomic term: the proper Lingala word for bat is ngembo (megabat / flying fox) or lipalata. The ndoki element carries the literal sense of "sorcerer," so the compound is read figuratively, never as straight description.

examples.lingala: Ngembo ebele bavandi likolo ya banzete ya mampa.
examples.english: Many flying foxes sat on top of the breadfruit trees.
examples.french: De nombreuses roussettes se sont posées sur les arbres à pain.

words.culturalNote: Ngembo — the large fruit-eating megabat (flying fox). Hangs by the hundreds in canopy roosts; the silhouettes against the dusk sky are one of the unmistakable images of the equatorial evening.

examples.lingala: Linzoko abombami na kati ya matiti pene na ebale.
examples.english: The water chevrotain hid inside the grass near the river.
examples.french: Le chevrotain aquatique se cache dans l'herbe près du fleuve.

words.culturalNote: Linzoko — the small, shy water chevrotain. Walks the riverbank at dawn; flees into the water at any disturbance. The males carry small fangs in place of horns — the trace of a deep evolutionary past.

examples.lingala: Mbuloko atamboli malembe na kati ya esobe ya monene.
examples.english: The swamp antelope walked slowly inside the large marshy plain.
examples.french: Le sitatunga marche lentement dans la grande plaine marécageuse.

words.culturalNote: Mbuloko — the sitatunga, the swamp-adapted antelope with splayed hooves that let it cross waterlogged ground other ungulates cannot. Rare to see; mostly known by tracks in the soft mud and the rare distant glimpse at dawn.

examples.lingala: Mbalapi alei makanga ebele na nse ya mabele.
examples.english: The giant pangolin ate many termites underground.
examples.french: Le grand pangolin a mangé beaucoup de termites sous la terre.

words.culturalNote: Mbalapi — the giant pangolin, larger cousin of likwaga. Solitary, nocturnal, armoured in heavy scales. Critically endangered; heavily trafficked for scales and meat. Sacred in many forest traditions — taking one is not a small act.

examples.lingala: Likoba akangi mbisi na makasi na kati ya moluka.
examples.english: The clawless otter caught a fish powerfully inside the stream.
examples.french: La loutre a attrapé un poisson puissamment dans le ruisseau.

words.culturalNote: Likoba — the African clawless otter of the slow rivers and swamps. Hunts fish, crabs, and frogs with dextrous front paws (no claws — uses fingers and snout). Rare sighting; mostly known by the smooth mud-slides on the riverbank.

examples.lingala: Ntatabi azali kokota na kati ya banzete ekauka noki.
examples.english: The elephant shrew is entering inside the dry sticks quickly.
examples.french: Le macroscélide entre rapidement sous les bois secs.

words.culturalNote: Ntatabi — the elephant shrew (sengi), tiny mammal with the long flexible snout. Bounds on improbable thin legs along forest-floor pathways it has memorised perfectly. Distantly related to elephants, despite the size.

examples.lingala: Noko ya zamba azali na mikuwa ya makasi na mposo.
examples.english: The porcupine has sharp quills on its skin.
examples.french: Le porc-épic a des piquants pointus sur la peau.

words.culturalNote: Noko ya zamba — literally "forest uncle," market nickname for the porcupine. (Noko on its own means maternal uncle.) The respectful nickname softens the dangerous reputation — those quills go in easily and come out hard.

examples.lingala: Eloli ya zamba abimisaki solo mabe mpo na mbwa.
examples.english: The striped polecat released a bad smell at the dog.
examples.french: Le putois rayé a dégagé une mauvaise odeur sur le chien.

words.culturalNote: Eloli ya zamba — "the forest mongoose," descriptive name for the striped polecat or zorilla. Cousin of eloli (mongoose), but with the skunk-family defence: a foul spray that drives off any predator that hasn't learned the lesson before.

examples.lingala: Mbuta ya zamba abangaka nioka ya mabe te.
examples.english: The honey badger does not fear dangerous snakes.
examples.french: Le ratel ne craint pas les serpents dangereux.

words.culturalNote: Mbuta ya zamba — "the elder of the forest," descriptive name for the honey badger. Famous for fearlessness against cobras, bee-swarms, and animals many times its size. The nickname is half-respect, half-warning: a small body but the temperament of an elder who fears nothing.

examples.lingala: Ekanya abombami na nse ya makasa ekauka mpo na koswa taba.
examples.english: The puff adder hid beneath the dry leaves to bite the goat.
examples.french: La vipère heurtante s'est cachée sous les feuilles sèches pour mordre la chèvre.

words.culturalNote: Ekanya — the heavy-bodied puff adder, lying still on warm paths and dry leaves. Slow to flee, fast to strike; the hiss-puff sound it gives when threatened is the warning to step well back.

examples.lingala: Imba atambolaka mbangu na mpeka ya banzete.
examples.english: The green mamba moves fast on the tree branches.
examples.french: Le mamba vert se déplace vite sur les branches.

words.culturalNote: Imba — the bright-green tree mamba, faster than most can react. Slips through the canopy as if water; bite is venomous but the snake itself prefers escape over confrontation.

examples.lingala: Kimbamba amati na efelo ya kuku mpo na kolia mpese.
examples.english: The gecko climbed the kitchen wall to eat cockroaches.
examples.french: Le gecko a grimpé sur le mur de la cuisine pour manger les cafards.

words.culturalNote: Kimbamba — the small house gecko, the night-shift kitchen worker. Pads on walls and ceilings hunting moths and cockroaches; welcomed in every household for keeping the bug count down.

examples.lingala: Libawu amingoti zingazinga ya nzete monene.
examples.english: The rock python coiled itself around the huge tree.
examples.french: Le python de Seba s'est enroulé autour du grand arbre.

words.culturalNote: Libawu — the African rock python, longest snake on the continent. Constrictor; takes prey by squeezing rather than venom. In some traditions, an animal of strong symbolism; killed only with great care.

examples.lingala: Likunda akoti na kati ya matiti moke kozanga koswa bana.
examples.english: The green bush-snake slipped into the short grass without biting the children.
examples.french: La couleuvre verte est entrée dans l'herbe courte sans mordre les enfants.

words.culturalNote: Likunda — the slim, harmless green bush-snake of gardens and undergrowth. Often mistaken for the venomous imba (green mamba); knowing the difference is part of forest-edge growing up.

examples.lingala: Lobefu abimi kowuta na nse ya mabele nsima ya mbula ya monene.
examples.english: The blind snake emerged from underground after the heavy rain.
examples.french: Le serpent aveugle est sorti de sous terre après la grosse pluie.

words.culturalNote: Lobefu — the small worm-like blind snake (typhlops) that lives buried in the soil and surfaces after heavy rain. Harmless; often mistaken for a large earthworm at first glance.

examples.lingala: Mboma azali komema mpiko makasi tango azali kokanga mboloko.
examples.english: The python brings intense stamina when capturing a duiker.
examples.french: Le python met une endurance intense quand il capture un céphalophe.

words.culturalNote: Mboma — broad term for the constrictor snake, used across regions for python and boa types alongside libawu. Patient ambush hunter; lies still for days waiting for the right passing prey.

examples.lingala: Mbwembwe abongolaka langi na ye na mposo ya banzete.
examples.english: The chameleon changes its colour on the tree bark.
examples.french: Le caméléon change de couleur sur l'écorce de l'arbre.

words.culturalNote: Mbwembwe — onomatopoeic regional variant for the chameleon (the standard word is ndamba). The doubled sound evokes the slow, swaying motion of the animal's deliberate walk.

words.french: vipère à cornes / vipère du sable

examples.lingala: Nkanga azali na solo mabe te kasi azali na ngenge makasi.
examples.english: The horned viper has no bad smell but its venom is intense.
examples.french: La vipère à cornes n'a pas de mauvaise odeur mais son venin est puissant.

words.culturalNote: Nkanga — the horned viper of dry, sandy regions. Buries itself in loose sand with only the horned brow ridge showing; strikes upward at anything passing. Distinct from kanga (the verb to close) and kanga (the crab) — pure homonym.

examples.lingala: Nsasa atwaki ngenge mbala moko na miso ya mbwa.
examples.english: The spitting cobra spat venom straight into the dog's eyes.
examples.french: Le cobra cracheur a craché du venin dans les yeux du chien.

words.culturalNote: Nsasa — the spitting cobra, capable of spraying venom into the eyes of a threat from over a metre away. The first defence is the hood-spread; the second is the strike. Treated with extreme respect.

examples.lingala: Ntulu akimi noki na kati ya mabanga tango ayoki makelele.
examples.english: The skink fled quickly into the rocks when it heard the noise.
examples.french: Le scinque s'est enfui rapidement dans les rochers en entendant le bruit.

words.culturalNote: Ntulu — the smooth, fast-moving skink of stone walls and woodpiles. The tail breaks off cleanly if a predator grabs it — and regrows over weeks. Harmless; widely tolerated around the home.

examples.lingala: Nyasa ezali kobina pete na kati ya mai ya moluka.
examples.english: The water snake is swimming softly inside the stream water.
examples.french: La couleuvre d'eau nage doucement dans l'eau du ruisseau.

words.culturalNote: Nyasa — the harmless freshwater snake that swims with its head just above the surface. Hunts small fish and frogs; the calm sight of it in a stream is part of the rural landscape.

examples.lingala: Nzofi abimi koluka mpese mpe bangungi na butu.
examples.english: The night adder emerges to look for cockroaches and mosquitoes at night.
examples.french: La vipère nocturne sort la nuit pour chercher cafards et moustiques.

words.culturalNote: Nzofi — the night adder, small and inconspicuous by day, active by night around lights that draw insects. Venomous but rarely deadly; bites tend to happen when a barefoot step lands on one in the dark.

examples.lingala: Keba na pili, azali kobatela mabele na ye na kanda.
examples.english: Watch out for the adder, it is guarding its ground angrily.
examples.french: Fais attention à la vipère, elle garde son territoire avec colère.

words.culturalNote: Pili — slang for the adder, particularly the puff adder. Not to be confused with pili-pili (the chili pepper, an entirely separate word); context tells which is meant. Heard in the bush more than in the city.

examples.lingala: Anana oyo ezali na mai mingi mpe etondi na sukali.
examples.english: This pineapple is very juicy and full of sweetness.
examples.french: Cet ananas est très juteux et plein de sucre.

words.culturalNote: Anana — the pineapple. Cut into thick slices and shared cold; the fragrance fills the room. Grown in lowland coastal and inland plantations; sold by the head in every market.

examples.lingala: Bana balokoti limfuka ekweyaki kowuta na nzete.
examples.english: The children gathered the wild forest fruit that fell from the tree.
examples.french: Les enfants ont ramassé le fruit sauvage tombé de l'arbre.

words.culturalNote: Limfuka — collective name for some of the wild forest fruits that ripen and drop in the wet season. Gathered by children on bush walks; eaten on the spot or carried home to share.

words.french: fruit du palmier / noix de palme

examples.lingala: Akati mbila na soka mpo na kolamba pondu.
examples.english: He cut a palm fruit with an axe to cook cassava leaves.
examples.french: Il a coupé une noix de palme à la hache pour cuire les feuilles de manioc.

words.culturalNote: Mbila — the individual palm fruit, dark and dense; pressed for mafuta ya mbila (palm oil) at the heart of so many household dishes. Counterpart to maba (the harvested cluster).

examples.lingala: Tosombi litungulu na wenze mpo na kotia na supu.
examples.english: We bought wild onion bulbs at the small market to put in the soup.
examples.french: Nous avons acheté des oignons sauvages au petit marché pour la soupe.

words.culturalNote: Litungulu — the wild onion bulb (related to tungulu, the cultivated onion). Sold at small markets when in season; smaller and sharper than the cultivated form; used in stews and broths.

examples.lingala: Paipai oyo ezali pete mpe esili kotela malamu.
examples.english: This papaya is soft and has ripened well.
examples.french: Cette papaye est molle et bien mûre.

words.culturalNote: Paipai — the papaya, eaten ripe with a squeeze of lime. Green papaya is grated into salads; the tree grows fast in any courtyard and bears fruit within a year of planting.

examples.lingala: Ditidi ezali monene mpe etondi na mai ya sukali.
examples.english: The watermelon is huge and full of sweet juice.
examples.french: La pastèque est énorme et pleine de jus sucré.

words.culturalNote: Ditidi — the watermelon, dry-season relief. Cut into wedges and shared on a tray; seeds spat into the courtyard or kept for next year's planting. Pale-fleshed regional varieties also called ditidi.

examples.lingala: Bandeke balei fiki nyonso ekweli na nse ya banzete.
examples.english: Birds ate all the figs that fell beneath the trees.
examples.french: Les oiseaux ont mangé toutes les figues tombées sous les arbres.

words.culturalNote: Fiki — the fig (from English/French via the Bible's circulation in mission schools). Wild fig trees feed birds, bats, monkeys; the cultivated fig is rarer, mostly in older mission gardens.

examples.lingala: Mbuma ya vinyo ezali na langi ya bule mpe moindo.
examples.english: Grapes have colours of blue and black.
examples.french: Le raisin a des couleurs de bleu et de noir.

words.culturalNote: Vinyo — the grape (from French vigne / Portuguese vinho). Not native; the word travels with imported grapes sold in city supermarkets and at festive tables. Same root as the word for wine across many African languages.

examples.lingala: Mpondunene ezali mbuma ya zito oyo akolaka na nzete ya molai.
examples.english: Breadfruit is a heavy fruit that grows on a tall tree.
examples.french: Le fruit à pain est un fruit lourd qui pousse sur un grand arbre.

words.culturalNote: Mpondunene — the heavy starchy breadfruit, roasted or boiled and served like potato. Grows on impressive tall trees; one fruit can feed a family. Not to be confused with mpondu (cassava leaves).

examples.lingala: Mbalasika ekweyi na nse tango mpepe makasi ebetaki.
examples.english: The wild plum fell to the ground when the strong wind blew.
examples.french: La prune sauvage est tombée au sol quand le vent fort a soufflé.

words.culturalNote: Mbalasika — the wild forest plum, smaller and tarter than the cultivated kind. Gathered after windy days when ripe fruit drops; eaten fresh or stewed with sugar.

examples.lingala: Ndimonene ezali na mposo ya makasi mpe mai na yango ezali bololo.
examples.english: The citron has a thick skin and its juice is sour.
examples.french: Le cédrat a une écorce épaisse et son jus est acide.

words.culturalNote: Ndimonene — "the big ndimo," the citron — thick-skinned, lumpy, more zest than juice. Used for marmalade and traditional preparations; the rind is the prize, not the flesh.

examples.lingala: Mwana akamati ntelamoke mibale na kati ya sani.
examples.english: The child took two small finger-bananas from the dish.
examples.french: L'enfant a pris deux petites bananes-figues dans le plat.

words.culturalNote: Ntelamoke — "the little ntela," the small, sweet lady-finger banana. Children's favourite; bunches small enough to finish in one sitting. Distinct from the larger eating banana and the plantain (makemba).

examples.lingala: Tolambi ndongondongo na mungwa mpe mafuta.
examples.english: We cooked okra with salt and oil.
examples.french: On a cuit le gombo avec du sel et de l'huile.

words.culturalNote: Ndongondongo (also written dongo-dongo) — okra, the slim green pod that thickens stews across Central Africa. Sliced into supu ya ndongondongo with palm oil and dried fish, or served alongside fufu. Homonym of ndongondongo the dragonfly (different entry) — same headword, completely different worlds; context tells which.

words.english: to peek / to peer / to spy a look
words.french: jeter un coup d'œil furtif / épier

examples.lingala: Azali kondoke na lininisa mpo na kotala libanda.
examples.english: He is peeking through the window to look outside.
examples.french: Il jette un coup d'œil furtif par la fenêtre pour regarder dehors.

words.culturalNote: Kondoke — to peek, peer, sneak a look through a crack, gap, or curtain. Urban/marketplace verb (slang contraction of kondonga / kondoke variants). Used when someone is secretly spying, looking where they're not meant to be looking, or keeping an uninvited eye on a situation. "Azo ndoke" is the further-contracted street form.

words.english: to stare wide-eyed / to bulge one's eyes / to glare
words.french: écarquiller les yeux / fixer du regard

examples.lingala: Azali kodongola miso na kanda tango aswanaka.
examples.english: He is bulging his eyes with anger when he argues.
examples.french: Il écarquille les yeux de colère quand il se dispute.

words.culturalNote: Kodongola — to open the eyes as wide as they go: shock, fury, intimidation. The expressive twin to kondoke (the secret look) — where kondoke is hidden, kodongola is the most visible facial action you can make. Common in marketplace disputes ("kodongola miso" — to pop out the eyes) and any moment of dramatic offence or surprise.

words.english: to twitch / to blink rapidly / to flinch

examples.lingala: Azali kofoti nkongi mpo na moi makasi.
examples.english: He is twitching his eyebrow because of the intense sun.
examples.french: Il fait tressaillir son sourcil à cause du soleil intense.

words.culturalNote: Kofoti — the small involuntary twitch: the eyelid in glare, the cheek from a stray fly, the shoulder from a startling sound. The body's quiet reflex, named.

words.english: to step on / to crush underfoot / to stomp

examples.lingala: Akebe noki mpo konyatola kanga-nkando te.
examples.english: He was careful not to step on the scorpion.
examples.french: Il a fait attention de ne pas marcher sur le scorpion.

words.culturalNote: Konyatola — the deliberate or careless crushing underfoot. Of a scorpion on a moonlit path; of a fallen mango in the courtyard; of pride, in the figurative usage.

words.english: to whisper secrets / to murmur gossip

examples.lingala: Balingi kosungila makambo ya bulubulu na matoi.
examples.english: They like to whisper messy matters into ears.
examples.french: Ils aiment chuchoter des affaires embrouillées aux oreilles.

words.culturalNote: Kosungila — the whispered gossip with a hand cupped to the ear. Sometimes friendly, often not; the verb carries its own small judgment. Elders warn against it; teenagers traffic in it.

words.english: to provoke / to taunt / to deliberately annoy

examples.lingala: Tika kotumola mbwa wana, ekoswa yo.
examples.english: Stop provoking that dog, it will bite you.
examples.french: Arrête de provoquer ce chien, il va te mordre.

words.culturalNote: Kotumola — the deliberate poking and prodding: a child teasing a tethered dog, a sibling jabbing a sibling, a customer needling a market seller until the price drops. The verb implies the speaker thinks the target should be left alone.

words.english: to become hoarse / to lose one's voice

examples.lingala: Mongongo na ye egwanti mpo na makelele ya zando.
examples.english: His voice became hoarse because of the market noise.
examples.french: Sa voix s'est enrouée à cause du bruit du marché.

words.culturalNote: Kogwanta — the voice gone rough from too much shouting: market sellers at the end of a long day, football fans after a derby, a preacher after a hot service. The hoarseness is its own kind of honest tiredness.

words.english: to squirm / to wriggle / to twist the body

examples.lingala: Limfunda azali komingota na kati ya potopoto.
examples.english: The earthworm is wriggling in the mud.
examples.french: Le ver se tortille dans la boue.

words.culturalNote: Komingota — the wriggling motion: a worm in the dirt, a child who does not want to sit still, someone caught in an uncomfortable conversation. The body's refusal of stillness, in one verb.

words.english: to slice open (for someone) / to rip apart on behalf of

examples.lingala: Apasweli ngai anana ya sika mpo na kolia.
examples.english: He sliced open a fresh pineapple for me to eat.
examples.french: Il m'a ouvert un ananas frais à manger.

words.culturalNote: Kopaswela — the applicative form of kopasola (to tear/split): to slice or open something for someone else. A small act of care: opening the pineapple, splitting the bread, halving the orange for the child.

words.english: to sag / to droop / to hang low

examples.lingala: Mpeka ya nzete ezali kosunza mpo na mbuma ebele.
examples.english: The tree branch is drooping because of the heavy fruit.
examples.french: La branche s'affaisse à cause des nombreux fruits.

words.culturalNote: Kosunza — the slow downward sag: branch under fruit weight, washing line under wet clothes, shoulders at the end of a long day. The verb is descriptive, often quietly sympathetic.

words.english: to toss around / to shuffle / to scatter back and forth

examples.lingala: Batika kobwakitinya biloko ya ndako ndenge wana.
examples.english: They should stop tossing household items around like that.
examples.french: Ils devraient arrêter d'éparpiller les affaires de la maison comme ça.

words.culturalNote: Kobwakitinya — the repeated, careless tossing of things: clothes flung from the suitcase, papers shuffled aside, dishes shoved across a counter. The grandmother's complaint condensed into a verb.

words.english: to chop into tiny pieces / to mince / to shred

examples.lingala: Mama akitinitinyi tomati mpo na kolamba supu.
examples.english: Mother chopped the tomatoes into tiny pieces to cook the soup.
examples.french: Maman a émincé les tomates pour cuire la soupe.

words.culturalNote: Kokitinitinya — the rhythmic mincing of cooking: onion, tomato, garlic, ginger all worked down small under the blade. The doubled syllables in the verb mirror the doubled chopping motion.

words.english: to scrutinize / to inspect intensely / to size up

examples.lingala: Motekisi azali kopitolo mbongo na ngai ya sika.
examples.english: The trader is intensely inspecting my new money.
examples.french: Le commerçant scrute mon nouvel argent.

words.culturalNote: Kopitolo — the long, suspicious look that takes the measure of something. Of a banknote at the market (counterfeit or real?), of a stranger at the door, of an unfamiliar dish. The verb of careful, distrustful examination.

words.english: to shake / to wag / to vibrate

examples.lingala: Mbwa azali koningisa mokila na ye mpo na kiese.
examples.english: The dog is wagging its tail out of happiness.
examples.french: Le chien remue la queue de joie.

words.culturalNote: Koningisa — the active shaking or wagging: tail in greeting, hand in negation, branch in the wind. Causative form of koninga (to shake intransitively).

words.english: to slurp / to suck in / to absorb liquid

examples.lingala: Mwana azali kofiba mai ya lilala kowuta na kopo.
examples.english: The child is slurping orange juice from the cup.
examples.french: L'enfant aspire le jus d'orange de la tasse.

words.culturalNote: Kofiba — the long pull on a straw, the noisy finish of a juicy mango, the slurp at the bottom of the soup bowl. Children do it without thinking; adults are told not to.

words.english: to soften / to weaken / to loosen

examples.lingala: Sukali ekolembisa bololo ya mai ya ndimo.
examples.english: Sugar will soften the sourness of the lemon juice.
examples.french: Le sucre adoucit l'amertume du jus de citron.

words.culturalNote: Kolembisa — the causative of kolemba (to grow weak). To soften the harsh flavour with sugar, to soften the harsh news with kind words, to soften the muscle that has gone tight.

words.english: to burst / to rupture / to shatter on its own

examples.lingala: Kopo ya baso epasuki tango mai ya moto ekoti.
examples.english: The glass shattered when the hot water entered.
examples.french: Le verre s'est brisé quand l'eau chaude est entrée.

words.culturalNote: Kopasuka — the intransitive bursting or shattering. The cup of a sudden temperature change; the sack from being overstuffed; the tyre on a sharp stone. The thing that breaks itself.

words.english: to be troubled / to feel deep anxiety

examples.lingala: Motema na ngai ezali kotungisama mpo na sango ya mabe.
examples.english: My heart is troubled because of the bad news.
examples.french: Mon cœur est troublé à cause de la mauvaise nouvelle.

words.culturalNote: Kotungisama — to carry deep anxiety, the heart in unrest. Passive of kotungisa (to trouble); the verb names the inner state when worry has settled and won't lift.

words.english: to leave to rot / to neglect to the point of decay
words.french: laisser pourrir / négliger jusqu'à la ruine

examples.lingala: Atiki mosala na ye mpe afwamikisi yango mobimba.
examples.english: He abandoned his work and let it rot completely.
examples.french: Il a abandonné son travail et l'a laissé pourrir complètement.

words.culturalNote: Kofwamikisa — to neglect something so badly it goes to ruin. Of a house left unrepaired, a relationship left unattended, a body left untended. Causative of kofwama (to rot). Street slang extension carries figurative force.

words.english: to crisscross / to be striped / to intersect

examples.lingala: Singa ebele ekatani likolo ya balabala.
examples.english: Many wires crisscross over the street.
examples.french: De nombreux câbles se croisent au-dessus de la rue.

words.culturalNote: Kokatana — the visual pattern of crossing lines: power cables over a Kinshasa street, the zebra's stripes, the loom's woven threads. Reciprocal of kokata (to cut/cross).

words.english: to anticipate / to prepare for an arrival / to lay groundwork

examples.lingala: Tozali kolengele koya ya bakolo lobi na pokwa.
examples.english: We are preparing for the arrival of the elders tomorrow evening.
examples.french: Nous préparons l'arrivée des aînés demain soir.

words.culturalNote: Kolengele — to prepare carefully in advance for someone or something coming. The chairs arranged, the food started, the gate swept; the verb covers all the small readinesses before the actual arrival.

words.english: to mock / to sneer / to show contempt

examples.lingala: Kofinga moto te, mpe kotiola ye liboso ya bato te.
examples.english: Do not insult a person, and do not mock them in front of others.
examples.french: N'insulte pas une personne, et ne la raille pas devant les autres.

words.culturalNote: Kotiola — the open mockery, sneering at someone's face or behind their back. Different from kofinga (insult) — kotiola is the contempt itself, the laughter and the dismissive wave. Considered a deep social wound when public.

words.english: to dry up completely / to shrivel / to desiccate

examples.lingala: Matiti ekauki mobimba mpo moi ezali makasi lelo.
examples.english: The grass dried up completely because the sun is intense today.
examples.french: L'herbe s'est complètement desséchée parce que le soleil est intense.

words.culturalNote: Kokauka — the going-completely-dry of the dry season: brush, riverbed, washing on the line, the last of the kitchen water. Both literal and figurative: hope can kokauka, a friendship can kokauka.

words.english: to be completely forgotten / to be lost to history
words.french: être complètement oublié / sombrer dans l'oubli

examples.lingala: Lisapo ya bankondo ekoki kobungama te.
examples.english: The story of the ancestors cannot be forgotten.
examples.french: L'histoire des ancêtres ne peut pas être oubliée.

words.culturalNote: Kobungama — to slip out of memory entirely. Of names, languages, songs, stories — what disappears when no one carries it. The fear and the duty bound up together in one verb.

examples.lingala: Namoni lipekapeka ya kitoko likolo ya avoka.
examples.english: I see a beautiful butterfly on top of the avocado tree.
examples.french: Je vois un beau papillon sur l'avocatier.

words.culturalNote: Komona — to see, in the everyday sense and in the deeper one (to understand, to recognise, to witness). The foundational verb of perception in Lingala; threads through countless idioms.

words.english: to guard / to protect / to keep watch over

examples.lingala: Sinzili azali kobatela ekuke ya lopango na kimia.
examples.english: The watchman is guarding the yard gate in peace.
examples.french: Le gardien protège le portail de la cour avec calme.

words.culturalNote: Kobatela — to keep, to guard, to preserve. Of a gate, of a secret, of a tradition, of a child. Used both literally (the watchman) and figuratively (the elder who carries the family's stories).

words.english: to breathe / to rest / to take a pause

examples.lingala: Vanda na kiti mpo na kopema moke nsima ya mosala.
examples.english: Sit in the chair to rest a bit after work.
examples.french: Assieds-toi sur la chaise pour te reposer un peu après le travail.

words.culturalNote: Kopema — to breathe, to rest, to take a pause. The end-of-day verb, said in invitation: pesa motema kopema (let your heart rest). Threaded into greetings and goodbyes alike.

words.english: to mourn deeply / to wail in grief

examples.lingala: Libota mobimba bazali kolela na mawa mpo na liwa ya mbuta.
examples.english: The entire family is mourning deeply because of the death of the elder.
examples.french: Toute la famille pleure de chagrin à cause de la mort de l'aîné.

words.culturalNote: Kolela na mawa — "to weep with mawa," where mawa is the deep word for sorrow and pity together. The phrase names the openly expressed grief of funerals and farewells; the community's tears, not the private ones.

words.english: to inhale deeply / to catch one's breath

examples.lingala: Atelemi na libanda mpo na kobenda mopepe ya malili.
examples.english: He stood outside to inhale the cool breeze.
examples.french: Il s'est tenu dehors pour respirer la brise fraîche.

words.culturalNote: Kobenda mopepe — "to pull the breeze in." To step outside after the day's heat and breathe deep; to take the long inhale that resets the body. The phrase is both literal and quietly meditative.

examples.lingala: Mwana asanzi bilei mpo na maladi ya libumu.
examples.english: The child threw up the food because of a stomach illness.
examples.french: L'enfant a vomi la nourriture à cause d'une maladie de ventre.

words.culturalNote: Kosanza — to vomit, in plain straightforward usage. Said matter-of-factly in the household when a child is sick; not shamed, simply named.

words.english: to rule / to reign / to dominate

examples.lingala: Mokonzi ya sika ayei kokonza mboka na bosembo.
examples.english: The new chief came to rule the village with justice.
examples.french: Le nouveau chef est venu régner sur le village avec justice.

words.culturalNote: Kokonza — to hold authority, to govern. Shares its root with mokonzi (chief, ruler). Used for political authority, household authority, and (occasionally, ironically) anyone strutting around acting like they're in charge.

examples.lingala: Keba, komila mokuwa ya mbisi te.
examples.english: Careful, do not swallow the fish bone.
examples.french: Attention, n'avale pas l'arête de poisson.

words.culturalNote: Komila — to swallow whole. The mother's warning at the fish dinner; the medicine pushed down with water; the rumour swallowed without question.

words.english: to burst out laughing / to crack up

examples.lingala: Bato nyonso bapasuki na koseke mpo na lisapo na ye.
examples.english: Everyone burst out laughing at his story.
examples.french: Tout le monde a éclaté de rire à cause de son histoire.

words.culturalNote: Kopasuka na koseke — literally "to burst with laughter." The full-body laugh of a circle around a good storyteller; not a polite chuckle but the kind that doubles people over. The verb of an evening at its best.

words.english: to be thrown away / to lie abandoned

examples.lingala: Bosoto oyo ebwami na libulu kala.
examples.english: This trash was thrown into the pit long ago.
examples.french: Ces ordures ont été jetées dans le trou il y a longtemps.

words.culturalNote: Kobwama — passive of kobwaka (to throw). The state of having been discarded; said of refuse, but also figuratively of a person or relationship left unattended.

examples.lingala: Azali komona pasi makasi na lino na ye.
examples.english: He is suffering intense pain in his tooth.
examples.french: Il endure une douleur intense à sa dent.

words.culturalNote: Komona pasi — "to see pain." The Lingala idiom for suffering, used for physical pain and life-hardship alike. The shared verb of so many family histories: "tomona pasi mingi" — we have seen much pain.

words.english: to lean heavily on / to depend on (out of exhaustion)

examples.lingala: Alembeli moninga na ye mpo makolo ezali kolenga.
examples.english: He leaned heavily on his friend because his legs were trembling.
examples.french: Il s'est appuyé sur son ami parce que ses jambes tremblaient.

words.culturalNote: Kolembela — applicative of kolemba (to weaken). To lean on someone because you cannot stand on your own; the friend's shoulder under the arm of someone tired, injured, or grieving.

words.english: to pull (someone's) ears / to discipline sternly

examples.lingala: Mbuta abendi matoi ya mwana mpo atika bulubulu.
examples.english: The elder pulled the child's ears so he would stop the chaotic behaviour.
examples.french: L'aîné a tiré les oreilles de l'enfant pour qu'il arrête le chahut.

words.culturalNote: Kobenda matoi — "to pull the ears." Used both literally (the parent's old reprimand) and figuratively (any stern warning). Carries the weight of generations of household discipline.

words.english: to open up / to be unlocked

examples.lingala: Ekuke ya ndako efungwami tango mpepe ebeti.
examples.english: The house door opened up when the wind blew.
examples.french: La porte de la maison s'est ouverte quand le vent a soufflé.

words.culturalNote: Kofungwama — passive/intransitive of kofungola (to open). The door that opens of itself, the parcel that comes undone, the closed mouth that finally opens to speak.

words.english: to be trapped / to be stuck / to be locked
words.french: être coincé / être pris au piège

examples.lingala: Mpese ekangami na kati ya molangi ya mai.
examples.english: The cockroach is trapped inside the water bottle.
examples.french: Le cafard est coincé dans la bouteille d'eau.

words.culturalNote: Kokangama — passive of kokanga (to catch / close). To be held fast: the bug in the jar, the foot in the trap, the person caught up in a situation they cannot get out of.

words.english: to trade insults / to curse at each other

examples.lingala: Batekisi mibale bazali kotukana na kati ya zando.
examples.english: The two traders are trading insults inside the market.
examples.french: Les deux commerçants s'invectivent dans le marché.

words.culturalNote: Kotukana — reciprocal of kotuka (to insult). The shouted back-and-forth of a market argument, two voices climbing over each other; usually ends with neighbours stepping in.

words.english: to scatter / to smash to pieces

examples.lingala: Mpepe makasi epanzi rido ya lininisa.
examples.english: The strong wind ripped and scattered the window curtain.
examples.french: Le vent fort a déchiré et dispersé le rideau.

words.culturalNote: Kopanza — to scatter forcibly, to break apart. The wind that scatters laundry, the stone that smashes the bottle, the rumour that scatters a friendship.

examples.lingala: Bato bapanzani noki tango bitumba-zoba ebandi.
examples.english: The people dispersed quickly when the brawl started.
examples.french: Les gens se sont dispersés vite quand la bagarre a commencé.

words.culturalNote: Kopanzana — reciprocal/passive of kopanza. The crowd scattering at the sound of police; the herd scattering at the sight of the leopard; siblings scattering across cities in adulthood.

examples.lingala: Mwana asopi mai ya kopo likolo ya mesa.
examples.english: The child spilled the cup of water on the table.
examples.french: L'enfant a renversé l'eau de la tasse sur la table.

words.culturalNote: Kosopa — to pour out (deliberately) or spill (accidentally). Same verb for the careful pouring of palm wine and the toddler's overturned cup; tone of voice carries the difference.

words.english: to overflow / to leak out completely

examples.lingala: Mai esopani na nse mpo elungi etondi mobimba.
examples.english: The water overflowed to the ground because the jug is completely full.
examples.french: L'eau a débordé au sol parce que la jarre est pleine.

words.culturalNote: Kosopana — reciprocal/passive of kosopa. The pot that boils over, the river that overflows its banks, the basket too full to carry. The unstoppable spilling that follows from filling too far.

words.english: to cross over / to ferry across

examples.lingala: Sofele akatisi mutuka na balabala ya potopoto.
examples.english: The driver crossed the car over the muddy road.
examples.french: Le chauffeur a fait traverser la voiture sur la route boueuse.

words.culturalNote: Kokatisa — causative of kokata (to cross/cut). To bring across: a vehicle through mud, a child across a busy street, a difficult message into the right hands.

examples.lingala: Mutuka elekeli na nzela ya moke mpo na kokima zando.
examples.english: The car bypassed through the narrow path to avoid the market.
examples.french: La voiture est passée par le petit chemin pour éviter le marché.

words.culturalNote: Kolekela — applicative of koleka (to pass). To take a specific route through or around something; the back-road verb of any Kinshasa driver who knows traffic patterns better than the maps.

words.english: to break someone's heart / to cause deep anxiety
words.french: briser le cœur / causer un profond chagrin

examples.lingala: Likambo oyo ezali kotungisa motema ya mama.
examples.english: This matter is causing deep anxiety to mother's heart.
examples.french: Cette affaire cause un profond chagrin au cœur de maman.

words.culturalNote: Kotungisa motema — "to trouble the heart." The phrase for deep emotional pain caused by another's actions; said both for romantic heartbreak and for the slower wound of a child's choices that disappoint a parent.

examples.lingala: Fandisa mopaya sika na kiti ya malamu.
examples.english: Seat the new visitor on the good chair.
examples.french: Fais asseoir le nouveau visiteur sur la bonne chaise.

words.culturalNote: Kofandisa — causative of kofanda (to sit). To make sit: a visitor offered the best chair, a child placed on the lap, a heavy basket set down. The verb of welcome and care.

words.english: to unfold / to spread out (cloth, mat)

examples.lingala: Tandola elamba kitoko oyo likolo ya mesa.
examples.english: Spread this beautiful cloth on top of the table.
examples.french: Étale ce beau tissu sur la table.

words.culturalNote: Kotandola — to unfold or spread wide: the tablecloth before a meal, the mat in the courtyard for sitting, the wrapper laid out for the baby. A gesture of preparation, of making ready.

words.english: to fall into deep sleep / to crash out

examples.lingala: Nsima ya mosala ya zito, abwami na mpongi noki.
examples.english: After the heavy work, he fell into a deep sleep quickly.
examples.french: Après le travail lourd, il est tombé dans un sommeil profond rapidement.

words.culturalNote: Kobwama na mpongi — "to be thrown into sleep." The crash-out at the end of a long day, sleep that takes the body completely. Different from the gentle kolala (to lie down) — this one is not chosen, it arrives.

words.english: to feel pity for / to have compassion
words.french: ressentir de la pitié / avoir de la compassion

examples.lingala: Mbuta ayokeli mwana moke mawa mpe apesi ye mampa.
examples.english: The elder felt pity for the small child and gave him bread.
examples.french: L'aîné a eu pitié du petit enfant et lui a donné du pain.

words.culturalNote: Koyokela mawa — "to hear/feel mawa for someone," where mawa is the deep word for both pity and sorrow. Not condescending pity but a moved-to-act compassion; the verb that turns into the gesture.

words.english: to calm / to reassure / to ease the heart

examples.lingala: Sango ya malamu ekitisi motema na ngai mobimba.
examples.english: The good news completely calmed my heart down.
examples.french: La bonne nouvelle a complètement apaisé mon cœur.

words.culturalNote: Kokitisa motema — "to bring the heart down." To calm anxiety, to soothe worry, to settle a troubled mind. Said both about an event (good news that arrives) and an action (the friend who knows how to do it).

examples.lingala: Bandeko mibale bapesani mbote na kiese na nzela.
examples.english: The two relatives greeted each other warmly on the road.
examples.french: Les deux parents se sont salués avec joie sur la route.

words.culturalNote: Kopesana mbote — reciprocal of kopesa mbote (to give hello). The mutual greeting between two people meeting: handshake, embrace, words, all together. The opening ceremony of every encounter.

words.english: to touch one's heart / to move someone emotionally

examples.lingala: Maloba na yo esimbi motema na ngai makasi.
examples.english: Your words touched my heart deeply.
examples.french: Tes paroles ont profondément touché mon cœur.

words.culturalNote: Kosimba motema — "to touch the heart." The phrase for being genuinely moved: by a story, a song, a small kindness. Spoken as gratitude, never as flattery.

words.english: to cross the line / to exceed boundaries
words.french: dépasser les bornes / aller trop loin

examples.lingala: Lofendo na yo elekisi ndelo, tika koswana!
examples.english: Your arrogance has crossed the line, stop arguing!
examples.french: Ton arrogance a dépassé les bornes, arrête de te disputer!

words.culturalNote: Kolekisa ndelo — "to make pass the limit." The verb of an offence going too far: the joke that wasn't a joke any more, the argument that drew blood, the disrespect a family will not forgive.

words.english: to waste time / to loiter pointlessly
words.french: perdre du temps / traîner sans but

examples.lingala: Tika kobungisa ntango na makambo ya bulubulu.
examples.english: Stop wasting time on chaotic matters.
examples.french: Arrête de perdre du temps avec des affaires embrouillées.

words.culturalNote: Kobungisa ntango — "to make time get lost." Causative; said with the impatience of someone who can see exactly what the listener could be doing instead. A standard parental reprimand.

words.english: to halt / to bring to a standstill / to park

examples.lingala: Sofele atemisi mutuka pembeni ya balabala.
examples.english: The driver stopped the car next to the road.
examples.french: Le chauffeur a arrêté la voiture au bord de la route.

words.culturalNote: Kotemisa — causative of kotelema (to stand). To bring to a halt: the car parked, the argument ended, the machine switched off. The verb of imposed stillness.

words.english: to open one's heart / to speak openly
words.french: ouvrir son cœur / parler à cœur ouvert

examples.lingala: Alingi kofungola motema mpo na koloba bosolo.
examples.english: He wants to open his heart to speak the truth.
examples.french: Il veut ouvrir son cœur pour dire la vérité.

words.culturalNote: Kofungola motema — "to open the heart." The verb of honest, vulnerable speech: confiding in a friend, finally telling an elder the real story, the difficult conversation a relationship has been waiting for.

words.english: to wrap up a conversation / to end a debate
words.french: clore la conversation / mettre fin au débat

examples.lingala: Mbuta ayei kosukisa lisolo mpo na kimia ya ndako.
examples.english: The elder came to wrap up the conversation for the peace of the house.
examples.french: L'aîné est venu clore la conversation pour la paix de la maison.

words.culturalNote: Kosukisa lisolo — causative of kosuka (to end). The elder's role at a debate that has run on long enough; the gentle but final word that brings the discussion to a close so the household can settle for the night.

words.english: to be startled / to flinch / to jump in surprise

examples.lingala: Mwana asutuki makasi tango nkuba ebeti na likolo.
examples.english: The child was deeply startled when lightning struck above.
examples.french: L'enfant a fortement sursauté quand la foudre a frappé en haut.

words.culturalNote: Kosutuka — the involuntary flinch of surprise: the body's reflex to a sudden flash, sharp noise, or unexpected hand on the shoulder. The verb of the small jump that goes through you before you can think.

examples.lingala: Elamba na ye ya moyindo etondi na putulu ya nzela.
examples.english: His black cloth is covered in road dust.
examples.french: Son tissu noir est couvert de poussière de la route.

words.culturalNote: Moyindo — phonetic variant of moindo (dark, black), heard in fast conversational speech where the o glides into a y before the i. Used interchangeably for dark colours, dark cloth, and dark complexions. Both forms are correct; moindo is the standard written form, moyindo the everyday spoken one.

examples.lingala: Asombi mwinda ya sika na wenze mpo na kotambola na butu.
examples.english: He bought a new flashlight at the small market to walk at night.
examples.french: Il a acheté une lampe-torche neuve au petit marché pour marcher la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Mwinda ya sika — "the new light." In a household where the power cuts often, the new flashlight or replacement bulb is its own small relief. The phrase covers everything from a fresh candle to a battery torch to a modern LED bulb.

examples.lingala: Niau oyo ezali na langi ya moyindo makasi.
examples.english: This cat is an intensely black colour.
examples.french: Ce chat est d'une couleur noire intense.

words.culturalNote: Langi ya moyindo — "the colour of dark." The everyday way to name the colour black in description: a black cat, a black cloth, a black sky before rain. Pair with langi ya pembe (white), langi ya motane (red), langi ya bule (blue) for the basic palette.

examples.lingala: Tango mwinda ekufi, molili makasi ekoti na ndako.
examples.english: When the lamp died, intense darkness entered the house.
examples.french: Quand la lampe s'est éteinte, une obscurité intense est entrée dans la maison.

words.culturalNote: Molili — the darkness itself, distinct from moindo (the colour black). The dark of a power cut, of a moonless village night, of the closed shutters at midday. Pairs with mwinda (light) as natural opposites.

examples.lingala: Pelisa mwinda moke mpo na kotala monoko ya ekuke.
examples.english: Light a candle to see the doorway.
examples.french: Allume une bougie pour voir l'entrée de la porte.

words.culturalNote: Mwinda moke — "the small light." The candle or small flame kept against power cuts, lit also at altars and during prayers. The phrase covers anything from a slim white candle to a match held up for a fleeting look.

words.english: to shine / to glow / to gleam

examples.lingala: Sanza ezali kongenga kitoko likolo ya ebale.
examples.english: The moon is shining beautifully over the river.
examples.french: La lune brille magnifiquement au-dessus du fleuve.

words.culturalNote: Kongenga — to give off light. Said of the moon, the polished metal, the eye of a happy child. Both literal (the lamp shines) and figurative (her face shone with joy).

examples.lingala: Semisi na ye ya pembe etondi na mafuta ya mbila.
examples.english: His white shirt is stained with palm oil.
examples.french: Sa chemise blanche est tachée d'huile de palme.

words.culturalNote: Pembe — white in colour; by extension light-skinned or clean. Pairs with moindo (black/dark) as the opposite end of the colour spectrum. "Mposo ya pembe" — white skin; "langi ya pembe" — the colour white.

examples.lingala: Likolo ezali langi ya bule tango moi ezali makasi.
examples.english: The sky is blue when the sun is strong.
examples.french: Le ciel est bleu quand le soleil est fort.

words.culturalNote: Bule — blue, borrowed from French bleu. The everyday colour word for sky, water, the DRC flag stripe. Standard in modern Lingala; older traditional speech sometimes used "langi ya likolo" (sky-colour) instead.

examples.lingala: Mbuma ya lilala ya kotela ezali langi ya tane.
examples.english: The ripe orange fruit is a yellow colour.
examples.french: L'orange mûre est de couleur jaune.

words.culturalNote: Tane — yellow, light brown, amber — the spectrum of ripe fruit, dry grass, honey, palm oil. Less saturated than the pure flag-gold; the everyday warm-tone word.

examples.lingala: Milinga ya fulo ezali kobima na lininisa ya kuku.
examples.english: The stove's smoke is coming out of the kitchen window.
examples.french: La fumée du foyer sort par la fenêtre de la cuisine.

words.culturalNote: Milinga — smoke. The thick cooking smoke that drifts from a wood-fired fulo at dinner time; the smell that announces a meal half a courtyard away. Also the smoke of bonfires, brush burning, and rituals.

examples.lingala: Yela mopaya mai ya peto na kati ya kopo.
examples.english: Bring the visitor clean water in the cup.
examples.french: Apporte au visiteur de l'eau propre dans la tasse.

words.culturalNote: Peto — clean, pure, the opposite of mbindo. Used for clean water, freshly washed clothes, and figuratively for a clean record or pure intention. "Motema ya peto" — a pure heart.

examples.lingala: Sapato na yo ekomi mbindo mpo na potopoto.
examples.english: Your shoes became dirty because of the mud.
examples.french: Tes chaussures sont devenues sales à cause de la boue.

words.culturalNote: Mbindo — dirty, soiled, the opposite of peto. Used for soiled clothes, unwashed hands, polluted water; also figuratively for a soiled reputation or a dishonest deal.

examples.lingala: Bana bazali kobwaka mabanga na kati ya ebale.
examples.english: The children are throwing stones into the river.
examples.french: Les enfants jettent des pierres dans le fleuve.

words.culturalNote: Mabanga — stones, plural; the rocky surfaces of riverbeds, the cobbles of an old courtyard, the gravel of an unpaved road. Singular libanga. A child's first throwing-target; an old testament of geology.

examples.lingala: Libota mobimba bamilongisi mpo na kobanda mobembo mosika.
examples.english: The entire family prepared themselves to begin a long journey.
examples.french: Toute la famille s'est préparée pour entamer un long voyage.

words.culturalNote: Mobembo — the long-distance trip, the voyage, the relocation. The word anchors the famous parting blessing "mobembo malamu" (safe journey), spoken at the door, the gate, the port whenever family or friends head out. Said with both hands; a small ritual of release.

examples.lingala: Sofele atemisi mutuka sika na nse ya nzete ya manga.
examples.english: The driver parked the new car under the mango tree.
examples.french: Le chauffeur a garé la voiture neuve sous le manguier.

words.culturalNote: Mutuka — phonetic variant of motuka (car), heard widely in everyday speech. Same word, the u/o vowel slides depending on speaker and region. From English "motorcar" via colonial-era trade routes.

examples.lingala: Mutuka oyo abungi nzela na kati ya zamba monene.
examples.english: This car lost its way inside the thick forest.
examples.french: Cette voiture a perdu son chemin dans la forêt épaisse.

words.culturalNote: Nzela — the path, the way, the route. Both literal (the road through the village) and figurative (the way through a difficult situation). Threads through countless idioms: "luka nzela" (find a way), "mobembo malamu na nzela" (safe travels on the path).

examples.lingala: Nauti na mboka sika mpo na kotala yaya na ngai.
examples.english: I have just come from the village to visit my older sibling.
examples.french: Je viens à l'instant du village pour rendre visite à mon aîné.

words.culturalNote: Mboka — the home place. Used for the ancestral village, the wider country (mboka na biso — our country), and sometimes the neighbourhood. For diaspora, mboka almost always means the home village or DRC itself — the place that holds the family stories.

words.english: visitor / stranger / guest (short form of mopaya)

examples.lingala: Bapaya ebele bakoti na kati ya ndako lelo na pokwa.
examples.english: Many visitors entered the house this evening.
examples.french: Beaucoup de visiteurs sont entrés dans la maison ce soir.

words.culturalNote: Paya — contracted form of mopaya (visitor, guest, stranger). The plural bapaya is especially common: the relatives arriving for a wake, the guests at a wedding, the unannounced cousins. A household always rearranges itself for bapaya.

examples.lingala: Pesa ngai falanga mpo na kosomba mampa ya sukali.
examples.english: Give me cash to buy sweet bread.
examples.french: Donne-moi de l'argent pour acheter du pain sucré.

words.culturalNote: Falanga — money, specifically cash, often the Congolese franc (FC). Same root as the franc; everyday speech word alongside mbongo (the broader "money/wealth"). Counted in bills, carried in pockets, exchanged at every wenze.

examples.lingala: Amemi sako ya makala likolo ya nkinga na ye.
examples.english: He carried a sack of charcoal on his bicycle.
examples.french: Il a porté un sac de charbon sur son vélo.

words.culturalNote: Sako — the large sack, usually woven (jute, polypropylene). The unit of bulk goods in the wenze: a sako of charcoal, a sako of rice, a sako of cassava. Always carried on the shoulder or strapped to a bicycle.

examples.lingala: Ntalo ya bilei emati makasi na zando lelo.
examples.english: The price of food rose sharply at the market today.
examples.french: Le prix de la nourriture a fortement augmenté au marché aujourd'hui.

words.culturalNote: Ntalo — the price, but also the value or worth of something. Negotiated daily at every market stall; spoken with the long sigh of any household facing inflation. "Ntalo moke" — cheap; "ntalo monene" — expensive.

examples.lingala: Monganga apesi nkisi mpo na kolongola tofina na elongi.
examples.english: The doctor gave medicine to remove the pus-filled acne from the face.
examples.french: Le médecin a donné un remède pour enlever l'acné purulente du visage.

words.culturalNote: Tofina — the cluster of pus-filled pimples, whiteheads, or pustules; the plural form (singular lifina). Named expressively from the verb kofina because it is the kind of pimple that gets squeezed or popped. Treated with antiseptic creams and the old grandmother's hot-compress remedies.

examples.lingala: Lifina moko ebimi ye na elongi lelo na tongo.
examples.english: A single pimple emerged on his face this morning.
examples.french: Un seul bouton est apparu sur son visage ce matin.

words.culturalNote: Lifina — a single pimple or boil, the singular form of tofina. The unexpected morning arrival on the cheek before an important day, the small inflamed bump that draws every finger to it. Comes from the verb kofina (to squeeze).

examples.lingala: Mpota na ye ebimisi mafina mpo ezali ya mbindo.
examples.english: His wound discharged pus because it is dirty.
examples.french: Sa plaie a suppuré du pus parce qu'elle est sale.

words.culturalNote: Mafina — the pus inside a pustule or infected wound. Same kofina root as tofina/lifina (the pimples themselves) — mafina is the substance, tofina the structure that holds it. Sign that an infection has set in and needs proper cleaning.

examples.lingala: Mobeli azali kopema malembe likolo ya mbeto.
examples.english: The patient is breathing slowly on the bed.
examples.french: Le malade respire doucement sur le lit.

words.culturalNote: Mobeli — the patient; the one carrying maladi. The word the household uses to organise care: the mobeli rests in the cool back room, meals are brought, visitors keep their voices low.

examples.lingala: Nzoto na ye ezali moto makasi mpo na fevere.
examples.english: His body is intensely hot because of a fever.
examples.french: Son corps est très chaud à cause de la fièvre.

words.culturalNote: Fevere — colloquial loanword from French fièvre. The everyday word for fever in modern Lingala, alongside the older descriptive phrase "nzoto moto-moto" (body hot-hot). Often the first sign of malaria; treated quickly.

examples.lingala: Azali komona moto-pasi mpo na fevere makasi.
examples.english: He is suffering a headache because of the intense fever.
examples.french: Il souffre d'un mal de tête à cause de la forte fièvre.

words.culturalNote: Moto-pasi — "head-pain." The everyday headache, from a fever, dehydration, or a long day in the sun. Treated with rest, water, and the soft hands of someone who cares.

examples.lingala: Mwana azali kolela mpo na libumu-pasi nsima ya kolia manga.
examples.english: The child is crying with a stomachache after eating mangoes.
examples.french: L'enfant pleure d'un mal de ventre après avoir mangé des mangues.

words.culturalNote: Libumu-pasi — "belly-pain." Cramps from too much fruit, the wrong water, or the first signs of an infection. The grandmother's first remedy is hot ginger water; the second is taking the child seriously.

examples.lingala: Mobeli azali kosukula makasi na kati ya suku.
examples.english: The patient is coughing heavily in the room.
examples.french: Le malade tousse fortement dans la chambre.

words.culturalNote: Kosukula — to cough. The sound that the whole household tracks: dry cough, wet cough, the cough that won't stop at night. Persistent coughing brings out the eucalyptus leaves and steam bowl.

words.english: scab / crust over a healing wound

examples.lingala: Likoka ekweli kowuta na mpota na ye lelo.
examples.english: The scab fell off his wound today.
examples.french: La croûte est tombée de sa plaie aujourd'hui.

words.culturalNote: Likoka — the dark crust that forms over a healing wound and eventually falls off on its own. The instruction is universal: do not pick at it. Plural makoka — the patchwork of scabs on a child who has spent the season running barefoot.

words.english: to swell up / to bloat (variant of kovimba)

examples.lingala: Lokolo na ye ezimbi nsima ya konyatola nzete.
examples.english: His foot swelled up after stepping on the stick.
examples.french: Son pied a enflé après avoir marché sur le bâton.

words.culturalNote: Kozimba — phonetic variant of kovimba (to swell), heard widely in everyday speech where v/z alternate. Used for any swelling: a stung face, a sprained ankle, the belly after too much food.

words.english: to burst a pimple / to lance a boil / to express pus
words.french: percer un bouton / inciser un abcès

examples.lingala: Mama afitoli lifina oyo ezalaki kosala pasi.
examples.english: Mother burst the pimple that was causing pain.
examples.french: Maman a percé le bouton qui faisait mal.

words.culturalNote: Kofitola — the careful action of bursting a pimple or lancing a small boil. Done with a clean needle and a steady hand; usually by the parent or the patient themselves. Causative variant of kofina (to squeeze).

examples.lingala: Mpota ya kala etikali soti na lipeka.
examples.english: The old wound left a scar on the shoulder.
examples.french: L'ancienne plaie a laissé une cicatrice sur l'épaule.

words.culturalNote: Soti — the scar; the permanent record of a wound long healed. Each carries a story: the childhood fall, the cooking burn, the run-in with a sharp branch. Often the first thing a grandmother points to when telling stories.

examples.lingala: Elongi na ye ezali na ntende ebele kowuta bomwana.
examples.english: Her face has many skin spots from childhood.
examples.french: Son visage a de nombreuses taches depuis l'enfance.

words.culturalNote: Ntende — the small dark or light spots on the skin: birthmarks, freckles, age spots, the patchwork that builds up across a face over the years. Often named affectionately as a sign of character.

examples.lingala: Azali kofoti nkongi mpo na miso-pasi.
examples.english: He is twitching his eyebrow because of sore eyes.
examples.french: Il fait tressaillir le sourcil à cause de mal aux yeux.

words.culturalNote: Miso-pasi — "eye-pain." The irritation from dust, smoke, long screen-time, or infection. The familiar end-of-day complaint of anyone who spent the afternoon by the cooking fire or the office computer.

words.english: bee sting / swelling from a bee sting

examples.lingala: Litama na ye ezimbi mpo na nzoi-eswi na elanga.
examples.english: His cheek swelled up from a bee sting in the field.
examples.french: Sa joue a enflé à cause d'une piqûre d'abeille dans le champ.

words.culturalNote: Nzoi-eswi — the bee sting and the swelling it leaves. The old remedies — wet clay, a smear of palm oil, a paste of crushed leaves — go on while someone hunts for the stinger. The swelling can last a day.

examples.lingala: Mbuta alembi makasi mpo na mokuwa-pasi.
examples.english: The elder is very weak because of bone pain.
examples.french: L'aîné est très faible à cause de douleurs osseuses.
