words.culturalNote: Mokuwa-pasi — "bone-pain." The deep ache that comes with fever, with age, with a long day of physical work. Treated with hot baths, ointments, and the practical kindness of being let to rest.

examples.lingala: Nzoto ya mwana ezali moto-moto lelo na ntongo.
examples.english: The child's body is feverish this morning.
examples.french: Le corps de l'enfant est brûlant ce matin.

words.culturalNote: Moto-moto — "hot-hot," the doubled descriptive for a feverish body. The first phrase a mother says when her hand touches the child's forehead. Older and gentler than the loanword fevere; carries the texture of being right at the bedside.

examples.lingala: Mpota-kanda oyo ezali kobimisa mafina ebele.
examples.english: This inflamed wound is discharging a lot of pus.
examples.french: Cette plaie enflammée laisse échapper beaucoup de pus.

words.culturalNote: Mpota-kanda — "wound-anger," the inflamed sore: red, swollen, hot to the touch. The sign that an infection has taken hold and proper care is needed soon — antiseptic, perhaps antibiotics, certainly not delay.

words.english: to lance a wound / to incise an abscess
words.french: inciser une plaie / inciser un abcès

examples.lingala: Monganga ayei kopasola mpota mpo na kobimisa mafina.
examples.english: The doctor came to lance the wound to drain the pus.
examples.french: Le médecin est venu inciser la plaie pour évacuer le pus.

words.culturalNote: Kopasola mpota — "to split the wound," the medical action of lancing an abscess so the pus can drain. Done carefully with a sterilised blade; brings immediate relief once the pressure is gone.

words.english: street gangster / hoodlum / violent gang member
words.french: voyou / membre de gang de rue

examples.lingala: Bakuluna bameki kobandisa bitumba-zoba makasi pene na wenze.
examples.english: The street gangsters tried to start a severe, chaotic brawl near the small market.
examples.french: Les voyous ont essayé de déclencher une bagarre violente près du petit marché.

words.culturalNote: Kuluna — the modern Kinshasa name for a street gang member, the violent neighbourhood delinquents who engage in armed robberies, street fights, and extortion. The plural bakuluna is a heavy word in urban security and street discourse — speaking it carries the weight of the real fear it names. Born in the post-war period; the phenomenon is one of the city's hardest unsolved problems.

examples.lingala: Mbwampoka akangi moyibi oyo akotaki na lopango butu.
examples.english: The domestic dog caught the thief who entered the yard at night.
examples.french: Le chien a attrapé le voleur qui était entré dans la cour la nuit.

words.culturalNote: Moyibi — the thief, in plain everyday usage. From the verb koyiba (to steal). The neighbourhood watch, the family dog, and the locked gate exist because of bayibi (plural). Said with the weight of real loss when something has gone missing.

examples.lingala: Bopolisi bayei noki mpo na kopekisa bitumba-zoba.
examples.english: The police came quickly to stop the brawl.
examples.french: La police est venue rapidement pour arrêter la bagarre.

words.culturalNote: Bopolisi — the police force as a whole, the institution. Distinct from polisi (an individual officer); the bo- prefix marks the collective/institutional sense. Citizens' relationship with bopolisi is complex — sometimes the answer, sometimes the problem.

examples.lingala: Polisi akangi kuluna moko na nzela ya zando.
examples.english: The police officer arrested one gangster on the market road.
examples.french: Le policier a arrêté un voyou sur la route du marché.

words.culturalNote: Polisi — the individual officer (from French police). The uniform on the corner, the checkpoint at the roundabout, the voice at the gate. Plural bapolisi.

examples.lingala: Bakatisi ye mibeko mpe batia ye na kati ya boloko.
examples.english: He broke the laws and they put him in prison.
examples.french: Il a enfreint les lois et on l'a mis en prison.

words.culturalNote: Boloko — the prison or holding cell. Slang short of the older word; commonly used in everyday speech. Going to boloko, coming out of boloko — both are heavy phrases that change a family's standing.

examples.lingala: Kuluna akamati machete mpo na kobangisa bato na balabala.
examples.english: The gangster grabbed a machete to scare people on the street.
examples.french: Le voyou a saisi une machette pour effrayer les gens dans la rue.

words.culturalNote: Machete — the wide-bladed cutting tool, borrowed from Spanish via French. The everyday farm and forest tool (for clearing brush, harvesting, butchering) — but also, regrettably, a weapon of street violence. Context tells which usage.

examples.lingala: Tokoki kofungola motema mpo na kopekisa bitumba.
examples.english: We can open our hearts to prevent fighting.
examples.french: Nous pouvons ouvrir nos cœurs pour empêcher les combats.

words.culturalNote: Bitumba — plural noun (singular etumba): fights, conflicts, battles. Spans the full range from a household quarrel to civil war. The eastern DRC's history sits heavy inside this word; said carefully.

examples.lingala: Polisi akamati chicot mpo na kotemisa mobulu ya bilenge.
examples.english: The officer took a whip to stop the youth rioting.
examples.french: L'agent a pris la chicotte pour arrêter l'émeute des jeunes.

words.culturalNote: Chicot — from French chicotte, the colonial-era whip of bound hippopotamus hide. A heavy historical word — used during Belgian rule for punishment of forced-labour workers. The implement persists today; the memory it carries is much older.

examples.lingala: Mwa shege moko akangami tango ameki koyiba saki.
examples.english: A small street child was caught trying to steal a bag.
examples.french: Un petit enfant des rues a été pris en train de voler un sac.

words.culturalNote: Shege — the street child. A heavy modern Kinshasa word; bashege (plural) are the children sleeping in markets and roundabouts, surviving by small theft, ferocious cleverness, and what kindness reaches them. The phenomenon is one of the city's deepest wounds.

examples.lingala: Akatisi ngai na phase moko ya zando mpo na kozwa falanga.
examples.english: He played a market scheme on me to grab cash.
examples.french: Il m'a roulé avec une combine du marché pour avoir de l'argent.

words.culturalNote: Phase — borrowed from French; the street-slang word for a trick, a scheme, a manoeuvre to extract advantage or money. "Akoti na phase" — he's running a scheme; "phase mabe" — a bad trick. Heard constantly in Kinshasa street talk.

words.english: to fight / to wrestle / to brawl

examples.lingala: Bilenge mibale bazali kobunda libanda ya nganda pokwa.
examples.english: Two youth are fighting outside the bar this evening.
examples.french: Deux jeunes se battent devant le bar ce soir.

words.culturalNote: Kobunda — to fight physically, to wrestle, to brawl. Used both for actual fights and figuratively for inner struggle (kobunda na motema — to wrestle in the heart). Different from kotumba (war) — kobunda is hand-to-hand, person-to-person.

examples.lingala: Kuluna azongisi lifuti epai ya moninga nsima ya koswana.
examples.english: The gangster brought retaliation to his peer after the quarrel.
examples.french: Le voyou a exercé des représailles sur son pair après la dispute.

words.culturalNote: Lifuti — the payback after an insult or injury. Street-slang sense extends from the older meaning of "payment/wage" (lifuta) — the debt the offender will pay in kind. Often the next chapter of an unfinished quarrel.

examples.lingala: Abeti ye likofi makasi na mbanga mpe abuki lino.
examples.english: He hit him with a heavy punch to the jaw and broke a tooth.
examples.french: Il l'a frappé d'un coup violent à la mâchoire et a cassé une dent.

words.culturalNote: Mbanga — the jaw, the bone of the lower face. Named most often when the news is bad: in fight talk, in dentist visits. Houses the lino (teeth) and gives the face its hard line.

examples.lingala: Bomoi ya mputu etungisaka mitema ya mabota ebele.
examples.english: A life of severe hardship troubles many families' hearts.
examples.french: Une vie de pauvreté afflige le cœur de nombreuses familles.

words.culturalNote: Mputu — the deep word for poverty, hardship, being broken. More serious than the casual mpamba (broke) — mputu names a long-standing condition, not a tight week. Spoken with weight and rarely lightly.

examples.lingala: Lelo nazali lofelo mobimba, nakoki kosomba mampa te.
examples.english: Today I am completely flat broke; I cannot buy bread.
examples.french: Aujourd'hui je suis complètement fauché; je ne peux pas acheter de pain.

words.culturalNote: Lofelo — the colloquial state of having no money at all. Often said with a laugh, between friends; the word is its own little signal that today is a take-care-of-me day. Variant of lofele.

examples.lingala: Nayoki nsunga ntaba kowuta na nganda.
examples.english: I smell the aroma of goat coming from the bar.
examples.french: Je sens l'arôme de la chèvre qui vient du bar.

words.culturalNote: Nsunga — the smell, scent, or aroma; a sensory word that covers everything from cooking smells to perfume to the smoke of tobacco. Often paired with the source noun: nsunga ntaba (aroma of grilled goat), nsunga ya mafuta (smell of oil). Named in the moment a smell catches the nose.

examples.lingala: Ntaba ya kotumba ezali bilei ya nganda na pokwa.
examples.english: Grilled goat is the food of the nganda bars in the evening.
examples.french: La chèvre grillée est le plat des bars le soir.

words.culturalNote: Ntaba — the goat. One of the most familiar domestic animals across the Congo: kept in the yard, sold at celebrations, grilled at nganda bars (ntaba ya kotumba). Goats appear in countless idioms — "akimi lokola ntaba" (he ran like a goat) — and on most household dinner tables for a wedding or a wake.

examples.lingala: Nsunga ntaba ezali malamu mingi na mbalasa pokwa lelo.
examples.english: The aroma of grilled goat is very good on the porch this evening.
examples.french: L'arôme de chèvre grillée est très bon sous la véranda ce soir.

words.culturalNote: Nsunga ntaba — the unmistakable aroma of goat meat over charcoal. The smell that draws customers to a nganda from a block away, that defines a Kinshasa evening as much as the music. A compound built from nsunga (aroma) + ntaba (goat); the phrase itself functions as both description and invitation.

examples.lingala: Elamba oyo ezali na solo ya malamu kowuta na sabuni.
examples.english: This cloth has a good smell from the soap.
examples.french: Ce tissu a une bonne odeur grâce au savon.

words.culturalNote: Solo (homonym) — the everyday word for any smell or odour. Standard Lingala marks the two senses tonally (solo = smell vs solo = truth); plain-Latin written form is identical. Paired commonly with mabe (bad) for a stench. Distinct from solo meaning "truth, really."

examples.lingala: Nyama ya kofwama ebimisaki solo mabe makasi lelo.
examples.english: The rotting meat gave off an intense stench today.
examples.french: La viande pourrie a dégagé une puanteur intense aujourd'hui.

words.culturalNote: Solo mabe — literally "bad smell." The phrase for any stench, foul odour, or off-smell: spoilt food, blocked drains, the dead rat behind the cabinet. The word a household uses to coordinate the search for what needs cleaning.

examples.lingala: Supu oyo ekomi mungwa-mingi, nakoki komela yango te.
examples.english: This soup has become too salty; I cannot drink it.
examples.french: Cette soupe est devenue trop salée; je ne peux pas la boire.

words.culturalNote: Mungwa-mingi — "too-much-salt." The standard kitchen complaint when the hand at the salt shaker got distracted. Recoverable by adding water, potato, or a piece of bread — the rescue tricks every cook learns.

words.english: tough / chewy / hard (of meat or food)

examples.lingala: Nyama ya pakasa ezali makasa mpo etikalaki na moto mingi te.
examples.english: The forest buffalo meat is tough because it did not stay long on the fire.
examples.french: La viande de buffle est coriace parce qu'elle n'est pas restée longtemps au feu.

words.culturalNote: Makasa — the texture word for tough, chewy food. Said of meat that needed longer cooking, of stale bread, of cassava that has gone past its day. Often the punchline at a meal where the cook was rushed.

examples.lingala: Masango ya kolamba ezali peto mpe kitoko mpo na bana.
examples.english: Boiled corn is clean and fine for the children.
examples.french: Le maïs bouilli est propre et bon pour les enfants.

words.culturalNote: Kolamba — the foundational verb for cooking, particularly the wet methods: boiling, stewing, simmering. Distinct from kotumba (to grill/roast over fire). The verb that opens the kitchen: "nazali kolamba" — I am cooking.

examples.lingala: Pesa ngai nguba ya nkalinga mpo na kolia na mampa.
examples.english: Give me roasted peanuts to eat with bread.
examples.french: Donne-moi des arachides grillées à manger avec du pain.

words.culturalNote: Nkalinga — the noun/adjective for fried or roasted items, from the verb kokalinga (to fry/roast in a dry pan). Most famously nguba ya nkalinga — roasted peanuts — eaten by the handful as a snack.

examples.lingala: Ti oyo ekomi sukali-mingi mpo mwana abakisaki tini mobimba.
examples.english: This tea has become too sweet because the child added a whole tin.
examples.french: Ce thé est devenu trop sucré parce que l'enfant a ajouté toute la boîte.

words.culturalNote: Sukali-mingi — "too-much-sugar." The mirror of mungwa-mingi (too-salty). The mug of tea you put down, the cake left after dessert; the cue to dilute or share around.

examples.lingala: Nsunga ya ndimo-bololo ezali kopetola solo ya kuku.
examples.english: The scent of sour lime is clearing the kitchen odour.
examples.french: Le parfum du citron acide rafraîchit l'odeur de la cuisine.

words.culturalNote: Ndimo-bololo — "sour lime" / "bitter ndimo," naming the sharp citrus flavour and its brightening effect on a kitchen. A squeeze of ndimo-bololo lifts a heavy stew, cuts a fishy smell, and resets the whole room.

examples.lingala: Fungola nzungu ya supu mpo na kopesa mbuta bilei.
examples.english: Open the soup pot to give the elder food.
examples.french: Ouvre la marmite de soupe pour servir l'aîné.

words.culturalNote: Nzungu — the everyday cooking pot, often aluminium or cast iron, large enough to feed the family with leftovers for tomorrow. The lid lifted is the first signal a meal is ready; the bottom scraped is the last.

examples.lingala: Mwasi-ya-zando abongisi manaka bilei ya fete lelo.
examples.english: The marketwoman arranged the party menu today.
examples.french: La marchande a préparé le menu de la fête aujourd'hui.

words.culturalNote: Manaka bilei — "food calendar / list," the rotation of dishes planned for the week or for a celebration. The household ledger that turns the wenze visit into the dinner table.

examples.lingala: Nzete oyo eza na misisa ya makasi na nse ya mabele.
examples.english: This tree has strong roots underground.
examples.french: Cet arbre a de fortes racines sous terre.

words.culturalNote: Misisa — plural for roots and root-like structures: tree roots, vein patterns, fibre strands. By extension in language study, the structural "root" of a word (its morpheme stem). Singular form is mosisa.

words.english: a single root / vein / nerve fibre

examples.lingala: Abendi mosisa ya nzete mpo na kosala nkisi.
examples.english: He pulled a tree root to make medicine.
examples.french: Il a tiré une racine d'arbre pour préparer un remède.

words.culturalNote: Mosisa — the singular root: a tree root, a visible vein on the back of the hand, a single nerve fibre. The healing-plant tradition relies on knowing which mosisa to dig up; the knowledge sits with elders and traditional nganga.

examples.lingala: Nazi ezali na mposo ya makasi mpenza mpe mai ya elengi.
examples.english: The coconut has a very hard shell and sweet water.
examples.french: La noix de coco a une coque très dure et une eau sucrée.

words.culturalNote: Nazi — the mature coconut, hard-shelled with white flesh and sweet water inside. Distinct from kokoti (which can also mean coconut more broadly); nazi names the fully ripened nut, often cracked open with a machete blow.

examples.lingala: Mama akitinitinyi mbala-poto mpo na kotia na kati ya nyama.
examples.english: Mother chopped potatoes to put into the meat dish.
examples.french: Maman a coupé des pommes de terre pour les mettre dans la viande.

words.culturalNote: Mbala-poto — "the European potato." Names the Irish potato by analogy with the native mbala (sweet potato / yam). The colonial-era loan: poto refers to Europeans or things European. Cooked the same ways as mbala — boiled, fried, in stews.

examples.lingala: Kolia te mbala-nsango soki olambi yango malamu te.
examples.english: Do not eat the wild forest yam if you haven't cooked it well.
examples.french: Ne mange pas l'igname sauvage si tu ne l'as pas bien cuite.

words.culturalNote: Mbala-nsango — the wild forest yam. Bitter and slightly toxic raw; must be boiled long with several water changes before it is safe. Famine food in hard seasons; the technique for safe preparation is passed down with the warnings.

examples.lingala: Nguba ya kashu ezali na ntalo mingi na kati ya zando lelo.
examples.english: Cashew nuts have a high price at the market today.
examples.french: Les noix de cajou ont un prix élevé au marché aujourd'hui.

words.culturalNote: Kashu — the cashew nut, from English/Portuguese cashew. Imported and expensive; sold in small bags at city markets. The cashew apple (the fruit attached to the nut) is rarely seen this far inland.

examples.lingala: Amande ezali na mposo ya tane mpe ezali na elengi ya kokoka.
examples.english: The almond has a light brown skin and a sufficient sweetness.
examples.french: L'amande a une peau brun clair et une douceur suffisante.

words.culturalNote: Amande — borrowed from French amande. Imported nut, sold mostly in city supermarkets; used in modern baking and seen on premium grocery shelves. Not native to the equatorial region.

examples.lingala: Mwana alingi kofiba shokola ya sukali mikolo nyonso.
examples.english: The child wants to slurp sweet chocolate every day.
examples.french: L'enfant veut manger du chocolat sucré tous les jours.

words.culturalNote: Shokola — chocolate, from French chocolat. The processed bar form is a city treat; the underlying cacao (kakao) is grown in the DRC but most of it is exported and returns processed. A child's birthday wish in many homes.

examples.lingala: Ngubamonene ekolaka na nse ya mabele ya elanga na biso.
examples.english: The Bambara groundnut grows beneath our field's soil.
examples.french: Le pois bambara pousse sous la terre de notre champ.

words.culturalNote: Ngubamonene — "the big peanut." The Bambara groundnut, a hardy West/Central African legume that matures underground like the regular nguba but with larger, denser pods. Drought-tolerant; carries families through hard rainy seasons.

examples.lingala: Tosombi mbuma-mabele ya sika na wenze pokwa.
examples.english: We bought fresh ground-nuts at the small market this evening.
examples.french: Nous avons acheté des arachides fraîches au petit marché ce soir.

words.culturalNote: Mbuma-mabele — "fruit of the soil," a descriptive umbrella for the underground-maturing seed crops: peanuts, Bambara groundnuts, and similar. Used in market talk for the whole category.

examples.lingala: Mbuta azali komona mokuwa-pasi mpe misisa-pasi mpo na koumela na makolo.
examples.english: The elder is feeling bone pain and nerve pain from standing too long.
examples.french: L'aîné ressent une douleur osseuse et nerveuse à force de rester debout.

words.culturalNote: Misisa-pasi — "vein/nerve pain." The deep ache along the nerves and veins, common in the legs after long standing and in old joint injuries. Treated with rest, hot compresses, and the traditional plant balms.

words.english: to stretch / to extend muscle fibres

examples.lingala: Atelemi na libanda mpo na kobenda misisa nsima ya kolala.
examples.english: He stood outside to stretch his muscles after sleeping.
examples.french: Il s'est tenu dehors pour s'étirer après avoir dormi.

words.culturalNote: Kobenda misisa — "to pull the fibres," the verb of stretching. The morning stretch on the porch, the long reach before lifting a heavy basket. Practical name for a universal action.

words.english: to dig up sweet potatoes / to harvest tubers
words.french: déterrer des patates / récolter des tubercules

examples.lingala: Bana bakei na lisala mpo na kotimola mbala ya kotela.
examples.english: The children went to the field to dig up ripe sweet potatoes.
examples.french: Les enfants sont allés au champ pour déterrer les patates mûres.

words.culturalNote: Kotimola mbala — the harvest action, hoeing up the ripe tubers from the field. Often a children's task at the end of the growing season; each potato lifted is a small triumph and the basket fills quickly.

examples.lingala: Tozali kofandisa bapaya mpe kofitola nguba na mbalasa.
examples.english: We are seating the visitors and shelling peanuts on the porch.
examples.french: Nous installons les visiteurs et décortiquons des arachides sous la véranda.

words.culturalNote: Kofitola nguba — the shelling of peanuts, often by hand in a slow, conversational rhythm on the porch. The kind of work that pairs naturally with talk: a basket of unshelled goes in, a bowl of clean nuts comes out.

words.french: rassembler les régimes de noix de palme

examples.lingala: Mosali akei kosangisa maba pembeni ya nzete ya limbila ya molai.
examples.english: The worker went to gather palm nut clusters next to the tall palm tree.
examples.french: L'ouvrier est allé rassembler les régimes de noix de palme près du grand palmier.

words.culturalNote: Kosangisa maba — the gathering of fallen palm-nut clusters at the base of the oil palm. Heavy work, done with a long pole or by climbing; the foundation of every batch of palm oil that fuels Congolese cooking.

examples.lingala: Mama abakisi sukali na tshayi ya pokwa.
examples.english: Mother added sugar to the evening tea.
examples.french: Maman a ajouté du sucre au thé du soir.

words.culturalNote: Tshayi — tea, the form heard widely in eastern DRC under Swahili influence (Swahili chai). Coexists with the more general Lingala ti / tii. Both refer to the same beverage; tshayi has a slightly more formal or eastern flavour.

examples.lingala: Ntango nazali na fevere, mbala mingi namelaka tshayi ya nseto mpo na komiyoka malamu.
examples.english: When I have a fever, I often drink lemongrass tea to feel better.
examples.french: Quand j'ai de la fièvre, je bois souvent une tisane de citronnelle pour me sentir mieux.

words.culturalNote: Tshayi ya nseto — "tea of nseto," the household lemongrass infusion. Nseto refers to the sour-citrus grass that gives the tea its distinctive bright, sharp flavour. Standard home remedy across the region for fever, cough, indigestion; drunk piping hot with honey or sugar.

words.french: feuilles de citronnelle / brins à infuser

examples.lingala: Buka matiti ya tshayi na elanga mpo totokisa yango lelo na mpokwa.
examples.english: Pluck tea grass from the garden so we can boil it this evening.
examples.french: Cueille des feuilles de citronnelle au jardin pour les faire bouillir ce soir.

words.culturalNote: Lititi ya tshayi — literally "the grass of tea," the lemongrass stalks and leaves picked fresh for brewing. Plural matiti ya tshayi. Grows wild and in gardens; the bunch tied at the kitchen window is the household pharmacy.

examples.lingala: Kamwela ngai ndimu na kati ya tshayi ya moto mpo na kosilisa kosukula.
examples.english: Squeeze a lemon into my hot tea to stop the coughing.
examples.french: Presse un citron dans mon thé chaud pour calmer la toux.

words.culturalNote: Ndimu — phonetic/regional variant of ndimo (lemon, lime), heard especially in eastern DRC under Swahili influence (Swahili ndimu = lemon). Both forms refer to the same citrus; the choice is regional.

words.english: Mondia whitei / mukombero / traditional tonic root

examples.lingala: Bilenge mibali balukaka limwete na zamba mpo na kobakisa makasi na nzoto.
examples.english: Young men seek out Mondia whitei roots in the forest to boost body strength.
examples.french: Les jeunes hommes cherchent la racine de Mondia whitei en forêt pour augmenter la force du corps.

words.culturalNote: Limwete — the local name for Mondia whitei root (known as mukombero in East African trade). A traditional tonic chewed for energy and male vitality; the bark of the root has a sweet vanilla-like flavour. Sold dried in small bundles at markets throughout the region.

examples.lingala: Kotokisa nsinda na mai mpo na kosala tshayi ya kitoko mpe ya nsolo malamu.
examples.english: Boil lemongrass in water to make beautiful tea with a wonderful aroma.
examples.french: Fais bouillir la citronnelle dans l'eau pour faire un beau thé avec un parfum agréable.

words.culturalNote: Sinda — borrowed regional variant for lemongrass / wild tea grass, used alongside lititi ya tshayi and nseto. Boiled into the household lemongrass infusion drunk for fever, indigestion, and the simple pleasure of a hot citrus-scented cup.

words.english: Mondia whitei / African white ginger root (East African trade name)
words.french: Mondia whitei / racine tonique (nom commercial est-africain)

examples.lingala: Batekisa mikolo ya mukombero na zando mpo na kopesa bato makasi ya nzoto.
examples.english: They sell pieces of mukombero root at the market to give people physical energy.
examples.french: On vend des morceaux de mukombero au marché pour donner de l'énergie.

words.culturalNote: Mukombero — East African trade name for Mondia whitei, the tonic root sold for energy and male vitality. The same root the Lingala-speaking interior knows as limwete. The bark has a distinctive sweet vanilla-like flavour; chewed slowly, sold in small dried bundles at city markets.

words.english: leaves / herbal foliage (for infusions or cooking)

examples.lingala: Amemi nkasa ya nkisi kowuta na zamba mpo na kotokisela mboka.
examples.english: He brought medicinal leaves from the forest to boil for the village.
examples.french: Il a rapporté des feuilles médicinales de la forêt pour les faire bouillir pour le village.

words.culturalNote: Nkasa — plural for leaves used for cooking and traditional healing both. The traditional healer (nganga-nkisi) sends for nkasa ya nkisi (medicinal leaves) by name — each plant family has its own preparation. The same word covers culinary herbs.

words.french: remède traditionnel / médecine de la terre

examples.lingala: Bampaka basalaka nkisi ya mabele na misisa ya banzete.
examples.english: The elders make natural earth medicine from tree roots.
examples.french: Les anciens préparent des remèdes naturels à partir des racines d'arbres.

words.culturalNote: Nkisi ya mabele — "medicine of the earth." The whole body of traditional plant-and-soil remedies carried in the knowledge of village elders and the nganga-nkisi. Distinct from modern pharmaceutical nkisi; the phrase honours the deeper, older lineage of healing.

examples.lingala: Tokolamba mulele na mafuta ya mbila mpo na kolia na fufu.
examples.english: We will cook wild spinach in palm oil to eat with fufu.
examples.french: Nous cuirons les épinards sauvages dans l'huile de palme pour manger avec le fufu.

words.culturalNote: Mulele — broad regional term for wild leafy greens harvested for cooking: a darker, mildly bitter cousin of cultivated spinach. Stewed with palm oil and dried fish; rich in iron and the seasonal taste of the rains.

examples.lingala: Mela bololo oyo ata eza elengi te mpo esilisa maladi na katikati.
examples.english: Drink this bitter-leaf tonic even though it is not sweet, so it cures the illness inside.
examples.french: Bois cette infusion de feuille amère même si elle n'est pas sucrée, pour guérir le mal intérieur.

words.culturalNote: Bololo (plant) — Vernonia amygdalina, the bitter-leaf shrub of West and Central Africa. The leaves are washed, squeezed, and stewed (washed less for stronger medicinal effect, more for cooking). A trusted remedy for malaria symptoms and stomach trouble. Homonym of bololo meaning "bitterness" (the taste) — the plant is named for what it does on the tongue.

examples.lingala: Bana bakei kobuka mondongo na zamba mpo elengi na yango eleki sukali.
examples.english: The children went to pick wild forest fruits in the jungle because its flavour is sweeter than sugar.
examples.french: Les enfants sont allés cueillir des fruits sauvages dans la jungle car leur saveur dépasse le sucre.

words.culturalNote: Mondongo — wild forest fruit gathered fresh from the trees, often during the school holidays when children roam the bush. Sweet and free; carried back in folded shirts. The fruits ripen in clusters and disappear quickly once spotted.

examples.lingala: Tshaku azali ndeke ya mayele mpo akoki komeka maloba ya bato.
examples.english: The parrot is a clever bird because it can imitate human words.
examples.french: Le perroquet est un oiseau intelligent car il peut imiter la parole humaine.

words.culturalNote: Tshaku — traditional regional name for the African grey parrot, alongside the standard nkoso / nkoo. The bird's gift for mimicking human speech is the source of countless household stories — the grandfather's most-repeated phrase often comes back from the cage in his exact tone.

words.english: fast-paced rumba rhythm / guitar solo style
words.french: rythme rumba rapide / solo de guitare

examples.lingala: Seben ya sika eza na tshatsho ya makasi mpo na kobalusa zando.
examples.english: The new musical bridge has a powerful rhythm to make the crowd dance.
examples.french: Le nouveau pont musical a un rythme puissant pour faire danser la foule.

words.culturalNote: Tshatsho — Congolese music vocabulary for the fast, driving rhythm in a rumba or soukous track, especially the high-energy section after the seben. Names the rhythmic surge that lifts dancers off the chairs; spoken with pride about a great band, a great night.

words.english: to leave / to let / to abandon (regional variant of tika)

examples.lingala: Tshika ngai na kimia mpo nazo pema pongi.
examples.english: Leave me in peace because I am resting from sleep.
examples.french: Laisse-moi tranquille parce que je me repose du sommeil.

words.culturalNote: Tshika — regional variant of the standard tika (to leave, let, abandon). Heard especially in eastern dialects; the tsh- pronunciation softens the standard t-. Both forms carry the same imperative weight: "tshika ngai" / "tika ngai" — leave me alone.

words.french: petit pont / passement entre les jambes (foot)

examples.lingala: Alibitele amoni te ndenge mwana akoti na ye tshobo na nzelo.
examples.english: The referee did not see how the kid nutmegged him on the field.
examples.french: L'arbitre n'a pas vu comment le gamin lui a fait un petit pont sur le terrain.

words.culturalNote: Tshobo — the football street-slang for nutmeg: pushing the ball between an opponent's legs and running around them to collect it. The most humiliating thing one player can do to another; followed by laughter, jeers, and a chase. Heard on every dust-pitch from Lemba to Lubumbashi.

words.french: anguille d'eau douce / anguille des marais

examples.lingala: Mokolo ya wenze, tata asombi nzombo ya mobimba mpo na kolamba na mafuta ya mbila.
examples.english: On market day, father bought a whole freshwater eel to cook in palm oil.
examples.french: Le jour du marché, papa a acheté une anguille d'eau douce entière à cuisiner à l'huile de palme.

words.culturalNote: Nzombo — the snake-like freshwater eel of Congo Basin rivers and swamps, prized in river cuisine. Cooked whole in palm oil with chili and onion; the rich, oily flesh is the centrepiece of celebration meals. Native Bantu noun; closely related to monzombo (eel / mudfish), with nzombo as the standalone form.

examples.lingala: Mama atongi mboto na kati ya nkasa mpo na kosala liboke ya kitoko.
examples.english: Mother wrapped the mboto fish inside leaves to make a beautiful steamed fish packet.
examples.french: Maman a enveloppé le poisson mboto dans des feuilles pour faire un beau liboke.

words.culturalNote: Mboto (fish) — the distichodus / Congo salmon, a fleshy, prized river fish wrapped in nkasa leaves and steamed as liboke. Homonym of mboto meaning corn / maize — same headword, two unrelated worlds; context (a kitchen vs a field) tells which.

examples.lingala: Batatoli bilombe ya ebale bakangi mompongo monene na monama lelo.
examples.english: The river fishermen caught a massive elephant-snout fish at the river bend today.
examples.french: Les pêcheurs ont attrapé un grand poisson-éléphant dans la courbe du fleuve aujourd'hui.

words.culturalNote: Mompongo — the mormyrid or elephant-snout fish, easily recognised by the unique downward-curving long snout. Lives in the muddy bottoms of slow-moving river bends; uses weak electrical signals to navigate. Prized for its tender flesh.

examples.lingala: Keba na bansinga ya ngolo ntango ozali kosukola yango mpo ezokisa yo te.
examples.english: Watch out for the catfish whiskers when cleaning it so you don't get hurt.
examples.french: Attention aux barbillons du silure quand tu le nettoies pour ne pas te blesser.

words.culturalNote: Ngolo (fish) — the mud catfish of the Congo Basin, named for the long whiskers (bansinga) that can sting if handled carelessly. Hardy and abundant; the staple river protein of inland households. Homonym of ngolo / ngolu meaning grace / mercy; same headword, completely different sense.

examples.lingala: Ntalo ya kamba emati makasi na zando mpo misuni na yango eza petee mpe elengi.
examples.english: The price of Nile perch rose sharply at the market because its meat is tender and delicious.
examples.french: Le prix du capitaine est monté en flèche au marché car sa chair est tendre et délicieuse.

words.culturalNote: Kamba — the massive Nile perch (capitaine), one of the largest predatory fish of African inland waters. Prized for the soft, white flesh; commands a high market price. A single kamba can feed a celebration table.

examples.lingala: Mondele ebale apunzi na kati ya mai mpo nzoto na ye emononaka katikati.
examples.english: The glass fish darts through the water because its body is transparent.
examples.french: Le poisson de verre file dans l'eau car son corps est transparent.

words.culturalNote: Mondele ebale — literally "the white-person of the river," descriptive name for the transparent or pale glass catfish whose internal organs are visible through the skin. The poetic compound is itself the joke; said with affection more than mockery.

words.english: a single blade of grass / leaf stalk

examples.lingala: Akati lititi moko ya sika mpo na komeka nsolo ya nseto.
examples.english: He cut a single fresh blade of grass to test the lemongrass scent.
examples.french: Il a coupé un brin d'herbe frais pour goûter le parfum de citronnelle.

words.culturalNote: Lititi — singular for a single blade of grass, leaf, or stalk. The base form of matiti (plural: grass, greenery, brush). Used in everyday speech for any single piece of foliage picked, chewed, or pointed at.

examples.lingala: Bilombe bakei kokata matiti makasi na nse ya banzete ya ndako.
examples.english: The workers went to cut the tall grass underneath the trees by the house.
examples.french: Les ouvriers sont allés couper les hautes herbes sous les arbres de la maison.

words.culturalNote: Matiti — plural for grass, leaves, brush, weeds. The general word for the green ground cover: lawn, scrub at the forest edge, the tall grass after the rains. Singular form is lititi. Hidden in the matiti is where children warn each other about snakes.
